papers.abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon
authors: Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Yue Zhao, Armin W. Thomas, Ehsan Adeli, Jiajun Wu, Juan Carlos Niebles, Li Fei-Fei, Michael Poli
bullets: Introduces early-fusion multimodal autoregressive Halcyon models trained from scratch on 100M image-text pairs.
Reports better gFD scores than cited baselines with substantially less pretraining compute.
Controlled experiments find that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation.
Adding image-to-text supervision enables competitive image captioning without reducing T2I quality.
The findings are scoped to Halcyon’s multimodal pretraining setup and GPIC data.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
bullets: Addresses flickering edges and discontinuous transparency caused by independently processing short video chunks.
Uses separate RGB and mask token streams with full spatio-temporal attention for adaptive conditioning.
Introduces learnable preserve and refine tokens to propagate previous mattes during sliding-window inference.
Adds a shared reference anchor to maintain global consistency and limit error accumulation without extra training.
Outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, including on long in-the-wild videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoMaMa++ training and inference. (Top) During training, RGB frames are paired with either a binary mask or the ground-truth alpha matte as guide input, encoded into separate token streams by a frozen VAE encoder E , and tagged with a refine token (R) or preserve token (P). The DiT processes both modes jointly within a single clip, supervised against the ground-truth matte. (Bottom) At inference, long videos are processed in a sliding-window manner. Each chunk receives the refine token on its non-overlapping frames and the preserve token on its overlap frames, which carry the previous chunk’s predicted matte. A globally selected reference anchor frame is additionally supplied as preserve input to every chunk, providing a stable anchor that prevents error accumulation across the sequence.

Figure 3: Long-video temporal consistency. Qualitative comparison between VideoMaMa++ and other methods. The comparison methods exhibits visible flickering at chunk boundaries or struggles to capture fine-grained details, while VideoMaMa++ produces smooth transitions across chunks while still capturing fine-grained details that emerge in later chunks.

Figure 6: Annotation noise in AM-2K [25]. The ground-truth alpha mattes in AM-2K often miss fine-grained internal details, that VideoMaMa++ correctly recovers. Because MAD averages pixelwise error over the entire image, these missing details penalize accurate predictions and inflate the reported error. MAD-T, computed only within the transition region, isolates the matting quality that actually matters and avoids the bias introduced by such annotation gaps.

Figure 7: Re-initialization of SAM3 on YouTubeMatte static_0017. Initializing SAM3 [3] on the first frame fails to track a sheet of paper that the subject begins holding mid-sequence, since the object is not yet visible at initialization. Initializing on a later frame where both are simultaneously visible recovers the correct mask track.

papers.title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token
papers.tldr: VideoMaMa++ improves long-video diffusion matting by preserving and refining masks across chunk boundaries for sharper, more temporally consistent results.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards provides task-level supervision but limited guidance for localizing visual-reasoning errors.
Privileged on-policy self-distillation adds token-level corrections, but these can be contaminated by linguistic priors, response style, or privileged-view effects.
Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG) validates corrections by comparing teacher outputs with evidence-present and evidence-degraded views.
VAG uses verifier-derived advantages as anchors and admits only directionally visually supported corrections.
Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD, achieving new state-of-the-art average performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the VAG framework. Stage 1: A verifier derives AORM from on-policy rollouts. Stage 2: Dual-view teacher evaluation yields the distillation margin δt and visual contrast vt; VAG retains same-sign corrections and discards conflicting ones. Stage 3: The retained correction modulates AORM for the clipped GRPO update.

Figure 6: Training prompt and paired visual inputs. The textual prompt, comprising the image placeholder, question, visual focus instruction, answer choices, and output format, is shared across all three passes. The student is conditioned on the original image, the positive teacher on the evidence-centered crop given by the red bounding box, and the negative teacher on a randomly masked version of that crop. The ground-truth answer is used only by the verifier.

Figure 8: Fine-grained attribute recognition and spatial localization. Top: VAG reads the small helmet region as orange-red and selects the closest option, red, matching the ground truth, whereas OPD-V reports yellow. Bottom: VAG correctly localizes the green region with two oval patterns in the bottom-left corner. OPD-V answers incorrectly in both cases.

Figure 10: Chart-based visual arithmetic. The x-axis is labeled only every fifth item. VAG detects that its initial reading yields a value absent from the answer choices, re-derives the bar-to-item mapping, reads Item 10 and Item 15 as 1 and 11, and returns their average 6 (option D). OPD-V uses unsupported bar values and returns 9 (option C).
Figure 2: Comparison of on-policy learning paradigms. (a) RLVR, (b) RLVR with distillation, (c) Visual contrastive distillation, and (d) RLVR with visual attributable distillation.
Figure 5: Prediction and token-importance comparison. VAG produces the correct evidencegrounded prediction and concentrates credit on decision-relevant visual tokens.
Figure 1: Illustrative contamination diagnostic. (a) A token-level conflict case and (b) the correction-evidence alignment used to motivate attribution.
Figure 4: Performance comparison on Qwen3.5-9B.

Figure 9: Object-part recognition. VAG rules out the parts that are not visible in the frame and identifies the part on the right side of the car as the taillight (option C), matching the ground truth, whereas OPD-V selects an incorrect option.

Figure 7: Training dynamics of VAG. Left: the mean verifier reward increases over training. Right: the mean response length fluctuates within a broadly constant band and shows no sustained growth. Both panels report raw per-step training statistics without smoothing.

papers.selection_reason: Uses verifiable rewards and privileged visual grounding to train an RL policy with action corrections; relevant to multimodal policy learning and embodied control.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: VAG improves multimodal reinforcement learning by filtering self-distillation corrections to retain only those supported by visual evidence.

papers.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $\Psi_0$, $\omega$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.
authors: Tianqi Liu, Hanfei Zhao, Qifeng Liang, Hui En Pang, Jiarui Xu, Sayang Mu, Penghao Qiu, YingSheng Zhang, Jun Wang, Ziang Cao, Mingze Sun, Yukang Cao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision in joint loco-manipulation modeling.
Introduces Xp-Data with 10k hours of human and 3k hours of robot egocentric data, plus unified multimodal annotations and quality control.
Uses a unified kinematic representation combining camera poses for locomotion with projected skeletons for manipulation.
Introduces Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon dexterous humanoid teleoperation benchmark.
Reports strong performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks and held-out human video; distilled models support real-time, minute-long rollouts and VR interaction.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of Xp-Data. Top: caption terms. Middle: environment and task distributions for robot (inner ring) and human (outer ring) data. Bottom: unified skeleton annotations across human hands, dexterous robot hands, and parallel grippers.

Figure 4 | Overview of Ropedia W0. Left: Human pose annotations and robot forward kinematics provide kinematic structure and wrist poses; manual robot-keypoint annotation and correction align robot skeletons with the observed images. Middle: Camera trajectories are encoded as Plücker-ray maps, while manipulation is represented by skeleton maps, optionally augmented with wrist-pose and wide-FOV renderings. Right: A video diffusion transformer predicts future frames from an initial image, a text prompt, and these control signals. Pixel-aligned conditions are fused through additive projections, while wide-FOV features are injected via cross-attention.

Figure 5 | Overview of Xp-Teleop. About one hour of dexterous-humanoid teleoperation spanning six everyday household activity groups, from tidying and food preparation to laundry and cleaning (a). Each take is a long-horizon episode that chains locomotion with manipulation, such as putting objects into a box or folding a jacket on the bed (b). Takes are recorded as a single synchronized multimodal stream (egocentric RGB-D, 6-DoF camera pose, projected hand/robot skeletons and masks, 29-joint robot state, time-aligned language segments, per-hand tactile, and head IMU; c), and their 543 annotated segments are dominated by loco-manipulation verbs such as reach, walk, and grasp (d).

Figure 6 | Scaling on held-out human video. Zero-shot evaluation of the 5B model on 200 held-out egocentric clips versus human-video pre-training hours (log scale). The eight panels report camera ATE, RPE, and RRE; hand PCK@0.1 and PCKm@0.1; and PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. PCK counts missed hand detections as failures, whereas PCKm scores matched hands only; see Sec. C.1 for the evaluation protocol. Dashed lines indicate fitted trends.

Figure 11 | Live teleoperation with Ropedia W0. On-site recordings show the headset user and the monitor displaying model-generated feedback. Five chronological keyframes show interactions with human (top) and robot (bottom) embodiments.

Figure 8 | Cross-evaluation scaling on the DreamDojo [34] benchmark. Colors and marker shapes distinguish evaluation sets; lines connect measured checkpoint results.

Figure 7 | Human-to-robot transfer scaling. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on Ψ0 [117], Xp-Teleop, and ωHOME [65] versus human-video pre-training hours (log scale); each point is a pre-training checkpoint post-trained on the target benchmark before evaluation. Colors and marker shapes distinguish benchmarks; lines connect measured checkpoint results.

(c,d) Task-progress scores for individual policies and world-model-based candidate selection; Random selects one candidate rollout uniformly at random, so its expected score equals the mean over candidates.

(a) Real-robot executions of the policy initialized from Ropedia W0, shown as four chronological pairs of recorded keyframes with different objects, containers, and placements. (b) Aggregate real-robot task progress for Ropedia W0 initialization, FastWAM [131], and the Ψ0 [117] policy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/
authors: Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yu-Lun Liu, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang

Evaluations across 100 object and 20 scene tasks show improvements on four perceptual metrics, supported by diversity, ablation, and human-preference analyses.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches. Project page: https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/
authors: Sheng-Wei Zhang, Hsi-An Chen, Yan-Ting Liou, Chih-Hsuan Chen, Shih-Chen Tseng, Yu-Lun Liu

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made tremendous progress and can produce high-quality images. However, a question which would be asked in any other discipline is where the frontier models fall short. We introduce GenOlympiad, a benchmark which provides the most challenging text prompts from nine capability axes for stress-testing frontier text-to-image models. The assessed capabilities include generating large quantities, performing deep reasoning, ensuring hard physical consistency, following complex rules and so on. The prompts are designed such that prompt alignment is visually verifiable (e.g., counting) instead of relying on subjectiveness (e.g., style). Based on this, we develop an automated evaluation framework which decomposes the prompt into easy and hard questions, and for most hard questions, draws help lines to ground evidence for accurate grading. We evaluate 20+ strong text-to-image models, including Nano Banana Pro, GPT-Image-2.5, Seedream-5.0 and so on. We report that even the best-performing T2I model (Nano Banana Pro) only achieves a strict score of 23.9 out of 100 and that coding models such as GPT-6 Astra have higher prompt alignment scores (but not as visually pleasing). We also derive insights in model evolution, alignment with Elo scores, and effectiveness of our grounding-based evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/GenOlympiad/GenOlympiad and the project page is at https://genolympiad.github.io/
authors: Xi Hu, Martin Bell, Liang Zheng
bullets: Benchmarks nine capability axes, including quantity generation, deep reasoning, physical consistency, and complex rule following.

Introduces automated grading that decomposes prompts into easy and hard questions and grounds evidence for difficult checks.
Evaluates 20+ leading text-to-image models; the top reported model scores only 23.9/100 under strict evaluation.
Also analyzes model evolution, alignment with Elo ratings, and the effectiveness of grounding-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have enabled GPT-6 Astra to perform robotic manipulation through in-context learning. Yet contact-rich control and tactile perception are often regarded as strengths of specialist policies, leaving open whether Astra can directly understand and use tactile observations. We provide, to our knowledge, the first demonstration that Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses their contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through its existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on nineteen simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting. With visuo-tactile input, Astra achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8%, exceeding the strongest reported specialist baselines in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points, respectively. Vision-only performance also leads these baselines, reaching 76.3% and 80.6%. Trajectory analysis reveals active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. Our findings challenge the exclusivity of specialist policies in contact-rich manipulation and show that fine-grained vision can partially compensate for missing touch. They also identify vision-based tactile sensing as an interface for scaling contact understanding with foundation models and reveal signs of benchmark saturation. These results motivate joint visual-tactile pretraining, harder contact-rich evaluations, and physical-robot validation.
authors: Chen Yang, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Mu Xu, Jiansheng Fan, Chen Wang
bullets: Demonstrates direct interpretation and use of tactile contact cues, challenging the view that specialist policies are necessary for contact-rich control.
Evaluated on 19 simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks using 210 sampled scene seeds per setting.
Achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8% with visuo-tactile input, outperforming compared specialist baselines by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points.
Vision-only control also performs strongly, with mean success rates of 76.3% and 80.6%.
Trajectory analysis shows active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, but difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution.

Left: a recorded camera view; center: enlargement of the green-marked region; right: the visible cue. Grasp Classify shows cylinder texture, Roughness Classify exposes surface ridges and contour structure, and Roughness-Guided Regrasp contains visually different surfaces even in the fixed-camera view. Figure 4. Pull-out Key: resistance-aware extraction. Seed 1000017, V+T, success. At step 60, the action note identifies torsional deformation and proposes unloading the twist. Continued axial resistance leads to reseating and finer angular adjustment at step 80; the later frame shows extraction. The sequence alternates extraction attempts with unloading and realignment as resistance persists. Full rollout.

Figure 5. Insert Hole: inferring the bore direction. Seed 1000028, V+T, success. Astra interprets the opposing slopes of the tactile bands together with visible shaft deflection to infer a direction different from the reference trajectory. Astra pivots the shaft while maintaining entrance contact, then advances along the inferred bore. The case illustrates adaptation to contact geometry rather than literal replay of the demonstrated motion. Full rollout.

Figure 8. Gear Assembly: resolving successive assembly constraints. Seed 10034, V+T, success. When the red gear tilts, Astra unloads contact and adjusts its center. A later yaw adjustment addresses possible tooth interference before seating and rotation. The correction strategy changes from centering to tooth engagement as the observed constraint changes. Full rollout.

Figure 9. Insert USB: verifying object progress. Seed 10066, V+T, success. The connector remains exposed while the tactile contacts shift, and the action note identifies finger slip along a blocked plug. Astra withdraws, recenters, and issues a submillimeter correction before insertion progresses. Hand motion is not treated as sufficient evidence that the connector has entered the socket. Full rollout.

Figure 6. Hardness Classify: probing while maintaining retention. Seed 10006, V+T, success. Astra slightly relaxes the grasp after lifting, detects slipping, and re-establishes contact. The subsequent action note associates the sharply defined loaded edge with the hard-object demonstration. The probe changes the contact condition, and the subsequent correction preserves retention before classification. Full rollout.

Figure 7. Grasp Chip: cautious convergence on a fragile grasp. Seed 10099, V+T, success. Unilateral contact triggers smaller closure increments and a commanded 0.5mm lateral correction at step 110, between panels (a) and (b). After bilateral contact develops, Astra avoids continued tightening and tests retention through a gentle lift. The episode later completes intact placement; the panels focus on the contact-establishment phase. Full rollout.

Figure 11. Insert Block v2: recovering from unsuccessful placement. Seed 10019, half-cylinder, V+T, success. After release, the part remains at the opening. Astra regrasps, lifts, and makes further alignment attempts until the part settles into the opening. The behavior demonstrates outcome verification and recovery from an incomplete placement. Full rollout.

Figure 10. Insert Block v1: a local correction after rim contact. Seed 10036, cube, V+T, success. Astra prepares the hand orientation before grasping, transports the cube, and then responds to possible rim contact with a small retreat and a commanded 2mm centering adjustment. The final frame shows the release-and-verification phase. The local retreat creates clearance for recentering before renewed insertion. Full rollout.

Figure 14. Recognizing misalignment does not ensure effective correction. Insert Block v1, seed 10016, V+T, failure. Repeated rim contact prompts regrasping and leveling. From step 240 onward, the cumulative commanded pitch increments total approximately 51.6◦, with compensatory translation, yet insertion remains incomplete at the action limit. Full rollout.

Figure 13. Limited sensitivity to tangential motion and load. Weight Classify, seed 10038, V+T, failure. Astra interprets small tactile changes during a lift as evidence of a light object and places the heavy block on the incorrect blue tray. The image pattern also depends on grasp position, aperture, and motion; a small shear response is therefore not an unambiguous weight measurement. Full rollout.

Figure 15. Recognizing obstruction without resolving the correction direction. Insert HDMI, seed 1000062, V+T, failure. Fixed-camera crops and paired tactile images show three stages of the same unsuccessful episode. The recorded notes identify pitch-sign uncertainty at action 235, a return toward an upright interpretation at 270, and persistent obstruction at 585. The changing contact patterns do not lead to successful insertion. Full rollout.

Figure 16. Repeated probing without timely convergence. Empty-Can Selection, seed 10034, V+T, failure. Astra compares load responses, changes the grasp after unstable contact, and repeats the comparison. It selects the correct blue can at step 370 and starts the final grasp-and-lift sequence at step 390, but exhausts the 400-action budget before transfer. Information gathering must be coordinated with a stopping rule and the remaining manipulation. Full rollout.

papers.abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.
authors: Jiaxin Ge, Junyi Zhang, Tianning Chai, Hanjun Yoo, Chenyang Wang, Xiuyu Li, Weijia Shi, XuDong Wang, Sewon Min, Luke Zettlemoyer, Trevor Darrell, Haiwen Feng

In four environments, it generalizes to harder unseen settings; in four-box Sokoban, SFT-only Agima solves 40% of puzzles versus 2% for an action-only planner under sparse observation.

papers.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
authors: Heejeong Nam, Divyat Mahajan, Quentin Le Lidec, Randall Balestriero, David Klindt
bullets: Problem: Expert-rollout data may not cover the state-action combinations required by new planning tasks.
Method: Introduces AnyGoal, a benchmark and open-source library of goal-shifted variants across established world-model environments.
Scope: Each task recombines state factors and actions that individually appear in training data but are underrepresented together.
Finding: Multiple world-model families consistently fail on these recombinations across environments and evaluation settings.
Contribution: Analyzes dynamics and representation failures to clarify current generalization limits and support future evaluation.

A world model trained on Push-T performs poorly on Avoid-T, despite Avoid-T requiring only familiar 2D navigation and having individually familiar states and actions. In Push-T, action interventions reveal reduced model sensitivity in biased regions, suggesting that the model learns shortcuts rather than reusable dynamics.

Figure 7: End-to-end degradation reflects representation effects. Compared with oracle-state predictors, end-to-end models degrade more under goal shifts, suggesting additional failures from observation-level shift and learned representation geometry. See Appendix I.1for absolute metrics.

Darker regions indicate higher density, and gray regions mark areas whose density is below 1% of the peak reference density. papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient's value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter's forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6x speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory.
authors: Javad Rajabi, Hakki Can Karaimer, David B. Lindell, Babak Taati, Michael S. Brown
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of repeated DiT evaluations during denoising.
Uses a 2D DCT to decompose outputs and tracks each frequency coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter.
Accounts for nonuniform denoising via band-specific time coordinates derived from the noise schedule.
Triggers transformer evaluations only when forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold.
Demonstrates a better acceleration–fidelity trade-off across four image and video generation models, with under 0.05 GiB extra memory.

papers.abstract: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide a highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into a fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal a Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns a function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose a staged training procedure for pre-training hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as a wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.
authors: Xingyu Shen, Yingfa Chen, Ziqing Qiao, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han, Zhiyuan Liu
bullets: Modern recurrence offers efficient, expressive mixing but is weaker than softmax attention for contextual retrieval.
Different mixer types compete to learn the same functions, and early learning by one suppresses learning signals for others.
Recurrence typically learns retrieval faster than attention, often preventing attention from acquiring retrieval capabilities.
Freezing recurrence updates mid-training enables attention to learn retrieval; the paper uses this insight for staged pre-training.
Experiments up to 1B parameters report improvements in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and retrieval tasks across context lengths.

papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
authors: Zhaoyang Wang, Qianhui Wu, Haorui Wang, Simon Yu, Baolin Peng, Canwen Xu, Hao Cheng, Wenlin Yao, Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Jianfeng Gao, Huaxiu Yao
bullets: Motivation: Training agents through real-world computer interaction is difficult to scale and poses security risks.

Method: Generates executable environments supporting graphical interfaces, MCP services, and command-line interaction, with execution-based gates for solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability.
Scope: Produces 341 long-horizon environment–task pairs, some requiring more than 100 steps and remaining difficult for frontier models.
Results: Qwen models trained only in WildAWM worlds show substantial gains across eight out-of-distribution web, claw, and computer-use benchmarks.
Availability: The pipeline uses open-source models and its code is publicly released.

papers.abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Experiments show that even with tailored prompting, the strongest models remain unreliable: despite context windows exceeding 100K tokens and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in only 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in only 61.6%. Performance also varies sharply across evidence structures, so conclusions from limited structures may be biased. We further introduce a metric, Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), to relate evidence recall to inference FLOPs, and find that it peaks at moderate scales (4B-8B), where recall remains low. Additional output budget mainly benefits already strong models and widens capability gaps, yet the stronger preservation of these models comes at a steep computational cost. These findings highlight the importance for future work to investigate compressors with strong information preservation under a small computation budget, rather than relying on a large output budget or model scaling.
authors: Ziqing Man, Di Wu, Jia-Chen Gu, Junyi Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Introduces a 4,102-case diagnostic benchmark covering reference resolution, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives.
Directly evaluates evidence faithfulness, addressing the gap between answer correctness and faithful compression.
Even the strongest evaluated models preserve all required evidence in only 66.8% and 61.6% of cases for the best open-weight and proprietary systems, respectively.
Evidence-preservation performance varies substantially by evidence structure, making narrow evaluations potentially misleading.

Proposes Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), finding that preservation efficiency peaks at moderate model scales but remains low; extra output budget mainly helps stronger models at high computational cost.

papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

papers.abstract: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides a suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with a parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future video and generate actions, yet remain sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations, i.e., changes in visual appearance that should not affect robot behavior. We identify a gap in conventional WAM training: video prediction encourages representations to preserve appearance information, while action generation does not explicitly enforce invariance to task-irrelevant appearance. Data augmentation exposes WAMs to such perturbations but does not require perturbed and nominal observations to produce consistent action representations, and alignment with external pretrained features does not guarantee the desired invariance. To address this gap, we propose PICA-WAM, a self-supervised training framework that casts perturbation invariance as an auxiliary cross-appearance self-alignment task for WAMs. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher processes the nominal observation to provide a deeper-layer target, while the online WAM processes a perturbed observation and aligns its shallower-layer action representation to this target through a lightweight projection head. Across four strong WAMs evaluated on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot, PICA-WAM consistently improves robustness under visual perturbations, preserves nominal performance in simulation, and raises the real robot success rate. PICA-WAM further reduces the sensitivity of video features to task-irrelevant appearance and its propagation into actions, as shown by paired layer-wise diagnostics. Consistently improves robustness to visual perturbations, preserves simulated nominal performance, and increases real-robot success.

papers.abstract: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.
authors: Chan Yan Ki, Yanran Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Zhu, Lei Chen, Jie Zhou, Jiwen Lu

Across 11 video backends, the best model succeeds on both required endings in 32% of pairs with rule-only prompting; the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model.
The approach targets interactive worlds where correct outcomes depend on hidden state, rather than visual appearance alone.

papers.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.
authors: Zhengyue Zhao, Liwei Jiang, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao1
bullets: Motivation: Safety learned mainly during post-training can be forgotten during later training and may reduce general capability.
Method: Between pre-training and post-training, models learn from structured safety and utility documents and reasoning traces generated by the base model.
Key result: The approach reduces average attack success rate by 72%–81% versus Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models while improving general capability.
Robustness: Models largely retain safety after general-only SFT and GRPO, even without safety rewards.
Implication: Treating safety and reasoning as shared capabilities can reduce the safety–utility trade-off and improve training robustness.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.
authors: Wenhao Zhang, Zhongliang Zhou, Yi Ping, Zirui Wang, Sheng Li
bullets: Adding a frozen embedding of a stage-redacted report improves survival prediction across 1,633 TCGA patients; restoring the stage statement adds no benefit.
With visual features and pooling fixed, zero-shot prompts perform no better than supervised linear probes for lung and renal cancer subtyping.
SlideChat answers 74.82% of VQA items with the slide versus 74.41% without it, indicating weak visual grounding; its language-only backbone reaches 43.52%.
Paraphrasing preserves accuracy but changes 8–23% of answers, revealing sensitivity to wording.
The authors recommend minimum controlled evaluations to distinguish genuine language contributions from self-reported gains.

papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.
authors: Zhuofan Josh Ying, Guanglong Sun, Nolan Ho, Kieran Liu, Rui Yang, Andrew Chen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Pony Ma, Hossein Adeli
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training or fully fine-tuning large models with scarce, costly neural data.
Uses LoRA adapters plus a lightweight readout, while exploiting causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in one pass.
Scales adaptation to multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters and improves encoding performance across nine backbones.
BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge using the Qwen3-Omni backbone.
A multi-LoRA kernel supports efficient joint training of 200+ adapted models; adapted models remain interpretable and show increased audio and cross-modal contributions.

papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
papers.tldr: BrainLoRA uses parameter-efficient adaptation and causal multi-timepoint processing to efficiently scale brain encoding to very large multimodal backbones, achieving state-of-the-art challenge performance and interpretable neural adaptation.

papers.abstract: Multi-chain reasoning is a challenging task not only because the multi-chain evidence is dispersed, but also because different parts of reasoning may require distinct, interacting chains of support. Flat retrieval can flood a model with loosely related text, whereas early selection of a single reasoning path can discard evidence that becomes useful only after other facts are considered. We introduce RESIN (Reasoning with Entity Structured Indexing), which uses structure to locate evidence while keeping the original source as the basis for reasoning. RESIN decomposes a question into focused one-hop needs, retrieves a small set of source-grounded units for each hop, and places only this relevant evidence in a compact reasoning buffer. The buffer preserves alternative supports until final composition, making intermediate decisions explicit without forcing a brittle path. On the full HolisQA benchmark, RESIN achieves 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy over all questions, with higher reported CR and AR across five domains and higher F1 in four domains than the published baselines. Ablations show that both typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition are essential, supporting a clear conclusion: Precise evidence organization and delayed commitment make multi-chain reasoning effective and auditable. Our code is available at https://github.com/RamonMeng/RESIN.
authors: Xuanyu Meng, Jash Rajesh Parekh, Jiawei Han
bullets: Addresses dispersed, interacting evidence that flat retrieval may over-select or prematurely discard.

Uses a compact reasoning buffer that preserves alternative supports for explicit final composition.

Ablations identify typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition as essential; the approach emphasizes auditable reasoning.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.
authors: Ruicheng Li, Qixiu Li, Yu Deng, Sicheng Xu, Jiaolong Yang, Baining Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating hand motion and camera egomotion together for metric, consistent 3D trajectories.

Achieves the lowest coverage-aware MPJPE among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard, with lower world-frame trajectory errors than compared SLAM pipelines.
Runs at 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000; ablations indicate benefits from video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision.

papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.
authors: Tianwei Luo, Yiming He, Hongjin Wu, Ting Pan, Debin Ren, Haorui Guo, Junlin Yang, Yuxin Zuo, Zhehao Kou, Kaisen Yang, Zhuoqun Lai, Yi Ding, Jiale Yu, Yuchen Zhang, Zijie Qiu, Haozhan Li, Ning Ding
bullets: Includes five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, about 200 varied assets, 18,000 human demonstrations, and 66 verified tasks.
Core-50 evaluates demonstration-based learning and execution; Transfer-16 tests asset/relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task demonstrations.
The best trained multi-task policy reaches 29.1% success on Core-50, while an untuned GPT-6 setup reaches 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16.
Diagnostics identify failures in contact establishment, action coordination, goal maintenance, and task sequencing.
Qualitative real-robot rollouts provide evidence of sim-to-real transfer, while highlighting limits of reliable physical interaction.

papers.abstract: We introduce DexOAK, a learning-based object-aware kinematic retargeting framework for generating contact-consistent robot hand references from human motion-capture data. DexOAK first minimizes an interaction-graph Laplacian objective over a joint hand-object graph, so the robot reproduces the demonstrated object-relative interaction geometry rather than the human hand pose alone. These per-frame solutions form seed retargeted references, from which a feed-forward network conditioned on human keypoints and object point clouds learns the retargeting function. Object-aware finetuning then refines the network under contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses that position the fingers on the demonstrated contacts and reduce artifacts destabilizing physics-based refinement. Once trained, the network transfers to unseen data by inference alone, without per-frame optimization. DexOAK references improve dynamic retargeting over the state-of-the-art across bimanual tasks with rigid and articulated objects. On the Inspire hand, success rises from 39.5% to 48.4% on OakInk-v2, and ADD-AUC rises from 62.7% to 77.9% on ARCTIC. Ablations trace the gains to object-aware kinematic retargeting and the amortized network refined with contact losses. Trained on OakInk-v2, it transfers to ARCTIC zero-shot and nears in-domain performance after fine-tuning. On hardware, 46/56 open-loop replays succeed across five tasks, enabling dexterous robot data generation from human data. Visualizations and interactive results are at: https://fspinola.github.io/dexoak/.
authors: Federica Spinola, Robert Katzschmann, Cordelia Schmid
bullets: Models the joint hand–object interaction geometry rather than matching human hand poses alone.
Uses graph-Laplacian optimization to create seed references, then trains a feed-forward network from human keypoints and object point clouds.
Refines predictions with contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses to improve physical plausibility.
Improves dynamic retargeting on bimanual rigid and articulated-object tasks, including gains on OakInk-v2 and ARCTIC.
Transfers zero-shot across datasets and achieves 46/56 successful open-loop hardware replays across five tasks.

papers.abstract: Continuous in-hand rotation requires coordinated contact maintenance and renewal, linking manipulation performance to both hand geometry and tactile feedback. We investigate these relationships through rotational progress, finger participation, and fingertip loading on two versions of the low-cost LEAP Hand with anthropomorphic and symmetric finger arrangements. Both hands are integrated with TacTip vision-based tactile sensors and use a shared reinforcement learning framework. Simulation evaluates full tactile, binary touch, and proprioception-only observations on 12 unseen objects; hardware experiments evaluate full tactile policies on ten objects under multiple hand orientations. In simulation, full tactile observations increase mean normalized rotation per episode over proprioception alone by 94.8% for the anthropomorphic hand and 66.9% for the symmetric hand, with longer mean episode durations and lower mean total fingertip loads. Hardware contact measurements reveal more differentiated finger participation in the anthropomorphic hand, while cumulative loading is more evenly distributed across the symmetric hand's fingers. Overall, the symmetric hand achieves a 32.0% higher mean rotation count and a 25.8% higher aggregate rotation rate, together with longer manipulation duration. Additional hardware force recordings show a 19.9% lower mean total fingertip load for this layout. These findings relate finger arrangement to contact organization and load sharing, and show that richer tactile information supports greater task progress at lower mean loading in both simulated embodiments.
authors: Wenhao He, Max Yang, Chenghua Lu, Yijiong Lin, David A. W. Barton, Nathan F. Lepora
bullets: The study compares anthropomorphic and symmetric versions of the LEAP Hand using TacTip tactile sensors and a shared reinforcement-learning framework.
Simulation tests full tactile, binary-touch, and proprioception-only observations on 12 unseen objects; hardware tests full-tactile policies on 10 objects and multiple hand orientations.
Full tactile observations improve normalized rotational progress over proprioception alone in both hand designs, while also increasing episode duration and reducing mean fingertip loads.
In hardware, the symmetric hand achieves higher rotation count and rate, longer manipulation duration, and lower mean total fingertip load.
The anthropomorphic hand shows more differentiated finger participation, whereas the symmetric hand distributes cumulative loading more evenly.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.

papers.tldr: Unisense extends MLLMs beyond vision and audio by unifying eight physical sensory modalities for embodied understanding and reasoning.

papers.abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.
authors: Alessandro Palma, Charles Jones, Tristan Cinquin, Fabian J. Theis, Frederik Wenkel
bullets: Addresses forgetting and replay-distribution degradation in sequential generative-model updates.
Trains a new velocity field to combine frozen historical and incoming-task velocities, weighted by a stability–plasticity coefficient.
Uses mean velocity distillation to access historical trajectories with only a few network evaluations per update.
The method outperforms generative-replay and distillation baselines for class-incremental image generation.
Biological case studies show adaptation across contexts and batches while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

papers.abstract: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps.

Achieves state-of-the-art recall among evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2.
