papers.abstract: Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
authors: Zhiwen Chen, Benjin Zhu, Yan Xie, Jun Ma
bullets: Driving logs show only the action taken, providing no direct supervision for feasible alternatives or infeasible instructions.

A scene-language compatibility gate regulates language conditioning, while a reward-trained language residual re-ranks trajectory candidates.
On WOD-E2E, Cartender improves paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.

papers.abstract: An inference budget is useful only when the system delivers an answer within it. We study a fixed-budget policy combining first-valid-box stopping with a charged finalization cue. On 100 fresh, independently audited GSM8K test questions per model, it improves delivered endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and 7.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. A prelocked repeat on the same questions gives 7.0 and 10.0 points; neither seed shows a gross harm relative to first-box stopping. The point estimates of incremental physical-slot savings are below one percent. A finalization-only ablation separates cue recovery from stopping, and a fixed scalar reader tests extraction as an alternative explanation. The cue is prior art; the contribution is a component and readout analysis with charged injections and verified paths. Results cover two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Linyuan Gao, Zhiyuan Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Evaluated on 100 independently audited GSM8K test questions per model using Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.
Improved endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 and 7.0 percentage points, respectively; a prelocked repeat yielded 7.0 and 10.0 points.
Finalization-only ablations and a fixed scalar reader distinguish cue recovery, stopping, and extraction effects.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling can improve LLM reasoning, but existing approaches typically adapt generation or apply answer selection after a predetermined generation schedule. We study within-instance allocation: under a hard per-instance prompt-plus-completion token cap, when should inference stop, generate another candidate, or spend residual tokens adjudicating candidates already observed? BOSS is a training-free policy for this three-way decision, with worst-case budget checks before every generation and judge call. Its key contribution is online generation-adjudication allocation under one shared token ledger. Across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks, BOSS attains the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget cells under the common hard cap. At Llama-3.1-8B and B=4k, it reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy versus 58.6 for Adaptive-Consistency, 59.1 for TALE-EP, and 58.9 for fixed-schedule League. On identical Stage-I candidate pools, randomized A/B judging with repeated voting improves plurality from 58.4 to 60.3, with the full BOSS selector reaching 60.5. Approximately matched-cost controls further characterize how the benefit of adjudication changes with available inference budget. Together, these results establish generation-adjudication allocation as a distinct design axis for reasoning under strict per-instance caps.

At Llama-3.1-8B with a 4k-token cap, BOSS reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy; its scope is reasoning under hard per-instance token caps.

papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-CTLite.
authors: Shusen Ma, Xudong Zuo, Yangchun Xie, Yun-Bo Zhao
bullets: Targets irregular multivariate time series with sparse, asynchronous observations and cross-variable dependencies.

Achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE on four real-world benchmarks using only 88–2,537 trainable parameters.
Reduces inference latency by 18.6–87.3% and cuts runtime by about 52% across 16 repeated forecasts when summaries are reused.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.

bullets: Studies PEFT design choices across three MoE backbones, downstream tasks, and general-knowledge tasks.

LoRA and DoRA form the strongest operating region for downstream accuracy; nonzero load-balancing coefficients do not Pareto-dominate zero.
A redesigned MoE²-LoRA that moves its bypass pool into expert weights improves four upstream endpoints by 2.4–17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
authors: Adri\'an S\'anchez-Freire, Gonzalo P\'erez-G\'omez, Aitziber Atutxa, Ander Barrena
bullets: Expanding retrieval collections can change performance patterns observed on small or controlled corpora.
Abstract retrieval works best for abstract-aligned evidence, while full-text is preferable when richer evidence is needed.
Hierarchical full-text retrieval usually matches or exceeds flat full-text performance while using 67% fewer indexed units and 44–56% less storage.
RAG improved most external benchmark configurations and all held-out test configurations, with gains of up to 9.6 and 30.3 percentage points, respectively.
Reranking benefits depend on the corpus and retrieval setting; design choices should reflect evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
authors: Surya Deep Singh, Ashutosh Tripathi, Gaurav Deep Singh
bullets: Represents legal documents as provision graphs, preserves clause boundaries, and resolves cross-references before embedding.
Combines BM25 and BGE-M3 retrieval using Reciprocal Rank Fusion for precise citation and semantic matching.
Achieves perfect boundary precision, preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references, and uses 40.3% fewer chunks while maintaining section coverage on GDPR.
Improves retrieval substantially across benchmarks, including Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% on LegalBench-RAG and higher Recall@5/HR@5 on Indian, European, and Thai legal queries.
Releases implementation, evaluation queries, annotation methodology, and chunking-quality metrics.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.
authors: Ruiyang Ren, Yuhao Wang, Yinan Zhang, Chunyan Miao
bullets: Controlled replays show that arrival timing changes what agents search for, even with identical initial evidence.
These differences persist after all initial results arrive and through subsequent searches.
The paper introduces CEA, which triggers local reasoning only when each subquestion’s evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order.
CEA reduces acquisition disagreement to near repeat variation, matches complete-input accuracy, and improves accuracy over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points.
Under contention, first-ready allocation reintroduces substantial disagreement, whereas CEA makes decisions earlier and responds faster than waiting for all initial evidence.

papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.
authors: Nikita Dragunov, Matvey Mikhalchuk, Anton Razzhigaev
bullets: Targets user-perceived latency rather than decoding cost alone.
Generates from incomplete requests and updates the response as more input arrives.
Evaluated with both autoregressive and diffusion language models.
Characterizes when the approach reduces latency and analyzes why it works.

papers.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
authors: Song-Li Wu, Chubin Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses robotic photography requiring intent understanding, motion planning, and aesthetic image composition.
Uses PhotoCoT for structured camera-action planning within a Vision-Language-Action framework.
Applies Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization to align camera behavior with human preferences.
Introduces OpenPhotography, a dataset of language-guided robotic photography demonstrations for training and evaluation.
Real-world experiments show effective generalization to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex instructions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. RoboPhoto-VLA model architecture. Given an image observation and a language instruction, the model predicts executable robot camera actions. The architecture follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with PhotoCoT for structured photographic grounding and multi-step action planning; (2) Reinforcement Learning (RL) with ADPO for refining action selection to better align with human aesthetic preferences.

Fig. 1. RoboPhoto-VLA first receives the user’s language request alongside a target scene (upper left: the user asks to capture a photo of themselves eating an apple). The system then detects the user, identifies incomplete framing of the pose, and initiates adjustments to its position and angle (upper right). Next, RoboPhoto-VLA precisely adjusts its robotic arm and camera orientation to align with the desired composition (lower left). The lower-right panel displays the final unretouched photograph captured by RoboPhoto-VLA.

Fig. 4. We evaluate the model under cross-subject and cross-view generalization settings. For cross-subject evaluation, we employ the instructions “Capture me smiling naturally” and “Photograph me laughing with a friend” to assess performance in single-person and multi-person scenarios, respectively. For cross-view evaluation, we use the instruction “Take a photo of me drinking water” to examine robustness to viewpoint variations.

papers.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.tldr: RoboPhoto-VLA unifies visual understanding, language reasoning, and camera control to autonomously produce aesthetically preferred photographs across varied real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
authors: Ridouane Ghermi, Vicky Kalogeiton, Ivan Laptev
bullets: Existing multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can enable shortcuts or lack reliable automatic scoring for causal reasoning.
Causal Chain Generation (CCG) requires models to produce intermediate events connecting a video’s cause and effect.
SODA-Embedding evaluates semantic similarity to reference chains, while Causal-QA tests whether generated chains contain essential causal facts.
Two benchmarks are presented: SF20K-CC, based on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, derived from movie audio descriptions.
State-of-the-art VLMs often hallucinate or omit key events; GRPO fine-tuning with a composite reward substantially improves performance over strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of the proposed framework. We introduce a unified approach to optimize AR diffusion generation for both storage and computational efficiency. Storage Management (Left): Tokens from historical chunks are selectively cached in memory based on a layer-wise threshold σl, discarding redundant information. The final frame of the immediately preceding chunk serves as a reference frame, with all its tokens unconditionally preserved. Computation Optimization (Right): This reference frame acts as an anchor to guide token selection for the current chunkC . Redundant tokens are filtered out via a threshold γ to reduce computational overhead. AR Diffusion Generation (Middle): Finally, the retained historical tokens from memory and the active tokens from the current chunk are concatenated and processed by the AR diffusion.

The videos are synthesized via Self Forcing, conditioned on a single text prompt provided at the initialization stage. (b) Attention distributions. Visualizations reveal the distribution of temporal attention scores, indicating that the generation process predominantly focuses on active dynamic elements alongside adjacent temporal context. (c) Cosine similarity between the currently generated frame and preceding frames. The consistently high similarity observed in static background regions demonstrates the potential for extensive feature reuse during computation.

Figure 3: Dynamics-guided Distribution Matching Distillation. To mitigate static bias, we introduce a dynamic weight mask based on temporal cosine similarity. By amplifying loss in high-motion regions, it penalizes static predictions and forces the model to learn complex dynamics.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
authors: Marwan Farag, Bin Yang
bullets: Targets the high cost of processing dense, long-form audio token sequences in Large Audio Language Models.
Scores tokens conditioned on the user’s question rather than relying on attention, similarity, or temporal-sampling heuristics.
Distills token rankings from a frozen LALM’s answer-gradient saliency and uses downstream answer supervision.
At 10% token retention, achieves the best or tied-best performance on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks.
Evaluated across speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification, among other tasks.

papers.abstract: We investigate multi-constraint policy optimization in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where interactions among constraint gradients often yield ill-conditioned update directions, causing numerically fragile steps and unintended cancellation or redundant overlap in constraint corrections. To address this, we propose LOCU, which mitigates numerical instability arising from constraint interactions by applying symmetric Lowdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. Combined with Fisher-geometric screening and near-collinear compression, LOCU yields a compact reduced space in which the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and constraints are handled symmetrically through a low-dimensional active-set solve. For infeasible iterates, LOCU constructs a Pareto-descent direction which preserves the local feasibility of satisfied constraints within the same reduced formulation. Experiments show that LOCU remains stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts, and generalizes across different cost critic architectures.
authors: Joonyoung Lim, Younghwan Yoo
bullets: Targets ill-conditioned, fragile update directions caused by interacting constraint gradients in CMDPs.
Uses symmetric Löwdin orthogonalization under the Fisher–Rao metric, plus gradient screening and near-collinear compression.
Solves a symmetric low-dimensional active-set problem where the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball.
Provides Pareto-descent directions for infeasible iterates while preserving locally satisfied constraints.
Experiments show stability under strong constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts across cost critic architectures.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
authors: Tiange Xu, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of diffusion transformers for high-quality video generation.
Uses training-free reciprocal correction: cached dense refinement fixes sparse-attention omissions, while fresh sparse statistics monitor input changes.
Employs online error feedback to coordinate sparse attention, hierarchical caching, and correction aging without changing the reuse schedule.
Evaluated across multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention, caching, and direct-composition baselines.
On HunyuanVideo at 720p for 5-second videos, reports a 3.05× speedup and better fidelity and speed than tested direct compositions.

papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.
authors: Gia-Bao Dinh Ho, Sekh Mainul Islam, Masahiro Kaneko, Timothy Baldwin, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: The work studies whether a document alone can override a model’s parametric knowledge.

They usually outperform decoding-based intervention and written instructions, and match activation steering.
Controls suggest the effect mainly operates through the passage; model-specific suffixes also transfer to unseen passages.

papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Kewei Fu, Yongqi Tong, Chenzhi Zheng, Wei Wu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li
bullets: Addresses wasted listening time and truncated tool calls in realtime voice agents.
Starts new Thinker invocations on updated partial transcripts while preserving ongoing reasoning and dispatched tools.
Shares completed reasoning and tool results to fill missing arguments and launch dependent calls.
Across three benchmarks, it improves speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse, with benchmark-dependent effects on final quality.
On FDBench v3, tool coverage rises by 16 percentage points and mean final-response latency falls by 36.4%.

papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
authors: Vijini Liyanage, Fran\c{c}ois Yvon

Experiments across corpora and downstream tasks find reduced model size with little degradation in performance.
Synthetic data is especially helpful for tokenizer quality in low-resource settings.

papers.abstract: RGBA video generation is essential for creating compositable visual assets in filmmaking, game development, and digital content production. However, generating high-quality RGB appearance alongside temporally coherent transparency remains a significant challenge. Existing text-to-RGBA video methods often entangle RGB and alpha distributions and offer limited control over the precise appearance of a target asset. In addition, incorporating image conditioning typically suffers from the emergence-disappearance effects, which fail existing first-frame or first-and-last-frame conditions due to their fully transparent boundary frames. To address these issues, we present Wan-Alpha++, a unified framework that brings controllable RGBA video generation to both text- and image-to-video diffusion backbones through a shared RGBA latent space, extending our conference version Wan-Alpha from the text-conditioned setting to image-conditioned generation with an interior reference frame. Our method first learns shiftable RGB-alpha distributions while preserving the pretrained RGB prior. Specifically, we introduce a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion objective to produce distinguishable RGBA latent representations, and a transparency-guided mean sampler that shifts the noise distribution to improve transparency generation and enable spatial controllability. Building upon this RGBA generation prior, we introduce temporal phase reparameterization for image-conditioned effect generation. By cyclically transforming a zero-positive-zero alpha pattern into a positive-zero-positive pattern, it relocates visible content to both temporal boundaries, facilitating effective appearance conditioning with limited RGBA data.
authors: Haotian Dong, Xin Wang, Wenjing Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Yan Tina Luximon, Ping Li, Wanchao Su, Ke Xu, Di Lin
bullets: Targets entangled RGB–alpha generation and weak image-conditioning behavior at transparent video boundaries.
Uses a shared RGBA latent space across text-to-video and image-to-video diffusion backbones.
Introduces transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion and a transparency-guided mean sampler for improved and spatially controllable transparency.
Applies temporal phase reparameterization to convert zero-positive-zero alpha patterns into boundary-visible positive-zero-positive patterns for image conditioning.
Extends Wan-Alpha from text-conditioned generation to image-conditioned transparent effects using an interior reference frame.

With Middle initialization, MatAnyone only processes the frames following the condition frame and discards the first half of the video. Moreover, it continues to propagate an object-shaped alpha artifact even after the RGB content has disappeared. In contrast, our method conditions on a user-specified visible frame and generates a complete RGBA effect that gradually emerges and then disappears with clean transparent states.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical world models plan over long horizons by passing predicted states from a coarse model to a lower-level controller. Choosing these states can be expensive: the upper-level planner repeatedly differentiates through candidate macro-action trajectories. We replace this search with a lightweight goal-conditioned network trained through the frozen high-level predictor. The network supplies a conditioning vector, while the predictor generates the next latent waypoint. Training uses hindsight goals and state-prediction losses on offline trajectories, without search-solution targets or macro-action labels. Inference retains an autoregressive high-level rollout, but requires no high-level candidate optimization. We evaluate this approach on the shared-latent HWM checkpoints distributed with H-JEPA, using three backbone seeds and three head initializations per backbone. With a common evaluation protocol, mean success is 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze. The method improves over the corresponding HWM search baseline on three environments and has the same mean on Push-T. Dedicated measurements on an NVIDIA L40S give 1.28-4.39x end-to-end speedups for batched evaluation. Ablations identify state-adaptive conditioning as a consistent contributor, while predictor-mediated subgoals and unrestricted conditions have environment-dependent benefits.
authors: Xiang Kaibo, Liu Qingfeng
bullets: Uses a frozen high-level predictor to generate latent subgoals from learned conditioning vectors.
Trains on offline trajectories with hindsight goals and state-prediction losses, without search targets or macro-action labels.
Maintains autoregressive high-level rollouts while eliminating candidate optimization at inference.
Achieves mean success of 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze.
Delivers 1.28–4.39× end-to-end speedups; state-adaptive conditioning consistently helps, while other components vary by environment.

papers.abstract: Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control. Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion. In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object. Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker. Such an attack scheme is "deploy-and-forget" -- the attacker can deploy the tag and leave. When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object. Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object. Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device. We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design. End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm. Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.
authors: Binbin Zhang, Yifeng Zhang, Xiaomeng Chen, Dongyao Chen

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) allows robots to learn new skills from human examples; however, many vision-based methods require large datasets and resource-intensive end-to-end training. This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images. The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos. These features are used to train a temporal deep learning model that predicts robot joint-angle trajectories for execution. The framework is implemented on a NAO humanoid robot, evaluated quantitatively in simulation, and demonstrated on physical hardware. In simulation, the robot achieves a 78% success rate on a pick-and-place task using only 16 demonstrations, which increases to 86% when trained with 100 demonstrations. The framework also achieves a 71% success rate on a pushing task using eight demonstrations, highlighting its effectiveness for data-efficient humanoid skill acquisition.

Implemented on a NAO robot, with evaluation in simulation and demonstration on physical hardware.

papers.abstract: Humanoid manipulation requires reusable arm skills, yet demonstrating every possible skill combination is impractical. We present Humanoid Semantic Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Policy (HS-MoDP), which composes separately demonstrated arm skills through independent semantic routing over a shared expert pool. This design preserves arm-specific skill control while sharing action-generation parameters across arms. A semantic scheduler integrates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller through alternating manipulation and repositioning stages, extending the effective workspace and enabling skill reuse across location changes. To acquire demonstrations of whole-body contact manipulation, we develop G1Exo, an isomorphic exoskeleton that provides direct joint-level control of arm configurations. Experiments on a Unitree G1 show stronger skill composition than the baselines. G1Exo enables more reliable contact teleoperation than end-effector VR-IK, and its demonstrations improve contact-skill learning across four policy architectures. For HS-MoDP, switching from VR-IK to G1Exo demonstrations raises full cabinet workflow success from 35% to 65%. All project hardware designs and source code will be released as open source after the review process.
authors: Yiming Wang, Peixian Yang, Lifeng Zhuo, Lai Wei, Xinling Du, Kun Song, Weiming Wang, Daolin Ma

papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.
authors: Xiang Wang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Xiang Chen, Liqiang He, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Targets rigid menu systems, fragmented services, and limited extensibility in public-service voice platforms.

Validated in China’s 114 hotline, demonstrating low-latency full-duplex interaction, scalable routing, and competitive speech naturalness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of VISAGENT. The framework comprises a full-duplex user interaction layer, a two-level hierarchical routing layer, and an extensible voice-agent marketplace. The user memory service provides shared context for agent selection and task execution, while the voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational agents and onboards them into the marketplace.

Figure 3: Request-processing workflow of VISAGENT. Spoken input is routed either to the end-to-end conversational model or to a domain-specific agent selected according to the request, dialogue context, and relevant user memory. During agent execution, failures return to the first-level router with the available context and failure feedback, while additional service requests explicitly introduced by the user are redispatched within the same session. After successful task completion, the system asks whether the user has another request. An affirmative response initiates a new request cycle, whereas a negative response triggers interaction summarization, memory update, and session termination.

Figure 4: Architecture of the speech interaction component used in VISAGENT. The primary speech-to-speech path integrates an audio encoder, an input adapter, an LLM, a streaming audio decoder, and a vocoder. An auxiliary CTC transcription branch supplies textual representations to the hierarchical routing layer and downstream service agents.

Figure 5: Three-phase training procedure for the speech interaction model. Stage 1 trains the input adapter to align the output of the frozen audio encoder with the representation space of the frozen LLM. Stage 2 trains the audio decoder to generate discrete acoustic features from the frozen LLM representations. Stage 3 jointly fine-tunes the input adapter, LLM, and audio decoder while keeping the audio encoder frozen. Snowflake and flame symbols denote frozen and trainable neural modules, respectively; the vocoder converts the decoder output into the final speech waveform.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.

papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn, Shubham Mittal
bullets: Covers five tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation.

Reasoning and summarization improve when models pivot through English rather than using target languages directly.
Provides cross-lingual error analysis and cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis to diagnose multilingual limitations.

papers.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.
authors: Tingting Zhai, Wei Liu, Renjian Yu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of choosing kernels when the data distribution is unknown in advance.
Learns an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers through structural risk minimization.
Uses alternating optimization: combination coefficients directly minimize the objective, while classifiers minimize surrogate upper bounds.
The method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best hindsight-selected single-kernel models.
Ablations and evaluations on 11 datasets using seven metrics show improvements over OKS-OMC and other online multi-label methods.

papers.abstract: We present PnP-Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative-free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP-RANSAC algorithms. PnP-Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi-dense 2D-3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP-Transformer into a zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP-Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co-op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP-RANSAC (similar to Co-op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP-Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy-latency trade-off. Code and pretrained models are available: https://github.com/ebylmz/pnp-transformer
authors: Emirkan Burak Yilmaz, Yakup Genc
bullets: Processes semi-dense 2D–3D correspondence fields and confidence scores in a continuous latent space.
Regresses 6D pose without iterative optimization and can be integrated into a zero-shot pipeline with separately trained components.
Achieves 41.2% mean AR at 0.46 s/object across seven core BOP datasets, outperforming most prior baselines but not Co-op.
EPnP-RANSAC reaches 52.2% mean AR with the same correspondence module, at an additional 60 ms/object cost.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Proposed architecture. (a) Method Overview: During an offline onboarding stage, RGB-D templates are rendered from the 3D CAD model and processed through a ViT encoder to acquire the template features. At inference, a query image crop is similarly processed using the same encoder to obtain query features. A transformer decoder and following heads then predict the patch-level match matrix M and displacement offset O across all query-template pairs. The template with the highest overall match confidence is selected, and its corresponding 2D–3D correspondence field with associated point-wise confidences (u,X, c) is fed into PnP-Transformer to regress the relative transformation ∆ = (R, t) ∈ SE(3) while producing the latent representation z of the recovered transformation. (b) PnP-Transformer Module: PnP-Transformer consists of three primary sub-modules: PnP-Encoder that processes input correspondences into a geometric latent vector z, Pose-Encoder used during training to map ground-truth target poses (Rgt, tgt) into target embeddings z̄, and Pose-Decoder that regresses final relative 6D pose parameters from z.

Fig. 2: Representative pose estimation results on BOP datasets. Predicted (red) and ground-truth (green) object contours overlaid on the input images. Rows 1 and 2 represent success cases for PnP-Transformer and PnP-RANSAC, respectively, while Rows 3 and 4 show their corresponding failure cases.

Fig. 3: Visualization of the learned pose latent space. (a) Trajectory Tracing : Background points represent camera poses sampled across an icosphere, color-coded by azimuth angle. The mapped trajectory of a continuous 360◦ camera orbit around the world Y-axis forms a closed loop in the latent space. (b) Latent Additivity : A relative displacement vector ∆z = zB − zA extracted from a source pose pair (blue) is applied to neighboring starting points zstart. The resulting transferred shifts (red arrows) demonstrate similar displacements.

papers.abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
bullets: Defines low-density sampling risk as unlikely events and high-density drifting risk as physically inconsistent but likely generations.
Explains that model-internal likelihood signals can reduce low-density errors but cannot ensure physical plausibility.
Introduces HA-Sampler, which applies external physical guidance during latent refinement.
Introduces HA-Scorer, a generator-based likelihood signal using continuous normalizing flows for video evaluation.
Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy support the analysis and report better performance than compared SOTA baselines.

papers.abstract: Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation.
authors: Yuanhang Lei, Baofei Liu, Xingxuan Li, Tao Cheng, Zixuan Wang, Boming Zhao, Yujun Shen, Siyuan Huang, Ruizhen Hu, Peter Yichen Chen, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generalizing real-time physics-based animation across shapes and spatial discretizations.
Uses a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder to predict shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object training.
Introduces self-supervised physics-informed learning with normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction, avoiding simulation trajectories.
Supports reduced dynamics with user control, contact interactions, and direct binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Also learns complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animation; experiments show cross-shape generalization and real-time simulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. PhysSkin++ is a generalizable physics-informed neural skinning framework for object animation. The framework is learned directly from static 3D geometries via physics-informed self-supervision without any annotated data. Once trained, PhysSkin++ can be applied in a feed-forward manner to perform neural skinning for diverse 3D shapes and discretizations, enabling real-time physics-based animation. It further supports interactive control, collision-aware multi-object interaction, and rig-complementary animation.

Fig. 9. Qualitative results on unseen 3D shapes from the RigNet [62] test set. We visualize blended skinning fields to demonstrate our method’s generalization to novel 3D shapes. A single PhysSkin++ model produces all results.

Fig. 4. Qualitative results for controllable and collision-aware reduced dynamics. (a) Dirichlet boundary conditions constrain prescribed regions during deformation. (b) Interactive dragging provides localized user control. (c) Boundary-penalty energies support contact with planar environments across diverse shapes. (b) Deformable– deformable contact among multiple objects, jointly resolved by the reduced collision formulation. We encourage readers to visit our project page for additional animation videos.

Fig. 2. Given a static 3D shape, we first sample volumetric cubature points for animation and surface points for shape encoding. A shape encoder processes the surface points to produce shape latents, from which a set of learnable queries extract handle latents via cross-attention. Subsequently, spatial queries attend to the handle latents through another cross-attention block to derive point-wise features, which are decoded into neural skinning fields. A geometry-only, physics-informed learning strategy optimizes the network in a self-supervised manner under physical and orthogonality constraints, enabling the learned skinning fields to support real-time, physics-based animation.

papers.abstract: Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4--1.8\% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.

papers.abstract: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood. We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.
authors: Qing Yang, Yuqi Xiong, Pengcheng Huang, Zhipeng Xu, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu

Layer-wise and activation analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence grows toward model output and involves architecture-specific components.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all evaluated models.

papers.abstract: Dense temporal audio-visual captioning is important for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior work is constrained by three main limitations: (1) the lack of a dataset combining high temporal resolution, longer videos, and bidirectional alignment between time and events; (2) the reliance of most existing RL methods on checklists; and (3) the lack of a benchmark that bidirectionally evaluates event semantic correctness and temporal accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVTime-50K, a high-quality 50K-scale dataset with temporally precise, semantically accurate captions and longer videos; (2) AVTime, a state-of-the-art model optimized with a novel Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward that imposes explicit bidirectional constraints between time and events; and (3) AVTime-Bench, a specialized benchmark that introduces a novel bidirectional evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avtime.

papers.abstract: Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
