papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of looped transformers with truncated backpropagation; relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.tldr: A large scaling study finds that full backpropagation through looped transformers is generally better than truncated training, with two fully trained loops offering an efficient tradeoff.

papers.abstract: We study regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While minimax-optimal algorithms are known, tractable approaches to instance-dependent optimality are still lacking. Motivated by this gap, we introduce $\pi_0$-PSRL, a variant of PSRL that uses posterior samples to decide when exploration is needed, while following a fixed reference policy $\pi_0$ during exploration episodes. This decouples the test for exploration, triggered when the sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies, from the choice of the policy used to gather information. The resulting design addresses a limitation of standard PSRL, where the sampled optimal policy may not be the optimal choice for exploration. We prove instance-dependent regret bounds for $\pi_0$-PSRL, identifying the logarithmic exploration cost induced by $\pi_0$ and taking a step toward matching asymptotic lower bounds for episodic RL. Our proof techniques showcase a novel proof structure to derive problem-dependent regret bounds in episodic MDPs, and concentration results for Dirichlet random variables, that may be of independent interest.
authors: Victor Boone, Cyrille Kone, Waris Radji, Odalric-Ambrym Maillard, Dorian Baudry
bullets: Addresses the gap between known minimax-optimal methods and tractable instance-dependent optimality.
Uses posterior samples to trigger exploration when sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies.
Follows a fixed reference policy π₀ during exploration, avoiding potentially poor exploration choices from sampled optimal policies.
Proves instance-dependent regret bounds that characterize the logarithmic exploration cost of π₀.
Introduces proof techniques involving problem-dependent regret analysis and Dirichlet concentration.

papers.selection_reason: Instance-dependent regret bounds for posterior-sampling RL in episodic MDPs; core reinforcement learning method transferable to robot learning.
papers.title: Towards instance-dependent regret optimality in Episodic MDPs with Posterior Sampling
papers.tldr: π₀-PSRL separates deciding when exploration is needed from choosing how to explore, yielding instance-dependent regret guarantees for episodic MDPs.

papers.abstract: Once historical clients become unavailable, a federation must serve newcomers through the artifact it leaves behind. How much of its knowledge remains useful in an architecture chosen afterward? We introduce FEDNBO, a seven-dataset benchmark that separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation under disjoint data roles. Controlled studies expose inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a gap between teacher accuracy and private-model utility. Ordinary public-response distillation provides a competitive reference without public task labels or newcomer samples: gains over strengthened local training are 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on 300 CelebA identities and 300 FedEMNIST writers, respectively. In a complete-pipeline FedEMNIST comparison, this reference reaches 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, versus 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for a HeteroFedTTA reconstruction at the same epoch budget. Equal-count public-input interventions extend support sensitivity to trainable visual backbones. Together, these results establish an auditable benchmark and a strong reference for evaluating the utility, cost and reliability of post-federation knowledge transfer.
authors: Xinyuan Zhao
bullets: Separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation using disjoint data roles across seven datasets.
Finds inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a mismatch between teacher accuracy and private-model utility.

Ordinary public-response distillation is a competitive reference without public labels or newcomer samples, improving over strengthened local training by 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on CelebA and FedEMNIST, respectively.
On FedEMNIST, it achieves 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, compared with 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for HeteroFedTTA at the same epoch budget.
Equal-count public-input interventions assess support sensitivity for trainable visual backbones.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.
authors: Jiaxuan Sun, Biao Wang, Shuai Li
bullets: Standard video GRPO gives every rollout the same frames, which can cause homogeneous rewards and weak group-relative learning.
Multi-Frame Rollouts create aligned, temporally subsampled views from one maximal-frame decode to diversify visual evidence without architectural changes.
Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit rewards a correct lower-frame-ratio trajectory only when all full-ratio reference rollouts fail.
Experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show robust improvements over standard GRPO.
The method uses no auxiliary networks or model-architecture modifications.

A shared policy generates {oi}Gi=1, and a verifier assigns rewards {ri}Gi=1. The outcomes of the fixed full-ratio subset jointly determine the gate for Temporal Efficiency Credit, which produces the modified advantages {Ãi}Gi=1. papers.tldr: FrameGRPO improves video reasoning by diversifying sampled temporal views during GRPO training and selectively rewarding efficient correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
authors: Abhinav Khattar (NVIDIA), Aishwarya Chhabra (NVIDIA), Ameya Velingker (NVIDIA), Anusha Kamath (NVIDIA), Brandon Norick (NVIDIA), Kanishk Singla (NVIDIA), Kiran Praveen (NVIDIA), Markus Kliegl (NVIDIA), Mohammad Qazim Bhat (NVIDIA), Mostofa Patwary (NVIDIA), Niket Agarwal (NVIDIA), Rajpreet Thethy (NVIDIA), Ramani Akkati (NVIDIA), Raviraj Joshi (NVIDIA), Sai Nishanth Padala (NVIDIA), Shuoyang Ding (NVIDIA), Sriharsha Niverty (NVIDIA), Utkarsh Vaidya (NVIDIA), Vitaly Lavrukhin (NVIDIA), Yev Meyer (NVIDIA), Anoop Kunchukuttan (AI4Bharat), Mitesh Khapra (AI4Bharat), Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan (AI4Bharat), Rudra Murthy (AI4Bharat), Sumanth Doddapaneni (AI4Bharat), Thanmay Jayakumar (AI4Bharat), Ujjwal Sharma (AI4Bharat)
bullets: The corpus contains approximately 2.83 trillion tokens across all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native scripts and 12 in romanized form.
A GPU-accelerated pipeline translates curated English data, evaluates and repairs low-quality outputs, preserves structure and technical content, and maintains source traceability.
Continued-pretraining experiments across 12 languages find that combining synthetic data with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline.
The Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite covers chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation using translated benchmarks plus native-speaker review.
Benchmarking open-weight models reveals substantial variation across tasks and languages; experiments also examine data volume, script coverage, and Indic-data share effects on English performance.

papers.abstract: Thin cylindrical objects offer little space for planar markers. We propose a dual-colour-stripe marker that uses the known curvature of an object to improve pose measurement with a single camera. The boundary between two colours provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges supply features at different depths. We analyse how this depth separation improves the estimation of rotation about the cylinder axis, or roll. For a camera-facing marker at 15 cm, the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound on roll standard deviation is 2.00{\deg}for a flat marker, 0.38{\deg}for a single curved marker and 0.21{\deg}for a wrap-around marker. Monte Carlo roll RMS errors are within about 10% of the corresponding standard-deviation bounds. A first-order relation connects the sagitta of the curved marker to the roll sensitivity provided by a stereo baseline. The analytical and simulation results explain how curvature improves monocular measurement and provide a basis for designing marker geometry.
authors: Jaesung Hong, Dong Won Lee
bullets: The marker addresses the limited space available for planar markers on thin cylinders.
Its colour boundary provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges offer features at different depths.
Analysis relates curvature-induced depth separation to improved rotation-about-axis (roll) sensitivity.
At 15 cm, the roll standard-deviation bound is 2.00° for a flat marker, 0.38° for a curved marker, and 0.21° for a wrap-around marker.
Monte Carlo errors closely match the analytical bounds, supporting marker-geometry design based on curvature.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-colour-stripe marker for monocular pose estimation of cylinders using curvature. Relevant to 3D perception and geometry.
papers.title: Curvature as a Baseline: Monocular Pose Measurement of Cylindrical Objects with Dual Colour Stripe Markers

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.
authors: Chenghao Liu, Wei Fan, Jindong Han, Dongjie Wang, Aniket Mahanti, Pengyang Wang, Hao Liu
bullets: Targets the high latency of long chain-of-thought reasoning over lengthy time series.
Defines System 1 sufficiency and compresses series while retaining important frequency patterns.
Combines sufficiency and realizability divergences to guide compression and embedding alignment.
Uses a gating mechanism to select sufficient information and align it with the System 1 model’s embedding space.
Across 13 datasets, it reportedly outperforms reasoning models by over 62% while reducing inference time by 62.9% versus fine-tuned versions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Keru Zhou, Ziyi Wang, Bing Hu, Li Wang
bullets: Identifies distinct expert-routing patterns associated with fast versus slow reasoning and shows they causally affect chain-of-thought depth.
Uses a training-free, two-stage tempo-contrastive analysis to identify these experts.
Redistributes routing weights within the original top-k experts based on input difficulty: favoring fast experts for easy inputs and slow experts for hard ones.
Evaluated on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks, improving accuracy by up to 2.6 points and reducing output tokens by up to 35.4%.
Scope: controls reasoning depth through expert routing without changing model training.

papers.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: TempoMoE adaptively steers fast- and slow-thinking experts to reduce unnecessary multimodal reasoning while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
authors: Kehang Zhou, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Bridges explicit CoT, which uses generated tokens, and latent thought, which uses recurrence in hidden states.
For loop count L=L(n) and fixed k≥1 with s(n)^(1/k)=Ω(L), the model simulates a time-t(n), space-s(n) Turing machine.
Uses context window O(s(n)/L) and O(t(n)s(n)^(1/k)/L) generated tokens.
These resources are each reduced by a factor of L relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation.
The construction also works with constant-bit-size softmax attention under the paper’s finite-precision kernel.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical construction of looped transformers that internalize chain-of-thought, reducing context and generated tokens; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A constant-bit-size looped transformer can internalize chain-of-thought into recurrent hidden-state computation while reducing context and generated-token requirements by a factor of the loop count.

papers.abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.
authors: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
bullets: Long-horizon procedural reasoning remains unreliable in large language models.
Procedural memory is proposed as distinct from semantic and episodic memory.
Goal-Oriented Graphs encode goals and prerequisite dependencies in inspectable symbolic structures.
The paper examines graph construction challenges and principles for integrating symbolic structure with neural reasoning.

The primary variation is in the source of procedural knowledge available for graph construction. The game domain (Minecraft) is the only one that has been empirically evaluated [15]; the other rows are conceptual illustrations of the representation pattern.

Table 2: Expected tradeoffs among procedural memory representations for LLM agents. A “∼” indicates partial or moderate support. These ratings are conceptual expectations based on representational properties rather than a quantitative benchmark comparison.

papers.selection_reason: Explicit procedural memory for language agents via goal-oriented graphs; relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
papers.tldr: The paper argues that explicit, modifiable procedural memory represented as Goal-Oriented Graphs could improve language agents’ reliability on long-horizon procedural tasks.

papers.abstract: Designing capable neural policies for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), which map local observations to action distributions, represents an important challenge in multi-agent learning, with practical relevance to scalable collective automation problems such as warehouse logistics. In contrast to prior studies focusing primarily on individual policy design, this study explores a meta-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approach to learning-based MAPF. Specifically, given a collection of compact yet high-performing experts specialised for different map distributions, our architecture learns a router that selectively fuses their outputs according to each agent's local situation. We instantiate and validate this MoE approach with a commonly used graph neural network-based policy as well as a newly developed recursive action-token refinement model. Combined with supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning of the experts, our experiments show that MoE generally improves upon the pretrained policy and outperforms existing leading methods. At the same time, our findings reveal that appropriately trained, parameter-matched monolithic models still outperform MoE, highlighting a nuanced role for map-distribution MoE for MAPF.
authors: Fumimaro Suzuki, Keisuke Okumura
bullets: Targets scalable multi-agent pathfinding for settings such as warehouse logistics.
Learns a router to selectively fuse compact experts specialized for different map distributions.
Evaluates the approach with a graph neural network policy and a recursive action-token refinement model.
Uses supervised learning and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning for the experts.
MoE generally improves pretrained policies and surpasses existing leading methods, but parameter-matched monolithic models perform better.

papers.selection_reason: Learning-based multi-agent pathfinding with mixture-of-experts; relevant to robot navigation policies.

papers.abstract: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.
authors: Jin Han, Mingfeng Xin, Feng Liang, Jingtao Yu
bullets: Builds a loop-collapsed action graph with forward transitions and recovery back-edges, then predicts the next declared option or stop in one pass without generating text.
On 3,875 held-out decisions, the typed encoder matched logged next hops on 32.2% overall and 34.9% within declared options, versus roughly 2.2 seconds per LLM hop.
Node-conditioned candidate restriction contributed a +3.5-point gain over a flat catalog; graph traversal showed no measurable additional gain within the reported interval.
Behavior is difficult to reproduce: 7.9% of realized hops were outside declared options, and repeated states often disagreed, limiting the state-conditioned ceiling to 25.6–44.9%.
The most confident 15% of predictions reached 91.9% accuracy, while broader agreement above one-third of the fleet required state information containing both the plan and observation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The induced action graph G at the level on which every node can be named: a capability-family structure over the released corpus. papers.selection_reason: Routing layer replacing expensive LLM hops with small-model decisions; reduces latency and token cost, fits efficient AI.
papers.title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
papers.tldr: NIOCIS accelerates tool-use routing by predicting a typed next action from a node-specific option set, replacing costly LLM decisions with millisecond-scale inference but achieving only partial agreement with logged behavior.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires models to chain intermediate conclusions while remaining cost-aware. Existing training-free self-reflective protocols (generate -> critique -> revise) improve accuracy but operate on a flat token stream: revisions cannot identify which prior step is unreliable, and early stopping cannot exploit structural convergence. We introduce GraphEvoResearcher, a training-free protocol that lifts EvoResearcher's self-reflective meta-reward onto an explicit reasoning graph - nodes are intermediate conclusions/evidence and edges encode support, contradict, and depends_on. A graph-aware meta-reward combines correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, and four structural signals (connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, path convergence) to decide whether to revise, backtrack, or stop. A graph-convergence early-stop terminates when evidence branches converge on a single conclusion. On a real LLM (DeepSeek), over GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (n=50 each), GraphEvoResearcher reaches 98%, 92%, and 82% respectively, the highest of all baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest set (MATH: +24 pp over single-shot, +12 pp over flat reflection), while keeping construction cost bounded at ~2 steps / 4.5-5 nodes. Our results indicate the structural signal of a reasoning graph is most valuable exactly where single-step reasoning is unreliable.
authors: Suxing Liu
bullets: Addresses flat generate–critique–revise protocols, which cannot localize unreliable reasoning steps or exploit structural convergence.
Represents intermediate conclusions and evidence as graph nodes with support, contradiction, and dependency edges.
Uses graph-aware rewards covering correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, and path convergence.
On DeepSeek across GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (50 examples each), achieves 98%, 92%, and 82%, respectively; MATH gains are +24 percentage points over single-shot and +12 over flat reflection.
Keeps construction cost bounded at approximately 2 steps and 4.5–5 nodes; evaluation is limited to the reported model and benchmark samples.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of a multi-hop reasoning graph produced by GraphEvoResearcher. The question root v0 spawns evidence branches; the premise of one branch is contradicted by another, so the protocol backtracks/revises; the surviving conclusion is supported by a converging branch and yields the final answer.
Table 1: Positioning of GraphEvoResearcher against closely related self-reflective and graphreasoning methods.
Table 3: Cross-model verification on MATH.
Table 4: Cost-accuracy tradeoff (n=50).

papers.selection_reason: Graph-aware self-reflective reasoning with structural early stopping reduces reasoning cost.
papers.title: GraphEvoResearcher: Graph-Aware Training-Free Self-Reflective Reasoning for Cost-Bounded Multi-Hop Question Answering
papers.tldr: GraphEvoResearcher improves cost-bounded multi-hop QA by using a self-reflective reasoning graph to target revisions and stop when evidence converges.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
authors: Xinyue Peng, Zhenlin Liang, Meng Cai, Hua Wang
bullets: Addresses unnecessary CoT generation, which increases serving cost and can turn correct intermediate reasoning into incorrect final answers.
Embeds completed reasoning segments on a unit sphere and analyzes their semantic trajectory online.
Uses a trial phase with short branch answers and confidence thresholds, followed by a trajectory phase that detects repeated reversals with little progress.
Across five tasks and two models, reduces output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time by 51.0%.
Achieves an 80.58% five-task average, comparable to Full CoT.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GLOBE, a training-free online algorithm over a single reasoning stream, in three steps. The example is a tool-calling irrelevance case, as the persona permits only science questions and the weather tool should not be called. In the trial phase, a get_weather trial answer at Wait is rejected for low confidence. In the trajectory phase, the reasoning wavers over calling the tool. Once reversals, marked by the red arrows, accumulate with little net displacement, further reasoning is redundant, so the trajectory stop ends the stream and the final answer declines the request.
Figure 1: Two mechanisms for triggering an early exit: a trial answer at a candidate signal (a) and a cut of the reasoning stream (b).
Figure 4: Operating-point evidence. (a) Diagnostic trial and cut evidence used to locate the phase switch. (b) Selection of τQ.

Figure 3: Stop reliability on separate analysis runs. (a) Harm and rescue of GLOBE early stops versus Full CoT on GSM8K, BFCL v4 Live, and Agent Memory. (b) Stop outcomes per controller: stopped and correct (green), stopped and wrong (orange), and natural close (grey).

Figure 5: Signal-specific analysis. Top: the share of candidate signals whose short trial passes the confidence test, split by signal type. Middle: the share that passes the test and is correct. The thinking-close signal keeps improving until 400 tokens (40% gate, 35% yield), while the two textual markers never exceed 27% and 17%; Wait peaks at 100–200 tokens and decays from there, and Actually is the weakest of the three throughout. Bottom, over a longer axis: the marker lane’s window. The share of passed confidence tests whose answer is correct falls from 78% to 45% beyond 800 tokens while the mean trial confidence stays flat at about 0.80. Bins are 100 tokens wide and hold at least 25 events.

The ten-pair mean gives the figures quoted in the abstract; the final row excludes Qwen BFCL v4 Live.

Table 6: Stop coverage versus stop quality on Qwen from separate analysis runs. Stop: stopped items over N (count in parentheses). Post-stop: accuracy among the stopped items. Yield: stopped and correct over N . N is 1,221 (CSQA), 1,319 (GSM8K), 2,251 (BFCL v4 Live), and 465 (Agent Memory). On Agent Memory an item counts as stopped when the request that ends it is stopped. Bold: best yield per task.

GLOBE thresholds are (Kphase,Kosc, τQ); Character-LLM has no trial phase, and its first entry nmin is the number of completed segments before the trajectory stop is armed.

Table 10: τQ sweep with Kphase = 4 and Kosc = 8. Tok: retained reasoning tokens per item. Traj.: trajectory stops. Bold: the selected setting.

Table 11: Sensitivity to the segment encoder (Qwen, reference configuration). The 8B rows use the default encoder; on BFCL v4 Live this is the run of Table 1. Tok: retained reasoning tokens per item. Traj.: items closed by the trajectory stop. Embed: embedding time per item.

Table 5: What the controller costs, per item, for the Qwen runs behind Figure 3b. Requests count the main stream, trials, and the continuation. The embedding share is the embedding time divided by the item’s wall time; because the observer runs alongside the main stream, it bounds the latency the observer can add.

The role-play harness has no trial phase (Appendix A.6), so there is no w/o trial answers row.

papers.title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
papers.tldr: GLOBE is a training-free early-exit method that uses confidence checks and geometric trajectory patterns to stop chain-of-thought reasoning earlier, reducing computation while preserving Full-CoT-level performance.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.
authors: Junhui Chen, Yu Zhang, Lantian Li, Dong Wang
bullets: Reframes swarm analysis from final utility to how agents process, integrate, and rely on information.
Uses ECS to measure external-context dependence and PKS to measure parametric-knowledge dependence.
ECS rises with input relevance and captures useful multi-source contributions, while PKS falls as informative context accumulates.
Probe-guided pruning reduces redundant communication and token use; probe-guided path search accelerates convergence versus utility-only baselines.
Demonstrates probes as auxiliary signals for swarm structure optimization across controlled and realistic settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Behavioral probes in multi-source aggregation and chain-reasoning settings. (a) Zstandardized segment-level ECS of the Critic with respect to upstream expert outputs; higher values indicate stronger reliance on the corresponding segment. (b) PKS trajectories along the reasoning chain, with labels indicating the last taxonomic level that introduces new information. Solid lines show means and shaded regions show the 15–85 percentile range. Overall, seg-ECS highlights domain-relevant upstream sources, while PKS decreases only when informative context continues to accumulate.

Figure 1: Node-level response patterns under four context conditions: irrelevant (bubble), related but unhelpful (rel), oracle denotes inverse relational evidence that is sufficiently informative for reverse inference, and answer denotes context directly containing the answer. Curves and translucent bars show score densities, dashed vertical lines mark group means, and the annotation boxes report mean and standard deviation. Overall, ECS increases with context relevance, while PKS decreases when the answer can be inferred from the provided context.

Figure 3: Behavioral probes in a realistic tool-augmented GAIA pipeline. Panel (a) compares ECS for decision-critical and non-critical tool evidence across WebSearch and FileAnalyse; panel (b) compares ECS for function-calling search-result segments labeled as useful or irrelevant by the corresponding WebSearch analysis output; panel (c) compares CombineAnswer PKS before and after removing WebSearch evidence.

Figure 5: ECS–PKS behavioral profiles of functional categories in the GAIA dataset. The x-axis is PKS, the y-axis is ECS, colors denote functional log categories, and black crosses mark category centers. The profile clusters align with functional roles, supporting a task-dependent region Ωtask for probe-guided pruning.

Figure 4: Critical edge weight trends under three warm-starts. After 50 utility-only warm-up iterations, the PKS-based convergence probe is introduced. The panels show good, moderate, and poor warm-starts, defined by the critical-edge weight before probe intervention. Solid lines denote the mean weight over critical edges, with shaded regions showing the 15–85 percentile range. Across all cases, the probe accelerates critical-edge growth compared with the utility-only baseline.

Table 1: Node-pruning results across baselines. DA/LA/BA denote cumulative inbound weights to the final decision node; Rdn sums redundant LA/BA weights; Tok/Q is average tokens per question. Table 4: Topic grouping of MMLU subjects used in the expert-specialization analysis. The first column gives the aggregated topic group used on figure axes, and the second column lists the original MMLU subjects assigned to that group. This grouping enables cross-domain comparison of expertconditioned ECS responses.
Table 8: Paired accuracy and communication comparison on 500 MMLU questions using the existing trained Qwen graphs. Probe-Joint achieves 80.2% accuracy (401/500).
Table 6: Comparison of simpler signals with ECS and PKS on the same 6,052 single-node records.
Table 2: Example context conditions for the node-level response experiment.

Table 3: Statistical summary for the node-level response experiment in Figure 1. Mean adjacent Cliff’s δ averages the three ordered comparisons bubble→rel, rel→oracle, and oracle→answer. Confidence intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals, and p-values are from paired permutation Spearman tests.

Table 5: Statistical summary for the GAIA tool-augmented reasoning experiment in Figure 3. Confidence intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals for mean differences. Positive differences indicate larger ECS for critical RAG evidence in panel (a), larger ECS for relevant WebSearch segments in panel (b), and larger PKS after removing WebSearch evidence in panel (c).
Table 10: Conditional escalation to an external reasoning Adapter on 300 held-out questions. Incremental tokens are measured relative to the No-Adapter workflow.

Table 9: Sparse expert selection using a fixed, few-shot-calibrated seg-ECS ranking. Accuracy, expert calls, and tokens are reported per test question.

papers.tldr: Behavioral probes based on ECS and PKS make information flow in LLM swarms measurable and support more efficient communication and reasoning-path optimization.

papers.abstract: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.
authors: Kesav Kumar Jayakumar, Karthigeyan Thilak
bullets: A two-token readout using unspaced “yes”/“no” IDs never matches LLaVA-1.5-7B’s generated space-prefixed tokens, distorting evaluation.
A tokenizer-derived eight-token readout yields LLaVA-1.5-7B F1 scores of 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on adversarial, popular, and random splits.
The adversarial readout shift is larger than gains reported by five of six surveyed papers, but comparisons remain unresolved because precision and readout settings differ.
Across four additional VLMs, copying LLaVA’s IDs causes F1 to fall to 0.00 for two models, while tokenizer-specific readouts produce 0.80–0.92.
Nine tested inference-time corrections did not improve the fixed baseline; attention analysis also challenges assumptions behind grounding-based interventions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Decision path at the POPE answer position for LLaVA-1.5-7B. The model always emits a space-prefixed surface form (‘ Yes’ or ‘ No’). The two-token check inspects two IDs the model never produces in this context, so every comparison is between two candidates the decoder excluded. On the adversarial split that comparison reads 924 of the model’s 1,644 ‘ No’ answers (56%) as yes, pushing the yes-rate to 0.760 on a 50% positive split.

Figure 3: Running yes-rate over the 3,000-question POPE adversarial stream. The eight-token protocol (blue) stabilises near the ground-truth yes-rate (dashed). The two-token protocol (red) stabilises around 0.760 because it reads 924 of the model’s 1,644 ‘ No’ emissions (56%) as yes.

Figure 2: Confusion matrices for POPE adversarial (3,000 questions) under each protocol. Under two-token evaluation, 660 of the 1,318 true-No predictions migrate to the FP cell, leaving precision at 0.6307. Under eight-token evaluation only 182 stay there, and precision is 0.8658. The model’s behaviour is identical across both matrices; only the readout changes.

Figure 7: Nine inference-time corrections on POPE adversarial, two views. (a) F1 against the corrected baseline at 0.8221. (b) The same methods on the precision-recall plane with F1 iso-curves. Every yes-suppression variant moves north and west of the baseline; no path crosses the F1=0.8221 iso-curve.

Figure 10: Yes/no surface forms map to different token IDs under each model. Blue rows are the forms the model actually generates first after ASSISTANT:; grey rows are valid single-token IDs that never appear; orange multi-token rows are space-prefixed forms the Mistral tokenizer splits into two tokens, so they cannot enter a first-token comparison.

Figure 4: Running yes-rate across all three POPE splits under both protocols. The two-token protocol (left) holds a yes-bias on every split, settling at 0.760, 0.707 and 0.644 on adversarial, popular and random; the eight-token protocol (right) tracks the underlying ground-truth mix.

Figure 6: Eight POPE adversarial samples from our run (question IDs 1, 7, 26, 72 on top; 14, 20, 35, 39 on the bottom), two per confusion-matrix outcome under eight-token evaluation. Blue borders mark predictions that match the label; red borders mark errors. The split queries objects that co-occur with present ones, which is what makes the FP and FN cases hard to fix with a generic visual-uncertainty signal.

Figure 9: Absolute logit gap |ℓyes − ℓno| at the answer position on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Left: per-category mean with one-standard-deviation error bars (TP n=1173, TN n=1317, FP n=183, FN n=327; means 2.07, 1.48, 0.70, 0.96). Right: kernel-density estimates. The order TP > TN > FN > FP at the mean separates confidence from correctness, which is why uncertainty-keyed corrections trade TPs for FNs at about the same rate as FPs for TNs.

Figure 5: First-token frequency at the answer position for all eight yes/no surface forms across the three POPE splits (log scale on y). The four right-side forms, including yes (3582) and no (1217), receive zero first-token mass in any split. The two-token protocol reads only 3582 and 1217.

Figure 8: Distribution of mean attention from the final text token to image positions, layers 14–20, on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Blue bars are correct (n=2490); red bars are wrong (n=510). Higher image attention associates with wrong predictions, so suppressing yes-logits when attention is low removes signal from the wrong side of the distribution.

Table 4: POPE F1 under the four readouts for four VLMs beyond the LLaVA-1.5-7B reference (top block, from Table 2). legacy_2tok and legacy_8tok hard-code the LLaVA-1.5 LLaMA-2 IDs; dynamic_single re-derives the single-token yes/no IDs from each model’s own tokenizer; string_parse greedily decodes and parses the first yes/no substring. papers.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
authors: Rui Wang, Zishen Lai, Jiayu Liu, Cheng Qian, Jeonghwan Kim, Heng Wang, Xuejun Zhang, Jiateng Liu, Bingxuan Li, Shujin Wu, Qing Zong, Tianshi Zheng, Chunyang Li, Qihan Lin, Chen Li, Dadi Guo, Xiusi Chen, Yangqiu Song

papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
authors: Chenhe Yang, Yuhuan Lyu, Tianyang Hu

papers.abstract: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
authors: Matthias Eder, Pantelis Emmanouil, Vivek Farias, Fabian Fischer, Adam Jozefiak, Tianyi Peng, Thomas Ulz, Raphael Watschinger, Fangyu Wu, Andrew Zheng

papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
authors: Moritz Wagner, Christophe Roux, Max Zimmer, Sebastian Pokutta
bullets: Existing methods evaluate cache entries independently, overlooking how deleting one entry changes attention over all others.
KV-Surgeon uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate to jointly choose greedy deletions and compensate remaining entries.
It improves the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier across QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena for dense and mixture-of-experts models.
At 50× compaction, it improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching at comparable cost.
A faster variant also surpasses the prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.

papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
authors: Minoo Ahmadi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: SMC enhances inference-time search by resampling partial generations according to internal confidence or external process rewards.
Multinomial resampling can duplicate high-weight candidates and eliminate alternative lineages, while ESS may miss this diversity loss.
LP-SMC combines Chopthin resampling with a weight floor to preserve unequal weights and give low-scoring lineages opportunities to recover.
Across two base models and multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, LP-SMC improved oracle coverage in every setting and end-to-end accuracy in 11 of 12 settings.
Coverage gains also persisted with an external reward model, indicating separate benefits from diversity preservation and reward guidance.

papers.abstract: In this work we focus on the problem of embodied task planning, which requires an agent to accomplish a complex task by separating it into atomic actions. Recent studies have developed LLM-based methods to address this problem. However, the executability and correctness of the generated plans remain suboptimal in complex environments and tasks. On the other hand, classical search algorithms have the potential to solve the planning problems perfectly, yet they require fully observable environments, known state transitions and goal state, which are often unattainable in general task domains. Therefore, we propose to implement an LLM-guided search algorithm that makes the search process possible and efficient by incorporating LLMs' commonsense knowledge. Our method leverages LLMs to (1) translate natural language instructions into formatted goal conditions, (2) facilitate efficient exploration in partially observable environments, (3) implement a rule-based world simulator, and (4) prune the space of candidate actions to improve search efficiency. Experimental results on VirtualHome and ALFWorld demonstrate its superior performance.
authors: Peiran Xu, Yixiang Yang, Jinghan Li, Fei Li, Cao Sheng, JiaZhong Yu, Yadong Mu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of LLM-generated plans and classical search when environments are complex, partially observable, or lack known transitions and goals.
Translates natural-language instructions into structured goal conditions and uses an LLM to guide exploration.
Employs a rule-based world simulator and prunes candidate actions to make search more efficient.
Demonstrates superior performance on the VirtualHome and ALFWorld benchmarks.
Scope: effectiveness is reported for these embodied task-planning environments; the abstract gives no further limitations.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models can jointly understand video, audio, and text, yet they remain weak at temporal grounding, a capability essential for real-world audio-visual applications. To understand this limitation, we look beyond final predictions and examine the model's internal temporal evidence. We identify a temporal generation gap: the internal attention of the model localizes the target moment more accurately than the timestamps it generates. To close this gap, we propose TACG (Temporal Attention-Consistency Grounding), a post-training method that treats internal attention as a reliable temporal pivot and aligns it with both the model prediction and the ground-truth annotation through attention-consistency training. We further build a 580K-sample training dataset by reconstructing temporal QA from dense audio-visual annotations and organizing general omni-modal instruction data. Using TACG and this training dataset, we train OmniGround, a general-purpose omni-modal model with stronger temporal grounding capability, without injecting any additional temporal cues. OmniGround reaches state-of-the-art omni-modal temporal grounding, including 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while staying competitive on both general audio-visual understanding and vision-only grounding.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Depeng Wang, Hao Lin, Ke Xu, Ya Guo, Huijia Zhu, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang
bullets: Identifies a temporal generation gap: internal attention localizes target moments more accurately than generated timestamps.
Introduces TACG, a post-training attention-consistency method using internal attention as a temporal pivot.
Builds a 580K-sample dataset from dense audio-visual annotations and general omni-modal instructions.
Achieves 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while remaining competitive in broader audio-visual and vision-only tasks.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of searching the open web and synthesizing evidence, yet they remain poorly suited to controllable report generation in multimodal deep research. This task requires agents to handle interleaved textual and visual inputs, gather multimodal evidence through multi-step web search, and deliver comprehensive illustrated reports under user-specified requirements. Existing systems face two limitations. During reasoning, they often underuse images discovered along the search trajectory; during generation, they tend to produce fixed-form answers with limited control over report granularity, multimodal composition, and evidence grounding. We introduce MIRA, a Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for controllable reports. MIRA integrates textual and visual evidence throughout research and writing. At its core, MIRA-Harness translates user requirements into generation contracts and connects four stages: evidence collection, report submission, feedback-driven revision, and final delivery. Building on this harness, MIRA-Data constructs high-quality multi-hop multimodal research trajectories, and we post-train foundation models to operate within the workflow. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art performance among open agents on 7 representative, established multimodal-search and deep-research-agent benchmarks, while producing user-aligned illustrated reports with traceable textual and visual evidence.
authors: Hongrui Wu, Kaiwen Tuo, Congcong Wang, Gen Li, Shuai Dong, Xinlei Yu, Yuqi Xu, Haowen Hou, Zelin Peng, Jiaqi Wang

Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art results among open agents on seven multimodal-search and deep-research benchmarks.
Produces user-aligned illustrated reports grounded in traceable textual and visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Video vision-language models (VLMs) have strong semantic understanding, yet remain unreliable at precise temporal grounding. Existing gains from explicitly aligning video frames with absolute time suggest that VLMs may already encode accurate temporal locations internally but lose precision when expressing them as timestamps. Our analysis across four VLMs and two grounding datasets confirms this hypothesis: attention intervals outperform predicted intervals on approximately 66% of valid examples. We term this discrepancy the temporal generation gap. Because precise temporal annotations are expensive, this finding motivates closing the gap to improve temporal grounding using only unlabeled video-query pairs. We propose Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses internal temporal attention as self-supervision for Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value samples. SAPO consistently improves temporal grounding across multiple datasets and models spanning weak to strong initial grounding ability. Relative mIoU gains reach 33.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 5.4% on the strong Time-R1-7B. The improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
authors: Howard Yen, Nitya Mani, Alex Renda, Christopher S. Hardin

Finds that models strong at recall can degrade sharply on state tracking and pattern learning with longer contexts.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.
authors: Haowei Zheng, Zhenyu Zhou, Jiawei Chen, Can Wang, Defang Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by coarse time discretization in accelerated diffusion sampling.

papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang, Kailong Fan, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Zhenan Sun, Renzhen Wang, Deyu Meng
bullets: Sequential editing can cause cumulative parameter interference and degrade general abilities.

Its Fisher-geometry formulation has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution.
Experiments across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 show strong performance and improved preservation of downstream accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
authors: Shengjing Liu, Feiyang Li, Yuxuan Yang, Yile Wang, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets overthinking caused by lengthy, redundant reasoning in large reasoning models.
Monitors trial-answer consistency at reasoning-step boundaries rather than forcing early termination.
Suppresses action transition point tokens such as “Wait,” “Alternatively,” and “Hmm” during decoding.
Training-free experiments across four models and five benchmarks reduce token use by 18.6%–25.0% while maintaining performance.
Results also report 0.07%–1.48% accuracy improvements and more coherent, concise outputs judged by LLMs.

papers.abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.
authors: Zihe Zhang, Weimiao Yu, Piumi Don Simonge
bullets: Addresses subtle morphology, class imbalance, and multi-scale context challenges in prostate WSI grading.
Uses frozen foundation-model features alongside ImageNet-pretrained, foundation-model-distilled FastVim features from raw crops.
Mamba encoders provide linear-time spatial context at each scale, followed by joint feature fusion for prediction.
On PANDA with 5-fold cross-validation, achieves 0.894 macro F1 and 0.802 Gleason 5 F1.
Improvements are consistent across tested foundation models and classifiers, with larger gains at smaller scales.

The representations from both branches are each encoded by a Mamba encoder and fused into one patch-level prediction, and a per-scale classification head supplies an auxiliary training signal (deep supervision). Only the Mamba encoders, the per-scale classification heads and the fusion head are trained, and the two feature encoders are kept frozen.
