papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.
authors: Nimeshika Udayangani, Flora D. Salim, Christopher Leckie, Sarah Erfani
bullets: Addresses OOD detection when past task data are unavailable and catastrophic forgetting must be avoided.
Introduces TA-KAN, a task-adaptive classifier designed to reduce recency bias and improve ID–OOD separation.
Adds a geometry-guided OOD score that complements classifier confidence without using past ID data.
Reports significantly improved OOD detection with strong ID classification and state-of-the-art OOD-CL results.
Scope: focuses on rehearsal-free continual-learning settings.

papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.
authors: Wonjun Yi, Wonho Jung, Junho Kim, Rismaya Kumar Mishra, Yong-Hwa Park
bullets: Targets simultaneous identification and severity classification of motor faults from shared vibration signals.
Uses task-specific feature extractors with cross-task information exchange instead of a fully shared trunk.
Time-frequency attention highlights informative within-task regions, while channel attention refines exchanged features.
On a rotor-bearing system, it achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898 and outperformed the evaluated baseline architectures.
Ablations supported using both attention mechanisms; the model used 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs.

papers.abstract: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
authors: Zezhong Jin, Xiaoyu Wang, Zhe Li, Chong-Xin Gan, Siqing Qin, Man-Wai Mak, Kong Aik Lee
bullets: MCRA splits residual states into groups, exchanges information using a Sinkhorn-normalized matrix, and learns a gate balancing original and adapted paths.
FALA uses a shared learned query to assign input-dependent layer weights separately for every speech frame.
The method targets efficient adaptation without full fine-tuning of large self-supervised speech models.
Relative EER reductions are 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb versus a frozen WavLM baseline.
Adaptation uses only 0.0009%–0.0016% of WavLM-Large’s parameters, depending on the evaluation set.

FALA then computes frame-dependent layer weights before the speaker encoder. Frozen LayerNorm and dropout operations are omitted from the diagram for clarity.

papers.title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification
papers.tldr: A highly parameter-efficient speaker-verification adaptation method jointly modifies residual paths and selects Transformer layers dynamically for each speech frame, substantially reducing EER over a frozen WavLM baseline.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement. We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.
authors: Lejia Ye, Bin Wu, Jingjing Gao, Yiyang Wu, Xiaohu Zhang
bullets: Reframes each 3D Gaussian primitive as a neuron, providing a unified perspective on sparse-view reconstruction.
Enriches supervision with optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization.
Uses motion-aware dropout and early stopping to suppress overfitting while maintaining dynamic-scene stability.
Outperforms reported optimization-based and feed-forward baselines on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset.
Won first place in the challenge’s sparse-view track.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our methodology. papers.tldr: A few-shot learning framework improves sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting by enriching supervision and regularizing training to reduce overfitting and geometry degradation.

papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.
authors: Xidong Wu, Qi Qi, Yuqiong Ji, Shangqian Gao
bullets: Synchronous rollout generation is a major throughput bottleneck in on-policy self-distillation.
AsyncOPSD decouples rollout generation and learner updates, avoiding multi-model coordination overhead because teacher and student share parameters.
It addresses stale buffered trajectories with staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting.
Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, it achieves 1.96–2.25× higher training throughput than synchronous OPSD and improves average accuracy.

(b) Asynchronous OPSD assigns Nr GPUs to independent rollout actors and Nl GPUs to a single distributed learner (N = Nr + Nl). Actors add rollout microbatches in a shared buffer, and the learner periodically updates policy to the actors.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao

Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],

papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

papers.abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.

papers.abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/
authors: Zhiyang Deng, Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feature-based action conditioning, which requires models to learn action-to-motion geometry from data.

Introduces Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling to stabilize observed regions earlier while synthesizing newly revealed content using them as reference.
More faithfully follows commanded motion and reduces revisit drift by 66% versus the strongest of four representative baselines.
Transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes.

papers.abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
authors: Zhaonan Li, Zelei Cheng, Amritansh Mishra, Chia-Hsuan Lee, Mann Patel, Sambit Sahu, Ben Zhou, William M. Campbell

Performance was comparable to separately trained fixed-K=20, the strongest fixed-support baseline tested.
Late widening to full support appeared most promising, but diagnostics and a single-run replay did not provide a clear explanation or consistently reproduce the gain.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.
authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu, Hope Yao
bullets: Studies continual learning for agents facing changing topics, workflows, and domains while keeping model weights frozen.

Memory retrieval localizes updates better, yet can retrieve irrelevant memories and collide when similar queries require different workflows.
Higher plasticity consistently trades off against stability.],

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can complete a task despite local execution errors that are corrected, bypassed, or carried forward without individually determining its outcome. We call these implicit failures (IFs) and study them as signals for process observability beyond final task outcome. Across 1,828 traces from nine MAS-benchmark configurations, IFs occur in 54.3% of successful and 75.2% of failed traces. We develop taxonomies of error types and subsequent absorption mechanisms, supported by human and cross-model annotation audits. Counterfactual replay further probes how repairing an IF changes the final outcome. To examine the practical value of IFs, we evaluate IF-based best-of-N trace selection against existing process reward models, and introduce a novel RL algorithm, IF-GRPO, that uses IF costs to refine preferences among successful trajectories in GRPO. Experiments show that IF-GRPO exhibits some gains in accuracy and process metrics. Importantly, it exposes trade-offs between task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density. Overall, our results show that IFs provide complementary process observability into how MAS reach their outcomes, including error recovery, propagation, and IF-based process differences that final task success alone does not expose.

bullets: IFs appear in 54.3% of successful traces and 75.2% of failed traces across 1,828 traces from nine benchmark configurations.

Results indicate some gains in accuracy and process metrics, while revealing trade-offs among task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density.

papers.abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.
authors: Chang Zhou, Jiarun Zhou, Xingtong Yu, Hong Cheng, Hui Zhang, Xinming Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that improving isolated trading decisions does not ensure long-term co-learning between trader and critic.

Links role-specific memories through shared trading records to evaluate critiques, revisions, and realized market outcomes.
Experiments on U.S. stock trading report higher cumulative return, the highest Sharpe ratio, and the lowest maximum drawdown among evaluated baselines and passive benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.
authors: Yanjin He, Cuifeng Shen, Wanzhou Lei, Maohua Li, Tao Lan, Kan Liu, Hanlin Tang, Qing Qu
bullets: Addresses the high training cost of diffusion models and the sampling cost of inference-time guidance.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show improvements across scales and representations; one ImageNet-256 setup reaches the baseline’s best FID with roughly half the total training compute, while RAEv2 achieves FID 1.15 without and 0.99 with inference guidance.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev, which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model's cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.
authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo

The released benchmark provides stimuli, logs, code, and per-model cue-price profiles for reproducible auditing.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supervises student-generated trajectories with a reference-conditioned version of the same base model. We ask whether every trajectory supplies distinct supervision that warrants its distillation cost. Gradient measurements on Qwen3-1.7B at initialization reveal that correct and incorrect responses have similar individual gradient magnitudes, but incorrect responses have approximately three times the coherent gradient share. Their estimated population-mean directions also largely overlap. A signal--noise model fitted at a small group size tracks alignment at larger group sizes without refitting. Motivated by these measurements, we introduce correctness-filtered OPSD (C-OPSD), which generates one response per problem and distills only a subset of incorrect responses. Removing unselected rows before both distillation forwards avoids their teacher/student forward and student backward work. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD achieves on-par performance with full OPSD. In a measured micro-batch-size-four implementation, executed rows decrease by approximately 68%, and with retained rows packed into full micro-batches, training takes about 40% less time while rollout generation remains unchanged. Together, the measurements and training results connect outcome-conditioned supervision redundancy to more compute-efficient distillation.
authors: Harrison Zhao, Lei Huang, Fei Liu, Wen Shi, Zijian Jin
bullets: Incorrect responses provide more coherent gradient signal than correct responses despite similar individual gradient magnitudes, suggesting supervision redundancy.
C-OPSD generates one response per problem and distills only a selected subset of incorrect responses.
Filtering rows before teacher/student forwards and student backpropagation reduces executed rows by approximately 68%.
Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD performs on par with full OPSD.
With packed retained rows, training takes about 40% less time; rollout generation is unchanged.

papers.abstract: Fine industrial robotic manipulation requires 6D pose, scale, and an operation-ready 3D model. Existing industrial pose estimation relies on CAD models, object-specific training data, or stable workcells, limiting use with unseen objects; zero-shot methods suffer from single-view occlusion, generative bias, and scale uncertainty. We present OV-PEAR, an observation-verified framework for 3D reconstruction and pose-scale estimation of unknown industrial objects. Its three-stage object-centric pipeline: (1) segments RGB-D instances and generates object-level 3D hypotheses; (2) anchors them to the robot frame via appearance-aware view retrieval, explicit scale search, and visibility-sensitive registration; (3) back-projects multi-view RGB-D evidence into the object-canonical frame to verify voxel occupancy, suppress hallucinations, and produce reusable trusted object models. On BOP-Industrial, OV-PEAR achieves 0.657 average AR and improves pose and voxel-level geometric consistency in real scenes; real-robot connector assembly reaches 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success. The model library and pose-scale log enable short-term object-level state maintenance at 0.02 ms/frame.
authors: Guoqin Tang, Qingxuan Jia, Yichen Tan, Zihang Lv, Ruiquan Wang, Zeyuan Huang, Gang Chen
bullets: Targets unknown objects under occlusion, scale uncertainty, and unstable workcell conditions.
Uses a three-stage pipeline for instance segmentation, object-level 3D hypothesis generation, robot-frame anchoring, and explicit scale estimation.
Verifies reconstructions by back-projecting multi-view RGB-D evidence to suppress hallucinated geometry and build trusted reusable models.
Achieves 0.657 average AR on BOP-Industrial and reports 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success in real-robot connector assembly.
Maintains short-term object-level state at 0.02 ms/frame using a model library and pose-scale log.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.
authors: Mohsen Fayyaz, Ali Modarressi, Daniel Israel, Lucas Bandarkar, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Across 10 tasks, copied or lightly edited text is cheaper to generate than open-ended writing.
In DiffusionGemma, story writing needs over three times as many forward passes per token as grammar correction.
Generation cost is largely explained by output novelty relative to the input and word rarity; this also applies to reasoning traces and final answers.
Highly tokenized languages require more passes per token, compounding their cost from producing more tokens.
Wrong math answers take more passes per token than correct ones; speed-weighted answer selection improves over majority voting by up to 4.2 points without extra cost.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and exploits decoding-cost variation in diffusion language models, offering a practical signal for more efficient inference.
papers.title: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models spend more decoding effort on novel, rare, highly tokenized, and incorrect outputs, making generation cost strongly task- and language-dependent.

papers.abstract: Autonomous codebase refactoring requires coding agents to restructure working software while strictly preserving externally observable behavior and prioritizing execution performance and compute efficiency over stylistic preference. Existing benchmarks: refactoring benchmarks assess functional correctness while overlooking runtime regressions, whereas code performance benchmarks target isolated micro-kernels that ignore codebase-scale complexity. We observe that refactoring scale is governed by the scope of the observable contract, the caller-visible interface fixing behavioral invariants while freeing private implementations for optimization. Building on this insight, we introduce FrontierRefactor, a benchmark of 60 qualified engineering tasks spanning four scales, from computational kernels to full repositories, across in-place optimization and cross-language rewriting. Evaluating frontier coding agents through a reference-free cascaded protocol across 1,080 execution runs reveals that correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions satisfy functional equivalence yet fail to deliver verified performance improvements, with 19.3% suffering performance regressions and 21.9% trapped in measurement noise. Refactoring paradigms reveal orthogonal engineering bottlenecks: while cross-language rewrites gain speedups from native compilation after passing functional checks, agents struggle with contract fidelity, with pass rates dropping from 65.0% on modules to 32.6% at package scale; conversely, in-place optimization reliably preserves behavioral contracts at 86.5% but rarely achieves acceleration without physical performance profiling. Trajectory analysis shows that agents fall victim to uncalibrated micro-benchmarking illusions, an operational blind spot that multi-turn execution-timing feedback directly resolves, raising strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%.
authors: Shijian Wang, Fanqing Meng, Jiajun Chen, Qiguang Chen, Linxin Song, Runhao Fu, Shuhang Zheng, Shuai Shao, Qizhe Xie, Jieyu Zhao, Mengkang Hu

Uses a reference-free cascaded evaluation protocol over 1,080 execution runs to assess correctness and performance separately.
Correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions preserve functionality but lack verified performance improvements.

Cross-language rewrites can benefit from native compilation but struggle with contract fidelity at package scale; in-place optimization preserves behavior more reliably but seldom accelerates without profiling.
Multi-turn execution-timing feedback improves strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%, addressing misleading micro-benchmark signals.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a benchmark for coding agents performing codebase refactoring. While focused on software, it represents the application of LLM agents to complex tasks, relevant to the general agent capabilities within language foundation models.
papers.title: FrontierRefactor: Benchmarking Multi-Scale Performance-Oriented Codebase Refactoring
papers.tldr: FrontierRefactor shows that autonomous code refactoring must jointly verify behavioral equivalence and real execution gains, which current agents often fail to achieve.

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
authors: Guanqun Jiang, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces procedural hallucination: producing retrieval-supported answers that violate a governing skill or procedure.
Presents SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains.
Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% with conflicting retrieval, versus 78.2% and 72.8% with supportive retrieval.
Mechanistic analysis finds the largest answer-preference divergence shortly after generation begins, with repair primarily attributed to value vectors.
Intervening in the identified value pathway improves final answer validity.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how language models handle conflicts between retrieved context and stored skills, framing skills as a form of memory. Relevant to LLM memory mechanisms and retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models often follow useful but skill-violating retrieval cues, causing procedural hallucinations that can be traced to early value-pathway dynamics.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm for Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks. However, deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over wireless edge networks presents distinct challenges: large model parameters increase uplink transmission latency over bandwidth-constrained fading channels, and non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data exacerbates client drift. Existing feature alignment solutions often introduce auxiliary computations that consume time slots allocated for wireless parameter transmission, increasing the likelihood of straggler dropouts under system delay constraints. To address these issues, we propose DPGR-GCAM, a communication-efficient federated domain generalization framework. By employing a dual-parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) architecture, we design a channel-aware tiered transmission mechanism that adaptively truncates payloads to maximize node survival rates under fading conditions. To mitigate client drift, we introduce the Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation (GCAM) mechanism. GCAM operates within the low-dimensional feature manifold to dynamically resolve multi-objective optimization conflicts with minimal edge computation latency, thereby reducing computation-induced network outages. Experiments demonstrate that DPGR-GCAM improves cross-domain generalization and sustains convergence under network fading scenarios with a 10\% client participation rate.
authors: Yuankun Xia, Hui Wang, Ling Yuan, Ziyu Hong, Di Yin, Yufeng Zhou
bullets: Targets high uplink latency, fading-induced dropouts, and client drift from Non-IID edge data.
Uses dual parameter-efficient fine-tuning and channel-aware tiered transmission to adaptively truncate payloads.
Introduces Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation to resolve optimization conflicts in a low-dimensional feature space with low computation overhead.
Experiments show improved cross-domain generalization and sustained convergence under fading with 10% client participation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The overall workflow of the proposed DPGR-GCAM framework for federated domain generalization over wireless edge networks. The system comprises three stages: (1) Global broadcast of lightweight tunable parameters and class prototypes; (2) Local training, where the GCAM mechanism dynamically resolves feature-level optimization conflicts to regulate the visual adapter update; and (3) Channel-aware aggregation, which adaptively truncates the uplink payload based on real-time Shannon capacity to maximize node survival rates under fading channels.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Domain Generalization in Edge Networks via Dynamic Prototype Regulation

papers.abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.
authors: Yun Shen, Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Addresses repetitive, task-local self-reflection and the grounding–generalization trade-off between retrieved and parametric memory.
Builds a bank of successful and failed reflections, then uses retrieved cases to generate failure hypotheses during training and inference.
Different retrieved cases provide grounded reflective diversity to guide future attempts.
Shows strong overall performance across two backbones and five math, code, and multi-hop QA benchmarks.
Also generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and helps smaller models guide stronger solvers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reflective memory designs and CoMem. Retrieved memory recalls past experience, parametric memory generates guidance from the task alone, and additive hybrids combine both. CoMem uses retrieved experience to construct supervision and train an experience-conditioned generator. At inference, different retrieved pairs elicit diverse failure hypotheses.

papers.abstract: Recovering from failures in long-horizon, stateful language agents is challenging because the action introducing a defect, the symptom exposing it, and the persistent state requiring repair frequently diverge. Existing methods largely focus on retrospective failure attribution, leaving sequential diagnosis and state repair poorly integrated under constrained budgets. We introduce TRACE-FIX, a unified recovery framework centered on versioned residual task state. Trace transforms execution logs into a structured dependency-linked ledger, prioritizing unresolved task requirements rather than salient surface errors. Fix formulates recovery as budgeted planning over admissible actions, incorporating outcome forecasting and explicit repair-reserve constraints to prevent premature budget exhaustion. To rigorously decouple localization accuracy from downstream repair capability, we present LongH-Debug, evaluating root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end closed-loop execution independently. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that structured residual tracking substantially improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines, while budget-aware sequential planning converts verified fault signals into more reliable task recovery without destructive trial-and-error. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/tracedp.
authors: Zile Huang, Ser-nam Lim
bullets: Targets failures where the triggering action, observed symptom, and state needing repair occur at different points in execution.
Trace converts execution logs into a dependency-linked ledger focused on unresolved task requirements.
Fix plans admissible recovery actions using outcome forecasts and repair-reserve constraints to avoid exhausting the budget prematurely.
LongH-Debug separately evaluates root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end execution.
The framework improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines and enables more reliable recovery without destructive trial-and-error.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.

Jev also performs competitively using only the question, though its advantage varies across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.
authors: Xinxing Zhou, Xiaojie Yuan, Yanlong Wen, Ming Jin
bullets: Targets controlled time series where future actions can be compared and optimized before execution.
Maintains variable-specific latent states, updates them with an action-conditioned transition and observations, then rolls them forward under candidate actions.
Trains without paired counterfactual outcomes or planning supervision.
Evaluated on building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory-management simulators across prediction, intervention, decision, and planning tasks.
Ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings; model rankings often change across factual prediction, intervention fidelity, and decision quality.

papers.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.
authors: Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Peng Zhang, Jochen Renz
bullets: Targets the trade-off between bounded memory and retaining older experience in continual in-context reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Self-consistency answers a question by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. Its evaluation requires both correctness labels and information about which responses agree; correctness labels alone generally determine neither voting accuracy nor the benefit of additional votes. For tasks in which all correct responses map to the same normalized answer, we derive sharp accuracy bounds using classical stochastic majorization, refined by abstention counts and answer-category limits. We also derive sharp bounds on accuracy changes across voting budgets that share a response pool. When answer-category counts are available, we introduce Plurality-U, a count-based dynamic program that exactly averages voting accuracy over all fixed-size subsets, eliminating finite-pool Monte Carlo error. On 1,403,520 stored outputs from recent reasoning models in Scorio Lite and Scorio Trace, recording abstention counts and answer options cuts the width of SuperGPQA accuracy intervals by more than half. For moving from 9 to 17 votes, our bounds reduce interval width by a median of 77.7% on SuperGPQA and 72.3% on 14 GPQA and Adaptive-Consistency pools, compared with a baseline that combines separate accuracy bounds. Exact computation has lower paired median runtime than 2,000-subset Monte Carlo in 14 of 15 tested pool-budget settings. These results clarify what incomplete logs can establish and provide an exact evaluation procedure when answer counts are retained.
authors: Zhengtao Gui, Zexi Chen, Weining Shen
bullets: Correctness labels alone are insufficient to determine voting accuracy or the value of additional votes; agreement information is needed.
For tasks with a shared normalized correct answer, the authors derive sharp bounds using stochastic majorization, abstention counts, and answer-category limits.
They introduce Plurality-U, a dynamic program that exactly averages accuracy over fixed-size response subsets when answer counts are available.
Across stored reasoning-model outputs, adding abstention and answer-option counts substantially narrows accuracy intervals, while exact computation often outperforms 2,000-subset Monte Carlo.
The analysis applies to incomplete logs and clarifies what can—and cannot—be established about self-consistency performance.

papers.title: Which Answers Agree? Evaluating Self-Consistency from Incomplete Logs

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.
authors: Jianhao Zhang, Ou Wu, Yi Du
bullets: Targets noisy, redundant synthetic candidate pools and the difficulty of preserving pretrained capabilities during single-stage fine-tuning.
Builds a navigator by applying the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization, revealing recipe-induced capability drift.
Scores candidates by predictive divergence between the navigator and pretrained model to estimate forgetting-aware utility.
Efficiently selects a utility–diversity constraint set, then distills pretrained behavior on it during new-task fine-tuning.
Experiments report a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation with lower selection overhead.

papers.abstract: Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.
authors: JooKyung Yuh, Byungmin Park, Eunseo Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Kyu Hyun Choi, Sung Ju Hwang, Kyong Hwan Jin, Hae Beom Lee
bullets: Targets the limitations of LLM methods lacking explicit model evaluation and Bayesian methods restricted to predefined candidates.
An LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits parameters, computes model evidence, and averages predictions.
Experiments are selected to maximize expected information gain over both model families and parameters.
Updated beliefs and residual diagnostics guide subsequent LLM hypothesis proposals.
Across four benchmarks, BMD achieved the lowest final prediction error and more often recovered exact functional forms; ablations supported its numerical feedback and joint objective.

papers.abstract: Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability $\varepsilon$, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change $k$ facts is accepted with probability $1/k$, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with $s$ premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by $r$ rules can cost order $r^{1-1/s}$ facts. For entity resolution with $m$ records of one entity, the first-order risk equals $\varepsilon$ times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order $m^{1/3}$; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large $m$, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.
authors: Zhengtao Gui (University of California, Irvine), Weining Shen (University of California, Irvine)
bullets: For single-premise implication rules, random pruning order adds no first-order risk; multi-premise rules can amplify errors substantially.
In entity resolution, first-order error risk is proportional to the Wiener index of the query-order spanning tree.
Pivot query orders are optimal and keep error amplification below 2; random orders can be much worse as the number of records grows.
Most-similar-first ordering is worst in one dimension and can underperform random ordering in two dimensions.
Simulations match the abstract’s predicted risk constants within sampling error.

papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical analysis of error propagation in constraint pruning with noisy LLM oracles, offering insights into LLM optimization and reliability.
papers.title: How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost? Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles
papers.tldr: Constraint pruning can save queries but amplify a single noisy LLM error, with risk determined by how many implied facts that error corrupts.

papers.abstract: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.
authors: Hengsong Liu, Liangyu Teng, Jingnan Cai, Yuntian Shi, Jingyu Zhang, Yang Liu, Jing Liu, Liang Song
bullets: Final-answer or single-message evaluations can miss complementary clues that jointly recover forgotten information.
The paper formalizes and empirically validates that controlling individual views does not guarantee low recovery from their combination.
Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU) trains on individual and pooled messages, prioritizes high-risk views, and uses replacement-based credit assignment.
On TOFU, ACU reduces full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training.
Retained-task performance remains comparable, with evaluation also conducted on WMDP-bio for native forgetting and utility.

papers.tldr: Collaboration can reconstruct information that appears forgotten from individual LLM outputs, and ACU reduces this team-level recovery while preserving utility.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
authors: Haoqun Cao, Yurun Yuan, Tengyang Xie
bullets: Off-policy updates are consistent only under two structures: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from horizon dependence, or KL regularization paired with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value.
The KL-based route corresponds to group-relative policy gradient (GRPG), connects to trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization, and yields a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage.
The analysis provides a theoretical interpretation of a GRPO-like objective used in practice.
Baselines have an additional off-policy role: shifting them downward induces pessimism, helping address partial data coverage.
Asymmetric REINFORCE instantiates this pessimistic baseline idea and obtains a regret bound under single-policy coverage.

papers.selection_reason: Off-policy policy gradient theory with KL regularization, baselines, and pessimism is transferable to RL-based robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
papers.tldr: The paper explains when off-policy policy gradients remain theoretically valid, showing that trajectory importance weighting or specially matched KL regularization and baselines can preserve optimal-policy stationarity while enabling offline-RL-style guarantees.

papers.abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. Probing and steering 25 open-weight base LLMs (0.13B-10.31B parameters; 14 families) on human-scored BESTEP English writing tasks, we find that holistic scores are decodable from model activations for the longer tasks (Parts 2 and 3) and only weakly for the shortest (Part 1). Furthermore, scoring rubrics have partly separable directions in representation space for the longer tasks, though not for short responses (Part 1). However, causal steering reveals a critical limitation: applying a matching intervention (e.g., steering "grammar" on a grammar-degraded response) yields only a negligible advantage (about 2% of the effect) over a mismatched intervention (e.g., steering "vocabulary"), and none that is detectable in any of the 10 testable comparisons across reliably measured rubrics. Rather than controlling distinct evaluative dimensions, the rubric directions share a dominant lever whose rubric-specific parts are not selective, which may mirror the halo structure of human ratings. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that analytic scoring rubrics designed for human raters do not behave as independent controls in base LLMs, even among the seven models whose scores agree best with human raters ($r \geq 0.6$). Second, we establish a methodology that shows that score agreement and decodability do not imply rubric-level control in LLM-based assessment.

bullets: Holistic scores are more decodable for longer essays than for the shortest responses.

The findings hold even among models with relatively strong agreement with human raters, indicating that agreement and decodability do not guarantee rubric-level control.
The shared rubric structure may reflect a dominant halo-like evaluation signal rather than independent scoring dimensions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Zilei Shao, Ian Li, Heng Zhao, Kewei Lian, Guy Van den Broeck, Zhe Zeng, Anji Liu
bullets: Factorized denoisers treat simultaneously predicted tokens as conditionally independent, leaving dependency errors unresolved.
Codpula combines a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer whose coupling parameters adapt to the input context.
The model jointly trains token potentials and coupling controls using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters.
Conditional queries adapt token commitments to dependencies without additional Transformer evaluations within a decoding step.
The method reports state-of-the-art results across reasoning benchmarks and advances the mathematical-reasoning and code-generation accuracy–latency frontier.

Figure 13: The deferral trace tracks name agreement. The deferred group spells the identifier string xor and its call literal: ’ >>>’, ’ string’, ’ x’, ’or’, "(’", ’0’, ’1’. These must agree with the function actually defined above, so committing them independently is exactly how a parallel decode invents a name that does not exist. Tokens with no such constraint (the word ’ string’ at position 21, a period, a newline, indentation) score identically 0.0000 and are committed in the same step. Note the two ’ string’ occurrences: position 26, part of the identifier, scores 1.1281; position 21, ordinary prose, scores 0. The signal is contextual entanglement, not the token’s identity.

Figure 12: What the deferral gate holds back, and why it lets go. At step t the gate defers exactly 4 of 16 proposed slots, and those four are precisely the tokens of the guard clause if not numbers: return ... mutually determined, and wrong in a way that compounds if any one is committed against a different choice of the others. The twelve it commits are indentation, newlines and list markers, scoring |dep| ≤ 0.0022 and most of them exactly 0. One step later the surrounding context has been written and the same three tokens score 20–1000× lower, so the gate releases them. Deferral is therefore not a rejection: it is a re-ordering that lets an entangled group be decided jointly rather than independently.
