papers.abstract: Micro-expert pruning reduces the capacity of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models by removing coupled channels within routed experts. However, finer pruning granularity alone does not guarantee the preservation of downstream capabilities, as similar language-modeling perplexity can accompany substantially different task performance. We revisit micro-expert mask construction as two distinct decisions: allocating retained capacity across experts and selecting channels within that capacity. We propose UC-RAMP, a two-stage post-training pruning framework that explicitly separates these decisions. CAPE uses cross-domain calibration evidence to redistribute expert widths under an exact layer-wise budget, while RAMP refines channel composition at fixed widths through one-out, one-in exchanges guided by a channel-interaction surrogate. Across three MoE models at 25% and 50% routed-expert channel pruning, UC-RAMP achieves the highest ten-task mean accuracy among evaluated pruning methods in five of six settings. At 50% pruning, it outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 8.19, 3.96, and 6.14 percentage points across the three models, respectively. In a single-A100 deployment at 25% pruning, UC-RAMP reduces measured time to first token by 19.7--23.9% and time per output token by 20.2--22.3% relative to the unpruned model. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/UC_RAMP.
authors: Zukang Xu, Xinpei Gao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Dawei Yang
bullets: Micro-expert pruning can maintain language-modeling perplexity yet degrade downstream tasks, motivating better mask construction.
CAPE redistributes retained expert widths using cross-domain calibration under exact layer-wise budgets.
RAMP refines channel selection at fixed widths via one-out, one-in exchanges guided by channel interactions.
Across three MoE models and two pruning levels, UC-RAMP achieved the best mean accuracy in five of six settings.
At 25% pruning, it reduced single-A100 time to first token by 19.7–23.9% and time per output token by 20.2–22.3% versus the unpruned model.

papers.abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.
authors: Qihan Huang, Lingxia Zhang, Guye Zhang, Zizhu Wang, Xiaowei Mao
bullets: Addresses fragmented medical data and the communication and parameter costs of independently learned low-rank adapters.
Builds reusable adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators via truncated matrix exponentials and QR orthonormalization.
Shares a full core across compatible projections while keeping lightweight residual coefficients local to each client.
Evaluated on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones.
Reports substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter uploads, with competitive performance on most tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of PFedQFT. The framework comprises a global server that coordinates sample-weighted aggregation and multiple clients that construct reusable adaptation subspaces while retaining private core residuals for personalized local training. (a) At communication round t, the server selects the participating clients St and broadcasts the shared parameters Θt. (b) Each selected client transforms the generators Bin g and Bout g associated with sharing group g into the orthonormal bases Vg and Ug through Taylor mapping and thin QR. (c) For each adapted projection ℓ, client k constructs the private residual operator Dk,ℓ = Rout ℓ diag(pk,ℓ)(R in ℓ )⊤ and the personalized subspace operator Ck,ℓ = Gℓ +Dk,ℓ. (d) Local optimization updates the shared parameter copy Θk and the private coefficients ϕk using Dk . (e) Client k uploads only (∆Θt k, nk), while Dk and pk,ℓ remain local. (f) The server performs sample-weighted aggregation to obtain the shared parameters Θt+1 for the next communication round.

papers.abstract: Curriculum learning, which organizes training samples according to their learning priority, has been widely adopted in reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency. However, existing methods commonly construct curriculum units using predefined data properties and estimate their utility by simply aggregating a single proxy signal from recent training history.Such designs may group samples with different optimization effects and fail to anticipate how their utility evolves in relation to the policy. We propose Predictive Gradient-based Bandit (PGB) Curriculum, which first discovers optimization-aware learning units by clustering projected sample-level gradients. PGB then employs a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast the future utility of each unit and converts the predictions into a Boltzmann sampling distribution for adaptive data allocation. Experiments across multiple model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that PGB consistently outperforms standard GRPO, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling strategies, demonstrating improved data utilization and training efficiency.

bullets: Addresses curricula that rely on predefined sample properties and single historical utility signals.

papers.abstract: Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. Prompt engineering can require task-specific prompt design, while fine-tuning requires additional optimization and data. These requirements can make repeated behavioral adjustments costly. To address this, we introduce NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework that enables flexible, quantitative adjustment of LLM preferences at inference time. NeuroSteer employs a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) as its controller. Comparing neuron activation frequencies between positive and negative examples isolates "feature neurons" that correspond to target preferences such as politeness and positive sentiment. During inference, the activations of selected SAE features are amplified in the latent representations to steer the output distribution. Users can adjust the strength of this steering on a per-scenario or per-user basis, granting the LLM fine-grained, quantifiable trait modulation. Our experiments show that NeuroSteer can alter sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness at inference time. It achieves higher target-direction steering scores than the compared baselines in several settings, with task- and strength-dependent trade-offs in generation quality.
authors: Keqi Chen, Zekai Sun, Yuhua Wen, Tianyi Tian, Xinyang Huang, Huijun Lian, Yingming Gao, Ya Li
bullets: Targets preferences such as sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness through feature-level activation amplification.
Identifies preference-related “feature neurons” by comparing activations on positive and negative examples.

Experiments demonstrate effective target-direction steering, with generation-quality trade-offs depending on the task and steering strength.

papers.abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. We propose CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs and ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk over heterogeneous evaluation conditions. Across three combinatorial optimization domains, CVaR-based selection improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while maintaining competitive mean performance. These gains persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks
authors: Ruodai Cui, Li Niu
bullets: Targets weaknesses of mean-based selection, which can hide rare failures across instances, seeds, and scales.
Uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs in an evolutionary search framework.
Ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) over heterogeneous evaluation conditions.
Across three combinatorial optimization domains, it improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while preserving competitive mean performance.
Benefits persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model's reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher's probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.
authors: Chu Zhao, Lei Tang, Yanming Wang, Jianzhe Zhao, Guibing Guo, Zhengzong Chen, Yuanyuan Zhao, Fei Huang
bullets: Standard on-policy distillation gives uniform supervision across long trajectories, missing critical decisions.
Counterfactual outcome reversals show that action credit can change substantially even when the trajectory is unchanged.
ToolOPD summarizes each trajectory and outcome into a hindsight skill, then uses its effect on teacher probabilities to derive outcome-aware token credit.
The method reweights action-level distillation and jointly trains with reinforcement learning.
Experiments across multiple long-horizon tool-interaction benchmarks show significant gains over reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines.

papers.abstract: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.
authors: Tung M. Luu, Tri Ton, Duc M. Nguyen, Xuan Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Gia Binh, Quang Tan Nguyen, Vu Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of expert demonstrations and the cost of human preference labeling.
Uses ordered coverage alignment against a small set of expert demonstrations to estimate sequential progress.
Extracts pseudo-preference labels and applies them to fine-tune pretrained generative policies.
Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning baselines on challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks.
Works with both diffusion and flow-matching policies, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation.

The resulting dataset Dpref provides structured, dense pseudopreferences to stably fine-tune generative policies πθ(a|s) without manual reward engineering.

papers.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
authors: Yihui Yang, Yuanhong Yu, Jiawei Wang, Zhongrui Yu, Jia Shi, Kun Zhan, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Yu Liu, Sida Peng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of real-robot data and the sim-to-real gap in local navigation.
Pretrains on instruction-conditioned Internet videos to learn goal-directed visual dynamics.
Aligns learned dynamics with executable action chunks using action-labeled simulation data, then jointly fine-tunes the navigation system.
Reports 86.5% success on a single-view Short-Horizon OVON adaptation and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Real-quadruped deployment results support generalization to physical-world navigation.

papers.abstract: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.
authors: Sungjun Yun, Yonghee Choi, Dong-Jun Han
bullets: Addresses miscalibration in continual learning, where confidence and accuracy change asymmetrically across tasks.
Uses a lightweight grouping network to assign multiple temperature parameters based on confidence statistics and task-aware signals.
Adds Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization to encourage consistency within groups.
Experiments show improved calibration performance while maintaining accuracy.
Scope: a post-hoc calibration framework for evolving class-incremental settings.

papers.abstract: Continuous vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is typically evaluated by goal-reaching success, assuming it reflects an agent's ability to execute language-grounded behavior. We show that this assumption can fail: permissive contact models in current simulators may mask physically infeasible actions, creating a physical executability gap between semantic competence and embodied realization. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual-Semantic Traversability Alignment (VeSTA), a framework that aligns VLN policies with physically executable futures. We define visual-semantic traversability as the ability to predict instruction-conditioned trajectories that are semantically valid, geometrically feasible, and physically robust. VeSTA addresses this misalignment through two complementary mechanisms: improving executable support in trajectory generation and risk-aware selection among multimodal futures. Specifically, Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization uses strict-contact feedback to reshape the candidate distribution toward executable regions, while the Traversability Risk Critic learns a risk-adjusted scalar utility for candidate-wise future selection. Experiments on R2R and RxR reveal substantial dependence of existing VLN agents on simulator contact semantics. Under strict-contact evaluation, VeSTA substantially reduces collision-induced failures while preserving or improving goal-reaching performance, and controlled real-world robot experiments provide evidence that the learned preference transfers beyond simulation.
authors: Gang He, Zhile Cheng, Kepeng Xu, Zhenyang Liu, Yu-Wing Tai
bullets: Current VLN success metrics can hide physically infeasible actions because simulators may use permissive contact models.
VeSTA aligns instruction-conditioned trajectories with semantic validity, geometric feasibility, and physical robustness.
Trajectory Relative Group Policy Optimization steers candidate generation toward executable regions using strict-contact feedback.
A Traversability Risk Critic selects among multimodal futures using risk-aware utility.
Experiments on R2R, RxR, and real-robot trials show fewer collision failures under strict-contact evaluation while maintaining or improving navigation performance.

papers.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly erode the safety alignment of large language models, creating substantial risks when aligned models are adapted to downstream tasks. Existing alignment-stage defenses use harmful examples and simulated harmful perturbations during safety alignment to prepare models for later harmful fine-tuning, yet the collective effects of harmful weight perturbations remain underexplored. We identify a collective failure pattern: disjoint parts of a harmful perturbation have limited effects in isolation, but their joint application increases the model's harmfulness beyond the sum of their individual effects. Guided by this observation, we propose Joint Weight Perturbations (JWP), an alignment-stage defense that masks different parts of a harmful perturbation estimated from the current model and trains the model to respond safely in the resulting states. This exposes the model to different combinations of harmful perturbations and reduces its sensitivity to their accumulation during subsequent harmful fine-tuning. Experiments across downstream tasks and model families show that JWP offers stronger resistance to harmful fine-tuning than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuezhi Zhou, Zhu Zhang, Zhixing Tan
bullets: Harmful fine-tuning can erode the safety alignment of large language models.
Disjoint harmful weight perturbations may have limited individual effects but produce greater-than-additive harm when combined.
JWP masks different parts of an estimated harmful perturbation and trains the model to remain safe across the resulting states.
Across downstream tasks and model families, JWP resists harmful fine-tuning more strongly than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot diffusion image compression based on reverse channel coding achieves high perceptual quality at low bitrates without retraining, yet its bitstream remains vulnerable to bit flips. Prior work has shown that a joint combinatorial representation can amplify a single bit flip into substitutions of multiple atoms and that indexing each atom independently confines this error propagation. However, independent indexing reduces the number of atoms that fit within the bit budget and gives the decoder no indication of which atoms are corrupted. To address these issues, we propose BitFlat, a training-free error-localizing bitstream framework with two components. Blockwise Locality Alignment (BLA) decomposes the globally coupled atom selection at each diffusion step into independent selection units, each describing one signed atom from a dedicated codebook with a fixed-width field, so that any bit error affects only the unit in which it occurs. Reliability-Aware Diffusion Control (RADC) uses the bits saved by BLA to impose structured valid-codeword constraints within each field and converts the decoding state of each field into a binary reliability gate, which turns detected corrupted atoms into erasures at known positions and excludes them from noise synthesis. BitFlat requires neither target residuals nor additional network forward passes and leaves the diffusion model unchanged. Experiments on Kodak, DIV2K, and CLIC2020 show that BitFlat outperforms conventional, learned, and diffusion-based codecs at bit error rates from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ and, even with $26.7\%$ fewer bits, surpasses Robust Turbo-DDCM.

bullets: Addresses bit-flip vulnerability in reverse-channel-coding diffusion compression at low bitrates.
Blockwise Locality Alignment isolates each signed atom in an independent fixed-width codeword field.
Reliability-Aware Diffusion Control detects invalid fields, gates corrupted atoms, and excludes them from noise synthesis.
Training-free: requires no target residuals, extra network forward passes, or diffusion-model changes.
Outperforms conventional, learned, and diffusion codecs across tested bit-error rates, and surpasses Robust Turbo-DDCM with 26.7% fewer bits.

papers.abstract: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. However, pruning directly to the target size can substantially degrade reasoning capabilities, making subsequent recovery more difficult under a limited training budget. Moreover, this paradigm separates layer selection from recovery, limiting the use of recovery information to guide selection and potentially hindering the recovery of reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LOOP, a Layer-level Recovery-Oriented On-Policy Pruning framework that interleaves pruning and recovery across multiple shots. In each shot, LOOP removes a single layer and performs short on-policy distillation, mitigating the abrupt degradation in reasoning capabilities associated with one-shot pruning. To guide layer selection in subsequent shots, LOOP reuses on-policy trajectories and optimization signals from recovery to jointly assess each remaining layer's reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity, thereby making layer selection recovery-aware. Evaluations on several benchmarks show that LOOP consistently outperforms one-shot baselines in average accuracy across different model scales and pruning ratios.
authors: Liang Xu, Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Yufei Zhang, Wei Lin, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: One-shot pruning can sharply damage reasoning, making capability recovery difficult under limited training budgets.
LOOP removes one layer at a time across multiple shots, applying short on-policy distillation after each removal.
Recovery trajectories and optimization signals help estimate each remaining layer’s reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity.
Across several benchmarks, LOOP consistently achieves higher average accuracy than one-shot baselines across model scales and pruning ratios.

papers.abstract: Accurate evaluation of LLM personalization is hindered by current evaluation paradigms that over- or under-constrain the response space, yielding frequent false rejections and false acceptances. To reduce these false rates, we introduce ConQual-Audit, an audit-based framework that evaluates LLM personalization through a three-stage process: (1) extracting semantic constraints from user profiles and task-grounded reference; (2) qualifying constraints by pruning unnecessary constraints and recovering missing constraints; and (3) verifying candidate responses against the audited constraints via natural language inference. Across PrefEval and LaMP, ConQual-Audit outperforms nine baselines, attaining top AUCs (0.88 and 0.90) and the lowest false rate (0.21) on the leanest constraint sets at an amortizable audit cost. Crucially, this constraint audit is portable: integrating it into ExPerT and PREF helps revise smaller, higher-quality constraint sets to reduce their evaluation false rates.
authors: Xuran Li, Guanqin Zhang, Imran Razzak, Hakim Hacid, Eleanna Kafeza, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Current evaluation methods can over- or under-constrain acceptable responses.
The framework extracts, prunes, and recovers semantic constraints from profiles and task references.
It verifies candidate responses against audited constraints using natural language inference.
On PrefEval and LaMP, it reports top AUCs of 0.88 and 0.90 and the lowest false rate of 0.21 among nine baselines.
The audit also transfers to ExPerT and PREF, producing smaller, higher-quality constraint sets and fewer evaluation errors.

papers.tldr: ConQual-Audit improves LLM personalization evaluation by auditing constraints to reduce both false acceptances and false rejections.

papers.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.
authors: Desheng Xu, Hanglin Li, Tianchen Song, Zhiyong Zhao, Kun Zhan
bullets: Addresses activation outliers and heterogeneous channel sensitivity in post-training quantization.
Uses a noise-weighted metric to identify sensitive channels.
Applies learnable rotations to sensitive channels and lightweight fixed rotations elsewhere.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across several LLM families under W4A4KV4.
For LLaMA-3-8B, calibration takes 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory; fused kernels provide up to 2.3× prefill speedup and 3.5× memory savings over FP16.

papers.abstract: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fr\'echet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fr\'echet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
authors: Yian Zhao, Yu Yan, Hongcan Guo, Ruochong Zheng, Jian Zhang, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and drift in long-horizon autoregressive video rollouts.
Fine-tunes the deployed multi-step sampler using generative anchoring, context-fidelity Fréchet distance, and reality-matching Fréchet distance.
Uses statistics from short real clips, avoiding external teachers, online critics, and recorded long futures.
Applied to MiniWorld-1B, the method produced stable rollouts beyond 4,000 frames while continuing to follow actions in manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Fréchet Forcing to train long-horizon streaming world models from short clips by enforcing realism and context fidelity without requiring a teacher model or long videos.
papers.title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
papers.tldr: Fréchet Forcing trains action-conditioned streaming world models to remain realistic, scene-consistent, and action-following far beyond their short-clip training horizon without requiring a teacher or long videos.

papers.abstract: Robotic simulation, navigation, and inspection need photorealistic and geometrically accurate maps. Radiance fields achieve photorealism, but building them from robot data raises three challenges. A robot's trajectory serves its task, not reconstruction, so images from few viewpoints leave the geometry under-constrained. Residual errors in camera poses and intrinsics blur the map. The map's GPU memory grows with scene size, which limits its level of detail in large scenes. We present \textbf{SpaRV}, a \textbf{Spa}rse \textbf{R}adiance \textbf{V}oxel map rendered by differentiable ray marching, which lets irregular LiDAR scans supervise it alongside images. LiDAR depth and occupancy anchor the under-constrained geometry, and normal and smoothness regularizers keep it smooth between LiDAR points. To correct camera errors, SpaRV alternates map training with photometric optimization of the camera poses and focal lengths. To bound GPU memory in training and rendering, SpaRV holds one submap at a time at full resolution and the rest at coarser octree levels. Experiments show that SpaRV keeps the geometry consistent away from the captured trajectory and sharpens textures by optimizing the camera parameters. On one 24\,GB GPU, SpaRV reconstructs a university campus captured in 63{,}582 images and simulates other cameras and LiDARs. Our code will be released at \url{https://github.com/hku-mars/SpaRV}.
authors: Jianheng Liu, Yunfei Wan, Fangming Cheng, Xiangyu Hong, Zuhao Zou, Haotian Li, Longji Yin, Chunran Zheng, Jiarong Lin, Fu Zhang
bullets: Addresses under-constrained geometry from task-driven trajectories, camera calibration errors, and GPU-memory limits in large scenes.
Uses differentiable ray marching with irregular LiDAR depth and occupancy supervision, plus normal and smoothness regularization.
Alternates map training with photometric optimization of camera poses and focal lengths to reduce blur and sharpen textures.
Maintains one full-resolution submap while storing others at coarser octree levels, bounding memory during training and rendering.
Reconstructs a university campus from 63,582 images on one 24 GB GPU and supports novel-camera and novel-LiDAR simulation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose \textbf{PoSTCache} (\emph{Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache}), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.
authors: Liwei Lan, Hui Chen, Jungong Han, Guiguang Ding
bullets: Existing caching methods commit forward-only approximations that cannot incorporate later feedback.
PoSTCache uses an existing cache for forward proposals, then propagates discrepancy-based corrections backward from later full-computation steps.
Its PVR strategy selects full-computation anchors by estimated reduction in trajectory uncertainty using offline denoising trajectories.
Experiments on image and video generation models show consistent improvements over representative caching methods.
The framework is training-free and plug-and-play, with results scoped to the evaluated models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/
authors: Yang Zheng, Zizhang Li, Boyang Deng, Jan Ackermann, Lei Shu, Yinghao Xu, Jiajun Wu, Gordon Wetzstein, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Targets fluid videos whose generated motion often lacks coherent vortices and physically plausible dynamics.
Combines high-fidelity simulated fluids with in-the-wild videos to provide both physical supervision and visual diversity.
Uses a dual-stream model that predicts RGB frames and per-frame velocity fields.
Further applies velocity-aware direct preference optimization using the predicted physical signal as a reward.
The authors report more realistic fluid dynamics than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student's pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain.
authors: Yuanze Xu, Tianzhu Ye, Hui Sun, Wenhui Wang, Li Dong, Furu Wei
bullets: Compares SFT, RLVR, and on-policy distillation across five pretrained models and varied teacher sources.
Evaluates mathematical learning, retention of general capabilities, and changes in predictive distributions.
RLVR-trained teachers improve target-task performance while better preserving prior capabilities; SFT-trained teachers cause more forgetting.
Out-of-domain distribution changes are more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain changes.
Post-training gives teachers task-specific preferences that concentrate student updates more strongly in-domain.

papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.
authors: Arber Zela, Artavazd Maranjyan, Pol Puigdemont, David Berghaus, Valentyn Boreiko, Volkan Cevher
bullets: Recasts Fixed-Point Reasoners in normalized-transformer geometry, replacing Euclidean residual updates with geodesic operations.
Hyperspherical updates provide boundedness by construction and remove coupled rescaling in input injection, damping, and halting.
Establishes fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection.
Reports 96.6% on Sudoku-Extreme, 87.9% on Maze-Hard, and 59.1% on Mini-ARC, outperforming FPRM and other baselines.
Converged token-input angles are interpretable, encoding puzzle structure and predicting correctness.

papers.abstract: Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of Decompose and Recompose text embedding (Dero), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, Dero realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, Dero can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.
authors: Sooyeon Park, Hemraj Singh, Kyunghyun Min, Youngjae Yu, Sung-Bae Cho
bullets: Negation is difficult for text-to-image diffusion models because implicit biases in text representations can override negative constraints.
Dero uses auxiliary prompts to construct semantic-preserving and bias subspaces, then disentangles them with bidirectional SVD.
It selectively recomposes semantic components while restoring stylistic features to maintain image quality and fidelity.
The inference-time method operates only on text representations and supports both U-Net- and DiT-based diffusion models.
Experiments on object- and concept-level negation show improved text-image alignment, semantic fidelity, and human preference.

papers.abstract: Few-shot segmentation (FSS) aims to segment target objects with limited annotated examples. Recent studies have begun to explore large foundation models to improve generalization for this task. In particular, SAM 3 provides strong visual representations and supports text-guided segmentation. However, its performance remains limited in specialized domains, where semantic prompts and visual representations are often poorly aligned. To address this challenge, we propose ViTA-SAM, a framework built upon SAM 3 that integrates visual memory and textual features through cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we construct a visual memory module that encodes support features together with their corresponding masks, providing support-aware visual guidance for query prediction. In parallel, we leverage the text encoder of SAM 3 to extract semantic features as complementary priors. To bridge the gap between semantic and visual representations, we introduce a cross-modal alignment module that conditions textual features on memory-enhanced visual representations, yielding more consistent and visually grounded predictions. In addition, we propose a pseudo-label refinement strategy that updates the memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ViTA-SAM achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods, outperforming the strongest competing method by over 5% in average mIoU.
authors: Tianqi Wei, Zhi Chen, Xin Yu, Scott Chapman, Zi Huang
bullets: Addresses poor alignment between semantic prompts and visual representations in specialized domains.

Uses SAM 3 text features as complementary semantic priors and aligns them with memory-enhanced visual features.
Refines pseudo-labels to update memory with predicted query masks, enabling query-adaptive learning.
Outperforms the strongest competing method by over 5% average mIoU across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.
authors: Jinbae Seo, Hyeongjun Kwon, Jiyoung Lee, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jungin Park, Kwanghoon Sohn
bullets: Addresses the problem that lengthy reasoning can dilute relevant visual evidence with broad scene descriptions and peripheral details.
Uses three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation from the compressed context.
Trains the framework with multi-stage GRPO and progressive rewards for structured outputs, information reduction, relevance preservation, and localization accuracy.
Evaluated on six multimodal grounding benchmarks, where it achieves substantial zero-shot performance gains.
Scope: focuses on retaining useful extended reasoning while distilling it for precise grounding.

papers.abstract: Long-term LiDAR place recognition in forests is difficult because repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain create severe structural aliasing. We diagnose Scan Context (SC) by separating candidate retrieval from fine matching: on the standardized TreeLoc++ Wild-Places protocol, a TNVD support key places a valid location in the top-25 set for approximately 99% of queries, while conventional SC matching on those candidates reaches only 61.84% mean R@1. With an identical raw-SC candidate set, terrain normalization improves max-height cells by only 1.21 points but vertical-distribution cells by 19.72 points. These observations motivate Terrain-Normalized Vertical Distribution Scan Context (TNVD-SC), which preserves the SC ring-sector topology while encoding terrain-relative vertical probability distributions. Under the standardized TreeLoc++ protocol, TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 and attains the highest R@1 mean and R@1 stability among the compared methods, while TreeLoc++ remains stronger in mean MR, MF1, and AUC. The unchanged method reaches 85.14% mean R@1 on the four-session CVTNet-style NCLT evaluation. A lossless count-coded implementation with exact hierarchical Jensen-Shannon search reduces descriptor payload by 3.86x and compute latency by 23.8% without changing the audited retrieval outputs.
authors: Jineon Kim, Jhonghyun An
bullets: Forest place recognition is hindered by repetitive vegetation and uneven terrain, causing structural aliasing.
Candidate retrieval is largely reliable, but conventional Scan Context fine matching achieves only 61.84% mean R@1 on retrieved candidates.

TNVD-SC reaches 91.83% mean R@1 on TreeLoc++ and 85.14% on the four-session NCLT evaluation.
A lossless count-coded implementation reduces descriptor payload by 3.86× and latency by 23.8% without changing retrieval outputs.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Joonghyuk Shin, Jonathan Tremblay, Chan Hee Song, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses exposure bias and compounding errors that cause streaming video quality to collapse over time.
Learns a counterfactual velocity gap shown to be largely deterministic across noise seeds.
Trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector using closed-loop, DAgger-style rollout aggregation and drift-contraction training.
Requires no real videos when using the frozen base model’s own single-shot generations, and adds no inference cost after merging.
In 50-second generation, reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to −0.16 with 40 real clips, outperforming prior reported results with far less data.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-domain person re-identification remains challenging because domain shifts generate noisy pseudo labels that are reinforced during iterative adaptation. Existing clustering-based methods often rely on limited reliability cues or global confidence criteria and may impose hard identity supervision on ambiguous target samples. To address these limitations, we propose CGPLR, a confidence-guided pseudo-label refinement framework for unsupervised domain-adaptive person re-identification. CGPLR estimates sample-level reliability by jointly modeling centroid compatibility, local neighborhood consistency, separation from the strongest competing cluster and temporal assignment stability. The resulting confidence distribution is used to derive cluster-adaptive upper and lower thresholds for a three-way selective decision. Reliable assignments are preserved, recoverable samples are reassigned only when an alternative cluster receives sufficient geometric and neighborhood support and highly ambiguous samples are deferred from hard identity supervision. The learning objective adapts to these decisions through confidence-weighted supervision for preserved samples, cautious corrected-label weighting for reassigned samples and label-free representation consistency for deferred samples. CGPLR achieves 76.4% Rank-1 accuracy and 47.6% mean average precision (mAP) on Market-1501 to MSMT17, and 95.1% Rank-1 accuracy and 87.7% mAP on MSMT17 to Market-1501, demonstrating effective reliability-aware selective adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/Sundas058/CGPLR.
authors: Sundas Iqbal, Danish Ali, Qing Tian, Yuhui Zheng, Jianping Gou, Weihua Ou
bullets: Addresses noisy pseudo-label reinforcement caused by domain shifts during iterative adaptation.

Uses cluster-adaptive thresholds for three-way decisions: preserve reliable labels, cautiously reassign recoverable samples, or defer ambiguous samples.
Applies confidence-weighted supervision to preserved and reassigned samples, plus label-free consistency learning for deferred samples.
Reports 76.4%/47.6% Rank-1/mAP from Market-1501 to MSMT17 and 95.1%/87.7% in the reverse direction.

papers.abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $\pi_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang, Maggie Wang, Fangneng Zhan, Manling Li, Qianqian Wang, Mac Schwager, Zhuang Liu, Li Fei-Fei, Mengyu Wang, Paul Pu Liang

papers.abstract: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy models can be trained without 3D labels by rendering their predictions into the images and supervising them with 2D pseudo labels. In sparse Gaussian representations trained this way, Gaussian positions are learned only through pixel-wise rendering losses, which we hypothesize give small foreground objects little weight. In trained GaussianFlowOcc models, the Gaussian density on foreground voxels is on average only 1.62 times that on background voxels. We propose a training-only foreground attraction loss that back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels with pseudo depth and pulls nearby Gaussians toward these 3D points, favoring Gaussians that already predict the target class; the inference network is unchanged. On Occ3D-nuScenes, the loss raises this concentration to 2.40 over three seeds. Over three seeds, the mean foreground IoU increases from 6.29 to 6.96 and is higher for each seed, whereas the change in mean mIoU (13.53 to 13.82) is within the seed-to-seed variation of the baseline. Single-run ablations further indicate that pseudo-label targets outperform targets placed at ground-truth voxels and that acting on the Gaussian positions alone is not sufficient, and a single-seed test shows that the model degrades less when fewer Gaussians are kept at inference.
authors: Jeagon Song, Jhonghyun An

Mean mIoU increases only from 13.53 to 13.82, within baseline seed-to-seed variation.
Ablations favor pseudo-label targets over ground-truth voxel targets; the method also shows less degradation when fewer Gaussians are retained at inference.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are envisioned to perform diverse human-level tasks through their anthropomorphic morphology. Their dual-arm configuration enables a broad range of everyday actions. Yet, as in humans, this morphology can constrain loco-manipulation when both arms are occupied or additional contacts are required beyond their reach. Supernumerary robotic limbs (SRLs) offer a way to extend these capabilities, but their integration requires the added limb to be coordinated with whole-body motion and balance. In this study, we develop and integrate a supernumerary arm into a humanoid platform to investigate how morphological augmentation reshapes its feasible action space. Through quantitative analysis and hardware experiments across two configurations, we show how the additional limb expands whole-body interaction capabilities by enabling manipulation and support to be coordinated beyond the constraints of the native dual-arm configuration. To control this augmented morphology, we leverage model-based trajectory optimization (TO) to generate dynamically feasible motions for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) controllers. The controllers are trained in simulation and transferred to hardware in a zero-shot manner, enabling coordinated whole-body skills for contact-rich tri-arm loco-manipulation. We further show vision-guided autonomous execution on selected tasks using diffusion policies trained from hardware demonstrations. Our findings suggest that humanoid morphology need not be restricted to human-like forms, but can be reimagined as an extensible design space for robotic augmentation.
authors: Fukang Liu, Feiyang Wu, Paul Barsa, Jaehwi Jang, Akshat Jain, Zhigen Zhao, Yipu Chen, Zhaoyuan Gu, Nikhil Vemuri, Anshul Chandaliya, Kaijie Zhu, Sean Lublinsky, Matthew Zhu, Tony G. Chen, Ye Zhao

papers.abstract: Vision-based object pose estimation is vital for conducting spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO). Recent research has demonstrated the robustness of event cameras against the harsh lighting conditions that often occur in orbit, thanks to the extremely high dynamic range of event sensors. However, event-based spacecraft pose estimation (EBSPE) suffers when the relative motion between the chaser and target is slow, since the event rate drops significantly, leading to data with low signal-to-noise ratio. Unfortunately, for safety reasons, real RPO trajectories often involve slow relative motions (e.g., down to 1 mm/s), and operating under low illumination exacerbates the problem. Addressing slow relative motions is thus crucial to raise the practicality of EBSPE. To this end, we propose using recurrent vision transformers (RVT) for EBSPE. The key idea is to exploit recurrent memory to capture longer-term information across sparse event streams, and to learn the temporal attention span from full trajectories rather than fixing the time window. We developed an RVT-based heatmap regressor to produce 2D-3D correspondences for pose estimation, which was validated on real event data collected under slow relative motions representative of RPO trajectories. Results indicate the superior pose estimation accuracy and stability of our RVT-based method, relative to previous per-event-frame-based or fixed-time-window EBSPE methods.
authors: Sofia McLeod, Mohsi Jawaid, Carl Seubert, Tat-Jun Chin
bullets: Slow relative motion sharply reduces event rates and degrades event-based pose estimation, especially under low illumination.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
authors: William L. Tong, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan, Eran Malach
bullets: Addresses performance degradation of vanilla SSMs and standard state souping on crowded, long contexts.
Learns query-dependent weights to compose independently encoded and cached context chunks.
Improves performance across document QA, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use.
A sparse variant offers near-constant encoding cost as context length grows while maintaining or sometimes improving performance.
Includes theoretical arguments describing why state souping works and when it may fail.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Computational cost of souping. We measure the time it takes to encode a set of input chunks on an AWS H100 node. For the souping models, we include the time it takes to encode a 128 token query and compute the softmax weights. The state encodings are retrieved from either GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM), system RAM, or system disk. We plot a subset of timings here, with the full results in Figure 7. We include two sparse souping variants, one that keeps the top Ntop = 4 documents and another that keeps the top Ntop = 32. (a) We hold the chunk length fixed at L = 512 tokens and increase the total number of chunks. Encoding time therefore grows linearly with increasing chunks for all models. For the HBM model, at low K encoding the query dominates the encoding time, resulting in a flat trend. (b) We hold the number of chunks fixed at K = 8 and increase the length of each chunk. Since the number of chunks is constant, souping retrieves the same number of chunks for each query, resulting in a flat trend across all L where the height is controlled by retrieval speed.

Figure 7 Additional measurements on encoding time across models. We plot additional sets of timings beyond those showin in Figure 3. In particular, we show full timings measured for full and sparse souping models retrieving from HBM (a, b), system RAM (c, d), and system disk (e, f). The timings for Transformer and sequential Mamba models in the main text are computed with batch size of 1. To give a sense for what the compute-bound timings look like, we plot the per-example timing for batch size 32 for Transformer and sequential Mamba models (dashed lines).

Figure 2 Weighted state souping benchmark results. Vertical gray dashed lines indicate the max pool size or context length observed during training. (a - c) Single-hop (SQuAD) and multi-hop (HotpotQA, MuSiQue) benchmarks. We plot accuracy as an exact match between the gold answer span and the model prediction. Dotted lines represent closed book accuracy, where no documents are prompted in-context. Sparse souping keeps top Ntop = 4 chunks. (d,e) NIAH subsets of RULER. In the easy version, a single needle consisting of a random number is hidden among a natural language haystack of variable size. In the hard version, the haystack consists entirely of needle-like distractors, requiring precise retrieval. Sparse souping keeps top Ntop = 20 chunks. (e) Variable tracking subset of RULER. The input consists of random variable assignments embedded in random noise sentences, and the model must infer the correct value of a randomly chosen variable. Sparse souping keeps top Ntop = 20 chunks. (f) Simple Python subset of BFCL. The model is prompted with a list of Python functions and descriptions, and must execute a correct function call given a user query. Sparse souping keeps top Ntop = 4 chunks. (g) Parallel subset of BFCL. The setup is the same as in (f), but the model needs to execute the function multiple times.

Figure 1 Sequential encoding versus state souping. (a) A typical SSM operates by concatenating input chunks together with the user query, and performs a single, long autoregressive pass to produce the answer. (b) A state souping SSM encodes each input chunk independently, then soups the resulting state encodings into a single encoding used to initialize the model as it processes the user query. (c) In our weighted state souping method, we augment the SSM with an additional linear readout that produces key vectors from the input chunks and a query vector from the user query. The soup is constructed as a weighted sum with weighting function σ.

Figure 4 Squad-n benchmark results. As a further test of souping when the task requires attending to multiple documents, we construct a task based on SQuAD called SQuAD-n. Each example consists of n individual SQuAD document-question-answer sets. The model is prompted with all n documents (mixed among max(k−n, 0) distractors) followed by the questions, and must produce the answer spans corresponding to each question. We plot both perquestion exact match accuracy in (a, c) as well as joint accuracy in (b, d) for n = 3 and n = 5. Souping generally performs competitively with vanilla Mamba, and sparse souping in particular maintains long context generalization better than full souping. However, both Mamba and souping underperform Transformers on in-context K in this setting. This may be in part due to the Transformer’s sharper ability to track its context, and determine which questions have already been answered and which require an answer still.

Figure 5 Ruler benchmark, additional results. In the main text, we present results on needle-in-a-haystack (a,b) and variable tracking (c). We additionally plot a sweep over the number of chunks Ntop kept by the sparse souping model in (d - f). For the NIAH tasks, where only a single chunk is relevant, the value of Ntop is irrelevant. However, for the variable tracking task, relevant variable assignments are distributed across many more chunks, so below a certain threshold, the model fails to learn the task well.

Figure 6 BFCL benchmark, additional results. In the main text, we present results on the Python Simple split of BFCL (a), in which the model must produce a single tool call given a list of tool definitions and a user query. Here, we also plot performance on the Parallel split (the model must call a single tool multiple times) and the Parallel Multiple split (the model must call multiple tools multiple times). We measure accuracy by BFCL’s built-in abstract syntax tree (AST)-based checker (a - c) as well as a match based on function name alone (d - f). In general, weighted souping performs well for both Python Simple and Parallel, but a substantial gap opens on small, in-distribution K for Parallel Multiple. Mean souping performs better than weighted souping at K = 1 (where only gold tool definitions are prompted), indicating that souping may still work well, but the model is struggling to simultaneously learn appropriate weights and use a souped state initialization.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes weighted state souping for efficient long-context retrieval, directly relevant to long-context language models and efficiency.
papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.tldr: Weighted state souping improves long-context retrieval in state-space models by selectively combining cached document or memory states based on the query.

papers.abstract: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Jimson Huang, Maxwell Nickell, Ruowang Zhang, Abulhair Saparov
bullets: Implicit reasoning lets LLMs search ahead within one forward pass, helping them choose correct proof paths and produce shorter CoT traces.
Fine-tuning on progressively larger vocabularies and longer lookaheads succeeds where matched-compute training without a curriculum fails.
Curriculum-trained Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy at lookahead 256, versus 45% without curriculum.
Progress follows a saturating exponential: larger models have higher apparent ceilings, pretrained models improve faster, and overly large curriculum steps hinder learning.
Capabilities learned on synthetic tasks transfer to natural-language reasoning benchmarks, where curriculum training performs better at matched compute.

papers.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.
authors: Jesson Wang, Zhanhao Hu, Minghao Lin, Yuchen Wu, Aylin Caliskan, Mengyuan Li
bullets: Safety degradation depends on the behavioral transition induced by supervision, not only on whether training data is harmful.
The key conditions are a large refusal–answer discrepancy and the absence of an easy surface-level shortcut.
With matched discrepancies, localized versus non-localized transitions can change harmful compliance by an order of magnitude.
The authors introduce SAFEOFF, benign refusal-triggering instructions paired with harmless answers.
Across three aligned LLMs and three safety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment without explicit harmful supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of three fine-tuning settings on an aligned LLM. Harmful fine-tuning pairs harmful instructions with harmful responses; the resulting model complies with harmful queries. Benign fine-tuning on ordinary safe instruction data preserves the model’s refusal behavior. SAFEOFF fine-tuning keeps the data benign at the content level, rewriting only the instructions, yet the fine-tuned model also complies with harmful queries.

Figure 4: Refusal loss and downstream harmfulness across four matched SAFEOFF datasets (L1–L4). Source examples, benign target answers, dataset size, and training budget are fixed. Lower initial refusal loss is associated with higher ADVBENCH HARMSCORE after 250 optimizer steps. Results use one fine-tuning seed.

Figure 6: Response-level HARMSCORE distribution on ADVBENCH before fine-tuning and at step 1000 after fine-tuning on representative datasets (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). The aligned model concentrates almost entirely at score 1, while SAFEOFF shifts a large fraction of responses into higher harmfulness bins. The distributional shift shows that the increase in mean HARMSCORE reflects more than a small number of outliers.

Figure 3: Keyword-position experiment through step 300 (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Keywordinjection variants create benign fine-tuning examples that trigger default refusal before fine-tuning but are paired with harmless target answers; Shuffle denotes random-position insertion. Suffix-position keywords induce early harmful compliance followed by substantial recovery, and prefix-position keywords transfer little, consistent with shortcut learning. Random placement also partially recovers but remains at a higher level through step 300.

Figure 5: Checkpoint dynamics for behavioral-transition-inspired data constructions and benign controls on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Under the evaluated setup, SAFEOFF produces larger and more persistent increases in ASR and HARMSCORE than OVER-CAUTIOUS, SUBLIMINAL, and SIMPLE REWRITE.

Figure 7: SAFEOFF ratio ablation with 1000 total training examples (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). The ratio denotes the fraction of the fine-tuning corpus drawn from SAFEOFF; the remaining examples are drawn from BASE. Larger ratios produce stronger and more persistent safety degradation, with the ratio-1.0 condition showing the highest sustained ASR and HARMSCORE.
