Dataset harmfulness is a binary summary derived from the training-data audit in Table 2: ✓ denotes explicit harmful supervision, while × denotes no explicit harmful-supervision dataset.

Table 1: Keyword position × keyword count on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. At a given count every position injects the same keywords, so placement is the only difference within a column. D is the aligned model’s refusal rate on that condition’s own fine-tuning inputs (300 rows) before any fine-tuning; T is ADVBENCH ASR (520 prompts) after 300 optimizer steps. Discrepancy barely orders transfer across the nine cells (Spearman ρ(D,T ) = +0.10). With the keywords at a fixed position, D ranges over 0.64–1.00 while T stays within 0.05–0.17; with them scattered, T rises sixfold as D rises from 0.33 to 0.91. Original and SAFEOFF denote paired input prompts to the same aligned model, not pre-/post-fine-tuning models. The fixed target is “I can’t fulfill that request.” (7 tokens, excluding EOS). Values are sample means in natural-log units, computed with teacher forcing; Delta is SAFEOFF minus Original. Increased reports the percentage of paired increases exceeding 10−6. The first token “I” is not refusal-specific.

Table 2: Training-data audit across fine-tuning conditions. The Llama Guard harm rate is the fraction of examples whose instruction or response is flagged as harmful. This content audit is separate from the downstream safety evaluation.

BASE denotes the matched-source benign control, which pairs the same source examples with their original instructions. The right panel selects the 5% of coordinates with the largest absolute update differences between SAFEOFF and BASE within each v_proj matrix, highlighting where SAFEOFF departs most from benign adaptation. All pairs use the same selected coordinates.

Table 9: Two-factor controls on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at optimizer step 300, varying only the supervised target. Distinct counts unique responses, and Refusal on held-out ALPACA-CLEANED is an over-refusal rate on benign instructions, where lower is better. Both refusal-target arms reach ASR 0.00, but neither does so as a selectively refusing model.
Table 10: Utility-data mixture ablations with 1000 SAFEOFF samples held fixed. We vary the number of added SAMSUM or GSM8K samples and report safety metrics on ADVBENCH for each run.
Table 11: Final-checkpoint safety metrics for the SAFEOFF ratio ablation in Figure 7. Values are reported at step 1000 on the Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct backbone.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how benign fine-tuning can misalign LLMs, contributing to understanding of LLM behavior and safety.
papers.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
papers.tldr: Benign fine-tuning can weaken LLM safety when it trains a sufficiently large, non-localized shift from refusal to compliance, even without harmful examples.

papers.abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.
authors: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors, large search spaces, and the difficulty of executing latent plans in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses vector-quantized latent states for discrete search and a learned visual-feedback controller to sequentially reach planned states and correct deviations.
Introduces a first-passage-time quasi-metric for quantization that better aligns the planning abstraction with controller capabilities.
Achieves 100% success on physical Tower of Hanoi using only short-play data and outperforms competing world models by 13.3–85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks.
Scope: evaluated on manipulation and locomotion benchmarks, with physical-robot validation on Tower of Hanoi.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of VQ-WM. The initial (green) and goal (red) images are encoded into latent states and vector-quantized according to controller reachability, so that each vector-quantized state serves as a target the controller is expected to reach. The planner performs discrete search over these vector-quantized states using a discrete latent predictor. A continuous controller then drives the robot toward each planned target in turn, using visual feedback to correct deviations along the way.
Fig. 5: State vector quantization with different codebook sizes.
Fig. 3: Real-world execution of VQ-WM on the four-disk Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
TABLE I: Long-horizon Manipulation success rates.
TABLE II: Success rate (%) on Walker with different observation inputs.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a vector-quantized world model for latent feedback motion planning in robot manipulation, directly relevant to world models and learned control.
papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: VQ-WM combines discrete latent long-horizon planning with continuous visual-feedback control to reliably solve manipulation tasks beyond the length of its demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
authors: Ankur Banerjee, Vishnu Guntakala, Danity Pike, Advay Roongta, Kevin Yang, Ruizhe Li
bullets: Across six models, text dominated mismatched text–audio inputs in most cases, especially when sarcasm was involved.
Speaker identity remained decodable at the language-model input, indicating that acoustic information was perceived but suppressed downstream.
Attention knockout partially restored audio-grounded outputs by disrupting an intermediate relay during open-ended generation.
Back-patching showed no measurable repair, but its null result was inconclusive because replication failed on its original task.
The effect was absent in multiple-choice evaluation, suggesting closed-set benchmarks can miss this failure mode and related interventions.

papers.abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.
authors: Bishoy Galoaa, Sarah Ostadabbas
bullets: Targets the common failure of videos to follow requested motion despite matching scene content.
Compresses dense trajectories into 64 discrete tokens and predicts them from language with a 28M-parameter transformer.
Uses zero-gated cross-attention adapters to condition frozen Wan 2.2 DiT blocks; a low-rank variant adds 1.45% forward-pass FLOPs.
Raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442, with similar measured generative quality; shuffled motion codes provide little benefit.
Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound motions improve less, and token-to-patch assignments are not explicitly preserved.

papers.abstract: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.
authors: Anshun Asher Zheng, Weili Cao, Fangcong Yin, David Beaver, Junyi Jessy Li
bullets: Tests 12 language models on curated Moorean sentences across varied contexts.
Models generally detect the sentences’ infelicity, even when the wording is not a memorized form.
Using the Rational Speech Act framework, the study finds models’ listeners do not reason about their own speakers.
Reasoning traces suggest models treat Moore’s paradox as factual knowledge about sentences rather than a speaker-level constraint.

papers.abstract: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.
authors: Nozomu Fujisawa
bullets: Targets small four-output interaction differences that can be obscured by rounding error.
Decomposes inputs into native, two single-intervention, and full-dimensional mixed-residual components at selected linear projections.
Reuses higher-precision single-intervention contributions across joint candidates and derives a local cancellation identity plus a conditional nonlinear error bound.
In reported Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct studies, it reduced interaction MSE by 94.4% on synthetic families and 99.35–99.85% in two four-image COCO studies versus a matched control.
Scope is limited to development inputs and tasks requiring extra interaction fidelity; higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic achieved lower aggregate error at similar query times.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that activation dynamics--how representations change during inference--might be more revealing about language model behavior than static readouts from individual layers. In this work, we investigate the layer-wise evolution of representations of factuality, using true and false statements when the model is prompted to either lie or to be honest. We report a geometric phenomenon in which the factuality directions extracted from the lying and honest conditions appear to rotate away from each other across layers. We find that such layer-wise rotation also occurs in a task that requires the model to take different visual perspectives in the 3D world, suggesting that the rotation phenomenon might be indicative of manipulating conceptual spaces in general, rather than unique to factuality. We then investigate the "real time" transformation of conceptual representations on a trial-to-trial basis. We show that it is possible to make strong predictions about the model's target task and behavior from trajectories alone. In addition, diverging points in single-trial trajectories correspond to the onset of rotation in aggregated-trial analysis. Finally, we show that both rotation and divergent trajectories occur in more naturalistic settings in which models are not overtly prompted to "lie" but rather report false statements in the course of completing a different task.
authors: Zhuonan Yang, Yik Siu Chan, Wannan Yang, Ellie Pavlick
bullets: Studies factuality representations when models are prompted to lie or tell the truth.
Finds that factuality directions in the two conditions rotate apart across layers.

papers.abstract: Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) requires both accurate question answering and precise temporal localization. Existing supervised methods rely on costly temporal annotations, while existing zero-shot approaches are primarily designed for Video Question Answering (VQA) and are not optimized for temporal grounding. We propose DiffGround, an action-driven zero-shot framework built upon frozen Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our framework first predicts an answer-relevant action cue that transforms the input question into an explicit semantic target for grounding. Action Cue converts a reasoningoriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Guided by the action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) efficiently selects informative keyframes for reasoning. Finally, we introduce Semantic Diff Refinement, a training-free temporal refinement method that exploits semantic differences between neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings to recover complete action segments from sparse predictions. Extensive experiments on NExT-GQA and STAR show that DiffGround consistently outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods, establishing a new state of the art for Video Question Grounding.
authors: Cheng-Han Lee, Amir Salimi, Hsiang-Wei Huang, Che-Chun Su, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo
bullets: Targets Video Question Grounding without costly temporal annotations.
Uses frozen multimodal models to predict answer-relevant action cues and select informative keyframes.
Applies training-free Semantic Diff Refinement to recover complete action segments from neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings.
Evaluated on NExT-GQA and STAR, where it outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods.
Scope: relies on frozen MLLMs/VLMs and is designed for action-centric temporal grounding.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. Given a video and a question, DiffGround first performs offline, question-agnostic action segment preprocessing to partition the video into semantically coherent action segments. A frozen MLLM then predicts an action cue describing the target action with a single MLLM call. Guided by the question and predicted action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) ranks video frames to select the most informative keyframes for Video Question Answering (VQA). Finally, Semantic Diff Refinement expands the initial grounding prediction by leveraging SigLIP2 semantic differences to align temporal boundaries with the complete action segment, producing more accurate Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) results.

Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. DiffGround consists of three stages. First, a frozen MLLM predicts an Action Cue from the input question and uniformly sampled video frames, converting a reasoning-oriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Second, a frozen VLM (SigLIP2) jointly matches the question and Action Cue to retrieve the Top-K most informative keyframes. Meanwhile, an offline Semantic Diff Segmentation module partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Finally, the retrieved keyframes are used for Video Question Answering, and the predicted timestamps are refined by the precomputed semantic segments to recover complete temporal boundaries for Video Question Grounding.
Fig. 4: Prompt Template Design. The prompt for our final VQG prediction, which is adapted from TStar [18].

Fig. 3: Visualization of the proposed Semantic Diff segmentation. By measuring semantic transitions between neighboring clips, our offline preprocessing partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Besides separating distinct scenes (e.g., piano playing versus woman and child), it further identifies fine-grained action boundaries, isolating the brief “touch child” interaction (38.8–40.9 s) from surrounding activities. During online inference, Semantic Diff Refinement aligns the retrieved keyframe with the corresponding action segment, producing accurate temporal grounding.
Fig. 5: Prompt Template Design for Object Cue. The prompt for generating object cues, which is adapted from TStar [18].

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.
authors: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu
bullets: Addresses tool grounding when multiple physical devices can provide the requested capability.
Uses adaptive context partitions and hierarchical endpoint trees to reuse feedback across related requests and devices.
Selection accounts for service cost, authorization, battery reserves, availability, and device capabilities.
Provides a finite-horizon regret bound and optional differential privacy for aggregated reward statistics.
In a simulated loading-dock workload, it improves step success and cost-adjusted service while reducing simulated energy and latency versus several baselines.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.
authors: Josif Grabocka
bullets: Existing TFMs either incur high costs from repeated row- and column-wise attention or lose detail by compressing each row into one embedding.
FTFM assigns one contextual latent to each row and each column.
Cells interact indirectly through their corresponding row and column latents rather than attending to one another directly.
The approach retains feature-specific cell representations while reducing repeated attention computation.
FTFM achieves competitive tabular-classification performance on benchmarks including TabArena and BeyondArena.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.
authors: Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Targets streaming video QA, where queries can arrive at any time and only a few preceding frames are typically relevant.
Encodes segments independently at varying representation levels, from inexpensive visual features to full KV caches.
Dynamically completes retrieved segments and pipelines computation across CPU and GPU resources using offline cost profiles.
Reports competitive accuracy with up to 10.4× lower time-to-first-token than prior methods and up to 5.9× lower than streaming systems.
Sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT below 0.5 s, or up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT below 2 s.

papers.abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.
authors: Yunlong Deng, Yan Li, Xing Hu, Yida Zhu, Sean Du, Weiyang Liu, Guangyi Chen
bullets: Motivates context editing as a native language capability for managing long reasoning and interaction histories.
Encodes editing operations with dedicated special tokens, allowing agents to invoke edits during generation.
Trains agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with edits conditioned on evolving context.
Evaluated on four long-horizon benchmarks, improving average success by 5.6 and 4.5 percentage points for two models.
Reduces average token usage by 36% and 15% for those models, respectively; scope is focused on long-horizon agentic workflows.

papers.abstract: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.

papers.abstract: Any-to-any generation seeks a single model that translates flexibly among text, image, and audio, yet existing approaches either require fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared representation that suppresses modality-specific structure. We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs while preserving each modality in its native latent sequence. Modaliff assembles conditions and targets into a unified token sequence, with per-token attributes to disambiguate token identities and role-based positional embedding to preserve each modality's internal structure across sequence layouts. This design enables a single denoiser to support diverse generation tasks without task-specific architectural changes or a shared cross-modal latent space. Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions either by combining single-condition predictions at inference or by lightweight finetuning on captions that jointly describe multiple inputs. Experiments across text, image, and audio show that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.

Supports multiple conditioning inputs through inference-time combination or lightweight caption-based finetuning.
Reports the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most tasks with substantially fewer parameters and training data.

papers.abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.

Evaluated with GPT and Claude executors on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset, against six general-purpose judges.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.
authors: Mobina Kashaniyan, Ali Jannesari
bullets: Fixed sampling budgets overlook both query difficulty and GPU contention, which can raise energy use by up to 4.1× for the same query.
ATEST-Online incrementally samples, estimates answer stability, monitors GPU conditions, and learns sampling cost online without offline calibration.
ATEST-Calibrated chooses per-query budgets from offline accuracy and cost models, making it better suited to stable workloads.
Across four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online stayed within energy budgets while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increased.

Online adaptation improves robustness but can increase tail latency and reduce throughput on short tasks; offline calibration used 42× less GPU time and 48× less energy in the evaluated workload when profiling was included.

(b) ATEST-Calibrated, the offline mode of ATEST, builds accuracy and cost models offline for each dataset and picks B once per query. (c) ATEST-Online starts with one sample and adds samples step by step (1→3→4→6→8). papers.abstract: We introduce ReDT, a feed-forward visual geometry transformer designed to scale multi-view reconstruction to high-definition (HD) inputs. Existing visual geometry transformers are typically trained at fixed, standard definition (SD) resolutions and exhibit degraded reconstruction quality and poor computational scaling to high input resolutions. While recent efficient architectures reduce the complexity of inter-frame attention, expensive intra-frame and encoder attention remain largely unaddressed, making HD reconstruction impractical with existing architectures. ReDT addresses both limitations with a resolution-aware architecture designed to scale to high-resolution inputs. The key idea of ReDT is to first map each view to a fixed-size set of basis tokens, compute correspondences in this compact constant-size basis space, and then project the outputs back to the original resolution for dense prediction. By decoupling the internal representation from input resolution during attention, ReDT substantially reduces the computational cost of high-resolution 3D reconstruction and improves model performance at all resolutions. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets spanning SD to FHD (2K) show that ReDT outperforms state-of-the-art visual geometry transformers in both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. For instance, on the ETH3D (2K) dataset, ReDT achieves a $16\times$ speedup, a $34\%$ reduction in peak GPU memory usage, and a $33\%$ reduction in chamfer distance over VGGT-$\Omega$. \href{https://redt.github.io}{Project Website.}

papers.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.
authors: Jithin VG, Ditto PS
bullets: Compaction replaces older agent turns with summaries to prevent long sessions from exhausting usable context.
On recall tasks, compaction improved accuracy for both 1.2B and 9B models versus truncation.
In 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, long-session resolution rose from 41% to 53%, with 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost.
Benefits appeared when compaction triggered early enough to preserve room for reasoning; short sessions did not benefit.
The gain disappeared under a 45-minute session budget because summaries took a median of 161 seconds; an 8B model often avoided compaction entirely.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
authors: SM Mazharul Islam, Manfred Huber
bullets: Observation reconstruction can overemphasize visual fidelity, weakening latent priors and long-horizon predictions.
A Beta–Bernoulli spatial mask stochastically occludes observations with varying visibility at each timestep.
The masked observation and binary mask are concatenated as encoder input, requiring minimal architectural changes.
Across pixel-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks, model-predictive control with open-loop rollouts shows improved planning performance and data efficiency.
Balanced observability performs better than training focused mainly on sparse or dense observations; results are robust to mask scale.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Posterior estimation under induced partial observability. By limiting observation access, stochastic gating prevents posterior collapse onto observations and drives learning in the prior.

Fig. 3. Comparison of task learning performance under induced partial observation and full observation. Each subplot shows test return versus environment steps. Stochastic gating improves learning efficiency and final performance on Cheetah, Reacher, and Walker, while matching on Cartpole. The lines show the average and the shaded area represent 1 standard deviation over 5 seeds.

Fig. 4. Comparison of scale factors with fixed Beta(2, 2). Performance curves are comparable across different scales, indicating that task performance is invariant to the spatial granularity of the mask when the expected observation density is constant. The lines show the average and the shaded areas represent 1 standard deviation over 5 seeds.

Fig. 5. Comparison of Beta prior configurations. The plot shows test performance over environment steps. The symmetric prior consistently outperforms the asymmetric alternatives, indicating that balanced exposure across the full range of observability during training is more critical than any specific directional bias in observability. The lines show the average and the shaded area represent 1 standard deviation over 5 seeds.
Fig. 2. Evaluation environments from the DeepMind Control Suite.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses learning latent dynamics and control policies for continuous control, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
papers.tldr: Stochastic masking during training improves the robustness and data efficiency of latent dynamics models for pixel-based control by aligning representations with predictive dynamics rather than visual reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Previous work has argued that multilingual LLMs encode language-specific features most strongly in their initial and final layers, implying that intermediate layers support language-agnostic representations. This paper reconsiders this finding by performing four different experiments: three that undertake a fine-grained analysis of representations of Portuguese and Spanish, two closely related languages, and one large-scale language identification experiment that covers over 200 languages. The results of these experiments challenge the strict separation between language-specific and language-agnostic layers in multilingual LLMs, using Llama 3.2 1B as a test case. By analyzing and manipulating contextual sentence embeddings, we demonstrate that language identity remains strongly recoverable throughout the model rather than being restricted to initial and final layers. Moreover, we find that the model tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, revealing a skew in model behavior that differs from human judgments.
authors: Mikaela Martins, Jonathan Dunn
bullets: Analyzes Portuguese and Spanish representations with three fine-grained experiments.
Uses a large-scale language-identification experiment spanning over 200 languages.
Finds strong language-identity signals across the model, not only in initial and final layers.
Shows ambiguous strings are classified closer to Spanish than Portuguese, unlike human judgments.
Results are demonstrated using Llama 3.2 1B and do not establish that all multilingual LLMs behave identically.

Spanish and Portuguese are most distinctive, thus having more languagespecific information, in the middle and final layers.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes language-specific feature representation across layers in multilingual LLMs, relevant to LLM interpretability.
papers.title: Where Are Language-Specific Features Represented in Multilingual LLMs? Everywhere
papers.tldr: Language identity remains recoverable throughout multilingual LLM layers, challenging the view that only the first and last layers encode language-specific features.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1's two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.
authors: Junzhe Shi, Yuan Gan, Shida Jiang
bullets: Frames reporting as a chain from model responses to decoded records, sets, and final task answers.
Uses task-compatible matching to identify missing candidates, lost representatives, and wrong selections.
Requires no target-task labels, relying on the task specification and a shipped configuration.
Reduces per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 50 dense synthetic scenes.
On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a three-model grounding tier lowers miss rate to 9.33%, outperforming the reported comparison protocols at similar cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: FSR for visual reporting with vision-language models. Top lane: the reporting chain of the default pipeline (Algorithm 1), from the image, task and budget to the answer, with the repair at each step (blue cards) and the result that governs it. Bottom lane: the same four steps for GUI grounding with three models (Algorithm 2), and where each kind of miss arises: F , no correct candidate after the calls; L, a correct candidate but no correct representative after construction; W , a correct representative that readout does not choose. The miss rate is F + L+W (Proposition 8). Calls determine coverage, what the responses contain; decoding, construction and readout determine what is delivered from it. F , L and W locate a miss; an operation can change more than one of them. Judge: choosing between configurations, for which the shipped defaults need no target labels. Detect: errors flagged without labels; in GUI grounding the alarm triggers the comparison. Every item is scored, and an item with no point counts as a miss.

Figure 1: Three repairs that change what a model delivers. (a) One response of GPT-6.1 to a dense synthetic scene (image 28 of SCP-dense, our dense synthetic counting scenes; 173 shapes of five classes): the list count, the records of each class in the model’s list counted by code, matches the truth, while the stated count the model wrote in the same response sums to 188; each of the 173 records matches a different shape of the same class (Section 7.2). (b) For the instruction “only allow values from a list” in an Excel menu, a single click by Gemini 3.8 lands on “Time”; a second call on a zoomed crop (ReGround, Li et al., 2025b) lands inside the target “List” (green box). On 200 ScreenSpot-Pro items, two-stage zoom cuts Gemini 3.8’s miss rate by 65% (Section 7.5). (c) Miss rate against cost per item at list prices on 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items: GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom, three such zooms with a cluster vote, a crop-first baseline in the style of GUI-Lens (Fu et al., 2026), a cluster vote over three models’ zoomed points, and FSR’s GUI-grounding tier (Algorithm 2), which selects among the same points with a scorer and a comparison; every item is in the denominator. Paired differences with intervals are in Section 7.7: the tier’s difference from the crop-first baseline has an interval that reaches 0, and its differences from the other flows exclude 0.

Figure 6: Risk-coverage of click alarms (260 items; point estimates). An alarm sets an item aside when the acted-on point and a second point for the same item are farther apart than δ of the longer image side; the system acts on the other items. Acceptance coverage is the share of items acted on, and the miss rate when acting the share of those items whose point is outside the target; lower and further right is better. Each curve traces δ ∈ {0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 8}%, and a smaller δ sets more items aside. Grey: the second point comes from a second call of the same model; blue: from the partner, the cheapest other model (Gemini 3.8 for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 for Gemini 3.8). Solid lines and filled markers: first clicks on the whole screenshot; dashed lines and open markers: both points after two-stage zoom. Rings: the shipped default δ = 1.5% (Table 12). Diamonds: acting on every item. The cross-model alarm reaches lower miss rates than the same-model alarm, at the price of setting more items aside.

Figure 3: One response, two answers. GPT-6.1 is asked to list every shape in a dense synthetic scene (SCP-dense image 28) and then give counts by type “for the shapes you listed”. (a) The scene has 173 shapes. (b) A detail of the scene with the records of the model’s list as dots, one colour per class: each record matches a different shape of the same class within 20 pixels. (c) The response itself, abridged; coordinates are on the model’s native 0 to 1000 grid. The list has 173 records, so the list count of every class is exact, while the counts the model states after it sum to 188, a per-type error of 21. Across 50 such scenes, list length misses the true total by 0.04 objects on average and the stated total misses by 7.78 (Table 8).

Figure 5: Selection and the deletion threshold. (a) Selection gain of deleting unconfirmed records, as a reduction of set error E per image (positive: deletion lowers E), against the marginal matching rate p1 of the deleted records, for the 54 base/partner pairs (symmetric log scale; grey circles: same-model partner; blue squares: cross-model partner; open markers: screen sources). With equal error costs the gain per image equals E[∆c](1− 2p1) (Proposition 2), so its sign follows the side of p1 = 1/2; the panel shows where each pair falls. (b) Reduction of E relative to one call when selecting among three calls of one model (detection sources, 60 images per cell): the constrained oracle, the cross-fitted logistic selector, and the logistic selector fitted on 10 labelled images (median of 40 draws). GPT, Son., Gem.: GPT-6.1, Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8.

Figure 4: Same-response readout across datasets (count-first prompts, lowest reasoning setting, one call; 100 images per dataset, 50 on SCP-dense). Bars: relative change of count error from the stated count to the raw list count of the same response, with paired image-bootstrap 95% intervals; negative means the list count is better. Blue: interval below 0; orange: interval above 0; grey and n.s.: interval includes 0. Error is per type on SCP and SCP-dense and total on PixMo-Count and FSC-147; numbers under dataset names are mean objects per image. Absolute errors are in Table B.1. The list count is better on the multi-class synthetic scenes for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5; Gemini 3.8’s lists degenerate there, so reading them is worse (Section 7.3).

Final default: what the pipeline ships. They coincide for set error on over-reporting families and differ elsewhere; the last column gives the reason. The prompts are in Appendix D, the settings of the GUI-grounding tier in Algorithm 2, and every value in the released configuration file.

Table 2: Task contracts. Scoring compatibility decides matches with the truth; association decides which records of different calls are the same object, and uses no labels. Coordinates are mapped from each model’s native frame to image pixels before scoring. The detection rows and the multi-class count row use overlapping datasets but different images and different contracts.

The raw list count counts the records of each class before the alias map, the mapped list count after it. Pure readout: stated count → raw list count of the same response. Alias map: raw → mapped list count of the same list. Protocol: mapped list count of a count-first response → that of a list-first response. Full method: stated count of a count-first response → readout of Section 5 on a list-first response, the effect of the reporting and decoding protocol. The shipped F1 configuration of each model is the highest F1 of its column (bold); for Gemini 3.8 the two default-setting configurations differ by less than 0.2 points.

Table 13: Choosing one click among several calls, on 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items that share no item or screenshot with the 260 click items of the GUI experiment. (a) Every flow, with every item in the denominator; a flow that returns no point counts as a miss, which happened only in single-model flows (column No point). Calls and cost: what the flow needs per item, every attempt counted, at list prices. The three-model flows use GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5 at the default setting and Gemini 3.8 at the lowest, unless marked “all lowest”. Cluster vote: the largest cluster of points within δ wins, ties go to the earliest model (GPT-6.1, Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8), and the earliest point of the winning cluster is returned; computed from the stored calls, no scorer. Per-type count error, lower is better; paired image bootstrap 95% intervals. Difficult DOTA objects and objects less than half inside the window are not targets, so records on them are counted like any other record, for every readout alike. List recall: share of true objects matched by a record centre inside a true box of the same class (list-first arm). Readout gap: mean per-type difference between the stated count and the list count of the same count-first response, which bounds how much switching readouts can change the error. Same response: stated count → list count of the count-first response. Full method: readout of the list-first response (list count, or the stated count if the list is flagged) against the stated count of the count-first response; the Gemini 3.8 default row is the shipped configuration. Table 5: Revisions of the model. Each row records the failed assumption and the evidence against it, the revised assumption and its direct check, and the new consequence with its test. The kind of evidence is named in each cell.

Table 14: Selection among three calls of one model (detection sources, list interface, lowest setting, 60 images per cell; reduction of E relative to the first call, in %, higher is better). The constrained oracle optimizes over the same feasible family as the selectors (Proposition 12); the unrestricted value lets two members of one cluster match two targets and is not attainable. The two oracles differ on 25 of 720 images. Selectors are logistic or boosted-tree record gates on output features; they read no labels at inference but are fitted with labels: cross-fitted (5 folds by image, persisted), in-sample, or on 10 labelled images (median over 40 draws, each evaluated on the images it did not use). Gap: constrained oracle minus cross-fitted logistic, with a 95% image-bootstrap interval for the fitted selector; it mixes information absent from the features with selector and estimation shortfall (Proposition 7).

Table 12: Disagreement alarms for clicks (ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, 260 items; partner set by a fixed rule as the cheapest other model; point estimates). The alarm compares the acted-on point with a second point for the same item and fires when the two are farther apart than δ = 1.5% of the longer image side; in this risk-coverage analysis the item is then set aside instead of acted on (in Algorithm 2 it triggers a comparison instead). Unzoomed alarms compare first clicks; after zoom, the acted-on point is the zoomed first click, and the second point is the same model’s zoomed second click or the partner’s zoomed first click. Miss rate, all items: miss rate when acting on every item. Acceptance coverage: share of items acted on. Miss rate when acting: share of acted-on items whose point is outside the target. Errors caught: share of the acted-on prediction’s misses that the alarm sets aside. Other values of δ are in Figure 6, and miss rates at matched acceptance coverage in Table B.3.

Entries are relative changes of the loss in % (for E, negative is better; for F1, positive is better). Bold: the paired 95% interval excludes 0 in the favourable direction; underlined: it excludes 0 in the unfavourable direction. ⋆: the user’s model is the strongest single model on that source and loss; every significantly worse cross-model entry carries a ⋆. papers.selection_reason: Inference-time procedures for reliable visual set generation in VLMs; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial/GUI grounding.
papers.title: From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: FSR treats visual reporting as part of VLM reasoning and improves counting, detection, parsing, and GUI grounding through task-aware inference-time procedures for frozen models.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning treats the expert demonstration or gold response as a one-hot target, suppressing valid alternative continuations that the model would otherwise assign probability to. We propose Gold-Conditioned Distillation (GCD), a method that turns expert demonstrations into model-native supervision. GCD uses one model as both teacher and student: the teacher conditions on a prompt containing the gold response in context, the student conditions on the original prompt as at inference, and the student is trained to minimize the forward KL divergence to the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold response token. This lets the model use its prior knowledge to teach itself the new task: correctness is anchored by the gold response, while the soft target preserves plausible alternatives. Across various training tasks on Qwen and Llama models, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Bang An, Shuming Liu, Wenqing Cui, Tianqi Xu, Bing Li, Yibo Yang, Peter Wonka, Bernard Ghanem
bullets: Standard supervised fine-tuning suppresses plausible alternative continuations by using one-hot gold targets.
GCD uses the same model as teacher and student: the teacher sees the gold response in context, while the student sees only the inference-time prompt.
The student matches the teacher’s next-token distributions via forward KL divergence at each gold-response token.
Across Qwen and Llama training tasks, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Gold-Conditioned Distillation (GCD). The student predicts the next token from the query x and the gold-response prefix y<t; the teacher predicts it from a privileged context that additionally contains the full gold response y and a repeat prompt. The student is trained with a forward KL loss to match the teacher’s gold-conditioned next-token distribution, and the teacher is an exponential moving average of the student.

Figure 4: Learning-rate sensitivity of SDFT versus our GCD on LiveNews. Each panel shows accuracy across four training epochs for one model. Gray curves are SDFT runs, darker for higher learning rates; the red curve is GCD at its single reported learning rate. SDFT’s best learning rate is model-specific and improves the method only marginally, while GCD dominates the entire SDFT envelope on every panel.
Figure 2: Learning New Knowledge from Scratch. We report evaluation accuracy as a function of training epochs for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on LiveNews dataset.

papers.abstract: Video large multimodal models have improved at identifying cross-frame visual evidence and conducting open-web retrieval, as reflected in recent video deep research (VDR) benchmarks. However, existing VDR benchmarks primarily evaluate tool-use trajectories and final responses without verifying whether a model actually uses the temporal video information or the retrieved web evidence. To fill this gap, we introduce \method{}, an evidence-grounded benchmark with three features. First, it combines human review with restricted-access probing across multiple models to exclude questions answerable from parametric knowledge or a single information source. Second, each question carries structured video-to-web evidence annotations that link the relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence. Third, its evaluation protocol separately scores video grounding, web evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness. Across eight multimodal agent systems, the best reaches 76.0\% answer accuracy, yet none recovers the complete required web evidence for more than 8\% of questions. Our benchmark is publicly available at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hh721/vdr_temp}.
authors: Xiyuan Liang, Yu Wang, Zuhao Yang, Ziting Wang, Duo Li, Sudong Wang, Zhongyu Yang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets a gap in existing VDR benchmarks, which assess trajectories and answers without verifying evidence use.
Filters questions through human review and restricted-access probing to require both video and web information.
Provides structured annotations linking relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence.
Separately evaluates video grounding, web-evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness.
Across eight multimodal agents, the best answer accuracy is 76.0%, while no system recovers complete web evidence for over 8% of questions.

papers.abstract: To determine where computation is needed in volumetric segmentation networks, we analyze block-level redundancy and stage-wise token-mixer contribution. Centered Kernel Alignment reveals high input-output representational similarity within blocks of representative convolutional, hybrid, and Transformer-style segmentation networks. Similarity-guided pruning reduces their parameter counts by 39-75% while decreasing mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points. To examine token mixers within blocks, we introduce Anatomical Relation Distortion, which quantifies how bypassing a mixer distorts feature relations between labeled anatomical positions. Applied to an unpruned candidate architecture, Centered Kernel Alignment indicates high representational redundancy in intermediate encoder mixers, whereas Anatomical Relation Distortion shows that they contribute little and the bottleneck mixer most. These findings motivate SlimFormer++, which uses Selective Mixing blocks with windowed Mamba mixing in the first encoder stage and only residual channel MLPs in deeper stages. At the bottleneck, Augmented Mixing injects similarity-weighted sparse long-range context into the axial taps of a depthwise convolution at cost linear in voxel count. Evaluated against 12 baselines across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets (1,809 cases), SlimFormer++ achieves the highest mean Dice (87.84%) and lowest mean HD95 (6.50 mm) with the fewest parameters (5.98 million). These results support stage-aware token mixing as a design strategy for improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in volumetric segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/WHHHHHY822/SlimFormerPlusPlus
authors: Yang Hong, Lei Zhang, Zhihong Liu, Jianqing Mo, Xujiong Ye
bullets: Block-level redundancy analysis shows 39–75% parameter pruning can reduce mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points.
Anatomical Relation Distortion indicates early and intermediate encoder mixers contribute little, while bottleneck mixing is most important.
The model uses windowed Mamba mixing early, residual channel MLPs in deeper stages, and augmented sparse long-range mixing at the bottleneck.
Across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets, it reports 87.84% mean Dice and 6.50 mm mean HD95 with 5.98M parameters.
The findings support stage-aware token mixing as a strategy for efficient volumetric segmentation.

papers.abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.
authors: Mingcong Ding, Babette B\"uhler, Tim F\"utterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Enkelejda Kasneci
bullets: Addresses the cost of retraining models for changing social-behavior taxonomies and VLMs’ weak sensitivity to fine-grained posture.
Uses human pose only during training to guide a lightweight adapter, while inference relies on RGB and text prompts without pose input.
Separates a shared transferable core from a VLM-specific projection head, enabling adaptation to new backbones by retraining only the head.
Reports improved recognition on the training domain, transfer across VLM backbones, and generalization to two unseen datasets.
Improved behavior predictions also correlate more strongly with human ratings of rapport and dominance; scope is limited to tested models and indoor datasets.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user-specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, an inference-time scaling method tailored for text-to-image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow-matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward-guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR-SMC.
authors: Wenyi Lian, Zheng Zhao, Thomas B. Sch{\"o}n
bullets: Addresses the challenge of applying standard SMC to flow-matching models, whose ODE-based inference uses deterministic proposals.
Perturbs resampled particles by changing their source noise and reconstructing an intermediate state that remains compatible with flow-matching interpolation.
Adds look-ahead refinement to improve resampled particles before reward weighting.
Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image show consistent reward-guided generation improvements.
Ablations support the roles of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement.

papers.abstract: Decision models answer typed questions, such as multiple-choice or yes/no questions, with a probability for each option. We add test-time search to frozen decision models, with no training: we show the model a complete proposed answer, read off its probability of saying "Yes" to the proposal's correctness, and search for answers that it rates higher. The search is done either by editing one answer at a time or by joint optimization, which changes several answers at once. Search raises accuracy for every model and test set we tried, and the gains are largest for exact correctness on logic puzzles, where every answer in a task must be right. On 128 such puzzles, it takes Qwen3.8-27B from 2 to 30 exactly correct puzzles ($15\times$) and its per-blank accuracy from 27.8% to 48.5%. On a shared set of 47 puzzles, searching over each model's own Yes/No score raises the per-blank accuracy of StartLux Instant, Perplexity Decider, Clef, and JEV, which we reach only through its public API, by 4.0 to 13.0 percentage points, and raises the number of puzzles they get exactly correct, out of 47 and averaged over three search seeds, from 10 to 35, 9 to 26, 2 to 11, and 9 to 31.7 respectively.
authors: Lev Stambler
bullets: Targets typed-answer tasks such as multiple-choice and yes/no questions without additional training.
Evaluates complete proposed answers and searches for alternatives rated more likely correct by the model.
Uses either single-answer editing or joint optimization to revise multiple answers simultaneously.
Improves accuracy across all tested models and test sets, with the largest gains on exact logic-puzzle solving.
On 128 puzzles, Qwen3.8-27B’s exactly solved tasks rise from 2 to 30, while per-blank accuracy increases from 27.8% to 48.5%.

papers.abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. We distinguish weak multimodality (the model can answer questions about an input image) from strong multimodality (the model's text representations themselves become vision-aligned, improving performance on text-only tasks with latent visual structure). To test for strong multimodality, we construct a task of shape-counting problems with paired equivalent text and image specifications. This task is trivial when the image is provided, but requires visualization when specified in text as line coordinates. We compare instruction-tuned Qwen-2.5 and Mistral models against their vision-aligned counterparts on the text variant of the task. We find that the multimodal models do no better in this setting, despite strong performance on the image version of the task. Probing experiments corroborate this: vision-aligned decoder embeddings carry no more visual structure than their text-only counterparts. Finally, we provide an optimization objective that distills in-context visual embeddings into text embeddings. This alignment induces gains on the text variant of the task without explicit task supervision, even on samples more complex than seen during alignment. This suggests that VQA-style alignment leaves available cross-modal transfer untapped.
authors: Shashwat Singh, He He, Tal Linzen
bullets: The paper distinguishes weak multimodality—answering questions about images—from strong multimodality, where text representations become vision-aligned.
On paired shape-counting tasks, multimodal models perform no better than text-only models when given coordinate-based text, despite performing well with images.
Probing shows that vision-aligned decoder embeddings contain no more visual structure than embeddings from text-only models.
A self-distillation objective aligns in-context visual and text embeddings without explicit task supervision.
This alignment improves text-based shape counting, including examples more complex than those used during alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Given paired text-image data our alignment method trains the model to predict from text (code) the embeddings it would’ve had given the image. During alignment (left) we provide no task context or answer labels. During evaluation (right) the model performs the shape counting task.

Figure 3: Vision-alignment does not add more visual structure to the embeddings of the multimodal model, compared to the text-only model. While probes trained on the embeddings from both classes of models show above-chance accuracy, the performance for the two classes of models is very similar.

Figure 2: When the problem is provided in text, for all the settings tested—with and without in-context examples (ICL), and with and without chain of thought (CoT)—the performance of the multimodal models is similar to their text-only counterparts, and far below the image ceiling. This indicates that vision alignment did not transfer visualization capabilities to the text decoder. Error bars are based on the 95% confidence interval on accuracy estimates using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution.

Figure 4: The trends on learnt retrieval corroborate that the multimodal decoder does not have better visual representations of textual inputs than the text-only model. Both the embedding sets get significantly above-chance and above-control retrieval accuracy against DiNo embeddings – at least in the middle layers. papers.title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help

papers.abstract: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.
authors: Owen Bianchi, Samer Aslan, Ryunosuke Saito
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized evaluation for long-range memory in conversational contexts.
Introduces 100 human-created conversations augmented by LLMs, extending beyond existing dialogue lengths.
Uses a fact-recall task: classifying 40 candidate dialogue facts as true or false.
Evaluates current LLMs and memory enhancements, finding that substantial memory improvements remain necessary.
Better long-context memory could support more coherent, relevant, and human-like conversations.
