papers.abstract: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
authors: Sagar Kumar, Shailja Sharma, Tirthajit Baruah, Punit Rathore
bullets: Problem: Dice alone may remain stable after compression even when uncertainty estimates change, which is risky in safety-critical MRI/CT segmentation.
Method: A post-training mixed-precision framework ranks quantization actions by benefit–risk score and validates each accepted change using full-model reliability checks on calibration data.
Contribution: Introduces reliability-constrained compression that explicitly preserves uncertainty-map agreement alongside segmentation quality.
Results: Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, it preserves FP32-level Dice and achieves 3.59×–7.8× compression in 2D and 4.73×–7.82× in 3D.
Scope: TensorRT runtime measurements are reported separately from reliability-preserving storage compression.

papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.
authors: Yong Wang, Kecheng Zheng, Xing Zhu, Chao Xu, Yujun Shen, Shengze Cai
bullets: Targets the limited characterization of dexterous manipulation in existing robotic action models.
Covers five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long-horizon tasks, and memory.
Pairs every task with an out-of-domain variant to test robustness to controlled visual and spatial changes.
Includes two high-DoF hand embodiments and 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations totaling 6.25 million frames.
Provides unified-protocol baselines from evaluating seven recent Vision-Language-Action models.

papers.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
papers.tldr: BiDex-100 is a 106-task simulation benchmark for evaluating bimanual dexterous manipulation across capabilities, robustness, embodiments, and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.
authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
bullets: Adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev decision readout and continues generation from the existing KV cache when selected or when confidence is low.
On Qwen3-0.6B, JevBench accuracy was statistically unchanged, while expected calibration error decreased from 0.292 to 0.169 and Bitext routing accuracy reached 98.3%.
KV-cache reuse reduced latency by 15–37% on an Apple M4 Pro; copied-cache option scoring matched full-sequence scoring within 1.4e-6 probability.
System X v4 with Qwen3-1.7B increased JevBench accuracy from 55.0% to 61.0% versus its base model, without a significant IFEval change.
Failure modes include state conflicts and unsupported reply details; broader validation with multiple seeds, human raters, and real support data is needed.

papers.selection_reason: Reuses KV cache to avoid prompt prefill, reducing latency for LLM decision models.
papers.title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
papers.tldr: System X lets an LLM decision model generate replies directly from its decision KV cache, improving calibration and reducing latency while preserving roughly similar decision accuracy, though unsupported details remain a limitation.

papers.abstract: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.
authors: Behnam Moradi
bullets: Addresses the tension between fixed, safe robot controllers and costly, non-deterministic runtime foundation-model reasoning.
Uses an LLM to propose minimal subtree patches only after node failures; CMA-ES tunes parameters and a contextual bandit selects stored patches versus new LLM calls.
Admits patches through static checks, invariant-monitored replays, and empirical recovery margins, then stores them in a reusable fleet library and crystallizes them into deterministic BTs.
In Project AirSim experiments, crystallized trees achieved 97±2% mission success with no online learning, versus 12% for the unpatched tree and 98% for a hand-coded expert tree.
Replay admission rejected some useful wind-recovery patches, while a static-only variant generalized better to held-out failures.

papers.selection_reason: Uses foundation-model-generated patches and online adaptation to improve autonomous drone control, fitting learned robot control and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
papers.tldr: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees convert foundation-model-generated drone-control patches into deterministic, inspectable BTs, reducing runtime LLM dependence while achieving high mission success in simulation.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
authors: Sravanth Kodavanti, Manjunath Arveti
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning every transformer layer the same KV-cache budget despite differing token needs.
Uses multi-objective neural architecture search to find per-layer allocations compatible with existing eviction methods.
A single search captures the budget–task-score trade-off and transfers across target budgets; an optional constrained search further refines allocations.
Across four eviction methods and two LLMs, it outperforms uniform allocation in 146 of 154 evaluated settings and can match uniform performance with up to 75% less cache.
Allocations consistently concentrate cache on a small set of middle layers; compared with EvolKV, MOSAIC searches a much larger space with fewer evaluations and GPU-hours.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The MOSAIC pipeline. Stages 1–3 run once per (task, eviction policy): an unconstrained search on a calibration subset yields a Pareto front of per-layer allocations, full-data re-evaluation selects a winner, and the winner is rescaled to every target budget without further search. Stage 4 optionally refines each budget with constrained BO seeded by the rescaled winner. Bar profiles are schematic.

Figure 2: Budget–score trade-off found by the unconstrained search (full data). Rows: eviction method; columns: task. Dashed: uniform allocation. Dots: configurations on the Stage 1 Pareto front, re-evaluated on full data in Stage 2. Ring: the winner carried to Stages 3 and 4.

papers.abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, it reports state-of-the-art task recognition and skill assessments correlated with expert evaluations.
Its scope includes automated surgical education, real-time feedback, and objective training or certification support.

papers.abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.
authors: Yifan Lu, Rubin Wei, Ziyun Zou, Junhong Liang, Haolin Yang, Xinlin Zhuang, Abhijit Das, Adinath Madhavrao Dukre, Shadab Khan, Zhouhan Lin, Imran Razzak
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of controlling, updating, and reliably eliciting knowledge stored in language-model parameters.
Uses a frozen base LM with latent hidden-state corrections and a lexical token-space memory pathway.
A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token memory weights using uncertainty and disagreement features.
Keeps post-hoc factual memory outside the router; new facts can be appended without retraining and are used when an answer-level gate accepts them.
Experiments report improved predictive accuracy and updateability with low inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Mixture-of-Memories architecture. The input is tokenized and each next-token prediction is formed from three core sources: a frozen Base LM, a hidden-space Latent Memory (LatM), and a token-space Lexical Memory (LexM). The Budget Router produces per-token mixture weights over these sources. The writable Explicit Memory (ExpM) stores appended facts in an external key–value store and bypasses the router. For each question, it retrieves the fact and injects its answer only when an answer-level gate accepts it; otherwise the routed core predicts alone. New facts thus take effect without retraining.

papers.abstract: Pedestrians differ in whether they respond to a robot, yet many RL policies assume all are non-reactive to prioritize safety. Policies trained without conditioning on local pedestrians' reactivity may therefore be unnecessarily conservative or rely on cooperation that does not occur. We propose RCRA, an online adaptation framework that modulates a learned residual around a frozen conservative navigation policy according to estimated pedestrian reactivity. A Transformer-based estimator infers latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context, providing a more accurate signal for navigation adaptation and improving scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by $12.62$ percentage points over the Bayesian baseline, which assumes known pedestrian goals. These estimates are spatially aggregated into an adaptation scale that gates LoRA modules, enabling cooperative behavior near reactive pedestrians and conservative behavior near non-reactive pedestrians. Among baselines achieving SR above $90\%$ in every scenario, RCRA reduces scenario-averaged path length by $16.7\%$ relative to the conservative backbone and by $7.3\%$ relative to randomized-training baselines. It improves mean SR by $14.88$ percentage points over the reactive-trained policy.
authors: Immanuel R. Santjoko, Benedictus C. G. Cinun, Jing Chen, Bin Hu
bullets: Addresses the conservatism and coordination failures caused by assuming all pedestrians are non-reactive.
Uses a Transformer to infer latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context.
Aggregates local reactivity estimates to gate LoRA-based residual adaptations around a frozen conservative policy.
Improves scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by 12.62 percentage points over a Bayesian baseline.
Reduces scenario-averaged path length while maintaining high success rates, and improves mean success rate over a reactive-trained policy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RCRA. A reactivity estimator is trained on mixed scenarios. Online, the robot estimates per-human reactivity beliefs from partial observations, aggregates them using spatial relevance weights, and uses the resulting scale κt to gate the LoRA residual to adapt the navigation safety–efficiency operating point.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.
authors: Shuochen Chang, Bingjie Gao, Qingyang Liu, Qianli Ma, Yibo Miao, Haonan Zhao, Zhaohe Liao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static keyframe-label supervision and the evidence needed for complex downstream reasoning.
Initializes a lightweight saliency policy with supervised learning, then refines it against a frozen MLLM environment.
Uses answer-token negative log-likelihood as a dense reward and a KL term to preserve consistency with the learned prior.
Achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based frame scorers while retaining lightweight inference efficiency on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
The selector is trained once and transfers across multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of our methods. (a) Keyframe Selector. The lightweight selector (fθ) comprises stacked Video-Text Fusion Transformers. It modulates frame features with query semantics to output importance logits, then parameterizing a Plackett-Luce distribution. (b) Stage I: Label Prior Elicitation. We utilize keyframe label annotations to construct a Label Prior. The selector is trained via pairwise ranking loss to align its predicted logits with the label logits, establishing a robust initialization. (c) Stage II:Task-Evidence Posterior Inference. We freeze the MLLM and treat it as a frozen task environment. The selector performs Group Sampling to propose discrete frame subsets (z). The MLLM evaluates these subsets to provide dense NLL rewards (R) and advantages (A). The policy is refined via Bayesian GRPO to maximize task evidence while maintaining KL-regularization towards the label prior.

papers.abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.
authors: Jaeseok Jeong, Kyungmook Choi, Sohyun Chung, Youngsik Yun, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Addresses ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint changes in interactive world models.
Represents spatial memory and user interventions together, while allowing camera trajectories to be chosen independently.

Experiments show more accurate joint object-camera control than existing methods.
Qualitative results indicate that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.

papers.abstract: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zhe Liu, Yuxuan Zheng, Jinzhe Qin, Ziqi Gao, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between onboard inference latency and UAV motion during VLA control.
Uses B-spline trajectories initialized from expert demonstrations for continuous position and yaw references.
Fuses new predictions with active trajectories while preserving derivative continuity and limiting deformation.
Applies execution-aware GRPO to adapt the policy to deviations caused by asynchronous execution.
Achieves a 76.56% success rate on UAV-Flow and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations versus waypoint tracking.

The onboard policy decodes B-spline proposals, which the asynchronous executor aligns and fuses with the active reference. (b) Closed-loop flight rewards yield groupnormalized advantages, while recorded action tokens and pre-update log probabilities support token-level clipped GRPO. papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. Using fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice QA as a seed task format, we synthesize automatically verifiable tasks from domain passages and reshape them into cross-lingual variants. These variants preserve the same evidence-answer relation but change how English and target-language evidence are presented during RLVR. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks across four target languages, code-switched training outperforms matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while maintaining comparable English performance. Additional analyses provide evidence of better target-language input understanding and stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations. These results suggest that code-switched training helps target-language inputs access domain reasoning learned more strongly in English.
authors: Cheonbok Park, Jihwan Kim, Shinyoung Joo, Joosung Lee, Hwiyeol Jo, Jeonghoon Kim, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of verifiable RLVR tasks in specialized non-English domains despite abundant English text.

Preserves the evidence–answer relationship while varying the languages used to present evidence during RLVR training.

Across Korean medical and four-language cybersecurity benchmarks, code-switched training improves average target-language performance over matched baselines while maintaining comparable English performance.
Analyses indicate stronger target-language understanding and cross-lingual alignment in outputs and internal representations.

papers.abstract: Turning a moving-camera perspective video into a 360{\deg} video requires more than just generating content outside the input frame: observations revealed over time must be preserved, unseen regions completed, and the resulting scene kept consistent as the camera viewpoint changes. Existing methods assign these different requirements to a single conditional video model, requiring them to be jointly learned from panoramic video data. We instead present a modular, 3D-driven framework that distributes these three responsibilities across specialized components, all connected through a shared scene representation. Input observations are reconstructed explicitly in 3D, while a pretrained panoramic image model completes unobserved content from a selected panoramic render. This generated content is lifted into the shared 3D scene, where it remains spatially anchored across camera viewpoints. Without requiring any additional panoramic-video training, our framework achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on a static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set. These results support our decomposed, 3D-driven formulation as a promising alternative to direct video generation in this setting.
authors: Michael Wakeham, Mrinmoy Kumar Das, Wenqi Wang, Ayush Tewari, Boqing Gong, Deepti Ghadiyaram
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving observed content, completing unseen regions, and maintaining consistency as the camera moves.
Explicitly reconstructs input observations in 3D and uses a pretrained panoramic image model to generate missing content.
Lifts generated content into a shared 3D scene representation, spatially anchoring it across viewpoints.
Achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on the static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set.
Does not require additional panoramic-video training; evaluation is scoped to static scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Framework Overview. A feed-forward 3D reconstruction model aggregates observations from the input perspective video into an observed-region 3DGS [16], which is rendered into incomplete panoramic frames (Sec. 3.1). To complete as much unobserved scene content as possible, we select the frame with the least observed coverage and complete missing regions using a panoramic image model (Sec. 3.2). After estimating and aligning its depth, the completed panorama is lifted into an unobserved-region 3DGS and combined with the observed-region 3DGS, allowing the completed scene to persist when rendered along the input camera trajectory. (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 3. Qualitative comparisons. (a) Given the input video (left), we show panoramic outputs at three timesteps. Colored outlines mark novel viewing directions, with the corresponding perspective views below each panorama. (b) Colored outlines mark regions explicitly projected from the corresponding input frames. We compare the consistency of the remaining panoramic content across three timesteps.

papers.abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
authors: Sen Gao, Yongan Li, Han Chen, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich, Shixuan Sun
bullets: Targets derived state that must be computed from multiple records rather than directly retrieved.
Uses symbolic scenarios, Datalog-generated gold answers, derivation DAGs, and supporting events for precise diagnosis.
Tests 10 scenarios with 4,692 events and 1,503 queries across access, evolution, and composition difficulty.
Finds final-answer benchmarks hide failures: all evaluated memory systems trail BM25 on derived state, while the answer model reaches 96.01% with supporting events.
Identifies missing retrieval of intermediate states and failure to propagate implicit changes as dominant issues.

papers.abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
authors: Mohammad Omama, Aeyan Ashraf, Sandeep Chinchali
bullets: Addresses the interaction bottleneck of deep feature matchers on edge devices, where each query must otherwise process every database image independently.
Defers inter-image interaction to the final layers, separating reusable intra-image Context Blocks from lightweight online Interaction Blocks.
Introduces E-SToRE, which reduces spatial tokens before cross-image interaction using entropy-guided token reduction and expansion.
Evaluated on HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen.
LateMatch achieves over 2× lower effective computation; E-SToRE adds 10–14% savings with negligible accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Rethinking visual localization with cacheable image matching via LateMatch. (A) Standard visual localization pipelines require matching a single query image against Top-K (e.g., K = 100) retrieved database images. (B) Traditional matching architectures interleave intra-image context building and interimage cross-attention across all layers, preventing any caching and causing a severe computational bottleneck. (C) Our proposed LateMatch architecture breaks this bottleneck by deferring cross-image interaction to the final layers, decoupling the network into offline-cacheable Context Blocks (CBs) and online Interaction Blocks (IBs), reducing the effective compute cost by over 2× without sacrificing much on performance.
Figure 6: MambaGlue-late consistently and significantly outperforms computationally equivalent MambaGlue-lite baselines. We show the trends on three datasets: A) MegaDepth, B) ScanNet, C) HPatches.

Figure 7: LateMatch outperforms token and model pruning. Performance-compute trade-off on the HPatches dataset. We compare it against structurally smaller variants shown in green (LightGlue-late2 and LightGlue-late3). We also compare against attention head pruning (black crosses). LateMatch outperforms both these approaches by a significant margin.

Figure 5: LateMatch consistently dominates the compute-accuracy Pareto frontier. Performance versus online computational cost (E-GFLOPs) evaluated on the ScanNet (A, B) and MegaDepth (C, D) datasets. Across all capacity levels, the -late models (green) achieve strictly higher matching accuracy than the equivalent -lite baselines (red) at the same computational budget.

Figure 2: Strategic positioning of LateMatch in the feature matching landscape. While direct nearest-neighbor matching (A) is extremely fast but highly inaccurate, and lightweight matchers (B) are fast but nowhere close to the accuracy of heavy, computationally prohibitive deep matchers (D), our proposed LateMatch paradigm (C) achieves the high performance of full-capacity models with the online computational footprint of lightweight matchers.

Figure 4: Cross-attention entropy naturally decays across Interaction Blocks, guiding the progressive token reduction in E-SToRE. (A) The cross-attention entropy across the four IBs of LightGlue-late4. Attention smoothly shifts from diffuse global consensus (high entropy) in early IBs to highly peaked, localized matching (low entropy) in later IBs. (B) Progressively decaying r has significantly better performance (homography estimation accuracy) compared to other r selection approaches.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.
authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
bullets: Full-video speech-vision decisions can fail despite useful evidence being available in nearby visual windows.
Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED) is a training-free diagnostic that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation.
TED uses ASR transcripts and utterance intervals to query audio-free windows for temporal forecasting, alignment, or cross-modal binding.
Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, temporal forecasting accuracy improves from 29.3–33.7% to 79.3–82.2% with TED.
Controls indicate that the observed temporal anchor—not merely query replacement or region availability—drives recovery.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses temporal composition in audio-visual LLMs, relevant to multimodal and video understanding.
papers.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models

papers.abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present \textbf{MCSplat}, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.
authors: Yifei Wang, Wei Tian, Wenhua Bao, Jia Zhou, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Jianhua Wu, Shuai Yuan, Zhipeng Zhang, Xingliang Liu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Bingzhao Gao
bullets: Addresses photometric inconsistency across cameras and unreliable normal supervision near depth discontinuities.
Builds a canonical appearance space using depth-guided correspondences to decouple geometry from camera-specific appearance.
Uses a multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer to restore raw camera appearance for cleaner photometric supervision.
Estimates Fisher-information-based uncertainty to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision.
Reports better reconstruction quality, cross-view depth consistency, surface-normal agreement, and fewer geometric artifacts across driving datasets.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
authors: Karthik Viswanathan, Plamen Dimitrov, Stefano Rocca, Sarayu Sirikonda
bullets: Defines head complexity as the minimum number of attention heads needed to represent a Boolean function.
Derives an exact linear-fractional normal form and proves a general lower bound based on threshold degree.
Provides a ten-bit function showing that the threshold-degree lower bound can be strict.
For symmetric Boolean functions, characterizes head complexity by the number of value changes across consecutive Hamming-weight levels, including with positional embeddings.
Uses frontier-model conjecture generation and theorem proving, with Lean formalization and research traces released publicly.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One-layer attention-only model. The input consists of n bit tokens followed by a dedicated query token q, which also serves as the readout position. Each position is represented by the sum of a token embedding and a positional embedding, and the resulting embedded sequence is shared by all H heads. The heads update all positions in parallel, but the linear readout uses only position q. At this position, the head outputs are added to the residual uq, yielding hq(x). Thus, f is represented exactly when the inputs labelled 0 and 1 are linearly separable at the readout position hq(x), and H∗(f) is the minimum H for which this occurs.

papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of multi-head attention expressivity, relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
papers.tldr: This work formally characterizes the head complexity of Boolean functions in a one-layer attention-only transformer and demonstrates model-assisted, machine-verified theorem discovery.

papers.abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.
authors: Wei Gao, Cheng Tian, Duan Yang, Jianqing Yin
bullets: Coverage depends on a sufficiently trained backbone, full-width readout, and trainable gates; table capacity is not the limiting factor.
At fixed budget, coverage drops from 98% for 50 facts to 12.7% for 1,000, consistent with load-related interference.
Two-hop composition shows no meaningful synergy beyond independent retrieval: 26% observed versus 25% expected, with a 15% distortion floor.
A 28-point gap between given and recalled intermediates localizes the main failure to retrieval-for-reasoning rather than memory access.
The study recommends reporting coverage, synergy, and distortion, and explicitly chaining stored atoms for multi-constraint queries; the mechanism of load interference remains open.

papers.abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content. Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.
authors: Kehan Lan, Kaining Ying, Henghui Ding, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Covers six tasks in two directions: inferring spaces from events and retrieving events from spaces or trajectories.
SENRI-Bench contains 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions from about 25.3 hours of uninterrupted self-recorded video.
Evaluates direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory; all remain challenging.
SENRI-Agent uses Target-Guided Visual Check with parallel verifiers and working memory to address evidence gaps.
Improves existing memory-system baselines without changing their stored memories.

papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
authors: Jize Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Xinyi Le, Cailian Chen, Xinping Guan, Dacheng Tao
bullets: JEPAs are evolving into latent world models for prediction, planning, and control, but their internal states lack human-interpretable interfaces.
Interpretability should examine how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally influence predictions—not only what they encode.
The proposed four-stage agenda is Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act.
Existing work offers initial evidence for Ground, while latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remain largely unexplored.
The scope is a research agenda and perspective rather than a reported empirical evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Evolution and positioning of interpretability for latent-space world models. Despite rapid advances in latent-space world modeling and a rich XAI toolbox, direct interpretation of learned world models remains sparse. Existing efforts largely focus on latent-content probing or isolated analysis and intervention techniques, leaving systematic understanding of latent worlds underexplored.

Figure 2. From decoding representations to understanding late t worlds. The proposed blueprint progresses through four stages: Ground connects latent factors to interpretable world variables; Structure recovers their relations and dynamics; Verify tests their causal roles through controlled interventions; and Act uses verified understanding to diagnose failures and improve model behavior.

Figure 3. Cross-domain instantiations of latent worlds. Representative JEPA-based models across robot manipulation, 3D localization, medical care, and scientific discovery illustrate how relevant world variables, relations, and dynamics depend on the application domain. Latent-world interpretation therefore requires grounding representations in domain-specific concepts and interactions rather than assuming a universal set of interpretable features.

Table 1. Representative work related to latent-world interpretability, mapped onto the proposed Ground, Structure, Verify, Act blueprint. We focus on work that directly analyzes the representations, dynamics, or causal mechanisms of learned world models, with particular emphasis on JEPAs. ✓ explicit coverage; ◦ partial coverage; × not addressed.

papers.selection_reason: Perspective on interpretability of latent world models, directly aligned with world model research.
papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
papers.tldr: This Perspective proposes shifting JEPA interpretability from decoding representations to understanding, validating, and acting on the latent worlds that drive prediction and control.

papers.abstract: Existing motion transfer methods excel at exact, rigid motion replication from reference videos to target scenes, whereas they often fail to account for the compatibility between the transferred motion and the target scene environment in accordance with physical laws. In this work, we propose MotionShift, a novel motion transfer framework that achieves high-fidelity motion transfer while ensuring physical compatibility with the target scene. In particular, we design a planner--evaluator iterative motion adaptation mechanism, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) acts as the planner to generate motion trajectories by leveraging its strong semantic reasoning capabilities, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) serves as the evaluator to rectify the motion based on its superior visual perception and scene understanding. Through this planner--evaluator synergistic reasoning process, the motion is adapted to the target scene in a training-free manner. The adapted motion is then used as a generative condition for an image-to-video (I2V) model to render videos in the target scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MotionShift achieves high-fidelity and physically compatible motion transfer across diverse and complex scenes. Moreover, we show that MotionShift can be readily integrated into existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models, endowing them with realistic motion transfer capabilities.
authors: Yanchen Liu, Junyao Gao, Yanan Sun, Wensheng Chen, Guangming Lu, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical and environmental compatibility in existing reference-video motion transfer methods.
Uses an LLM planner to generate motion trajectories and a VLM evaluator to visually assess and rectify them.
Iteratively adapts motion to the target scene without additional training.
Feeds the adapted motion as conditioning to an image-to-video model for target-scene rendering.
Experiments report realistic, physically compatible transfer across diverse complex scenes and integration with existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MotionShift. Given a reference video and a target image, we first initialize a motion trajectory for the target scene. Then, through planner–evaluator iterative adaptation, we refine the trajectory to produce an environment-compatible trajectory and a corresponding motion prompt. Finally, these are progressively rendered into the output video: a motion generation model converts the trajectory into a semantic mask sequence, and an appearance rendering model synthesizes the final video from the masks and target image.

Fig. 5. Visual comparison with baseline methods. MotionShift exhibits superior motion consistency and environmental adaptability, accurately capturing perspective variations, realistic reflections, and synchronized hand movements compared to baseline approaches.

Fig. 4. Illustration of Planner–Evaluator Iterative Adaptation. At the beginning of each iteration, we leverage the semantic reasoning capability of the planner (LLM) to infer object–environment interactions and perform detailed motion planning along the given trajectory, producing a corrected motion trajectory. We then construct a pseudo video based on the target image and the corrected trajectory, and feed it to the evaluator (VLM) to assess visual consistency and physical plausibility, which then outputs revision suggestions. These suggestions are then appended to the planner’s instruction prompt, and we iteratively refine the motion trajectory until the evaluator detects no major issues.
Fig. 9. Visual results of Go-with-the-Flow using the initial trajectory vs. the environment-compatible trajectory produced by MotionShift as a plugin.
Fig. 3. Illustration of environment-compatible motion transfer, where identical reference motions adapt naturally to different scenes, yielding contextually consistent behaviors.
Fig. 7. Ablation on planner–evaluator adaptation. We compare variants by disabling adaptation, removing the evaluator, or replacing the planner.
TABLE I QUANTITATIVE COMPARISON. OUR METHOD SIGNIFICANTLY OUTPERFORMS THE OTHER LEADING METHODS.

papers.selection_reason: LLM/VLM planner-evaluator motion transfer for image-to-video generation, enabling physically compatible motion in target scenes.
papers.title: MotionShift: Environment-Compatible Motion Transfer via Planner-Evaluator Synergistic Adaptation
papers.tldr: MotionShift enables high-fidelity motion transfer that adapts to target-scene constraints through training-free planner–evaluator reasoning.

papers.abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
authors: Jiaxi Jiang, Matthias Heyrman, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz
bullets: Addresses missing robot proprioceptive data caused by privacy, ownership, or communication constraints.
Combines pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics to predict embodiment-specific joint configurations.
Uses synthetic human-to-robot motion retargeting across 16 humanoid embodiments and self-training on unlabeled online videos.
Improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over evaluated baselines, reducing joint-angle error by 18–32% across three real humanoid platforms.
Demonstrates improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments.

(b) Pseudo-labels from unlabeled online videos adapt the detector through self-training. The pose decoder is trained solely on synthetic data.

papers.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases on our benchmark between July and September 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by a factor of 4.4 and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
authors: Christopher Leet, Achyutha Menon, Sravanthi Machcha, Sven Koenig, Tzu Kit Chan, Jay Chooi
bullets: Evaluates seven models across six RoboDojo manipulation tasks on physical robotic hardware.

The findings suggest general-purpose embodied models could eventually approach specialized robotics systems, with associated safety risks.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.
authors: Yushi Lan, Zeren Jiang, Koichi Namekata, Xingang Pan, Chuanxia Zheng, Andrea Vedaldi
bullets: Addresses monocular video synthesis along new camera trajectories with newly visible content.
Builds a holistic 4D scaffold from reconstructed 3D scene trajectories and motion.
Projects scaffold geometry and source appearance into target views to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Uses source video and target cameras to ground generation in observations while delegating unsupported regions to the generative prior.
Experiments show trajectory-based conditioning improves camera control and novel-view synthesis; the generator requires no retraining for different reconstructors.

papers.tldr: Holo4D combines feed-forward 4D reconstruction with video diffusion to generate novel-camera videos while preserving observed geometry and plausibly completing unseen regions.

papers.abstract: Camera-conditioned video diffusion models often suffer from inaccurate camera control and geometric inconsisten- cies because camera constraints and estimated geometry are only weakly enforced during denoising. Existing reme- dies often require costly geometry-aware fine-tuning or ad- ditional 3D supervision. We introduce GeoART, a training- free self-refinement framework that improves camera con- trollability through geometry-aware test-time scaling. At selected denoising steps, GeoART generates multiple can- didates within the Predict-and-Perturb cycle and eval- uates them using a geometry prior, without directly modify- ing the denoising trajectory. A confidence gate suppresses unreliable geometric evidence, while rank-calibrated prob- abilistic selection combines score magnitude and relative rank to choose the next refinement state. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in camera controlla- bility, multi-view consistency, and visual quality over exist- ing sampling and self-refinement methods, without training or modifying the pretrained video diffusion model
authors: Liudi Yang, Ziyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses weak enforcement of camera constraints and estimated geometry during denoising.
Generates and evaluates multiple candidates at selected denoising steps within a Predict-and-Perturb cycle.
Uses a confidence gate to suppress unreliable geometry signals.
Applies rank-calibrated probabilistic selection to combine score magnitude and relative rank.
Reported experiments show consistent gains in camera controllability, multi-view consistency, and visual quality without modifying or retraining the pretrained model.

papers.abstract: In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.
authors: Boxin Bu, Simon Boche, Haoming Zhang, Jaehyung Jung, Jiaxin Wei, Hannah Schieber, Daniel Roth, Angela P. Schoellig, Stefan Leutenegger
bullets: Targets scalable visual mapping for autonomous navigation with both geometric awareness and high-fidelity appearance.
Anchors 3D Gaussian primitives to occupancy submaps, applies pose corrections, and optimizes only active submaps to limit GPU memory use.
Introduces a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation for online primitive sensitivity estimation, Gaussian pruning, and next-best-view planning.
Demonstrates high-quality real-time mapping on public datasets and real-world drone flights, including autonomous exploration for map refinement.
Scope: evaluated for visual-inertial SLAM-based mapping and drone exploration; quantitative performance details are not provided in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
authors: Hans Peter Lyngs{\o}e Raaschou-jensen (University of Copenhagen), M. Onurcan Kaya (Technical University of Denmark), Desmond Elliott (University of Copenhagen)
bullets: Addresses the limitation that parallel scaling streams reason independently and cannot share discoveries during processing.
Introduces an attention mechanism for sparse information exchange among parallel sequence streams.
Evaluated on a Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmark, pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks.
Masked pretraining beats an unmasked single-sequence baseline, while fact-retrieval performance remains unclear.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
authors: Yonatan Gideoni, Yoav Gelberg, Tim G. J. Rudner, Yarin Gal
bullets: Existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable.
Because the misalignment is inherent to the data, increasing model scale or alignment complexity is unlikely to eliminate it.
The misalignment induces predictable generalization failures and correlates with known VLM failure modes.
VLM backbones with better representational alignment exhibit fewer failures.
The findings challenge the strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

papers.abstract: The success of chain-of-thought (CoT) in complex reasoning can be attributed to a textual scaffolding effect: explicit intermediate results can be examined, reused, and composed to support subsequent reasoning, much as scaffolding supports a building under construction. However, mainstream multimodal LLMs lack an equivalent scaffold for visual distinctions that are difficult to express in concise verbal descriptions. We therefore ask: Can native visual representations become first-class citizens alongside language, providing a visual scaffold for reasoning? We define native multimodal reasoning as reasoning in which native visual representations and language jointly carry reusable intermediate states. As a concrete implementation, the visual scaffolding mechanism we proposed lets the MLLM autonomously initiate a retrieval action at any reasoning step. A lightweight retriever selects native visual features, which are then incorporated directly into the evolving CoT and remain available to subsequent steps. To evaluate this mechanism under controlled visual demands, we introduce NMR-Bench, comprising Burden Counting and Path Tracing. With 88M added parameters (approximately 2%) on Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, our model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy, respectively, surpassing the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines. Controlled interventions show that changing selected visual content affects task accuracy and can redirect subsequent visual selection even when intervening text is held fixed. These findings show that native visual states can function as intermediate reasoning material and point toward reusable scaffolds for additional modalities.
authors: Run Shao, Zhaoyang Zhang, Ziyu Li, Linrui Xu, Ji Qi, Xiu Su, Yichao Cao, Chao Tao, Haifeng Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of reusable visual intermediate states in mainstream multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces a mechanism that autonomously retrieves native visual features during reasoning and incorporates them into the evolving CoT.
Presents NMR-Bench with Burden Counting and Path Tracing to evaluate controlled visual demands.
With 88M added parameters, the model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy and surpasses the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines.
Interventions show that selected visual content influences accuracy and later visual selection, supporting native visual states as reasoning material.

(b) During inference, the model initiates each request and selects the features inserted before generation resumes. Training allows up to 64 evidence tokens per request; the main evaluation caps predicted selections at 8.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis under trajectory changes is essential for autonomous driving simulation, yet existing methods struggle to generate consistent videos when extrapolating to unseen viewpoints such as lane shifts. Reconstruction-based approaches maintain geometric consistency but degrade in visual quality under large viewpoint changes, while reconstruct-then-restore methods often produce visually plausible frames yet suffer from geometric and temporal inconsistencies. We present GeoV2V, a geometry-grounded video-to-video diffusion framework that synthesizes temporally coherent driving videos along novel trajectories by integrating LiDAR and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 backbone. A key challenge in learning cross-lane transformations is the lack of synchronized multi-trajectory supervision in real-world datasets. To address this, we also introduce Para4D, a synthetic dataset capturing synchronized multi-lane driving videos within dynamic scenes, which provides explicit supervision for lane-shift generation and serves as a strong training prior for geometry-consistent view synthesis. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics under large trajectory shifts. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/
authors: Yuchen Xi, Yuhan Guo, Chenwei Hou, Zixu Liu, Jin Fang, Jason Liu, Ruigang Yang
bullets: Targets novel-view synthesis for autonomous-driving simulation under large trajectory changes.
Uses LiDAR- and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 video diffusion backbone.
Introduces Para4D, a synthetic dataset with synchronized multi-lane driving videos for explicit lane-shift supervision.
Evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D show strong visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics.
Scope: the method addresses trajectory extrapolation, especially cross-lane transformations, where real-world synchronized supervision is limited.
