papers.abstract: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.
authors: Yulin Dai, Yuqian Fu, Tianwen Qian, Zhen Xing, Bojia Zi, Xiaoling Wang
bullets: Reframes embodied navigation video generation as bird’s-eye-view (BEV) map-to-video synthesis.
Provides a benchmark and dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes.
Pairs egocentric videos with BEV maps, camera trajectories, and language instructions.
Uses a unified multi-signal control framework with curriculum training that supports full conditioning or map-only inference.
Experiments across multiple foundation video-generation models show BEV-map control is viable for navigation video generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the framework and training strategy. (Top) Architecture: We adopt a hybrid condition injection on a DiT-based backbone. Instruction q and the first frame x0 are injected through the model’s native pathways, while camera trajectory τ and BEV map m are encoded via Plücker embeddings and temporal broadcasting with a VAE Encoder, respectively, and then fused via a fusion layer. (Bottom) Training: A progressive masking schedule gradually weakens non-map conditions, with modality-specific designs.

Fig. 2: Overview of the benchmark. It consists of three components: (1) Data Construction: synchronized multimodal data collection in the Habitat simulator. (2) Dataset Statistics: covering diverse scene semantics and a wide range of navigation distances, highlighting both the diversity and scale of the benchmark. (3) Evaluation Metrics: comprehensive assessment along two complementary dimensions, visual fidelity and geometric consistency.

Fig. 4: Quantitative comparison of training strategies. We compare our method with four ablation variants: w/o Aggressive Masking, Constant Masking, w/o Warmup, and w/o Fusion. The results demonstrate that our proposed curriculum strategy significantly improves geometric alignment without compromising visual quality compared to the baselines.

papers.tldr: Map2Vid introduces BEV-map-controlled video generation to make embodied navigation videos more intuitive to specify and evaluate.

papers.abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20--30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10--15%.
authors: Zixuan Qin, Qi Qin, Erbo Li, Ting Wei, Yifan Sun, Zhaoxin Fan
bullets: Targets costly expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources for domain adaptation.
Progressive Candidate Expansion iteratively selects unlabeled examples for annotation using a hidden-state proxy.
Exact Cartography Pruning ranks annotated candidates by exact training-dynamics scores to form the final subset.
Across medical, legal, and financial domains, it reports the highest average accuracy among budgeted baselines.
Uses annotation for 20–30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on 10–15%.

papers.title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: Hidden Cartographer uses hidden-state-guided annotation followed by training-dynamics-based pruning to select effective instruction-tuning data under separate annotation and fine-tuning budgets.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.
authors: Haotian Gan, Yudong Li, Xintian Li, Jiarui Han, Weidong Tang
bullets: Addresses hidden failures on subtle findings and overlapping conditions caused by linguistic shortcuts and modality imbalance.

Analyses indicate the selected data increases image-dependent learning and reliance on image-level and evidence-region information.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory turns prior interactions into durable agent state, but existing systems provide limited control over whether that state remains valid and whether it should influence a later query. We argue that reliable memory requires governance over both state formation and query-time influence. We introduce PLACE, a factorized governance layer that adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization to a memory backend. A factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates the contribution of each mechanism. Results show that write-side governance substantially improves lifecycle state correctness, while read-side governance eliminates measured causal leakage from ineligible memory in the state-correct setting. Their combination achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support. These findings show that reliable persistent memory requires explicit control over both maintained state and query-time information influence.
authors: Chen-Fang Hu, Hong-Han Shuai, Woan-Shiuan Chien
bullets: Targets two gaps in persistent memory: invalid lifecycle state and unauthorized query-time influence.
Adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization as separate governance mechanisms.
Factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates each mechanism’s effect.
Write governance improves lifecycle state correctness; read governance eliminates measured causal leakage in the state-correct setting.
Combining both achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support.

papers.tldr: PLACE makes persistent-memory agents more reliable by governing both which memories are retained and which are allowed to influence each query.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in sequential deep learning arises from a fixed-capacity architectural constraint: parameter updates encoding new tasks perturb weight subspaces supporting prior representations. We introduce the Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN), which mitigates the stability-plasticity trade-off in class-incremental learning through novelty-gated structural expansion rather than parameter negotiation within a shared capacity budget. KFN decouples task acquisition from knowledge consolidation: each incoming task is learned in an isolated lightweight specialist network (2.8M parameters) and integrated into the global model via a Structural Fusion Module that allocates dedicated channel capacity conditioned on a quantitative novelty score. Dual structural isolation--channel-space separation with temporally phased gradient unfreezing--protects consolidated knowledge. On ten-task Split CIFAR-100, KFN achieves 11.94% minimum task accuracy and 71.16% task-10 accuracy, whereas shared-parameter baselines degrade severely: LwF to 9.07% average accuracy (0.00% min), Replay++ to 8.91% (85.08% forgetting), and Replay to 16.21% (73.44% forgetting); KFN's forgetting (57.92%) is 15.5 pp lower than Replay. Furthermore, KFN prevents logit-scale drift, maintaining near-symmetric task performance. Across CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT satellite imagery, KFN's class-incremental retention (72.7% and 42.5%) substantially exceeds the best baselines (29.6% and 0.94%). Crucially, KFN achieves parameter-efficient linear scaling, adding 25% of the base parameter count per step and requiring 25.1% of naive backbone duplication over ten tasks (28.1M vs 112.0M). With a 37.1% peak GPU memory reduction over full retraining, KFN establishes novelty-gated expansion as a practical path beyond fixed-capacity architectures.
authors: Kanishk Bakshi, Amitansu Pattanaik, Kathiravan Srinivasan
bullets: Sequential task updates can disrupt weight subspaces encoding earlier task knowledge under fixed model capacity.
Each task is learned in a lightweight specialist, then integrated through a novelty-conditioned Structural Fusion Module.
Channel separation and phased gradient unfreezing help protect consolidated representations during fusion.
On Split CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT, KFN reports substantially stronger retention than the cited baselines while reducing parameter and peak-memory growth versus naive retraining.
The approach scales linearly by adding 25% of the base parameter count per task, but forgetting is reduced rather than eliminated.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method's capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.
authors: Jianghao Yin, Lang Yu, Qianxi Yu, Qin Chen, Jie Zhou, Zhikai Lei, Liang He
bullets: Targets hallucinations involving nonexistent objects, incorrect attributes, and faulty spatial relationships.
Uses three CLIP-based LoRA visual experts specialized for objects, attributes, and inter-object relations.
Employs an instruction-aware gate to adaptively fuse multi-aspect image features.
Introduces GIFT, a manually annotated, GPT-4-independent benchmark for fine-grained hallucination evaluation.
Experiments across multiple LVLM types and sizes report reduced hallucinations, minimal inference latency, and better performance than advanced baselines.

papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting models based on spectral graph convolution offer an interpretable account of how information is mixed between sensors, but they rely on an eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian. It costs cubic time, is fixed by the road network, and provides a symmetric operator that cannot represent the directed propagation of traffic congestion. Attention-based spatio-temporal transformers remove these limitations but generate a dense sensor-by-sensor attention map at each layer and time step, so memory, rather than accuracy, becomes the binding constraint on large networks. We introduce the spectral adaptive graph transformer, whose spatial operator is learned rather than derived from the Laplacian, directed rather than symmetric, and conditioned on the current traffic state rather than a static state, at a cost linear in the number of sensors. A sparse road graph diffusion branch provides the strictly local propagation that a low-rank operator cannot express, and a zero-initialized gate learns the balance between the two. Before spatial mixing, a unit-mean-gain frequency-bin attention module reweights each sensor's short-term periodicities according to its identity and current context. Across six public benchmarks spanning 170 to 1843 sensors, evaluated over three random seeds, the proposed model attains the lowest error of any single end-to-end model on one benchmark and remains competitive with the strongest current attention models on the others, while using about a quarter of their memory and training about twice as fast.
authors: Amirhossein Ghaffari, Susanna Pirttikangas, Ekaterina Gilman
bullets: Addresses cubic eigendecomposition costs, static symmetric propagation, and dense attention memory demands.
Learns a directed, traffic-state-conditioned spatial operator with linear scaling in the number of sensors.
Combines low-rank global propagation with sparse road-graph diffusion through a zero-initialized balancing gate.
Reweights each sensor’s short-term periodicities using context- and identity-dependent frequency-bin attention.

Across six benchmarks, achieves the best single-model error on one benchmark, competitive results elsewhere, about one-quarter the memory use, and roughly twice the training speed of strong attention models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a learned low-rank spatial operator plus sparse diffusion to replace dense attention, reducing memory and compute for spatio-temporal forecasting.
papers.title: Spectral Adaptive Graph Transformer for Efficient and Scalable Traffic Forecasting
papers.tldr: A scalable traffic forecasting transformer replaces costly spectral decomposition and dense attention with state-adaptive directed low-rank mixing plus sparse local diffusion, reducing resource use while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test-time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross-model average final checklist score over the reference is $1.51\times$ that of TIR prompt refinement and $1.81\times$ that of Dynamic CFG.
authors: Shuo Xu, Hanrui Ying, Debin Liu, Jianjun Li, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Addresses test-time optimization when existing generations contain errors from noise, prompts, or trajectory deviations.
Converts output-level reflection into corrective interventions during the image sampling process.
Adapts interventions at each sampling step and evaluates generated candidates against a reference.
Under matched additional-generation budgets, achieves larger checklist-score gains than TIR prompt refinement and Dynamic CFG.
Scope: focuses on fine-grained rectification starting from an existing base trajectory and reflection.

papers.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.
authors: Xiaoyu Wu, Zhaoxin Yu, Xinglin Xiao, Nan Xu
bullets: Addresses the cost of expert-designed problems and hallucination risks in LLM-generated supervision.
Uses reusable physical formulas and applicability conditions to control laws, scenarios, and numerical configurations.
Executes reference solutions before problem generation, grounding answers for SFT and reinforcement learning.
Produces TIRE-19k across nine physics subfields; it outperforms five equal-sized datasets across three LLM backbones and four benchmarks.
Further GRPO improves Qwen3-8B accuracy over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird's-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE.
authors: Zeqi Li, Xunyi Zhao, Zerui Li, Sihao Lin, Qi Wu, ShiJie Li
bullets: Small models show useful visual goal judgment but unreliable route reasoning, distance estimation, and stopping decisions.
The agent asks directional and stopping questions, plus a gated route query, and treats responses as evidence rather than actions.
A bird’s-eye semantic field, skeleton graph, geodesic frontiers, and a two-stage terminator convert these signals into navigation behavior.
It outperforms four zero-shot baselines on both VLNVerse evaluation granularities, although the interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero.
Termination is the main ablation lever; additional navigation queries provide no reliable gain, and the system runs on a Unitree Go2 with off-board inference.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. One navigation step in four lanes. Inputs (grey): the instruction, twelve RGB views, the matching depth views and the pose. The model (orange): a five-point sector score per view, a stop vote on the best-scoring view and, on route-bearing instructions, a gated chain-of-thought query over the frontier list. Structure (blue): depth becomes a range scan and an occupancy map, the map a skeleton graph with frontier nodes, and the sector scores a route-blind belief field; the proposal enters the field through a gate closed on coarse-grained instructions, and a utility over the waypoint candidates picks the move. The terminator (green): a vote is accepted only within a tolerance δ of the best trail score; otherwise the agent walks back to that position when the budget runs short. The model, structure and terminator panels and the strip below them are real data from one fine-grained episode.

papers.title: Structure over Reasoning: Unified Zero-Shot Navigation with a Small Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: A small vision-language model can support zero-shot navigation when structured mapping, frontier planning, and reliable termination—not direct action selection—handle route reasoning.

papers.abstract: Memory serves as the core component of LLM-based agents, enabling personalized responses via extracting and using user preferences from past interactions. However, its use may reduce response diversity, thereby narrowing the range of information available to users. Existing evaluations rely largely on synthetic interactions and cover few memory systems, leaving the effects of memory on response diversity insufficiently evaluated in real-world scenarios. We introduce MemBubble, a benchmark of 1000 instances built on preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations. To measure the extent to which memory concentrates response distributions, we construct test queries in scenarios distinct from user preferences while preserving topical relevance through shared preference categories. Across multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms, entropy decreases by 34.7% on average compared with directly providing the full interaction history, highlighting the important role of memory processing in diversity loss. We also explore simple user-side interventions and changes in information availability but find that these do not effectively close the diversity gap. Our findings highlight the need to consider preserving diversity and user access to information alongside improvements in personalization when designing and using agent memory systems.
authors: Jiajun Tan, Fei Sun, Xinyu Ma, Shixuan Zhang, Du Su, Qi Cao, Daiting Shi, Huawei Shen, Xueqi Cheng
bullets: Introduces a 1,000-instance benchmark built from preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations.
Tests queries that are topically related to user preferences but distinct from the original preference scenarios.
Evaluates multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms by measuring response-distribution entropy.
Memory reduces entropy by 34.7% on average versus providing the full interaction history.
Simple user-side interventions and increased information availability do not eliminate the diversity gap.

papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.
authors: Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang, Kai Mei, Riyang Bao, Shichao Zhu, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses redundant, harmful, or internalized skills and unreliable attribution from co-retrieval and task confounding.
Uses randomized skill injection and within-group contrasts in GRPO to estimate each skill’s contribution.
Tracks both skill utility as external scaffolding and model mastery of the corresponding capability.
Applies evidence-gated transitions for skill admission, incubation, retention, retirement, and removal, with a soft library-capacity bound.
Outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluations; analyses show skill values shift during learning.

papers.abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. This non-locality of invalidation turns memory into a liability: in long simulated chats, an agent reading a memory of atomic facts publishes 62% of the objects whose failure lies upstream, each backed by a record that was true when written. Yet derivation is local even when invalidation is not. Tether records, at write time, the exact versions each verdict derives from, and at read time withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store; the agent reads the same fields as before. On Fallout, a generator of versioned worlds with hypothesis-blind simulated histories shared by every memory, Tether publishes 0.3% of upstream-failing objects across three domains when relations are stated with their verdicts, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything. A-Mem and Graphiti re-verify most candidates (0.83-0.86 checks per candidate), which limits their savings, yet publish 9% of upstream-failing objects; Mem0 relies on memory more and publishes 42%. Flushing every verdict on any failure is as safe as Tether but costs 32% more checks. The gain over fact memory holds with three open-weight backbones and against a whole-store window. These gains depend on capturing dependencies: when relations arrive in sessions apart from their verdicts, Tether's downstream unsafe publication rate rises to 9.4-22.1%, and a weak writer that misses edges loses safety in the same way.
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang, Zhangkai Wu, Yiqun Duan, Zequn Sun, Taotao Cai, Mingkai Zheng
bullets: Problem: Stored facts can remain locally true but become unsafe after non-local dependency failures, such as key revocation.
Method: Record the exact versioned supports for each verdict and withdraw it at retrieval if any support has failed.
Result: On Fallout, upstream-failing publications fell to 0.3%, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything.
Compared with A-Mem, Graphiti, and Mem0, Tether achieved lower unsafe publication rates while requiring less re-verification.
Scope: Safety degrades when dependencies and verdicts arrive far apart or the memory writer misses dependency edges.

papers.tldr: Dependency-tethered memory lets tool-using agents invalidate stale verdicts when upstream premises fail, sharply reducing unsafe publications while avoiding full re-verification.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.
authors: Yiming Xu, Qian Yang, Zihan Chen, Yuefei Wu, Wenhan Zeng, Bin Shi, Bo Dong
bullets: Existing memory valuation based on retrieval success can miss context dependence and uncertainty from limited evidence.
BEAM evaluates each memory through a parameterized cognitive inference process conditioned on the current task.
Execution feedback serves as empirical evidence to continuously calibrate memory-value beliefs.
Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks show improved memory utilization and continual agent self-evolution.

papers.abstract: Embodied AI lacks the data-rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author; hidden validation layouts; no-feedback and inherit-only controls; tamper-evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29-8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered 150-layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78-95 of 100 but had 3-16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit-only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at USD 0.00028-0.00054 per episode; no direct-control baseline was run.
authors: Jingwen Bai, Guochao Bai, Canbo Zhang, Shuangqi Li, Minchao Hu, Weichun Huang, Shuang Liu
bullets: A strong model writes, tests, diagnoses, and repairs skills in simulation; frozen skills then run as code or with a low-cost caller.
Across 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, 4 tasks produced 7 frozen skills, while 3 failed to meet the safety gate despite extensive campaigns.
Inheritance-based repair beat from-scratch rewriting in all 8 controlled campaigns; development feedback added only a small, uncertain benefit.
Compiled skills achieved 148/150 successes without a model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller on hidden layouts.
Authoring cost was low per successful campaign, but repeated failures substantially increased cost; no direct-control baseline was run.

papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
authors: Rubin Wei, Siyuan Sun, Hao Sun, Yuliang Liu, Xiang Shi, Jiarui Wang, Junming Zhang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Addresses the cost of offline retrieval for parametric memory and the limited fusion of output-level methods.
Predicts chunk-level memory from preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings as supervision.
Fuses predicted memory into intermediate hidden states through gated cross-attention shared across chunk tokens.
Trains the memory module end to end while keeping the backbone frozen; inference requires no explicit retrieval.
Reports improvements across six QA tasks and gains for domain adaptation, alongside 32× fewer queries and 2048× fewer retrieved items for training-data construction.

papers.abstract: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.
authors: Pranav Singh, Prashant Singh
bullets: Studies fixed-length retention paired with an immutable archive under worst-case read limits.
Characterizes one-bit-read memory cells and gives encoders covering all possible records.
Shows that supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query.
For multiple reads, combines explicit encoders, decision-tree counting, and entropy-based lower bounds; word-read bounds are nearly tight.
Dialogue-agent experiments show that task-specific sufficient statistics or indexes can reduce private storage and decoding latency, with trade-offs in shared storage.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.
authors: Hui Yang, Wan Tian, Tao Ren, Zhongyi Li, Yijie Peng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between token-level clipping and response-level rewards, plus fixed clipping bands that fail to adapt as score distributions evolve.
Uses recent training statistics and conformal prediction to set sequence-level clipping bounds for a target marginal tail budget.
Provides bounds on out-of-band probability, with terms for target miscoverage, CDF discrepancy, and policy drift.
Under additional moment assumptions, also bounds objective and gradient errors relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate.
Experiments on Qwen3-1.7B models report improvements over GSPO on difficult math reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}
authors: Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the video reference gap between language-based reasoning and visual evidence across frames.
Builds a chronological chain of video primitives linking entity references with temporal support and spatial evidence.
Uses selected primitives to generate box prompts and temporal guidance for video mask prediction.
Trains the representation with supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning.
Shows strong performance across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones.

Figure 3: Chain-aligned training and mask execution. The policy generates multiple serialized TCoVP completions. papers.abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.
authors: Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Addresses the decoding latency caused by sequential dependencies in looped language models.
Uses a prediction slot for the current token and a latent slot that prepares the next token’s deep state in parallel.
Applies a small number of Jacobi iterations during training to refine latent states across the sequence while retaining token-level parallelism.
Experiments on dense and MoE Qwen-style models report better language modeling and downstream accuracy, with high retained decoding throughput.
Scope: results are reported for the evaluated 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models and batch sizes.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Dual-Slot training and inference. 1) Parallel Training (left). The prefix processes the full sequence once, and an initial warm pass through the core produces the initial latent slots. Jacobi updates then refine the slots at all positions in parallel, with next-token loss computed only from the final prediction states. 2) Autoregressive Decoding (right). At decoding step 𝑡, the shared Loop Core processes 𝑥𝑡 and 𝑥𝑡 + ℎ𝑡−1 in one invocation. The prediction-slot output 𝑦𝑡 predicts token 𝑡 + 1, while the latent-slot output ℎ𝑡 is carried to the next step.

Figure 2 | Language modeling performance of the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models. From left to right: perplexity on Pile validation, WikiText-2 (word-level), LAMBADA-OpenAI, and LAMBADAStandard. Lower is better. Dual-Slot improves over Vanilla across all four benchmarks for both model families.

papers.abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.
authors: Lahiru Wijayasingha
bullets: Addresses diffuse attribution across near-duplicate frames in video understanding.
Masks all frames outside each candidate subset and tests whether the prediction is preserved.
Evaluated on UCF101 and Something-Something v2 with CNN- and transformer-based models.
Finds highly compact, effective subsets and links reliance on more sufficient subsets with better model performance.
Supports failure analysis, inspection of learned visual emphasis, and future training improvements.

papers.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
authors: Jiaqi Su, Guibin Zhang, Jie-Jing Shao, Cong Pang, Tiankuo Yao, Ivor Tsang, Haiyan Yin, Shuicheng Yan
bullets: Addresses brain–body mismatch: harnesses may demand unlearned behaviors or constrain existing model capabilities.
Uses a shared evolutionary archive, execution feedback, and a meta-agent to coordinate harness evolution with model checkpoint selection or merging.
Adapts selected models under evolving harnesses using only supervised fine-tuning on self-generated rejection-sampled trajectories.
Reports competitiveness with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following.
Exceeds cited baselines on TraceElephant and HomeBench VM, supporting the importance of brain–body alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CoEvo-RSI. Left: The Curator draws on archived designs, checkpoints, and outcomes to guide evolution. Center: Harness editors choose historical harness bases; checkpoint selection or merging supplies the paired models. Right: Each round evaluates candidate pairs, tracks TIMR, adapts the selected model to its harness, and promotes improvements by validation performance. Outcomes return to the archive.

Figure 4: Co-evolution on Who&When Algo. Dashed/solid curves show AA/SA, and marker labels give TIMR (%). Panels show harnesses at rounds 6–8. papers.abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
authors: Yiqin Hao, Boyi Zeng, Zitong Wang, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Targets stronger reasoning for mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents without adding model layers or substantial test-time computation.
Adds the previous token’s deep hidden state to the current token’s shallow representation, creating cross-token depth recurrence.
Trains the recurrence with parallel Jacobi updates in a middle-layer core.
On 1.5B-parameter Qwen-style models, improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points with nearly unchanged decoding latency.
Also reports benefits for language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of P2N. The Transformer is divided into prefix, core, and suffix layers. Autoregressive decoding (right). At each token, the previous token’s core output is added to the current token’s prefix representation before entering the core layers. Since the previous token’s state is already available, this cross-token feedback is naturally compatible with autoregressive decoding; however, directly applying it during teacher-forced training would introduce a sequential dependency across token positions. Parallel training (left). The prefix processes the full sequence once, and an initial warm pass through the core produces the starting states. A small number of Jacobi updates then refines these states in parallel: in each iteration, the preceding iteration’s core outputs are shifted one position to the right and added to the fixed prefix representations to form the new inputs. Finally, the suffix layers are applied once to the final states to compute the language-modeling loss.

Figure 4 | Language modeling at the 1B and 1.5B scales. Perplexity of Vanilla and P2N dense models on (a) Pile validation, (b) WikiText-2, (c) LAMBADA OpenAI, and (d) LAMBADA Standard; lower is better. WikiText-2 uses word-level perplexity, and LAMBADA uses final-word perplexity. P2N uses three Jacobi updates at evaluation time. Numbers above the bars denote perplexity values. P2N achieves lower perplexity at both scales on every benchmark, indicating the effectiveness of this cross-token feedback method.

Figure 5 | Instruction-following ability. Category-wise MT-Bench scores for 1B (left) and 1.5B (right) dense models after Alpaca fine-tuning, evaluated by GPT-5.5. Each category score averages both conversation turns; legends report the overall mean across all 80 questions and both turns. P2N improves the overall score at both scales, with gains across all eight categories at 1.5B. Both panels use the same radial scale.

Figure 7 | Effect of sampling the number of Jacobi iterations. (a) Validation loss over 𝑘 = 0, . . . , 5 evaluation-time Jacobi iterations. (b) RMSE between consecutive core states, Δ𝑘, over 𝑘 = 1, . . . , 32 iterations. Random 𝐾 ∈ {2, 3} yields stable loss and state differences approaching zero, whereas fixed-𝐾 models deteriorate beyond their training iteration count.

Figure 1 | Mathematical reasoning at the 1B and 1.5B scales. At 1.5B, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy over Vanilla by 10.9 and 11.1 percentage points under zero-shot and eight-shot prompting, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of 52.2% and 65.8%.

Figure 6 | Convergence diagnostics of Jacobi iteration on the 1.5B P2N model. (a) Validation loss on 4096 eval samples under different numbers of Jacobi iterations. (b) RMSE between consecutive core states, Δ𝑘 = ∥𝐻 (𝑘) − 𝐻 (𝑘−1) ∥F/ √ 𝑇𝑑. (c) RMSE between Jacobi and sequential core states, 𝑑𝑘 = ∥𝐻 (𝑘) −𝐻seq∥F/ √ 𝑇𝑑. Validation loss quickly stabilizes, while both state errors continue decreasing toward zero as additional iterations are applied.

Figure 3 | Scaling behavior. (a) Final Pile validation loss across parameter scales (lower is better). (b) Pile validation loss over training tokens at the 1.5B scale (lower is better). (c) Mean zero-shot accuracy across parameter scales (higher is better). Overall, P2N exhibits consistently favorable behavior across all three scaling views.

Figure 8 | Scaling behavior of MoE models. (a) Final Pile validation loss across active parameter scales, from A0.15B to A1B. (b) Training loss over training tokens for the matched A1B models, with each point averaged over 500 consecutive optimizer steps. (c) Mean raw accuracy over all nine downstream task configurations across active parameter scales. Lower is better in panels (a) and (b), and higher is better in panel (c). P2N achieves lower final validation loss, lower training loss at the reported token budgets, and higher average downstream accuracy.

Figure 9 | Language modeling at the A0.6B and A1B scales. Perplexity of Vanilla and P2N MoE models on (a) Pile validation, (b) WikiText, (c) LAMBADA OpenAI, and (d) LAMBADA Standard; lower is better. Numbers above the bars denote perplexity values. P2N achieves lower perplexity at both scales on every benchmark, with the largest relative improvements on the LAMBADA variants.

Figure 10 | Evaluation loss under additional Jacobi iterations at the A1B MoE scale. Loss is evaluated on 4,096 examples for 𝐾 = 0, . . . , 5, where 𝐾 counts updates after the initial warm pass. After the initial reduction, evaluation loss changes only slightly as further iterations are applied.

Table 1 | Downstream performance at the 1B and 1.5B scales. Zero-shot and five-shot raw accuracy (%) of dense models. Avg. is the unweighted mean over the nine task configurations. Bold indicates the higher score within each matched scale and shot setting. P2N consistently improves average accuracy at both scales in both settings.
Table 6 | Dense model configurations. Vanilla and P2N use identical physical architectures and parameter counts. The P2N core is reported using zero-based layer indices.

Table 2 | Autoregressive decoding efficiency of the 1.5B dense model on a single GPU. TPOT denotes time per output token, and throughput counts generated tokens per second across the batch. Results are averaged over five paired runs generating 2,048 tokens per sequence. Rel. latency is the ratio of P2N TPOT to Vanilla TPOT. P2N maintains near-vanilla latency across batch sizes.

Table 4 | Recurrent core depth. Validation loss and estimated training compute relative to Vanilla on 600M model trained for 120B tokens. Compute ratios use the layer-based approximation 1+ 2.5𝐶/21, where 𝐶 is the number of recurrent layers. The middle-third core provides most of the gain from the 11-layer core at a lower estimated compute cost.

Table 5 | Recurrent core placement. Validation loss and loss gaps relative to Vanilla on 600M model trained for 120B tokens to ablate different seven-layer core placements. Among recurrent configurations with the same compute budget, the middle-third placement achieves the lowest loss.

Table 3 | Feedback formulation. Validation loss on 600M model trained for 120B tokens to ablate residual-scale treatments (a) and learnable mixing strategies (b). Loss gaps are measured relative to direct sum; negative values indicate improvement. Scale treatments increase loss, while learnable gates offer only small gains.

Table 8 | Downstream performance at the A0.6B and A1B scales. Raw accuracy (%) of Vanilla and P2N MoE models. Avg. denotes the unweighted mean over the nine task configurations. Bold indicates the best score within each matched scale, including ties. P2N improves average accuracy at both scales.

Table 9 | Mathematical reasoning at the A1B MoE scale. GSM8K test strict final-answer EM (%) under zero-shot and eight-shot prompting after supervised fine-tuning. Gains are measured in percentage points relative to Vanilla and calculated before rounding. P2N improves accuracy in both settings.

papers.abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.
authors: Lahiru Wijayasingha
bullets: Extracts keyframes conditioned on the model’s prediction.
Represents videos with few keyframes without changing the model’s belief.
Uses game-theoretic Shapley values to distribute importance fairly across keyframes.
Experiments show keyframe attribution outperforms traditional frame attribution.
Also explores highlighting important changes between adjacent keyframes.

papers.abstract: Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured. The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at 25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat's 33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the GPU's time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training accelerator.
authors: Que Haohua, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets GPU-dependent scene memories for resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles.
Co-designs an INT16 scene-coordinate regression accelerator and a fixed-point, bit-exact ordered 3DGS renderer for the AMD KR260.
Preserves DSAC* localization accuracy with 25.42 ms latency and achieves 34.11 dB on Cambridge and 27.84 dB on RealEstate10K.
Outperforms the Jetson Orin NX by 1.9×–5.7× in performance per watt at roughly one-quarter the power.
On-device training matches ACEsplat quality but remains slower and less energy-efficient than GPU training.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. LENS system overview. Posed RGB frames enter the PL SCR engine, which produces scene-coordinate point clouds for CPU pose solving and Gaussian initialization. The ARM CPU performs pose solving and tiling, while the PL LSE render engine rasterizes fixed-point Gaussian streams for reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. All outputs are board-measured on the KR260.

Fig. 3. Qualitative reconstruction rendering on all ten Wayspots scenes. Each scene shows the ground truth and the LENS integer render (bit-exact to the emulator), with the board PSNR overlaid. Every scene exceeds the 29.11 dB ACEsplat average.

Fig. 5. Analysis. (a) Integer precision recipe on ShopFacade; the 4096-entry covariance LUT is the dominant lever and the final configuration (star) clears the ACEsplat PSNR. (b) Stream compaction removes 24 to 60 percent of streamed Gaussians per scene with no change to any output bit. papers.abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.
authors: Vahid Jebraeeli, Jonathon Romero, Yijin Wang, Adrian Chan, Jianbang Zhang
bullets: The study examines ten guardrail models trained with identical architectures and optimization families but two different operational definitions of “unsafe.”
Many benchmark prompts were already present in training data, including 88% of JailbreakBench-benign and 82% of OR-Bench-hard; analyses were otherwise decontaminated.
Benchmark outcomes varied dramatically by labeling policy: HarmBench-copyright ranged from 0–100, while OR-Bench-hard over-refusal ranged from 3.4–56.4%, despite unchanged detection capability.
Only 0.03% of parameters and teacher soft-label provenance were sufficient to shift benchmark scores across their range, making checkpoint lineage a potential confound.
The authors recommend reporting benchmark contamination, a seed floor, and the policy definition used for grading.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Two audits of one safety suite, benchmarks ordered by (b). (a) how much of each benchmark was already inside the guardrail’s own training or validation data: the two most contaminated are over-refusal benchmarks, in red (§3). Exact match only, so a lower bound. (b) the range of each benchmark’s score across the ten label-source arms, on decontaminated subsets, at fixed architecture, averaged over the two model scales; n is the clean prompt count. The grey band is the seed-only floor Φb of §4, from the median over all 37 seed triplets to the median over the four of §4; Φb is measured on the full benchmarks, ∆b on the clean subsets (Appendix C). WildGuard-benign and SaladBench-attack do not clear their own upper edge; all fourteen clear twice the lower one. JailbreakBench-benign has 12 clean prompts and is excluded from (b) and from every aggregate.

Figure 5: (a) the deployment frontier: over-refusal against detection, bubble area proportional to parameters. Ours are two single arms selected on these same benchmarks, E8 at 149M and E10 at 395M; the grey points are the other nine 149M arms (catch 80.0 to 89.1, over-refusal 4.5 to 29.8). Both dashed arrows move one contested class and retrain nothing: in orange, the 8B guard’s Controversial verdict counted unsafe, which is that vendor’s strict mode, 29.7 to 48.5; in blue, our own BOUNDARY_SAFE counted unsafe, 5.7 to 96.0, with catch 91.1 to 97.2. Our convention is worth 90.3 points where the one we criticise is worth 18.8. The Qwen3Guard points are its loose mode. (b) one benchmark, six systems, 75 identical prompts: whether reproducing copyrighted text counts as harm is a taxonomy decision, and these systems made different ones.

Figure 1: The guardrail, and the three places an operational definition can enter it. Which of the three routes actually installs a policy is the subject of §5: route 1 does not, for a distilled student; routes 2 and 3 do, the last by re-fitting 0.03% of the parameters.

Figure 3: Accuracy on the one policy-A split that grades all 20 arms, against the two things it might be measuring. It tracks agreement with the annotator’s policy more closely than detection capability, though at n=20 neither association is resolved on its own (Appendix A). Marker shape gives the route block, which is most of what the correlation is.

Figure 4: One 149M student, four routes to install the same policy, on decontaminated subsets. Datalevel interventions (orange) do not install policy A even when every hard label carries it; a policy-A distillation teacher or a frozen-backbone head-only pass over 0.03% of the parameters (blue) does.

Table 2: Our guardrail against current open guards [25, 22], on identical decontaminated prompts, same host. The two “Ours” rows are single arms, E8 at 149M and E10 at 395M, each selected on these same benchmarks; across our four policy-A-last 149M arms CAP spans 81.0–91.1 and OVER-REF 4.5–6.3. CAP and POLICY are means over the capability-loaded and policy-loaded sets (Appendix A); OVER-REF is the mean over the two usable benign benchmarks (JailbreakBenchbenign is excluded at 12 clean prompts); COPY is HarmBench-copyright (n=75). Bold is best in column among the main systems; COPY is deliberately unbolded, because which end of it is better is the policy choice under study. DEPLOY is on-disk size in decimal GB and mixes precisions: ours is a measured INT8 ONNX export (150.1MB, taken from the shipped 149M checkpoint, which shares E8’s architecture and 149.05M parameters), the baselines are the vendors’ released bf16 weights, and the 397MB teacher cell is extrapolated at 1.007 bytes per parameter because no teacher export exists. Latency is median over 180 single-prompt requests on one H100 and is not like-for-like either: ours is eager PyTorch on the fp32 checkpoint padded to 512 tokens, the baselines run under vLLM with CUDA graphs, and the mismatch favours the baselines. The same checkpoint under a CUDA graph runs at 6.4ms at that sequence length and 2.6ms at a 64-token bucket (the prompts median 14 tokens). Decontamination is defined by our pools only. The retained subset is harder for every system, raising OR-Bench-hard over-refusal by 3.0 points for our student, 7.4 for our teacher and 7.3–19.1 for the baselines, so the clean OR-Bench-hard gap against Qwen3Guard-8B (49.6 points) is wider than the full-benchmark gap (34.3), which is itself inflated in our favour by that benchmark’s 82% training overlap. Size-matched random subsets of the same benchmark (2,000 draws) move that gap by +0.1 points (sd 2.9), so the widening is a property of which prompts our pools contain and not of subsetting. The lower block applies one lever to every system that emits a contested verdict, with no retraining and no data: Qwen3Guard’s Controversial counted unsafe (the vendor’s strict mode, against its loose mode above) and our BOUNDARY_SAFE counted unsafe. Granite Guardian emits no third class and so has one row. COPY does not move for our arms because no arm assigns any of the 75 prompts to BOUNDARY_SAFE: 0.00% at all twenty arms, and at all 100 prompts before decontamination. OVER-REF saturates instead: under the remap all ten arms land between 97.9% and 100.0% on OR-Bench-hard at both scales, against 3.4–56.4 and 9.3–71.2 under the shipped mapping, and the policy-A-last group of §5 moves from 24.6 and 11.4 points below the rest to 0.4 points above it.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.
authors: Lei Gao, Hossein Entezari Zarch, Chaoyi Jiang, Murali Annavaram
bullets: Addresses the computation and activation-memory costs that remain in LoRA fine-tuning, especially for frozen projections.
Uses native NVFP4 GEMMs, quantized activation storage, and reuse of quantized RMSNorm outputs to reduce memory and overhead.
Preserves BF16 inputs for nonlinear operations and applies GPTQ-style offline calibration to limit quantization error.
Fuses nonlinear kernels and caches weight layouts to reduce quantization/dequantization costs.
Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on an RTX 5080 report lower memory use and faster fine-tuning with competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multiobject tracking (MOT) is a fundamental capability in autonomous navigation, radar and sonar systems, as well as 6G integrated sensing-and-communication (ISAC) networks. In this paper, we propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (TkBD) framework that operates directly on complex-valued raw signals and learns a latent representation of unmodeled propagation effects during runtime. We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. To enable scalable inference, we make use of a recently introduced Bayesian TkBD framework that combines belief propagation, which avoids high-dimensional operations, with sequential Monte Carlo methods for efficient low-dimensional updates.
authors: Shaoxiu Wei, Bhaskar Rao, Florian Meyer
bullets: Targets multiobject tracking in autonomous navigation, radar, sonar, and 6G ISAC settings.
Operates directly on complex-valued raw signals while modeling unmodeled propagation effects through a latent representation.
Represents each object’s environment-dependent signal intensity with a normalizing flow trained online and unsupervised.
Optimizes the flow using an ELBO-derived variational Bayes objective to capture inference uncertainty.
Combines belief propagation with sequential Monte Carlo for scalable Bayesian inference.
