papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.
authors: Sicheng He, Yi Pan, Qiuting Yu, Jiaming Huang, Qi Lu, Shuyan Wu, Hongyan Feng, Xuanyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Jie Zhang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Action tails retain useful denoising progress instead of being regenerated from fresh noise.
The framework combines tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided renoising/refinement.
It operates during inference with the underlying VLA model frozen.
Across 16 model–benchmark pairs, it reduces inference cost in every case, with up to 1.48× speedup.
Success rate improves in 14 pairs, by up to 15.08 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass-rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same-layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested-language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian-hoang-04/anonymous-release.
authors: Jiwon Jeong, Anjelo Jann Laroza, Chaewoon Yoon, Arjun Pillai, Pranav Kokati, Christian Hoang, Seunghyeok Hong

The identified heads also reduced Language Confusion Benchmark pass rates, though their effects weakened under mean ablation and were smaller in base models.
Replacing language-related values or head outputs could make replies fail or redirect them into another language, supporting a causal role for these heads.
Improvements for crosslingual replies over control heads appeared only in the two Gemma models, limiting the generality of that effect.

papers.tldr: A small number of attention heads strongly influence which language an LLM uses, with effects that generalize across several model families.

papers.abstract: Multi-quadrotor passage planning requires coordinated spatial routes and passage times under vehicle dynamics and actuation constraints. Optimizing these decisions jointly couples temporal allocation, nonlinear motion, and inter-vehicle interactions, creating a computational challenge for local trajectory generation. We propose a learning-optimization framework that predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor planners. A common physical time grid aligns the vehicles, with intermediate events fixed by the networks and terminal progress optimized locally to permit different completion metrics. Differentiable sequential convex programming incorporates rigid-body dynamics and rotor-thrust bounds, allowing collision and completion gradients to train both networks through the generated trajectories. In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, the adapted policy passes physical feasibility and sampled separation checks in all five held-out layouts. Their mean completion metric decreases by 1.52% relative to the inherited policy. The median forward time is 21.01 ms on the held-out exchange layout with matching numerical trajectory references. These results demonstrate that learned spatial and event parameters can coordinate independent rigid-body planners while preserving local vehicle constraints in the evaluated scenarios.
authors: Yunhan Shi, Jia Deng, Zehao Jia, Lin Cheng, Shengping Gong
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of spatial routing, passage timing, nonlinear dynamics, and inter-vehicle interactions.
Predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor trajectory planners.

In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, all five held-out layouts met physical-feasibility and sampled-separation checks.

papers.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state. We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.
authors: Zunzhi You, Linwei Tao, Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Ambient L2 terminal costs work near the goal but create misleading low-cost basins farther away.
Latent representations retain physical state while apparently lying near a curved, low-dimensional manifold.

NGC changes only the terminal cost and improves success across all four benchmark tasks, nearly solving TwoRoom and Reacher.
Scope: evidence is reported for LeWM and four benchmark tasks; NGC relies on the training-latent neighborhood graph.

papers.abstract: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Rohan Mahapatra, Christopher Priebe, Hanyang Xu, Manya Ghobadi, Christopher Rossbach, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
bullets: Targets the lost optimization opportunities when draft and target models are compiled independently despite sharing execution.
Uses an LLM-driven search loop that edits optimization plans, compiles and measures co-located execution, and applies Monte Carlo tree search to guide exploration.
Introduces interleaved operand layouts that place blocks from both models in common tiles while preserving mathematical correctness.
Across six single-GPU configurations, achieves 1.37× geometric-mean per-round speedup, rising to 1.45× with interleaved kernels and 1.59× in the best case.
Improves average GPU utilization by 1.46× on RTX 5090 and 1.50× on NVIDIA B300.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.
authors: Hyebin Kim, Hwasik Jeong, Joonhyuk Park, Gyeongjin Kang, Jungwoo Kim, Younghyun Kim, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Targets the difficulty of recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance in feed-forward 3DGS.
Uses view-wise grouping for efficient neighboring-view interaction and 3D spatial grouping to reconnect geometrically related tokens.
Uses rendering reconstruction error as explicit feedback to refine structures and appearance beyond one-pass prediction.
Generates a compact set of Gaussians to retain fine-detail benefits without unnecessarily increasing primitive counts.
Reports state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets, according to the abstract.

Compact Gaussian generation predicts fewer Gaussians per token than existing pixel-aligned methods, maintaining a compact 3DGS representation. Finally, direct error feedback incorporates reconstruction errors obtained by rendering the input views to further refine token representations.

papers.abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.
authors: Shifei Duan, Zhe Wang, Francesco De Pace, Minas Liarokapis

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu, Miao Liu, Panwang Pan, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Visual token compression can harm reasoning by permanently deleting tokens that appear unimportant in early layers.
Layer-wise analysis reveals visual backtracking: stable visual pivots later retrieve context from previously low-saliency tokens.
ReTrace adds a dormant token state, caching non-pivot tokens outside expensive computation and restoring them during a backtracking window.
Tokens are pruned only after their information has been absorbed, preserving more visual context for reasoning.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 report nearly 90% lower FLOPs and KV-cache usage, a 2.83× prefilling speedup, and strong benchmark performance retention.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overall architecture of ReTrace. ReTrace follows a cache–inject–prune schedule. (3) Post-Absorption Task Pruning removes task-irrelevant enriched pivots after context absorption.

papers.abstract: Looped large language models trade parameter storage for recurrent computation, but most are trained from scratch. In practice, pretraining with looped depth is expensive, making post-training upcycling of a pretrained non-looped LLM an attractive alternative. We introduce \textbf{UpLoop}, a post-training recipe based on \emph{layer-wise} recurrence. Instead of looping a whole model or a middle block, UpLoop loops each selected layer locally, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch. To make loop execution useful, we add hidden-wise gates on the attention and MLP residual branches, so later loops act as progressive refinements rather than redundant rewrites. Empirically, UpLoop breaks the commonly observed saturation at two loops ($R=2$) in prior looped models. Starting from Qwen3-4B Base and applying SFT, UpLoop improves the average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17\% at $R=3$. We use $R=3$ as the main setting for the best accuracy--cost trade-off, while both native and extrapolated $R=4$ yield further gains.
authors: Tieyuan Chen, Huabin Liu, Yingtao Zhang, Shijie Li, Tengyu Pan, Weiyao Lin, Jianguo Li
bullets: Addresses the high cost of pretraining looped LLMs from scratch through post-training upcycling.
Uses layer-wise recurrence, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch.
Adds hidden-wise gates to attention and MLP residual branches so later loops progressively refine representations.
On Qwen3-4B Base with SFT, improves average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17% at three loops.
Three loops offer the main accuracy–cost trade-off, while four loops provide further gains in both native and extrapolated settings.

Gating suppresses late-layer write amplification, preserves better hidden-state continuity, and still allows gradual progress toward the final representation.

Different clusters exhibit distinct round- and branch-dependent patterns, indicating that recurrent refinement is distributed non-uniformly across hidden dimensions.

papers.abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. The resulting importance score protects selected tokens as anchors and calibrates bipartite matching between the remaining tokens. Three variants use external uncertainty at both training and inference, during training only, or neither stage. In ERA5 72-hour forecasting at two spatial resolutions, UtoMe improves Overall error over train-time ToMe at matched token budgets. At $1.40625^\circ$ and 50% token reduction, UtoMe-E lowers Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at the same 0.55x encoder FLOPs. Small reductions remain close to the full-token baseline; larger reductions incur measurable accuracy losses. Component ablations and spatial uncertainty controls support combining dynamics with aligned uncertainty when allocating a weather transformer's token budget.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Janet Wang, Xi Xiao, Jihun Hamm, Xiao Wang
bullets: Weather inputs have heterogeneous reliability, which similarity-only token merging does not capture.
UtoMe combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data-assimilation spread to score token importance and protect anchor tokens.
It supports uncertainty use during both training and inference, training only, or neither.
In ERA5 72-hour forecasting, UtoMe-E reduced Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at 50% token reduction and 0.55× encoder FLOPs.
Accuracy remains near the full-token baseline for small reductions but declines at larger compression levels.

The framework supports three uncertainty-availability regimes: external uncertainty at both stages, during training only, or neither stage.

papers.abstract: Recursive Transformers depend not only on how many parameters are shared, but also on how shared parameters are organized across depth. Existing static schemes adopt two extreme reuse topologies: layer-wise repetition, where each layer is reused independently, and global cyclic reuse, where the entire stack is repeatedly applied as a single shared function. We argue that sharing granularity is an important factor in recursive parameter sharing. This study proposes Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which partition layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuse each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement within blocks while preserving depth-wise transitions, without adding routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. Across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, with additional encoder-decoder and encoder-only studies, BRT improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth-wise differentiation. Project website: https://aim-skku.github.io/BRT/
authors: Josep Marques, Hyunyoung A. Cho, Youngeun Kim, Youjia Zhang, Aecheon Jung, Kyuhong Shim, Sungeun Hong
bullets: Recursive Transformers depend on how shared parameters are organized across depth, not just how many are shared.
BRT partitions layers into contiguous blocks and recursively applies each block before progressing to the next.
The approach requires no routing modules, auxiliary states, or additional training objectives.

Experiments across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, plus encoder-decoder and encoder-only settings, show improved validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive-sharing baselines.
Ablations and representation analyses indicate that intermediate block granularity provides a better balance between local refinement and depth-wise differentiation.

papers.abstract: The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade-off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.
authors: Yongchao Long, Chunrui Zheng, Yuxuan Zhou, Guangkun Nie, Tian-Chi Ma, Chao Pang, Shuohuan Wang, Yuchen Ding, Xianbin Wen, Dianhai Yu, Junyuan Shang, Yuxi Zhou, Shenda Hong

DCore is presented as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead.
The throughput payoff depends on task uncertainty, serving conditions, drafter choice, and computation budget.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading few keys of the KV cache, but existing methods do not control the error of a query, and on real KV caches their errors have heavy tails. We show that perturbing the score of every key with an independent Exp(1) variable turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys with probability proportional to their attention weights. Lowering the threshold along a geometric grid gives nested samples, a Horvitz--Thompson estimate of the output at every level, and confidence bounds that hold simultaneously over all levels, so each head stops at the first level whose certificate meets the target error $\varepsilon$. With fresh perturbations at every decoding step, each certificate fails with probability at most $\delta$ during generation. At a suitable threshold, the estimator reads $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ values regardless of the context length, and no adaptive method reads fewer, up to constants. A 4-bit scan with deterministic bounds, shared across a grouped-query-attention group, generates the candidates exactly but reads every key. On three LLMs and ten settings at 16K--128K tokens, no certificate is violated, and at equal keys read our 90th-percentile error is 4.6--7.9$\times$ lower than that of the best of 15 baseline families. At equal bytes, the best baselines have 0.6--1.6 times our 90th-percentile error and at least 4.9 times our largest. End to end, our method stays within one point of dense attention on tasks and within 0.1\% in PG-19 perplexity, and the strongest baselines at equal bytes score as well. On CPU, decoding steps at 32K--128K tokens run 1.1--1.4$\times$ faster than dense attention on the same 16-bit cache.
authors: Runguo Li
bullets: Perturbing key scores with independent Exp(1) noise converts threshold retrieval into sampling proportional to attention weights.
Nested samples across thresholds enable Horvitz–Thompson output estimates and simultaneous confidence certificates.
Each head stops when its estimated error is below ε; with fresh perturbations, certificate failure is bounded by δ during generation.
The estimator needs O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)) reads, independent of context length, and this read complexity is optimal up to constants.
Across 16K–128K contexts, certificates were never violated; decoding was 1.1–1.4× faster than dense attention on CPU while maintaining near-dense task quality.

papers.abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.
authors: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du, Jiajun Wu, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible video predictions and actions a robot can actually execute.
Uses a hierarchical policy: a video-model-based high-level planner plus a low-level visuomotor controller.
Learns subgoal reachability and task utility from offline, action-free robot videos, selecting subgoal sequences via dynamic programming without manual annotations.
Sparse subgoals are more reliably achieved than uniformly spaced ones, and the system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners.
Achieves 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long and handles challenging real-world bimanual tasks such as box folding and packing with unseen object combinations.

papers.abstract: Checklist rubrics applied by large language model (LLM) judges have become a standard instrument for evaluating open-ended outputs and for rewarding them during training. Two assumptions surround this practice: that leniency or strictness is a property of the judge model, and that a rubric can be improved by asking a model to review it. We test both in a controlled grading task with planted flaws and on two human-labeled datasets, SummEdits and RAGTruth. Holding the judge and the outputs fixed, rubric content moves the pass rate of correct outputs from 2% to 100%, whereas changing the judge model or the rendering of the same checks moves it by a few points. Model self-review then drifts the rubric toward the reviser's own standard: it adds requirements the task never stated and deletes checks that human labels had taught, with three reviser models and on all three datasets. To measure and control this, we show that under all-must-pass aggregation the Shapley value of each check has an exact closed form, which yields per-check catch credit, false-fail blame and unique catches in linear time. Attribution shows that self-review deletes the checks that do unique work and keeps the checks that cause false fails. A change-control gate that combines these quantities with a provenance freeze on label-derived checks holds nearly every drifting revision chain at its starting quality, with identical decisions under three judge models.
authors: Saeid Asgari, Rui Ying, Sara Malvar, Rakshanda Agarwal, Bruce Sun, Claire Wang, Leonardo de Oliveira Nunes, Ranveer Chandra
bullets: In a controlled grading task, rubric content shifted correct-output pass rates from 2% to 100%, while changing the judge or check rendering had only minor effects.
Across SummEdits and RAGTruth, model self-review added unstated requirements and removed checks supported by human labels.
For all-must-pass rubrics, each check’s Shapley value has an exact closed form, enabling linear-time attribution of catch credit, false-fail blame, and unique catches.
Self-review tended to delete uniquely useful checks while retaining checks responsible for false failures.
A change-control gate using these attributions and a provenance freeze preserved nearly every revision chain’s starting quality across three judge models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Strictness on Recon-72 (24 correct, 48 flawed reports). (a) Operating point of each rubric under a Sonnet judge. Hand-written and generated checks form two clusters that rendering does not move. (b) Correct reports passed under the same rubrics by three judges, which agree within a few points except with a generic scale and a pass threshold of 5. Takeaway: what the checks ask for moves correct passed from about 4% to about 96%, while rendering and judge model move it by a few points, as claimed: strictness is set by rubric content.

Figure 4: Self-review over four rounds on Recon-108. (a) From the hand-written rubric, free revision adds requirements and correct reports stop passing. (b) From the label-taught rubric, free and fixed-count revision remove or narrow the open coverage check and unplanned misses stop being caught. Delete-only revision is flat in both. Takeaway: drift runs in opposite directions from the two starting rubrics, too strict from one and too lenient on omissions from the other, each time toward the reviser’s own idea of a good report; only the arm that cannot add requirements avoids it, consistent with the claim that self-review moves the standard rather than refining it.

Figure 2: Generic checklists of increasing length under a Sonnet judge, mean of two runs. (a) On SummEdits each added check trades a few consistent summaries passed for inconsistent ones caught. (b) On RAGTruth, going from 3 to 10 checks costs 36 points of faithful responses passed for at most 4 points of catches; the same 10 checks read as a paragraph pass 75%. Takeaway: the content effect replicates on human labels, small where generic checks rarely demand anything a correct output lacks (SummEdits) and large where they forbid the light synthesis annotators accepted (RAGTruth); RAGTruth is also the one place where rendering mattered, through the aggregator.

Figure 6: Quality of the gated rubric after four rounds of revision, scored on the 8 evaluation environments. (a) From the hand-written rubric the failure mode is strictness; (b) from the label-taught rubric it is lost coverage. Only Gate S+P stays near the starting level (dotted) in both panels. Takeaway: each single signal protects one failure direction (Gate R only what its calibration labels see, Gate P coverage, Gate S strictness), and only their combination protects both, with one exception (Sonnet’s label-taught chain) discussed in the text; this supports gating revisions check by check rather than trusting either labels or attribution alone.

Figure 3: Accuracy of three Recon rubrics as a function of the flawed share of the validation set, computed from their two rates. The generated draft has balanced accuracy 52, the level of chance, yet outscores the hand-written rubric whenever more than 80% of the set is flawed. Takeaway: accuracy on a defect-heavy validation set can rank a rubric that fails almost everything above one that works, which is why we report the two rates throughout.

Table 2: Gate replay under three judge models on all 12 Recon environments. Each cell: correct passed / flawed caught / unplanned caught (%). Takeaway: under every judge the ungated rubric collapses in the same way, and Gate S+P keeps each metric within 6 points of that judge’s own starting value, so the gate’s decisions do not depend on which model applies the rubric.

papers.title: Rubrics Carry the Standard: Shapley Attribution for Checklist-Based LLM Judges
papers.tldr: Checklist rubric content—not the LLM judge—dominates evaluation outcomes, and Shapley-based change control can prevent rubric self-review from degrading quality.

papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target-aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target-relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model-specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population-level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.
authors: Changho Lee, Janghoon Han, Rajdeep Mukherjee, Yeda Song, Lening Nick Cui, Xinya Du, Honglak Lee
bullets: Target-aware data selection uses a small reference set to specialize reasoning post-training more efficiently.
Existing gradient-matching methods can struggle to distinguish target-relevant variation in long trajectories.
DeGMatch applies a target-relevance gate, then reranks candidates with centered gradients after removing leading principal directions.
It outperforms heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific baselines across mathematics, science, and code.
The method remains effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of DeGMatch. DeGMatch constructs a target-relevant gate, deconfounds the candidate gradient geometry, and ranks candidates using target-conditioned directional alignment and target-subspace magnitude to select the final training subset.

Figure 10: Deconfounding reduces concentration on the same highly ranked candidates across targets. t-SNE visualization of the top-1K candidates selected for each of five mathematical targets under raw-gradient matching (left) and after mean-centering and removal of the top 50 candidate principal directions (right). Black points denote candidates selected by at least two targets. Raw matching yields a union of only 1,317 distinct candidates across the five top-1K subsets, of which 54.0% are selected by all five targets. After deconfounding, the union expands to 2,950 distinct candidates, of which only 2.4% are selected by all five targets. Figure 9: Dominant-component removal reveals finer target-conditioned structure in candidate rankings. Each point represents the ranking induced by a disjoint 10-example reference subset over the same fixed 30K candidate population. Quantitative target-identification results are computed in the original ranking space rather than from the two-dimensional projection.

Figure 5: Why DeGMatch removes the dominant candidate-gradient directions. (a) The raw AIME ranking is almost completely reproduced using only the dominant population component (the mean direction and top 50 centered candidate PCs), whereas (a′) the orthogonal residual alone produces a substantially different ranking. (b–b′) A length- and NLL-matched non-target reference set induces a ranking highly correlated with the AIME ranking in the raw gradient space, but this correspondence is sharply reduced after dominant-component removal. (c) The effect is specific to the leading principal directions: after population centering, removing the top 50 PCs reduces the matched-control rank correlation from 0.87 to 0.28, whereas removing 50 random directions or lower-ranked PC blocks leaves it essentially unchanged.

Figure 6: Shared gradient structure becomes more prominent with reasoning-trajectory length. The truncation analysis holds the underlying examples fixed while varying the observed response length, whereas the decile analysis measures the corresponding association in the original data.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. We introduce MemPrice, which treats active context as a shared resource and dynamically allocates it across memories and representation levels. MemPrice turns accumulated memory pressure into an adaptive price on context, encouraging detail only when its estimated retention value justifies the additional footprint. This pressure persists across memory refreshes, allowing the contents of memory to evolve while preserving long-run control over context usage. We show that irreversible compression can force linear worst-case regret against hindsight following its own memory trajectory, and introduce a same-state benchmark to evaluate allocation on MemPrice's realized memory states. MemPrice enforces the hard context budget at every round and regulates long-run occupancy through adaptive pricing, without prior knowledge of the interaction horizon. Under priced-frontier regularity, its average allocation-regret bound against this benchmark vanishes when accumulated estimation error is sublinear. We evaluate the framework under matched memory budgets on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop across three foundation models, spanning both query-blind memory construction and goal-directed agent context management.
authors: Yiming Zong, Shiyuan Piao, Jiashuo Jiang, Fugee Tsung
bullets: Addresses the growing-context trade-off between retaining information, representation granularity, and context usage.
Converts accumulated memory pressure into a price that favors additional detail only when its estimated retention value warrants the cost.
Maintains pressure across memory refreshes, enabling evolving memories while enforcing a hard context budget each round.
Introduces a same-state benchmark and shows vanishing average allocation regret under priced-frontier regularity and sublinear cumulative estimation error.
Evaluates matched-budget performance on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop with three foundation models.

papers.abstract: We present \'{E}pi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. \'{E}pi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. \'{E}pi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, \'{E}pi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with \'{E}pi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, \'{E}pi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. \'{E}pi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.
authors: Yue Huang, Zhangchen Xu, Xiaonan Luo, Zheyuan Liu, Lichi Li, Yiping Wang, Peiyang Song, Eric Gabriel Ramos, Enze Xie, Olexandr Isayev, Paul Liang, Nouha Dziri, Huan Sun, Jianfeng Gao, Ying Liu, Misha Sra, Xiangliang Zhang, Alex Pentland, Zichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining continuity and improving methods across autonomous research sessions.
Uses persistent history, hierarchical memory, branching, independent review, and a fixed output verifier.
Reports 120 record-setting mathematical results, including tighter bounds, exact dual certificates, and a computer-assisted partial result related to Tuza’s conjecture.
Its coding variant, Épi-turbo, outperformed Codex by 5.4% on 30 FrontierOR tasks while using 64% of its model cost.
Designed to expose explicit methods and mathematical arguments for human inspection and further development.

papers.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research

papers.abstract: Poisson equations frequently appear in various fields, such as mathematics, physics and informatics. Solving Poisson equation, however, is challenging. Traditional methods are not data-specific, although have high certainty. They require a large number of iterations due to the CFL numerical stability. In contrast, deep learning methods are data-driven and more efficient, but require accurate training data and suffer from heavy computation. To tackle these issues, we propose a wavelet-inspired Poisson solver with 24 trainable scalars. The proposed network has several advantages. First, it is compact. It has four independent $5\times5$ kernels, each represented by six parameters, leading to 24 scalars in total. Such compact format can be deployed on most devices. Second, thanks to the loop design, it achieves higher accuracy than previous methods. A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without increasing its parameters. Numerical experiments confirm that such loop indeed improves the solving accuracy. On 10000 images, one, two, and three loops of the wavelet block lead to PSNRs of $47.27$, $74.14$, and $100.74$ dB, respectively. Third, the proposed method is computationally fast. Thanks to the wavelet transform, the proposed method has linear computation complexity, leading to high computation performance. In short, we propose a novel looped wavelet neural network with compactness, accuracy and efficiency for solving Poisson equations. Our method can be applied in various fields, such as computational fluid dynamics, image reconstruction, biomedical engineering, electromagnetic field simulation.
authors: Yuanhao Gong
bullets: Addresses the high iteration cost of traditional Poisson solvers and the data and computation demands of deep-learning methods.
Uses four independent 5×5 wavelet-inspired kernels, each encoded by six learnable parameters.
A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without adding parameters, improving solution accuracy as loop count increases.
On 10,000 images, one, two, and three loops achieved PSNRs of 47.27, 74.14, and 100.74 dB, respectively.
Wavelet-based computation has linear complexity, supporting fast deployment across devices and application areas.

papers.abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. We show that the exact T-MUON update is a steepest-descent direction under the $\star_M$-spectral norm and establish a convergence guarantee. Across GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu, head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform consistently achieves lower validation perplexity than AdamW, Muon, and variants using DFT, DCT, or DST transforms. These gains persist in additional experiments with longer context lengths and larger token budgets, although the preferred tensorization mode varies across settings.
authors: Dongyang Li, Mingsong Yan, Zheng Zhang, Sui Tang
bullets: Groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors instead of updating parameter matrices independently.
Defines a Muon-style update through the M-transform; the exact update is a steepest-descent direction under the star_M spectral norm.
Provides a convergence guarantee for the proposed optimizer.
Head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform outperforms AdamW, Muon, and DFT-, DCT-, and DST-based variants in reported experiments.
Performance gains persist with longer contexts and larger token budgets, while the best tensorization mode varies by setting.

papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang
bullets: Targets overconfident RFF errors when receivers, distances, collection days, or environments change.
Uses a frozen I/Q classifier and requires no target-domain labels.

An LLM planner selects diagnostic actions under evidence, trust, cost, and budget constraints.
Evaluations across five datasets and classifier backbones show a 38.7% average source-to-target accuracy drop and frequent high-confidence target errors.

papers.abstract: Jev and its open replicas choose among the options a caller supplies with a single forward pass, fast enough to decide inside an agent loop. We ask what such a model cannot decide, and find a simple limit: Jev cannot make a decision that an LLM makes only by writing out intermediate steps. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. Given a stale summary of the state, Jev follows it. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.
authors: Wang Yang, Xinpeng Li, Yanyan Zhang, Chuang Ma, Shouren Wang, Jianzhe Wei, Liqin Ye, Xiaoran Cai, Mohsen Hariri, Vipin Chaudhary, Xiaotian Han
bullets: Jev selects records accurately up to 20k tokens and 64 options when only one factor changes.

Jev solves 97.5% of items solvable by a reference LLM in one pass, but only 74% of items requiring more reasoning.
Confidence detects some self-made errors but not errors inherited from stale inputs; evaluated open models show the same limits.

papers.selection_reason: Probes the limits of one-pass decision models (Jev) in terms of context length and reasoning steps. This is directly relevant to Long-Context Models and the constraints of LLM inference.
papers.title: What Can't Jev Decide? Probing the Limits of One-Pass Decision Models
papers.tldr: One-pass decision models handle simple selection well but fail when decisions require multi-step state updates or reasoning beyond their inputs.

papers.abstract: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.
authors: Sen Fang, Liwei Che, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses limited facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific deformation, and loss of fine visual detail in existing avatars.

papers.selection_reason: Presents Stable Signer V3, a system for sign language production using 4D deformable primitive splatting. This directly connects visual and language understanding to physical actions (avatar generation), fitting Vision-Language-Action and 3D Vision.
papers.title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
papers.tldr: Stable Signer V3 enables interactive, high-resolution sign-language avatars with richer expressions, more accurate signer-specific motion, and finer appearance details using 4D deformable primitive splatting.

papers.abstract: Few-shot audio classification requires audio--language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. PALM's main formulation adapts encoded class representations without changing pretrained encoders, but its class representations remain input-independent and classification uses audio features without class-conditioned refinement. We introduce DF-PALM, a dynamic feature-space prompting framework that combines audio-conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross-attention for audio refinement. Class representations are conditioned after text encoding, held fixed across fusion layers for each input, and reused for final scoring. Both pretrained encoders remain frozen, avoiding audio-conditioned text-encoder passes. With PENGI as the frozen backbone, the main 16-shot evaluation covered 11 benchmarks and six baselines. DF-PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark-level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF-PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro-averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt-learning methods. The gains extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator-counted inference floating-point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance-conditioned feature-space adaptation as an effective approach to few-shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF-PALM.
authors: Yulin Sun, Shenghua Li, Yong Dou, Xinwang Liu, Cheng Yang, Kele Xu
bullets: Addresses PALM’s input-independent class representations and lack of class-conditioned audio refinement.
Uses audio-conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross-attention in feature space; representations are reused for final scoring.
With frozen PENGI, evaluation across 11 benchmarks at 16 shots achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-F1.
Outperformed PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively, with benchmark-level statistical support after Holm correction.
Improvements extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM; inference FLOPs increased by only 0.39% at 50 candidate classes.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. We evaluated five state-of-the-art LLMs across six scientific domains and constructed Read-Aloud Math, a balanced multi-domain corpus with LaTeX formulas, manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, multiple variants, textual context, domain labels, and formula complexity levels. Using multi-reference BLEU, GPT-5.2 achieved the highest score for simple transcriptions (75.9% without context, 64.9% with context), although without context it did not significantly outperform Grok 4.1 Fast or Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the highest score for extended transcriptions without context (36.5%), and Grok 4.1 Fast with context (48.8%). For extended transcriptions, Statistics and Mathematics scored highest across the two context settings, while Physics scored lowest. Formula length was significantly negatively associated with BLEU for simple transcriptions without context, but not with context, whereas BLEU increased significantly with formula length for extended transcriptions in both settings. Grouping symbols were most frequently involved in transcription differences, while variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were associated with lower BLEU scores. Overall, LLM-based formula verbalization is promising but remains sensitive to transcription type, textual context, and formula characteristics.
authors: Peter Volbach, Tim Schlippe
bullets: The study evaluates five LLMs across six scientific domains for spoken-style formula transcription.
It introduces Read-Aloud Math, a balanced corpus with validated simple and extended transcriptions, variants, context, domain labels, and complexity levels.
GPT-5.2 led simple transcriptions, while Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Grok 4.1 Fast led extended transcriptions under different context settings.
Extended transcription performed best in Statistics and Mathematics and worst in Physics.
Grouping symbols, variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were common sources of differences; formula complexity showed type- and context-dependent effects.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the ability of LLMs to verbalize mathematical formulas. This is a specific evaluation task for Large Language Models, relevant to their capabilities in structured reasoning and generation.
papers.title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
papers.tldr: LLMs can verbalize mathematical formulas, but accuracy varies substantially with transcription type, context, domain, and formula characteristics.

papers.abstract: Agent networks require reliable ways for requesting agents to verify where data is located, how it can be accessed, and whether the data received matches what the data owner made available. Checksum mismatches can reflect either altered content or serialization differences that preserve data equivalence under specified rules. Data identification mechanisms for agents, such as DataFacts, describe where data can be accessed and provide checksums for checking received data against published references. We propose a serialization-invariant identification method that assigns the same identifier to data representations equivalent under explicit rules. We use DataFacts as a case study, retaining its existing checksum alongside the proposed identifier. In a controlled agent study, we compare the proposed configuration with ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent re-encodings, altered content, and unavailable references. The study includes three model tiers from each of two providers. For equivalent re-encodings, the proposed configuration increased expected-outcome rates by 80.4 percentage points over the ordinary-tool baseline and by 70.2 percentage points over the checksum baseline. The proposed configuration also increased evidence-supported rejection of altered content by 3.5 percentage points over the checksum baseline. We contribute a serialization-invariant identification method with explicit equivalence rules, an integration approach illustrated through DataFacts, and an empirical evaluation against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines.
authors: Jin Gao, Maura Clark
bullets: Addresses checksum failures caused by harmless serialization differences in agent-published datasets.
Defines explicit equivalence rules and assigns one identifier to equivalent representations.
Integrates the identifier with DataFacts while retaining its existing checksum.
In a controlled study across model tiers and providers, improved expected outcomes for equivalent re-encodings and slightly improved rejection of altered content.
Evaluates against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent, altered, and unavailable-reference cases.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.
authors: Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Xinyu Lian, Fan Shu, Sida Li, Feng Yan, Mingjia Zhang, Yuxiong He, Zhewei Yao
bullets: Targets the difficulty of separating algorithmic gains from an under-tuned RL baseline for long-horizon agents.
Uses small-pool overfitting to expose failures hidden by early reward gains and integrates gated rewards, importance-weight control, aligned training/inference engines, and consistent policy state.
Reaches 62.0% pass@1 with Qwen3.5-4B on raw R2E-Gym data, comparable to FrogNano while using about one-sixth as many rollouts.
Filtering and refining multiple datasets improves Qwen3.5-4B to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% and Qwen3.5-9B to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2.
Controlled comparisons find that curation and stronger tests improve held-out performance, while stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for long-horizon agent training (Arctic-SWE) using reinforcement learning. It addresses the challenges of training agents over long horizons and domain shift, fitting both Robot Learning and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
papers.tldr: Arctic-SWE co-designs asynchronous RL infrastructure and training practices to provide a reproducible long-horizon software-engineering baseline, achieving strong SWE-bench performance without new algorithms.

papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.
authors: Daniil Gurgurov, Akansh Maurya, Josef van Genabith, Simon Ostermann, Hitomi Yanaka
bullets: Addresses the challenge of composing several training-free steering vectors for simultaneous behavioral control, especially across languages.
Jointly trains contextual gates that adjust each fixed steering direction based on the current hidden state and intervention interactions.
Outperforms constant-strength steering and four baselines, including prompting, across languages, behaviors, and models.
Better preserves general knowledge and keeps internal computation closer to that induced by prompting.
Analyzes how gate contributions change during composition to explain the method’s effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) often prioritizes model fidelity over user intelligibility, yielding explanations that satisfy technical transparency yet fail to support human sense-making. We propose a human-centered approach, MIND-X (Mental-model INtegrated Design for eXplainability), which aligns explanations with users' mental models, commonsense concepts, and judgment heuristics. Using fake review detection as a case study, we contribute: (1) a qualitative study (n=10) that elicits how people assess review credibility and produces an actionable, design-guiding taxonomy of perceptual cues; (2) a set of design principles that link those cues to explanation strategies and prompt LLMs to generate adaptive, language-based explanations; and (3) a quantitative evaluation (n=166) showing that these explanations offer distinct advantages over token-level transparency methods widely used in explainable text classification in terms of understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision-making support. Rather than claiming general superiority, our evaluation illustrates how grounding explanations in users' everyday reasoning practices can produce more intelligible and context-sensitive accounts. Our findings advance human-centered explanation design beyond a mere "gloss of transparency," demonstrating that a mental-model-aligned design process can improve intelligibility and support accountability across user-centered explanation tasks.
authors: Sidra Naveed (University of Siegen, Germany), Md Shajalal (University of Siegen, Germany), Gunnar Stevens (University of Siegen, Germany, Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg), Alexander Boden (Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg)
bullets: Addresses the gap between technically faithful explanations and explanations people can understand and use.
Elicits how people judge review credibility through a qualitative study of 10 participants, yielding a taxonomy of perceptual cues.
Translates these cues into design principles that guide adaptive, language-based explanations generated with LLMs.
A quantitative study with 166 participants found advantages over token-level transparency methods in understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision support.
The findings illustrate the value of mental-model alignment without claiming universal superiority or general applicability beyond the studied context.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots often switch gaits to traverse mixed terrain safely. Many practical supervisors enforce hardware constraints (e.g., dwell or guard intervals) using a transition handler. However, the switch decision itself is often driven by near-field thresholds, which can delay commitment when rough terrain is only detected shortly before contact in the local height map. We propose a lightweight height-map-only gait supervisor that unifies look-ahead and locomotion constraints in a single decision policy. A robot-centered height map is partitioned into near-, mid-, and far-field bands, each discretized into a terrain class, and band evolution is modeled as a Markov process. Gait selection is cast as a look-ahead Markov Decision Process whose transition model and cost explicitly encode platform-specific switching constraints. Indoor and outdoor experiments on a Unitree Go2 platform show reduced late switching, lower time spent using ineffective gaits on rough terrain, and improved roll stability compared to tuned reactive baselines. Overall, the MDP formulation yields anticipative constraint-aware gait switching that improves robustness without course-specific retuning.
authors: Kelvin Aladum, Justin Peel, Nisar Ahmed
bullets: Addresses delayed gait changes when rough terrain appears only shortly before contact.
Partitions robot-centered height maps into near-, mid-, and far-field terrain bands modeled as a Markov process.
Selects gaits with a look-ahead MDP whose transition model and cost encode platform-specific switching constraints.
Indoor and outdoor Unitree Go2 experiments report less late switching, less ineffective rough-terrain gait use, and improved roll stability versus tuned reactive baselines.
Improves robustness without course-specific retuning; evaluation is scoped to the tested platform and environments.

papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.
authors: Yue Dai, Sarah Zhou, Youtao Zhang
bullets: TGNN training becomes costly because rapidly growing event streams create sequential memory dependencies that limit parallelism.
RAFT identifies redundancy through the stability of node memories associated with prediction targets and historical inputs.
A root-event filter removes selected prediction targets, while a support-event filter excludes redundant historical context during sampling.
Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%.
Recorded training time falls by up to 52.56% with negligible changes to model precision.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a redundancy-aware input filtering framework for training Temporal Graph Neural Networks. This falls under Efficient AI (Token Pruning and Eviction) and offers a method to reduce computational load in dynamic graph learning, which is transferable to other sequential data processing tasks.
papers.title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
papers.tldr: RAFT accelerates temporal graph neural network training by filtering redundant target and historical events based on node-memory changes, substantially reducing processing with negligible precision loss.

papers.abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $\tau^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.
authors: Adarsh Vatsa, William Eiers
bullets: LLM agents repeatedly encounter the same states but typically re-derive decisions from context each turn.
“Discretize, Then Decide” extracts states, outcomes, costs, and transitions from workflow or agent logs, then solves the resulting MDP.
A controller reuses fixed actions for known states and delegates unseen states to the LLM.
On τ²-bench telecom, Qwen3.8-27B improved from 29% to 96% task success with 93% fewer model calls; Claude Opus 5.5 reduced calls and cost by about 98%.
The approach helps less on tasks dominated by generating novel content, such as resolving SymPy issues.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces LLM agent compute and cost by solving recurring decisions as an MDP; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Bellman Language Models pre-solve recurring agent decisions as a Markov policy, making bounded workflows faster, cheaper, and often more reliable.

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.
authors: Zhaoqi Wang, Zijian Zhang, Jiamou Liu
bullets: Targets the coordination of actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments across long animations.
Builds each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, then uses runtime and visual feedback for revision.
Reorchestrates scene drafts onto production assets and engine capabilities while preserving events, geometry, and timing.
Uses sequence inspection and frozen replay to transfer accepted performances into the final video.
Demonstrated through three complete animations lasting approximately 9.9–14.3 minutes.

Fig. 3. Sequences from the three complete animations. Rows show The Empty City Stratagem (37 to 62 s), Sending Jingniang Home (312 to 337 s), and Pinocchio (424 to 449 s), from top to bottom. Each row proceeds from left to right at intervals of five seconds.
