papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-horizon animation generation, a core challenge in video generation and world models. The framework of progressive scene programming and engine reorchestration is technically relevant to video synthesis and predictive modeling.
papers.title: SpriteStage: Long Horizon Animation Generation via Progressive Scene Programming and Replay
papers.tldr: SpriteStage generates long-form animations by progressively scripting, executing, inspecting, and revising scenes while carrying accepted world states forward.

papers.abstract: Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.
authors: Dimitrios Liakopoulos, Prasoon Sinha, Neeraja J. Yadwadkar
bullets: Generative AI workflows must jointly optimize structure, model assignment, and deployment configuration because these choices affect latency, cost, and accuracy.
Existing systems often optimize these decisions separately or commit to them early, resulting in poorer cost and goodput.
FlowMaker provides a task-level interface and selects workflow variants—workflow, model, and deployment combinations—on demand.
Its constraint-guided, load-aware pruning algorithm enables fast decisions while reusing deployed LLMs when current load and resource availability permit.
Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14× and reduces cost by up to 2.77×.

papers.title: FlowMaker: From Tasks to Cost-Efficient Generative AI Workflow Deployments

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models increasingly use multi-step search to solve knowledge-intensive tasks, yet existing systems typically expose retrieval through fixed pipelines or collections of atomic tools. We introduce Retrieval Program Learning (RPL), a programmable search framework that allows a policy to compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow. This enables adaptive search that can retrieve broadly, process intermediate results, and selectively construct model context without tying retrieval breadth to context consumption. However, the resulting flexibility creates a difficult exploration problem: useful programs may require several coordinated decisions, while reinforcement learning often supplies only sparse feedback. To address this challenge, we propose program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that generates local variants of suboptimal programs sampled during RL, converts them into training trajectories, and distills them back into the policy. We evaluate RPL on open-domain question answering and corpus-level reasoning tasks, comparing it with a range of retrieval and reasoning baselines. RPL consistently improves open-domain QA performance across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with particularly large gains on multi-hop tasks. Notably, a 4B model trained with RPL outperforms all 8B model baselines. On corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the highest answer F1 and document-coverage F1 for both model sizes while substantially reducing context consumption and retrieval turns. Our results show that programmable search expands the retrieval strategies that agents can learn, while program mutation provides an effective mechanism for exploring useful program structures beyond direct on-policy sampling.
authors: Kyuyoung Kim, Zilin Xiao, Zhiyuan Wang, Avinash Atreya, Ke Yang, Jinwoo Shin, Kecheng Hao
bullets: Problem: Fixed retrieval pipelines and atomic tools limit adaptive, multi-step search, while sparse RL feedback makes useful search programs difficult to discover.

Method: A policy composes search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow; grammar-constrained, execution-verified mutations generate useful training trajectories from suboptimal programs.
Results: RPL consistently improves open-domain QA across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with especially large gains on multi-hop tasks.

Results: A 4B RPL-trained model outperforms all evaluated 8B baselines; on corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the best answer and document-coverage F1 while using less context and fewer retrieval turns.
Contribution: A programmable search framework and program-mutation procedure that expands the retrieval strategies agents can learn beyond direct on-policy exploration.

papers.selection_reason: Programmable retrieval programs for RAG; relevant to external memory and context construction for LLMs.
papers.title: Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Retrieval Program Learning uses reinforcement learning and verified program mutations to teach language models adaptive, multi-step search strategies that improve accuracy while reducing context use and retrieval turns.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce **MisleadQA**, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA).
authors: Hui Wang, Bohao Chu, Qianli Wang, Shuning Zhang, Norbert Fuhr
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic multiple-choice dataset with abstention, pairing gold context with true out-of-scope or false in-scope distractors.
Evaluates six open-weight LLMs under misleading-context conditions.
True out-of-scope context causes wrong-answer switches in 29.3% of initially correct cases, versus 75.4% for false in-scope context.
Gold context nearly eliminates out-of-scope misdirection, but false context still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when presented first.
Context-faithful instructions mainly reduce errors through abstention and can lower accuracy even when gold context is available.

papers.title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner's dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker's execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling 99% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning.
authors: Shafeef Omar, Sebastian Sanokowski, Elham Daneshmand, Dian Yu, Daniel Cremers, Cordelia Schmid, Majid Khadiv
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction in humanoid loco-manipulation.
Pretrains a diffusion planner on human-to-humanoid retargeted motions and trains a low-level tracker with RL.
Uses SD:DPO to remove dependence on strong task conditioning, then DA:PPO to improve success and match plans to tracker capabilities.
Generates plans using only state history and goal conditioning, including for unseen object goals.
Evaluates kicking and pushing/pulling tasks and deploys successfully on a Unitree G1 without real-world fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion planner and RL tracker for humanoid loco-manipulation; fits robot learning and control.
papers.title: DiPLO: Self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation
papers.tldr: DiPLO combines self-distilled diffusion planning with RL-based whole-body tracking to enable robust humanoid loco-manipulation from limited demonstrations, achieving 99% simulated pick-carry-place success and successful hardware execution without real-world fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning (ACL) methods such as ACIL and GACL fit a ridge-regression classifier head on frozen features via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, achieving exemplar-free, exact updates. A separate line of work, Progressive Neural Collapse (ProNC), shows standard continual classifiers benefit from a progressively expanding Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) target. It is natural to ask whether fusing the two ideas, exact analytic updates and ETF targets, would yield a better closed-form continual learner. We show this is not the case as the fusion turns out to be identical to plain one-hot ACIL. Further, Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts, so the literal "progressively expand the ETF" construction stops yielding an ETF as new tasks arrive, and it introduces catastrophic forgetting ($4\times$ that of a classic ACIL head). We therefore separate an ETF's two defining properties, equiangularity and equinormality, and apply each on its own to the classifier weights rather than the targets, where the invariance above does not hold. Equinorm post-processing of the fitted weights recovers both tail-class and overall average accuracy across the long-tailed regime from 5:1 to 100:1 imbalance (e.g. +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points at 100:1 on CIFAR-100/ViT), transferring in sign across two backbones and two datasets, at a mild cost of 5.4 average-accuracy points on CIFAR-100/ViT on near-balanced streams (below $\approx 3{:}1$). Equiangular geometry, by contrast, is exactly inert on the target side but actively harmful on the weight side, usually losing to plain one-hot. Hence, the generally useful part of Neural Collapse geometry in Analytic Continual Learning is equinorm post-processing of the weights, becoming more useful as class imbalance grows; and equiangularity is at best a no-op and induces catastrophic forgetting at worst.
authors: Berk Sezer
bullets: Fusing ETF targets with exact ACIL updates is equivalent to plain one-hot ACIL.
Progressively expanding Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts and can cause substantially more catastrophic forgetting.
Equinorm weight post-processing improves tail and average accuracy under 5:1–100:1 class imbalance, with gains increasing as imbalance grows.
At 100:1 imbalance on CIFAR-100/ViT, it yields +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points.
Equinorming costs accuracy on near-balanced streams, while equiangular weight geometry is generally harmful.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses analytic continual learning, class-imbalance, and closed-form updates with a proposed equinorm remedy.
papers.title: An Impossibility Result for ETF Target Geometry, and an Equinorm Remedy for Imbalanced Analytic Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Equinorm post-processing of analytic continual-learning classifier weights improves long-tailed performance, while ETF/equiangular target geometry is ineffective or harmful.

papers.abstract: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z/r = 2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact. A frozen entrapment detector, trained on 81,771 windows spanning three materials and six sinkage levels, supplies a three-state belief to the policy observation. A separate simulator mobility latch gates training rewards. Across five training seeds, mean action evaluation achieves 62.5% escape (range 28.1-81.3%; 32 trials per seed) versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise. A numerical audit identifies a coupling-buffer fault that silently discarded 9.7% of contact nodes at 16 parallel environments. Results establish recovery in the tested simulation regime; physical transfer remains unverified.
authors: Meraj Hossain Promit, Chandak Chakma, Md Jubair Ahmed Sourov, Sejuti Rahman
bullets: Addresses terrain-specific scripted recovery and the risk that naive driving worsens entrapment.
Uses a recurrent policy informed by a frozen three-state entrapment detector and a simulator mobility latch for reward gating.
At the verified trap condition, the learned policy averaged 62.5% escape across five seeds, versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise.
A numerical audit found a coupling-buffer fault that discarded 9.7% of contact nodes in parallel simulation.
Physical transfer is unverified, and results are limited to the tested simulation regime.

Normalization and scaling are omitted; traces and probabilities are schematic.

papers.title: Escape Without a Recipe: Maneuver-Agnostic Mars Rover Recovery from Granular Entrapment
papers.tldr: A recurrent policy learns maneuver-agnostic Mars rover escape from simulated granular entrapment, substantially outperforming scripted maneuvers in the tested regime.

papers.abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
authors: Anna Pramod
bullets: Across 11 Indic scripts, TinyLlama’s tokenization ranges from 1.34 tokens per Latin-script word to 22.60 per Kannada word.
Its vocabulary covers 0% of Odia, 1% of Telugu, and 2% of Kannada codepoints; five scripts reach the byte-fallback ceiling.
The failure is silent: TinyLlama reports 0% UNK even when 93.6% of emitted tokens are raw bytes.
Low fertility can be misleading: mBERT’s 1.10 tokens/word on Odia accompanies 87.9% discarded text as UNK.
MuRIL handles all tested scripts at 1.23–2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and byte fallback, despite having one-fifth as many parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Fertility across eleven scripts, sorted. TinyLlama’s 32k Latin-trained vocabulary degrades monotonically to 22.60 tokens/word; MuRIL (fewer parameters, but a 197k Indic vocabulary) stays flat. (b) The fraction of emitted tokens the vocabulary cannot represent. TinyLlama substitutes raw UTF-8 bytes (expensive but information-preserving); mBERT destroys Odia as UNK (irrecoverable). Table 1: Measured tokenisation, n=400 sentences per script. cov.: percentage of the script’s assigned Unicode codepoints present in the vocabulary. fert.: mean subword tokens per whitespace-delimited word. fall.: percentage of emitted tokens the vocabulary cannot represent: <0xXX> byte tokens for SentencePiece (TinyLlama), UNK for WordPiece (mBERT, MuRIL). † The two fallback mechanisms are not equivalent: byte fallback preserves information at ≈3 tokens per character, whereas UNK destroys it irrecoverably; see Section 5. Coverage is computed over each full Unicode block and is therefore conservative for Latin, which contains many characters absent from this corpus; it should be read within a script, across tokenisers.

papers.selection_reason: Shows tokenizer vocabulary coverage bounds effective context and efficiency for Indic scripts, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
papers.tldr: For Indic scripts, small-model efficiency depends more on tokenizer vocabulary coverage than parameter count, and English-based metrics can hide severe byte-level fallback.

papers.abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.
authors: Xu Zheng, Wei Cheng, Zhuomin Chen, Dongkuan Xu, Mo Sha, Jingchao Ni, Dongsheng Luo
bullets: Targets private, on-device LLM personalization without uploading user data.
Runs forward, activation-recomputation, and input-gradient products with resident NPU weights, avoiding transposed weight copies.
Uses gradient-sensitive precision selection and FP16 per-row range guarding to preserve gradient quality.
Fuses CPU work, overlaps NPU and adapter computation, and supports resumable, thermally paced background training.
Evaluated on two Snapdragon platforms with four Qwen and Llama models across personalization and LaMP-2 workloads.

(a) A nightly update trains its LoRA adapter; (b) the same frozen 𝑊 serves forward, recomputation, and backward, and the CPU adds d𝑌𝑊 to the adapter input gradient; (c) the CPU trainer and the NPU service run as separate processes on the phone: the CPU owns the graph and optimizer, the NPU holds one weight copy, messages over a local Unix-domain socket carry projection requests, and shared memory carries their input and output tensors.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io
authors: Yizheng Xie, Yalda Foroutan, George Shramko, Daniel Rebain, Shrisudhan Govindarajan, Andrea Tagliasacchi
bullets: Addresses the failure of static 3D representations under object interactions and the sequence-replay limitation of time-conditioned dynamic methods.
Decomposes the scene into a shared static Gaussian base plus per-object slots representing two states, such as on/off.
Differentiably discovers which Gaussians belong to each object state without manual annotations.
Allows users to freely combine learned slot states and render the resulting scene from arbitrary viewpoints.
On a new casual-capture dataset, it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality.

papers.abstract: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.
authors: Yimeng Dou, Adam M. Saunders, Andre T. S. Hucke, Michael E. Kim, Adam W. Anderson, Eric R. Tkaczyk, Bennett A. Landman, Daniel Moyer
bullets: Targets active-light capture settings such as camera flashes, underwater vehicles, and endoscopy, where light direction changes with camera pose.
Separates per-point color into albedo and spherical-harmonic illumination within NeRF or other NVS pipelines.
Uses differentiable SH evaluation and closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion for joint optimization of lighting, albedo, and geometry.
Analytically generalizes illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining.
Achieves the best reported mean PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across five held-out scenes among compared methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed method. Given a co-located capture that produces N images I and the extrinsic camera parameter matrix c2w (I. Capture), the method factors appearance into albedo and illumination before volumetric rendering. The albedo branch (IIa) samples a global coordinate position x through a scene MLP to predict per-sample albedo ρ(x), density σ(x), and a global normal n from the density gradient. The illumination branch (IIb) starts from a single trainable l=4 SH code Esh ∈ R25×3 shared across all frames, and rotates it analytically into each frame via the Wigner-D matrix D(l) derived from the known rotation Rt ∈ SO(3), so that the rotated coefficients become Ẽt. Albedo ρ(x) and illumination factor α(xc,nc) are multiplied into the factorized radiance ρ′ = α⊙ρ and composited through volumetric rendering, producing a full render C(r), a clean albedo render∑ i wi ρ (i.e., a render without illumination effects), and an illumination map α.

Fig. 1. (a) Robots that operate in dark environments, such as subterranean exploration (SubT challenge) [1], deep-water surveys by the remotely operated vehicle Hercules [2], and nighttime driving [3] rely on onboard lights that move with the platform. (b) In standard novel view synthesis (NVS, left), hundreds of images are captured while the camera moves around the scene under fixed illumination field L, and a radiance field is reconstructed with methods such as NeRF, 3DGS, or their derivatives. However, in co-located capture (right), the camera and a light source are rigidly attached, so the surface illumination changes with every pose, as the light source is moving as well. We model this moving illumination through the irradiance E(n), so the irradiance for a given normal is computed by analytically rotating the coefficients with a Wigner-D matrix of the known camera motion, where the residual spatial variation from the near-field source is absorbed by a learned per-sample MLP (see III for more details). (c) DaFISH can reconstruct the scenes while attributing frame-varying brightness to the illumination branch. The brightness of ground truth and rendered images is increased by 40% for visualization.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison across three co-located captures (rows: Lab1, Outdoor1, and FourLights) and all methods plus ground truth (GT) are split over two stacked panels of four columns (top 4: 2DGS [7], 3DGS [6], GS-W [24], DarkGS [8]; bottom 4: SpotlessGS [21], relative-illumination [10], DaFISH, and GT). The red bounding box highlights the reconstructed detail. Our factorization keeps albedo stable while the directional SH irradiance travels with the camera.
Fig. 5. The row shows the original capture (left) next to the learned illumination field (right) at the same camera orientation.

Fig. 4. Clean scene recovery on held-out frames across three DarkRobotic scenes (columns). For each scene, a held-out GT frame (top) is shown next to the clean albedo (no illumination effect render) of the baselines (SpotlessGS [21], relative-illumination [10]) and DaFISH.

papers.title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
papers.tldr: DaFISH factorizes pose-dependent illumination from surface albedo using rotated spherical harmonics, enabling consistent novel-view rendering under camera-mounted lighting.

papers.abstract: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose \sysname, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of $70\%$, \sysname achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52\% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24\% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.
authors: Sankalp Parashar, Preethi Jyothi, Sunita Sarawagi
bullets: Targets far-field conversational speech errors through selective clarification rather than full re-utterance.
Uses pair-HMM alignment between noisy and clean decodes to create soft, counterfactual supervision.
Combines acoustic and language features into token-level gain scores, which are grouped into intervention spans.
An LLM revises only the selected span using the transcript of the repetition.
At 70% precision, it finds up to 52% more erroneous tokens than the strongest baseline and reduces WER by up to 24% under a recourse budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PARDON overview. As the speaker talks, the CF-Gain Scorer assigns every emitted token a score ej and two deletion estimates dj and ℓj , and the scores are grouped into spans. Once a span closes, PARDON asks the speaker to repeat it, using an anchor-based question. An LLM corrector puts the repeated words into the transcript.

Figure 4: Recourse on the AMI (a) and CHiME-6 (b) eval sets (β = 0.05, spans of at most six words): relative WER reduction against the re-utterance burden with synthesized (solid) or close-talking (dashed) replies. PARDON uses the CF-Gain Scorer; Peng et al. uses the same recourse pipeline with the detectors of Peng et al. (2026). Horizontal lines: the zero-interruption N -best correction of HyPoradise and the N -best oracle. We also report WER reductions achieved through speech enhancement (which is quite poor) in Appendix K.

Figure 7: Recourse on the AMI and CHiME-6 evaluation sets with a higher weight on re-uttered words (a, b) and with longer spans (c, d): relative WER reduction against the re-utterance burden, at the operating points selected on the development set, with synthesized or close-talking replies. Horizontal lines: the zero-interruption N -best correction of HyPoradise and the N -best oracle.

Figure 3: Training supervision. The same frozen transducer decodes the noisy audio X̂ and the counterfactual audio Xc. A pair-HMM channel aligns the noisy decode Ŷ to Y c and gives, for each token, the targets ẽj , d̃j and ℓ̃j of the scorer’s three heads; only the scorer receives gradients (§3.2.2).

Figure 2: The CF-Gain Scorer (shaded) and the frozen transducer it reads (dashed). The emission and dwell posteriors q and r̃ of the streaming alignment lattice pool frame-level evidence to each token. The pooled vector h̄j is concatenated with the predictor state g[j] to form fj . A unidirectional LSTM then scores each token as it is emitted via three heads: giving fixable error score ej and the deletion estimates dj and ℓj (§3.2.2).

Figure 6: The pair-HMM channel at noisy token ŷj . A correct token (C) is written unchanged. An erroneous one is preceded by a run of deleted tokens (D, possibly empty) and is then an anchor (A, written unchanged; only after a deletion), an insertion (I, nothing written) or a substitution (S, a different token written). C has Ej = 0; A, I and S have Ej = 1.

Figure 5: An ambiguous deletion. Two alignments explain the noisy decode equally well: the second that was deleted and is anchors the deletion (solid), or the first was deleted and the surviving that anchors it (dashed). The hard alignment labels only one token and treats the other as clean; the soft label splits the mass between them, so neither is penalized, and a span covering both carries the same label mass either way.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework for targeted clarification in ASR, using an LLM to revise specific error spans identified by a counterfactual gain scorer.
papers.title: Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
papers.tldr: A streaming ASR framework identifies error-prone spans worth asking speakers to repeat, then selectively revises those spans to improve recognition.

papers.abstract: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Chungwoo Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Addresses adapter and task-selection module growth under fixed onboard storage and compute budgets.
Reuses frozen adapters and adds new adapters only at selected layers, with a penalty discouraging redundant information.
Uses activation-statistic signatures for one-time task identification, then merges the task update into the backbone for control.
Across four LIBERO suites, matches or exceeds adapter baselines while using up to 4.5× less on-disk state per task.
GPU memory and control frequency remain comparable to the backbone as tasks accumulate; retention is also shown on a real UR5 arm.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of SARAM. Top: each task reuses the frozen library (Phase 1), allocates new adapters to a sparse subset of layers (Phase 2), trains them under a duplication penalty (Phase 3), and stores coefficients, adapters, and a task signature. Bottom: at deployment, one adapter-free pass selects the task and its update is merged, so only the backbone runs.

Fig. 1. Two growth axes of adapter-based lifelong robot learning. Prior methods accumulate adapters and selection modules on disk and keep them available on the GPU during control. SARAM adds new adapters sparsely and deploys a single merged backbone, adding up to 4.5× less on-disk state per task in our experiments.
Fig. 4. Layers allocated on LIBERO-Long. Colored bars mark layers that keep an adapter for each task (rows) and seed (blocks).

Fig. 3. Deployment cost versus tasks learned. GPU memory and control frequency stay at the backbone’s level for SARAM, and its stored parameters and on-disk state grow more slowly than adapter-based baselines.
Fig. 6. Task performance across the UR5 stream.
Fig. 5. Real-robot task stream. Seven UR5 manipulation tasks learned sequentially.

papers.title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning

papers.abstract: Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift: learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.
authors: Isabel Guan, Dingyuan Zhang, Shipeng Lyu, I-Ming Chen
bullets: In a 20-seed tray-placement experiment, success increased from 66.8% to 97.0%, while accepted hover failures fell from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions.
Despite fewer failures overall, the judge accepted 50.0% of remaining hovers, up from 31.1% under untrained sampling.
Residual failures more often occurred below the tray rim, where the grasped cube can conceal the gap.
A boundary probe found 148/160 below-rim hovers accepted versus 0/160 above-rim hovers.
Across nine judges, 1,392 stimuli, and eight settings, effects of state-dependent acceptance were heterogeneous.

papers.abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.

bullets: The study tests lookup in identical 256-cell tables rendered in row-major or column-major formats across five aspect ratios.

At 64×4, row-major leads by 42.3–54.0 percentage points; at 4×64, column-major leads by 35.0–59.0 points across three models.
Errors show that row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, whereas column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row.
The findings motivate “relational locality”: linearization makes one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.
authors: Xujun Che, Farsheed Haque, Depeng Xu, Xi Niu, Haopeng Zhang
bullets: Commit rules influence both which tokens are generated and when, introducing bias beyond the model’s own beliefs.
A single forward pass can estimate the model’s belief about a binary fork and provide a sampler-independent baseline.
Peeking and confidence-based samplers amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions.
Confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, especially with faster parallel decoding.
Fork-First Sampling can follow the model’s belief or a target distribution and avoids explicit gender commentary induced by prompt-based fixes, at the cost of one forward pass.

papers.abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
authors: Francesco Morri, Adel Abusitta, Quentin Cappart, Margarida Carvalho
bullets: Targets general-sum settings where defection can trap agents in low-welfare equilibria.
Uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment each agent’s Q-function with estimated effects of its actions on others.
Learns both cooperative and defecting policies using only the agent’s own Q-function.
Experiments across four social dilemmas show faster and higher cooperation than fully cooperative methods with shared rewards.
A single RQA agent can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.
authors: Kien T. Pham, Yuhao Liu, Chong Hou Choi, Zhenqi He, Yanghao Wang, Chenyang Lei, Rui Liu, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen

Uses independently warped noise schedules so video can denoise longer while audio settles earlier.
Trains asymmetric workflows where one clean modality guides synthesis or editing of the other.
Supports intent-aware editing that preserves one modality while modifying the other.
Enables post-inference self-refinement by regenerating only an unsatisfactory modality, without task-specific adapters.

papers.abstract: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model's native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.
authors: Benedetta Liberatori, Lorenzo Vaquero, Elisa Ricci, Paolo Rota
bullets: Addresses the challenge of concept-based video similarity, such as comparing activity or location, which is not directly handled by most LMMs.
Uses two branches, each processing one video with a caption of the other to assess concept-specific video–language alignment.
Fuses both entailment outputs into a similarity score and an explanation of the model’s reasoning.
Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show improved performance over models that process both videos simultaneously.
The approach is scoped to leveraging single-video understanding for cross-video comparative reasoning.

papers.abstract: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural-language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention-selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object-centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high-resolution frame-level attentions that capture spatial information with low-resolution video-level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U-Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM-based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen-backbone methods. Code and models are available at \url{https://hamidreza-136.github.io/atlas/}.

papers.abstract: Quadruped locomotion requires coordinating body motion,contact forces, foothold placement, and gait timing. We present a hierarchical controller in which reinforcement learning adapts these structured locomotion references while a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and whole-body impulse controller retain responsibility for high-frequency execution. The model-based backbone can sustain a nominal trot independently, allowing the policy to focus on when and how to modify an already functional locomotion controller. We train the complete hierarchy in a vectorized controller-in-the-loop environment using a six-direction disturbance curriculum. Under a common simulator and evaluation protocol, the proposed controller achieves 77.29% mean survival across the tested disturbance grid, compared with 50.35% for the model-based reference controller. Training-time channel ablations identify adaptive foothold placement as the largest marginal contributor to grid survival and reveal direction-dependent effects of gait-rate adaptation. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of the proposed hierarchical controller architecture for integrating learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control through structured locomotion references.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.

Diagnostics identify bottlenecks in object-level dialogue grounding, correct-entry retrieval, and spatial localization.
Even perfect object linking does not match ground-truth memory performance, indicating additional retrieval and localization challenges.

papers.abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhou, Junyuan Shang, Tianyu Wang, Chunrui Zheng, Zichang Liu, Wenbin Chang, Shuohuan Wang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Existing MTP methods rely on auxiliary modules, adding parameters, passes, and limited supervision to the backbone.
ECHO uses the backbone’s final layer to predict every future horizon, directly training the next-token-generating parameters.
Dynamic Depth Sampling samples training depths with probabilities that decay by depth, reducing the cost of deeper-horizon supervision.
The approach improves downstream accuracy, especially on reasoning and code, at half the overhead of training every depth.

At inference, the pretrained model drafts beyond its training depth while maintaining alignment in open-ended, high-entropy generation; benefits persist with more tokens, repeated pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project
authors: Hangwei Zhang, Nathan Rouill\'e, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Targets errors in iterative flow-matching sampling, where predictions are not typically revisited using intermediate representations.
The refiner predicts residual corrections from the base clean prediction, conditioning, noise level, and same-pass hidden states.
Corrections are applied before each sampling update, enabling subsequent predictions from the corrected state at one extra lightweight evaluation per step.
Theory analyzes when feature reuse and refiner training provide greater residual-risk reduction than simpler predictors or continued base-model training under matched compute.
Experiments across class-conditional image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation report consistent gains in visual quality and physical consistency.

papers.abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Zhiqing Tang, Hanlin Zhao, Siu Hing Lui, Tao Yang, Jingsong Lin, Huxin Gao, Yeung Trevor, Raymond Tang, Hongliang Ren

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.
authors: Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Shilin Shan, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide arbitrary token removal and reliance on textual shortcuts.
Equal retained-token budgets can produce different real inference costs depending on pruning location and procedure.
Random-Pass@k measures how often examples remain correct under random pruning, revealing when token selection matters.
Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) compares maximum end-to-end speedup at a shared preservation target.
Across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks, compression strength, speedup, and method rankings do not consistently align.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.
authors: Renxi Liu, Yiming Li, Shengyin Sun, Chen Chen, Xian Wang, Shuai Yang, Huiling Zhen, Xianzhi Yu, Yaoyuan Wang, Weizhe Lin, Xiaosong Li
bullets: Addresses the efficiency challenge of safely committing parallel token predictions in discrete diffusion language models.
Uses two confidence thresholds to classify tokens as directly decoded, speculative, or unresolved.
Applies progressively stronger verification: single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch.
Across three models and three benchmarks, reduces sequential model forward passes by 8%–37% versus confidence-based decoding, with at most a 1.3% accuracy drop.
Improves throughput by 7.0%–13.6% for 1-batch and 2-batch variants on Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K; multi-batch is slower in the reported runtime.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of PV-Decoding under block diffusion decoding. Two thresholds, τspec and τdec, partition masked positions by confidence ci into unresolved tokens (ci < τspec), speculative tokens (τspec ≤ ci < τdec), and directly decoded tokens (ci ≥ τdec). The speculative tokens are then processed by progressively stronger verification policies: single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.
authors: Qisheng Zhou, Zhen Xiong, Qiaoyu Tan
bullets: Targets the mismatch between diffusion models’ bidirectional reconstruction ability and append-only AR-style agent state.
Maintains one editable planning state and reconstructs only steps affected by resolved entities or changed search routes.
Introduces Expansion-Partition Marginalization to handle revisions that change plan length.
Adapts diffusion trajectory reinforcement learning to multi-turn search.
Achieves 50.24 average F1 across four multi-hop QA benchmarks; editable planning improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 under matched training.

papers.abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.
authors: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
bullets: Pure sampling always retains a positive escape chance, but top-p can lock a loop when its continuation probability reaches the threshold.
Penalties that do not outgrow the model’s preference for repetition may leave positions permanently locked.
DRY’s breaker-based penalty is capped for short breaker-free runs, so many locked loops remain locked.
Across 11 open models, 66% of locked units with run length g=6 stayed locked under DRY, versus 1% with g=8.
DRY-C adds recurrence-based exponential penalty growth; none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the limit while task completion remained close to DRY’s.

papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of repetition-loop lock-in and sampler blind spots in LLM decoding, relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.tldr: Repetition loops can become mathematically unescapable under truncation sampling and bounded penalties, revealing a blind spot in DRY that DRY-C addresses.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.
authors: Chaoran Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Chenglin Cui, Yazhe Wan, Taein Kwon, Changjae Oh
bullets: Directly matching VLA and 3D foundation-model features can cause severe rank collapse.
The proposed method aligns pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise feature equality.
It integrates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning without compromising original expressivity.
Experiments across public benchmarks, a new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation show robust spatial understanding across diverse tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. We extract self- and cross-attention (attn.) maps from both the VLA and the 3D foundation models to serve as relational affinity matrices described in Sec. 3.1. The 3D foundation model is kept frozen, and the VLA model is trained via LoRA. Other parts are fully trainable. More views can be naturally incorporated.

Figure 1: Spectral and rank analysis of different alignment methods. (a) Traditional 3D knowledge distillation aligns the point-wise magnitudes (i.e, vector norm) or angles (i.e, cos-similarity) across feature spaces, which often leads to rank collapse (b). In contrast, we align pair-wise relationships to achieve a rotation-invariant alignment that effectively prevents feature collapse. See Sec. 3.1 for details. VGGT [16] is used as the 3D teacher model.

Figure 3: Robustness to camera view changes. We evaluate results on camera view change by level on LIBERO-Spatial. Our method outperforms the Spatial Forcing across most levels, showing particular robustness at higher difficulty tiers, mitigating the performance degradation.

Figure 7: Our robot environment and task examples. We use a 7-DoF robotic arm with a twofinger gripper, a side-view camera, a wrist camera, and an agent-view camera (used only for visualization). We evaluate on six tasks in a complex kitchen environment.

papers.title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: A relational alignment method injects 3D spatial awareness into vision-language-action models while preserving their representational expressivity.

papers.abstract: LeJEPA derives an isotropic Gaussian embedding target by minimizing, under its task assumptions, a Fisher information criterion that controls the task-averaged squared prediction bias. This enables unimodal self-supervised learning without reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. However, its isotropic task prior does not account for the cross-modal structure of multimodal tasks that read shared content. We introduce MM-LeJEPA by extending LeJEPA's task assumptions to multimodal learning. Specifically, we model multimodal tasks as strength-weighted combinations of components that read independent information from the two modalities and components that read the same content from both. Under explicit gradient-moment, correspondence, and symmetry assumptions, we derive a correlated Gaussian target that minimizes a weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance constraint. An analytic transform adapts Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) to this target, yielding a two-term objective that combines distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction. The extension adds a single scalar hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation, and retains the simplicity of LeJEPA. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, our results are competitive with representative open-source methods. Code will be released.
authors: Haowen Bai, Rui Gong$, Meichen Liu, Ming-Xuan Weng, Bihan Wen, Kim-Hui Yap
bullets: Addresses LeJEPA’s isotropic prior, which overlooks cross-modal structure in tasks sharing content between modalities.
Derives a correlated Gaussian target from multimodal task assumptions and a weighted Fisher-information objective under fixed total variance.
Uses an analytic SIGReg adaptation combining distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction.
Adds one scalar hyperparameter controlling target cross-modal correlation.
Shows competitive results on public audio-visual classification benchmarks against representative open-source methods.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in 2D visual understanding tasks, yet the passive view-centric perception paradigm limits their capacity for 3D spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often requires actively acquiring spatial evidence beyond the currently visible views, such as camera poses and cross-view spatial relationships, to infer 3D relationships that are not explicitly represented in 2D images. However, existing methods either lack active exploration or merely provide additional views during inference, without explicitly acquiring such spatial evidence beyond 2D images. In this paper, we propose View-to-World (V2W), an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to actively explore 3D worlds and lifts VLMs from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric spatial reasoning. Given a spatial reasoning task with multi-view images, V2W first reconstructs an explicit 3D world with geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics, and exposes it to VLMs through visual and linguistic interfaces. Through multi-turn interaction with these interfaces, VLMs iteratively acquire spatial evidence from the constructed 3D world, enabling active world-centric spatial reasoning. V2W can be integrated with existing VLMs in a training-free manner and can be further enhanced by optimizing the exploration policy via reinforcement learning. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training-free setting and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the learned exploration policy, highlighting the importance of active exploration for spatial intelligence. Project page: \url{https://fangzhou2000.github.io/projects/v2w}.
authors: Qijian Tian, Jiayu Ying, Ke Fan, Lizhuang Ma, Xin Tan
bullets: Addresses the limits of view-centric VLMs for 3D spatial reasoning, where key cross-view relationships are not explicit in individual images.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world from multi-view images and provides visual and linguistic interfaces for interactive exploration.
Supports training-free integration with existing VLMs, with optional reinforcement learning to optimize exploration policies.
Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks show substantial gains over VLM baselines and state-of-the-art performance with learned exploration.
Scope: performance depends on the quality of the reconstructed 3D world and applies to tasks with multi-view images.
