papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of FIBER. (a) Heterogeneous interaction experts are acquired through motion imitation, reward shaping, or successorfeature-guided behavior reuse. (b) Action-aligned latent policy projection maps their short-horizon control responses into a frozen adaptivehorizon BFM; closed-loop rollouts produce executable latent trajectories. (c) These trajectories train a unified perceptive planner entirely offline. Language commands or waypoint conditions are encoded as steering tokens, and a DiT planner predicts future latent trajectories. During deployment, the planner replans from onboard observations while the frozen BFM provides high-frequency feedback.

Fig. 4: Qualitative real-world behaviors of FIBER. (a) During box carrying, the robot reacts to an unstable grasp by briefly lifting the box and repositioning its hands underneath for more secure support, illustrating high-frequency closed-loop adjustment. (b) After picking up the box, the same policy follows waypoint commands while carrying it; after stumbling, the robot stabilizes on its knees and recovers before continuing, demonstrating interaction-preserving skill chaining, steering, and recovery. (c) For a heavy door, the robot leans its whole body into the interaction to generate sufficient pushing force, showing adaptive whole-body realization of contact-rich tasks.

Fig. 3: Skill chaining with FIBER. In a single rollout, the policy sequentially opens the door in (i), picks up the box in (ii), and carries it back through the doorway in (iii), demonstrating closed-loop chaining of multiple interaction skills under changing high-level commands.

papers.title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: FIBER enables one perceptive humanoid planner to coordinate diverse loco-manipulation skills by planning in an executable latent space that preserves low-level feedback.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention propagates position uncertainty instead of treating corrupted 3D tokens as exact.
Simulated sensor-corruption benchmarks and real-robot tasks with transparent and reflective objects show improved noise robustness.
The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: NISE framework. Per-camera RGB-D is encoded by a frozen visual backbone ViT and a trainable DPT-style head [21] into a shared spatial feature map. NISE acts on this shared map: during training, Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision attaches a cross-view geometry head to encourage view-consistent geometry in the same features consumed by the policy; at deployment, this head is removed. Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention remains in the deployed policy and carries per-token coordinate uncertainty into 3D attention, so lifted tokens influence action features according to their spatial reliability.
Figure 4: Real-robot Success Rate. Each task group compares DP3, 3DDA, RVT-2, and NISE, with N = 30 trials per task and method.

Figure 1: Realistic depth corruption breaks what 3D policies can trust. (a) In a transparent test-tube manipulation scene, raw depth contains missing and geometrically wrong measurements; a standard 3D policy consumes this corrupted geometry as exact and fails, while NISE succeeds. (b) Depth-noise robustness on RLBench PerAct-18 [1, 2] and MetaWorld [3]. NISE maintains higher success rates as depth corruption increases, with a smaller clean-to-saturated decline than the compared baselines.

This is the practical difference between a raw cross-camera noisy target and GCVSS: the auxiliary signal is still noisy, but it is expressed in the same camera frame as the target feature map.

papers.abstract: Explicit memory systems transform conversation history into persistent representations intended to improve future access, often at substantial construction cost. Yet it remains unclear whether this added complexity yields better answer accuracy than retrieving directly from raw history. This study compares six state-of-the-art explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled retrieval settings. We find only localized gains for particular question types and tight run-time context budgets, with no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines. Oracle retrieval shows that some systems fail to preserve answer-supporting information during explicit memory construction, while others preserve it but fail to retrieve it effectively, despite construction costs reaching hours per conversation. Our findings suggest that while many existing memory systems for AI agents emphasize increasingly elaborate explicit memory construction, they are often evaluated without strong controlled comparisons to raw-history RAG and may underemphasize retrieval. Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.
authors: Yongjie Zhou, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
bullets: Compares six explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled settings.
Finds no consistent accuracy advantage for explicit memory, except for some question types and tight context budgets.
Oracle retrieval reveals two failure modes: losing answer-supporting information during construction or failing to retrieve preserved information.
Some systems require hours of construction per conversation, highlighting substantial overhead.
Results suggest improving retrieval may be as important as building richer persistent memories.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a controlled comparison of explicit memory systems against raw-history RAG, finding that retrieval efficiency often outweighs the benefits of complex memory construction.
papers.title: Do Conversational Agents Need Explicit Memory? A Controlled Comparison with Raw-History Retrieval
papers.tldr: Explicit memory systems offer only localized benefits over strong raw-history retrieval, while costly construction and retrieval failures limit their overall advantage.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.
authors: Siyu Zhang, Yuquan Lu, Yoshua Y. Li, Yifan Ding, Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Yifu Guo, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: On 120 AIME problems, power sampling within the same output limit adds no gain over greedy decoding.

Replacing the base model’s tokens only where its greedy choice differs from the RL model—about 4% of positions—recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 improvement; this also holds across three model pairs on MATH-500.

Forcing the opening token to “Alright” recovers 35% of the RL gain, while later replacements add a further 5.2 percentage points; fixed insertion rules for words like “Wait” do not reproduce this benefit.
Sparse replacement preserves much of the base model’s diversity and reaches 67.5% at k=256, versus 61.4% for the RL model and 61.45% for a matched whole-response mixture.
The comparison uses equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, because the replacement method consults both models at every decoding step.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what RL adds to LLM reasoning through sparse token-level interventions, directly relevant to LLM training and decoding.
papers.title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
papers.tldr: A small number of token-level choices—especially the opening token and later divergent decisions—accounts for much of RL’s reasoning improvement over the base model.

papers.abstract: Digital medicine now captures data that traces individual health trajectories and reveals population health dynamics through electronic health records, claims, remote monitoring, wearable devices, mobile devices, social sensing data, medical images, etc. But much of its modeling still centers on task-specific, outcome-specific, and prediction-specific estimation. The next frontier is not simply better prediction, but action in an evolving health world shaped by multiple decision-makers, heterogeneous populations, resource constraints, and feedback in care delivery. This is why digital medicine now needs world models: not only to estimate what will happen, but to represent how actions change what can happen next -- whom to prioritize, how to allocate scarce resources, how to adapt care across subgroups, and how interventions reshape future health trajectories and population dynamics. We call such a model population health world model (PHWM): a more foundational representation of an evolving health world in which health states, individual trajectories, population health dynamics, interventions, constraints, and feedback are intrinsically coupled. Building a PHWM endows three unmet structural gaps in current digital medicine: dynamic health-state modeling, population-level intervention intelligence, and validation, equity, and governance for action-oriented use. We argue that addressing these gaps requires three minimal capabilities: representation learning under action-dependent observation, multi-scale intervention intelligence, and validation with explicit decision boundaries, while highlighting the importance of social, contextual, and public-health sensing data for action-oriented digital medicine.
authors: Xike Xie, Yu Li, Weizhong Yang, Amalie Dyda, Shaohua Kevin Zhou
bullets: Current digital medicine is largely task-, outcome-, and prediction-focused, limiting action-oriented decision-making.
A PHWM jointly represents health states, individual trajectories, population dynamics, interventions, resource constraints, and care-delivery feedback.
It targets three gaps: dynamic health-state modeling, population-level intervention intelligence, and validation, equity, and governance for action.
The proposed minimum capabilities are action-dependent observation learning, multi-scale intervention intelligence, and validation tied to explicit decision boundaries.
Social, contextual, and public-health sensing data are highlighted as important for action-oriented digital medicine.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Population Health World Model: Observed health signals—including electronic health records, claims, wearable and remote-monitoring data, patient-reported outcomes, and social or contextual signals—feed into a population health world model that distinguishes latent health state from recorded observations. The model represents intervention space, transition dynamics, uncertainty, and hierarchy across levels and time scales, linking patient-level health trajectories to subgroup patterns and population health dynamics. Interventions and real-world constraints jointly shape intervention-conditioned dynamics, which in turn support action-oriented outputs such as prioritization, scenario analysis, coverage planning, and resource allocation. Validation and governance form an integrated layer spanning the framework, emphasizing predictive validity, intervention sensitivity, counterfactual plausibility, robustness under shift, usefulness, and equity.

Figure 2: Structural Gaps and Minimal Required Capabilities in Population Health World Model. Current digital medicine models rely on assumptions that observed features approximate health state, that decisions can be modeled at the patient level, and that evaluation under observed processes is sufficient. These assumptions lead to three structural gaps: (1) representational challenges arising from latent state being confounded with intervention-dependent observations, (2) multi-scale coupling challenges due to interactions across individuals, subgroups, and populations under shared constraints, and (3) validation challenges under intervention, feedback, and distribution shift. Addressing these gaps requires minimal capabilities rather than optional directions: representation learning under action-dependent observation, multi-scale intervention intelligence, and validation frameworks with explicit decision boundaries. These priorities correspond to core problem classes in artificial intelligence, including partially observable modeling, multi-agent and hierarchical systems, and off-policy and uncertainty-aware evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Population health world model with action-conditioned intervention dynamics.
papers.title: From Prediction to Action: Population Health World Model for Digital Medicine
papers.tldr: Population health world models aim to move digital medicine beyond predicting outcomes toward modeling how interventions, constraints, and feedback reshape individual and population health.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. However, these methods often lack systematic management of evolved skills, making it difficult for agents to reuse and accumulate skills across domains, thus limiting performance on subsequent tasks.To reliably accumulate, reuse, and maintain useful skills across tasks, we present SELM (Self-Evolving Library Management), a framework that formulates skill evolution as library-level management. SELM jointly manages skill retrieval, updating, and lifecycle by maintaining skill confidence and utility signals. It introduces utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills, a Map-Reduce framework to generate targeted updates from task-specific experience, and lifecycle controls to retain or remove skills based on their effectiveness. These mechanisms enable the skill library to continuously accumulate useful experience while preserving and pruning skills across tasks, improving agent performance on complex tasks across diverse domains. We evaluate SELM on four agent benchmarks covering diverse tasks and execution environments, and SELM consistently outperforms in most settings.
authors: Mengxi Hu, Yuxuan Hu, Jinbo Su, Ke Wang, Honghao Shi, Wenli Wu, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of accumulating and reusing evolved skills across domains.
Uses confidence- and utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills.
Applies Map-Reduce updates to incorporate targeted experience from task trajectories.
Manages skill lifecycles by retaining effective skills and removing ineffective ones.
Evaluated on four diverse agent benchmarks, with consistent improvements in most settings.

papers.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

papers.abstract: Visual accuracy leaves open whether predicted motion obeys dynamics. We introduce a framework for measuring and diagnosing mechanical consistency in visual dynamics. An independent SI audit of rigid closed chains separates geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work--energy balance. Continuous scoring measures progress against fixed engineering targets, while reference replay quantifies measurement error. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above measurement error. With exact states, KeyCLD preserves geometry and RK4 training raises its score from 52.65 to 64.30. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. The interventions distinguish gains in visual prediction and geometric admissibility from remaining force and energy errors.

bullets: Evaluates mechanical consistency through geometric admissibility, reaction-free actuator effort, and work–energy balance.
Uses continuous engineering-target scores and reference replay to separate model error from measurement error.

Exact-state inputs and RK4 training improve KeyCLD’s consistency score, while CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry but leaves large actuator residuals.
The framework distinguishes visual and geometric improvements from unresolved force and energy violations.

papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
authors: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao, Yue Feng, Jian Yu, Pengyang Shao, Yijun Tian, Xiaoyu Du
bullets: Cross-lingual safety gaps can let attacks bypass LLM guardrails, while existing alignment methods offer limited neuron-level interpretability.
SCAR scores from parallel safe and unsafe prompts identify language-specific safety neurons; their intersection forms the shared Safety Kernel (SK).
Activation suppression and state-transfer interventions validate the SK’s role in cross-lingual safety behavior.
SK-Masked LoRA restricts adaptation to FFN output dimensions associated with the SK.
Experiments report lower attack success across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, with generally limited effects on general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Pedipulating a freestanding articulated object requires controlling its pose and internal configuration while maintaining balance. We demonstrate this capability by autonomously solving a giant Rubik's Cube with a quadruped using only its feet. The task demands repeated precise interactions, since unintended layer motion can invalidate subsequent operations. We develop an onboard RGB-D perception pipeline that estimates the cube's metric pose and its full color state from partial views acquired through locomotion and flipping. A planner converts the computed solve into robot-executable skill sequences. Learned whole-body skills reorient the cube while preserving its layer configuration and turn its layers with one foot pinning the cube as the other pushes. We train these skills using reinforcement learning with privileged observations and distill them into policies that map onboard depth and proprioception to joint targets. The deployed policies tolerate variations in relative robot-cube placement and recover from external disturbances. The system completes three autonomous hardware solves, each about 30 steps over 8-9 minutes. These results show that combining onboard perception with coordinated pedipulation enables a quadruped to complete extended multi-step physical tasks. Additional material can be found at: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rubik-skills/

Reinforcement-learned whole-body skills are distilled into policies using onboard depth and proprioception, with recovery from placement variation and external disturbances.
The system completed three autonomous hardware solves of roughly 30 steps each in 8–9 minutes.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric 3D geometry from images is fundamentally ill-posed due to perspective projection ambiguity. Current geometry models incorporate supplied or predicted intrinsics during inference, but do not use them to supervise model adaptation. To refine these predictions, test-time adaptation (TTA) typically relies on external depth measurements. In this paper, we instead use camera intrinsics as an output-side geometric verifier. Comparing the point cloud's viewing rays with those defined by the known intrinsics yields a direct measure of geometric inconsistency. We propose \textit{IntriAdapt}, a TTA framework that minimizes this closed-form geometric residual. By optimizing a lightweight LoRA adapter on a frozen geometry foundation model, our method aligns the prediction with the specific camera model without depth sensors or external priors. We further extend this approach to video sequences, demonstrating that adapting a short sequence generalizes to other sequences captured by the same camera. The adapted model processes held-out images in a feed-forward pass, without repeating optimization for each frame. Experiments on ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks across multiple base models show that \textit{IntriAdapt} consistently outperforms both unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.
authors: Jiaxing Chen, Zizheng Yan, Jingyu Zhuang, Jinwei Chen, Shuguang Cui, Guanying Chen, Qingnan Fan
bullets: Addresses perspective ambiguity in image-based metric 3D geometry estimation.
Minimizes a closed-form residual between predicted point-cloud viewing rays and rays implied by the camera intrinsics.
Optimizes a lightweight LoRA adapter while keeping the geometry foundation model frozen.
Sequence adaptation generalizes across images from the same camera, enabling feed-forward inference on held-out frames.
Across ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks, it outperforms unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is emerging as a practical way to build a representation for robotics applications. However, deploying it on real-world platforms exposes multiple challenges. Rapid maneuvers of a robot induce motion-blurred images, which corrupt the reconstructed geometry and cause camera pose drift. Furthermore, the number of Gaussians grows without bound during continuous online mapping. In this study, we present RoMo-GS, an online 3DGS system designed to address these challenges. Instead of averaging N discrete sub-frames as in prior motion blur-aware 3DGS, we analytically integrate each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, yielding an O(1) complexity per Gaussian. Building on this, we bound the Gaussians' growth with a Hessian-based pruning score, while jointly refining pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam and an online LM step over the Gaussians. On multiple public datasets and a self-collected dataset, RoMo-GS matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS methods in rendering quality while running 15--150x faster, and operates online at competitive quality with about 20% fewer Gaussians than the online 3DGS baseline.
authors: Sangwoo Jung, Di Deng, Jiahui Fu, Laura Herlant, Ayoung Kim, Yafei Hu

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, risking either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction's sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents' rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule. In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.

bullets: Addresses compound instructions that mix safe and unsafe actions or hide hazards in longer task sequences.

papers.abstract: Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element-wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory-efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. Consequently, Adam remains a dominant and reliable choice for LLM pre-training. We propose AdamPM (Adam with Pooled Moments), a simple and memory-efficient variant of Adam that groups adjacent moment entries along the row or column dimension and represents each group by a single shared mean. AdamPM can well inherit Adam's hyperparameter settings and is readily integrated into existing Adam optimizer implementations, with less memory overhead. We systematically investigate pooling of both first and second moment estimates and identify second moment pooling as the effective design. With a group size of $s$, AdamPM reduces second moment memory to $1/s$ of the original requirement. Extensive experiments on language model pretraining, fine-tuning and multimodal learning demonstrate that AdamPM maintains model performance and training speed while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/jixiaowei95/AdamPM}.
authors: Xiaowei Ji, Lishan Xu, Jianing An, Jie Luo, Wenjun Wu, Lei Huang
bullets: Addresses Adam’s substantial memory overhead from element-wise first- and second-moment estimates in LLM training.

Experiments across language-model pretraining, fine-tuning, and multimodal learning show maintained performance and training speed.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.
authors: Deevyanshu Malu, Deeptanshu Malu, Sunita Sarawagi
bullets: Standard in-context training develops in-context term learning only weakly.
RareCipherFT pairs targets with context examples sharing rare terms, then replaces those terms with matching character-shuffled ciphers.
The cipher forces models to recover translations by copying from context rather than relying on lexical resources or shortcuts.
Across seven English–low-resource language directions and four 1B–7B models, term recall improves by 5–15 points without reducing COMET.
Probes with synonyms, nonce words, and surface-context controls support genuine source-to-translation linking.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan, Yang Li, Tiange Fu, Xiaoyuan Fu, Guiyang Luo, Jinglin Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large VLA models for real-time autonomous driving.

A budget scheduler allocates a real-time computational budget b based on intermediate qb features from the middle prefix layers. At the final prefix layer, a routing scheduler utilizes qlr to generate a binary mask M, dynamically activating specific layers and bypassing others via residual connections to yield final predictions.

papers.abstract: LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation policies. However, strong performance on LIBERO does not necessarily indicate robust embodied capabilities, as models may exploit benchmark-specific regularities rather than generalize to diverse operating conditions. In this work, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of embodied foundation models under distribution shifts. LIBERO-Pro2.0 encompasses 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six dimensions: Condition, Environment, Observation, Execution, Robot State Configuration, and Language, yielding 1,648 validated shifted task instances. To support robustness-oriented learning, we further collect 39,390 training trajectories through model-generated and human demonstrations. All shifted task instances undergo six rounds of iterative human review and correction to ensure physical plausibility and task validity. We evaluate 17 representative robot policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Our results reveal substantial robustness gaps across all evaluated paradigms: under runtime distribution shifts, the evaluated models exhibit an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points, with individual drops reaching 32.5 points. These findings highlight the gap between nominal benchmark performance and robustness under distribution shifts, underscoring the need for systematic robustness evaluation of embodied foundation models.

papers.abstract: Most simulation benchmarks for robotic manipulation keep target objects static and treat policy inference as instantaneous. These assumptions simplify evaluation but hide how a moving target evolves during computation and how stale an observation is when an action is executed. We introduce LIBERO-Dynamic, a dynamic extension of all 40 LIBERO tasks. It drives objects through contact friction along three trajectory families and speed tiers, while advancing the physical world according to calibrated, model-specific inference latency. The same mechanism supports training by replaying verified static demonstrations and compensating robot actions online for target displacement, producing 9,000 quality-filtered dynamic trajectories. We evaluate six pretrained policies on 1,800 dynamic conditions per configuration, compare execution strategies and action horizons with fixed checkpoints, and fine-tune three architectures using dynamic and mixed data. Faster motion degrades every policy but not uniformly; execution timing and horizon can change the behavior of the same policy; and asynchronous replanning benefits from frequent feedback only when the action queue avoids underflow. Dynamic demonstrations improve each architecture under at least one recipe, with gains varying by temporal conditioning, data composition, and training budget. A small-scale physical study shows task-dependent execution-strategy differences consistent with simulation. LIBERO-Dynamic makes object motion, inference latency, and action execution explicit and controllable for evaluating and improving robot policies in moving-target manipulation.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.
authors: Jinming Wang, Ruiheng Zhang, Yong Wang, Zipan Xiong, Keyuan Luo
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen VLA policies to learn from prior failures without updating the model.

Failure analysis highlights endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the absence of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline; physical safety improvement remains unestablished.

papers.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6$\times$ and 20.2$\times$. Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.
authors: Jiancong Ma, Kun Li, Jin Jiang, Shengcai Liao
bullets: Frames social co-action as an end-to-end agent task involving perception, dialogue, verbal response, and atomic action planning.

SocialCoAct-Bench contains 423 human-verified questions covering episode understanding, speaker intention, and coordinated action planning.

papers.abstract: Intelligent warehouse systems have transformed logistics by integrating robots with minimal infrastructure changes, boosting efficiency and optimizing workflows compared to traditional human-only operations. However, human-robot collaboration introduces new challenges, particularly due to human uncertainty, which leads to dynamic interactions and unpredictable behavior. To address these complexities, this paper presents the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, an extension of the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) problem that incorporates human unpredictability. This problem adds key constraints, such as dynamic obstacles caused by robots temporarily blocking paths when interacting with humans, and the need for real-time responsiveness. We formalize the MAPDwHC problem with additional constraints and properties. Based on this problem setting, we propose the CARVS algorithm, which improves task assignment and path planning by integrating task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. CARVS reduces congestion, enhances adaptability to human-robot interactions, and ensures real-time responsiveness. Simulation results show that CARVS significantly reduces timeouts of path planning in large-scale scenarios where traditional MAPD algorithms fail, improving both efficiency and scalability.
authors: Chaoran Li, Zeyuan Zhao, Shao Zhang
bullets: Introduces MAPDwHC, an extension of MAPD that models human unpredictability, temporary robot blockages, and real-time responsiveness.
Proposes CARVS, combining task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization for congestion-aware task assignment and path planning.
Simulation results indicate substantially fewer path-planning timeouts in large-scale scenarios than traditional MAPD algorithms.
Targets improved efficiency, adaptability, and scalability in human-collaborative warehouse operations.

papers.abstract: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) reduces training computation by skipping backpropagation for examples whose losses have stabilized, but the second-order loss-difference criterion used by IES lacks a theoretical justification. We develop Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping (TG-IES), which analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions and derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and a conditional stability bound for instance exclusion. We show that second-order differencing has a favorable bias-variance trade-off over first- and third-order differences in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and that its signal contains both gradient-drift and curvature terms. TG-IES derives its stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics rather than using the manually selected threshold of IES. Across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, TG-IES saves 53-58% of backpropagation instances in its main convolutional settings while keeping accuracy within 0.1-0.9 percentage points of full training; in the primary ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setting, this corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings. The method also transfers to ViT-Tiny, where it achieves smaller savings and incurs a modest accuracy cost. These results provide a theoretical basis for second-order instance-dependent early stopping and show that theory-guided calibration can substantially reduce training computation under the assumptions and experimental settings studied.
authors: Ahad Bin Islam Shoeb, Jamal Uddin Tanvin, Kamrul Hasan, Alve Reduan, Imtiaz Ahmed
bullets: Analyzes the bias-variance trade-off of second-order loss differences and identifies contributions from gradient drift and curvature.
Derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and conditional stability bound for excluding stabilized instances.
Sets stopping thresholds and patience from training-run statistics instead of manual tuning.
Saves 53–58% of backpropagation instances in reported convolutional settings, with accuracy within 0.1–0.9 percentage points of full training.
Transfers to ViT-Tiny with smaller savings and a modest accuracy cost, indicating scope-dependent effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
authors: Kerui Chen, Jinglu Wang, Yun Wang, Xinjiang Wang, Yan Lu
bullets: Addresses long-video context limits and the cost of reprocessing videos for each query.
Represents videos with time-anchored text and sparse images across multiple temporal scales.
Uses separate Writer and Reader workflows, optimized respectively for source fidelity/coverage and evidence localization/utilization.
Evolving the workflows improves average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness.
Reduces storage by about 99.86% while improving QA accuracy over direct frame input and a comparable agentic method.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. (a) Answering multiple questions about the same video incurs repeated processing costs: VLMs repeatedly process long visual contexts and also often omit details due to context limits, while agentic methods revisit the raw video through multiple retrieval and reasoning rounds. (b) To reduce query and storage costs, we adopt a write-once, query-many paradigm, encoding the video once into light-weight memory that preserves information for unknown future questions and supports efficient access across queries.

papers.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.
authors: Kevin Chen, Yu-Wei Zhan, Haoran Liang, Sen Cui, Changshui Zhang
bullets: Problem: Unconstrained latent transitions can drift from coherent physical evolution during recursive long-horizon prediction.
Method: Represent latent states with generalized coordinates and momenta, propagate them using dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, and map them back through a learnable inverse interface.
Training integration: HWM can augment existing world models without changing their perception or decoding components, while multi-step supervision aligns imagined and observed latent trajectories.
Results: HWM improves velocity, acceleration, and jerk estimates and reduces long-horizon energy drift in controlled simulations.
Embodied evaluations show gains across three settings, including 2.7% higher task success on RoboCasa, 9.7% higher nDTW with Ctrl-World, and 8.4% higher Logic with EVAC.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Hamiltonian latent dynamics framework. Given an observation ot, the encoder Eϕ maps it to a latent state zt, which is decomposed into generalized coordinates and momenta, (qt, pt), and evolved over multiple future steps using a learned hamiltonian energy function and a Symplectic Euler integrator. The resulting latent trajectory is mapped to latent representations and decoded by Dϕ to predict future observations. Training is jointly guided by the latent reconstruction loss, latent transition loss, and world-model reconstruction loss.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N methods improve text-only LLM reasoning by sampling multiple trajectories before selecting an answer. For Vision-Language Models (VLMs), answer frequency and model confidence alone can be insufficient, as sampled generations also vary in their engagement with the visual input. We find that distributional confidence and visual attention are complementary indicators of rollout quality. Each is limited on its own, while trajectories that show strong signals in both are more likely to be correct. Motivated by this, we introduce VisConf, a rollout-quality score that multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing rollouts that are weak in either signal. We incorporate Rank-Weighted Consensus (RWC), a tuning-free aggregation rule that converts within-question VisConf ranks into answer-level vote weights. Across three VLMs on MathVista, MMMU-Pro, and MMStar, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong BoN baselines. Our analysis shows particularly large gains when correct trajectories are present but underrepresented in the candidate pool.
authors: Muhammad Usman, Muhammad Qasim Ayub, Usman Ahad, Muhammad Tahir
bullets: VLM rollout quality depends on complementary signals: attention to visual input and distributional confidence.
VisConf multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing weakness in either signal.
Rank-Weighted Consensus converts within-question VisConf rankings into tuning-free answer vote weights.
Across three VLMs and three multimodal benchmarks, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong Best-of-N baselines.
Gains are especially large when correct trajectories exist but are underrepresented among sampled candidates.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VisConf and RWC framework. Given multiple sampled VLM rollouts, VisConf aggregates calibrated confidence and visual engagement independently over each trajectory, and combines them into a rollout-quality score, rewarding trajectories that are both confident and visually engaged. papers.abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.
authors: Diyi Hu, Ruizhong Qiu, Lin Qiu, Hanghang Tong, Hanqing Zeng
bullets: Addresses the coarse credit assignment of terminal rewards and GRPO’s uniform token-level advantages.
Selects partial-solution states using a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their verifier rewards with capped continuation probes.
Redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO’s trajectory advantage while preserving each trajectory’s mean token-level advantage.
Outperformed GRPO across evaluated models and achieved the highest accuracy in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons.
Beat dense-probing VinePPO on all six tested benchmarks while using 76% less end-to-end training time.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ProbePO improves cost-quality tradeoff by assigning within-trajectory credit with a sparse-probe budget. GRPO incurs no auxiliary-probe overhead but provides only trajectory-level credit. Dense per-boundary probing, exemplified by VinePPO, provides fine resolution at high rollout cost, while finite-sample Monte Carlo differences remain noise-sensitive. ProbePO instead caps the auxiliary-probe budget, concentrates it on selected pivots, and shrinks their value estimates before deriving segment-wise credit. The pipeline first fixes the policy-update trajectories, then ranks and probes candidate boundaries under the group-wide budget, and finally adds a token-mean-zero segment residual to the GRPO base advantage.

The detour (I2, a) receives negative credit; the answer reversal (I3, b) receives the strongest penalty. Each ProbePO profile preserves the GRPO token mean; in (b), r = 0.10 denotes a boxed but incorrect answer. Appendix D.5 provides the full contexts and pooled-M = 32 check.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Defines eight recurring skill categories for everyday contact-rich manipulation.
Introduces 36 reference tasks and over 40 reproducible object assets with physical and simulation support.
Uses tunable resistance loads and controlled task variations to test policy generalization.
Evaluations show vision-only policies struggle with contact perception and reaction, while visual-tactile policies provide no meaningful improvement on the tested tasks.
The benchmark is open-sourced for shared, reproducible research.

papers.abstract: Concept erasure removes harmful, private, or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models while preserving their other abilities. Leading models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 are trained with flow matching, and erasure methods for them fine-tune the model toward a guided teacher's velocities under a Euclidean loss. Yet the squared distance is only one member of a larger family: Bregman divergences are exactly the losses under which flow matching recovers the correct velocity field, and each member shapes differently what is erased and what is preserved. We introduce BEM (Bregman erasure matching), which is, to our knowledge, the first to learn this divergence through bi-level optimization, so that the fine-tuned model forgets the concept on unseen prompts while its unrelated generations stay unchanged. In the experiments we target the suppression of nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters. Under the evaluation protocol of GEM, BEM removes more of the concept than GEM on most settings, cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4% and the FID on nudity from 8.64 to 6.64, while retention holds on some concepts and degrades on others.
authors: Mohamed-Hicham Leghettas, Markus P\"uschel
bullets: Targets concept erasure in models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3, where existing methods use Euclidean velocity matching.
Uses bi-level optimization to learn a Bregman divergence that balances forgetting the target concept with retaining other abilities.
Evaluated on nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters under the GEM protocol.
Outperforms GEM on most settings, including reducing bloody-gore unsafe rate from 53.9% to 14.4% and nudity FID from 8.64 to 6.64.
Retention is preserved for some concepts but degrades for others.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies. Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free. Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors. The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.
authors: Anupam Pani, Wang Yuan, Qifan Wang, Yanchao Yang
bullets: Introduces a real-robot, multi-view gaze dataset with 12,000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains.
Synchronizes 300 Hz human gaze with images, proprioception, and actions, then transfers gaze targets across camera views.
Uses gaze as soft supervision to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training; inference requires no gaze.
Improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6% across 18 real-world tasks, with gains up to 25 percentage points.
Benefits transfer to LIBERO-Spatial and different VLA backbones; real gaze outperforms generic attention-shaping priors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of GazeAct. Left: We collect teleoperation demonstrations with synchronized robot observations, proprioception, actions, and eye gaze recorded on the active robot camera view. Middle: Recorded gaze is first aligned to the remaining camera views and converted into patch-level gaze distributions. During training, these distributions regularize the policy’s language-conditioned visual attention toward task-relevant regions. Right: At inference, gaze is not required as a signal and the policy predicts actions from standard VLA inputs: images, language, and proprioception.

Fig. 2. Data collection and synchronization system. During ALOHA teleoperation, robot observations, proprioception, and actions are logged on the robot side, while a screen-based eye tracker records the operator’s gaze on the displayed camera feed. Hardware triggers define shared trial boundaries, and synchronized timestamps support post hoc alignment of gaze with images, proprioception, and actions.

Fig. 4. Attention Regularization. Top: the transformer-based policy processes language and image patch tokens, producing visual attention over robot observations while learning to predict actions. Bottom: during training, recorded teleoperation gaze is converted into patch-level heatmaps and used as an auxiliary signal to guide the policy’s visual attention toward human-fixated, task-relevant regions. At inference, gaze is not required and the policy predicts actions from standard VLA inputs.

Fig. 5. Attention Visualization. Qualitative attention maps for ricecooker and injection-tray rollouts. Warmer regions indicate higher languageconditioned visual attention. Compared with the baseline, the attentionregularized policy places more attention on actionable regions, including the rice-cooker button and the injection tool, while using no gaze input at inference.

Fig. 3. Cross-View Gaze Alignment for Multi-View Robot Observations. We visualize a teleoperated trajectory for the task “open the rice cooker and pour the contents of the bowl inside.” At each timestep, gaze is recorded only on the active camera view (blue edges); our cross-view alignment propagates it to the remaining synchronized views (orange edges). The overlays show that the propagated gaze remains spatially consistent across viewpoints and task-relevant regions.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation remains challenging due to the loss of fine-grained details and limited adaptability to varying scene structures. In this paper, we propose SAP-Depth, a novel architecture based on Scene-Adaptive Probabilistic. Unlike traditional methods, we introduce a Dynamic Bins mechanism powered by a Learnable Parameter Predictor, which adaptively estimates scene-specific depth distributions conditioned on the input image context. Furthermore, a Bin-wise Probability Distribution Decoder is designed to effectively fuse multi-scale representations to predict dense depth probability distributions, significantly enhancing boundary sharpness and structural recovery. Through the collaborative coupling of these proposed modules, our model achieves dynamic prediction of scene-specific depth distributions. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset show that SAP-Depth outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, particularly in its ability to better preserve complex edge details. Further, tests on the Make3D dataset validate the model's excellent generalization capability and robustness.
authors: Bowen He, Li Zhang, Yujie Chen, Chang Cheng
bullets: Addresses lost fine details and limited adaptability across varying scene structures.
Uses Dynamic Bins with a Learnable Parameter Predictor to estimate image-conditioned, scene-specific depth distributions.
Employs a Bin-wise Probability Distribution Decoder to fuse multi-scale features and predict dense depth probabilities.
Reports improved accuracy and complex-edge preservation on KITTI, with generalization and robustness validated on Make3D.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong performance on multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), yet their reliability under biased conditions remains underexplored. We investigate length bias, the systematic preference for longer answer options, through controlled benchmarks spanning fine-grained visual domains. LVLMs consistently favor longer options even when visually inconsistent, with accuracy dropping 2--38\% when correct answers are shorter and increasing 1--70\% when longer. This bias persists across model scales. Through layer-wise mechanistic analysis, we reveal that length bias emerges from late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-side length priors. Blurry-image experiments show that bias intensifies when visual evidence weakens, while abstention tests reveal that LVLMs struggle to refuse incorrect predictions. We propose and evaluate multiple inference-time mitigation strategies; while these provide partial improvements, none achieves deployable bias mitigation without relying on oracle information unavailable at inference time. These results underscore that inference-time interventions are insufficient, pointing to the need for architectural solutions and bias-aware training.
authors: Md. Atabuzzaman, Hani Alomari, Chris Thomas
bullets: Controlled benchmarks show LVLMs prefer longer answer options, even when those options conflict with visual evidence.
Accuracy changes substantially depending on whether the correct option is shorter or longer, and the bias persists across model scales.
Layer-wise analysis links the bias to late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-based length priors.
The bias becomes stronger with blurry images, while models also struggle to abstain from incorrect predictions.
Inference-time mitigation methods offer only partial improvements and require unavailable oracle information for reliable deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our framework for investigating length bias in LVLMs. We create length-controlled MCQA variants to systematically expose length bias, conduct layer-wise analysis revealing late-layer suppression of visual evidence, perform diagnostic experiments using abstention and blurry images to localize bias sources, and evaluate mitigation strategies like ELED, caption-guided MCQA and Yes/No QA.

Figure 7: Example multiple-choice questions from the Dogs dataset illustrating four length-controlled variants: Equal Long, Equal Short, Shorter Correct, and Longer Correct. Despite this increased visual grounding, long incorrect options are preferentially selected, demonstrating that length bias operates through override of visual evidence in the language decoder rather than insufficient visual information retrieval.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates length bias and robustness in large vision-language models for multiple-choice QA.
papers.title: Investigating Length Bias and Robustness in LVLMs for Multiple-Choice Question Answering
papers.tldr: LVLMs exhibit persistent length bias in multiple-choice visual QA, often overriding visual evidence, and current inference-time fixes only partially mitigate it.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
authors: Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Targets high transient memory from full-prompt KV-cache construction, which limits long-context inference.
Processes prompt chunks layer by layer, retaining full-prompt KV only for the active layer before evicting it.
Preserves full-prompt-aware cache selection while reducing activation and temporary memory.
At 64K context, cuts construction-time transient memory by 83.89% on A100; on RTX 4090, TTFT increases only 1.06%.
Enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.

papers.abstract: While a LLM's chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT's content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.
authors: Arav Dhoot, Yixiong Hao, Zephaniah Roe
bullets: Replicates the necessity effect across 11 models from six model families, beyond the originally tested Gemini models.
All models follow simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while following concealed complex cues generally returns near baseline.
Extends evaluation to five cue families and three difficulty levels, including four new cue types.
The link between CoT necessity and unfaithfulness varies by cue type and model; some models verbalize hint-following even when it is computationally simple.
Supports CoT monitoring for unsafe behavior requiring non-trivial computation, but cautions that monitoring reliability is context-sensitive.
