papers.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
papers.tldr: Across 11 models, concealed cue-following usually breaks down when it requires complex computation, making chain-of-thought monitoring useful but strongly dependent on the task and model.

papers.abstract: Visual imitation policies can organise task motion, yet contact-rich object use demands gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing. We study fine-grained gripper control as a local feedback problem within ongoing task execution. Our approach assigns tactile feedback a dedicated control role during contact-rich task stages. We introduce ContactPolicy, a learned local controller that takes over the gripper while a visual base policy continues to control the arm. ContactPolicy combines tactile and force histories with current robot state to jointly predict gripper increments and their modulation, updating the gripper target from each new observation. An Intent policy manages control handover between the visual base policy and ContactPolicy. Real-world experiments on container opening, object handling, and tool operation show improved task success over both the Visuomotor Policy and Tactile-Force Policy baselines. Execution analysis illustrates how the gripper adjusts contact within an ongoing task, including periods of target retention and fine-grained changes as interaction conditions evolve. Arm-state ablations and failure analysis further examine how execution context supports local regulation. These results support task-local tactile policies for fine-grained gripper control within visual manipulation.
authors: Mingyuan Ba, Yanan Zhou, James Zhao, Weiming Zhi
bullets: Addresses the need for gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing during contact-rich tasks.
Combines tactile and force histories with robot state to predict gripper increments and their modulation.
An Intent policy hands gripper control between the visual base policy and the tactile local controller.
Real-world tests on container opening, object handling, and tool use report higher task success than two stated baselines.
Analysis shows target retention and fine-grained contact adaptation, while ablations and failure analysis examine the role of execution context.

papers.abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.
authors: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu, Chaochen Gao Tinghao Yu, Feng Zhang, Lilin Wang
bullets: Random sampling of natural long documents outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths under matched training budgets.
Within the same candidate pool, LongPPL key-token-density selection improves downstream performance, while evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors do not.
truncLongPPL scores only a truncated prefix, achieving performance close to full-span scoring with a measured 2.28× end-to-end scoring speedup at 128K.
Across context-extension, mixed-length training, and SFT evaluations, selected documents yield consistent gains, particularly on retrieval-focused tasks.
The study evaluates Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo 3-7B across 128K–256K target contexts, with short-context performance largely preserved.

papers.abstract: Individually competent robot skills can fail when composed: tools may lack a required capability, completion signals may misrepresent physical progress, and one skill may leave a state that violates its successor's prerequisites. We introduce Recursia, a recursive self-improvement framework that treats the shared executable stack, rather than individual task programs, as the persistent unit of improvement. The stack integrates tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers. Source-side execution traces guide failure attribution and the generation of missing tools or repairs to existing shared components. Generality checks, mechanism tests, and paired selection and regression gates determine which changes become the next parent. The resulting stack is frozen and reused through declarative task adapters, allowing source-derived changes to support new compositions without target-side code repair. Experiments cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 equipped with a Franka Hand. In simulation, Recursia improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 percentage points under Pos perturbations and 15.1 points under Task perturbations. Across three physical compositional target tasks, it improves mean success over the Skill Document Only baseline by 40 percentage points. Analyses of constituent execution, candidate rejection, and inference drivers distinguish local mechanism improvements from complete task success and characterize the cost of feedback-conditioned orchestration. These results examine shared executable interfaces as a concrete mechanism for compositional transfer in robot programming.
authors: Yangzhi Chen, Feiran Liu, Zishuo Wang, Zijian Jin, Xin Zhu, Lecheng Ruan, Wenjuan Han
bullets: Targets failures in skill composition caused by missing capabilities, misleading completion signals, and incompatible handoffs.
Uses source execution traces for failure attribution, generates repairs or new tools, and filters updates with generality, mechanism, selection, and regression checks.
Freezes the improved stack and reuses it through declarative task adapters, avoiding target-side code repair.
Improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 and 15.1 percentage points under two simulation perturbation settings, and by 40 percentage points over a document-only baseline across three physical tasks.
Evaluations cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 with a Franka Hand; analyses separate local mechanism gains from complete-task success.

papers.abstract: Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O-SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O-SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi-view fusion to an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self-supervised objective that O-SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label-free per-frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective-prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.
authors: Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Timothy Patten, Donald G. Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller
bullets: Addresses online change detection from unconstrained viewpoints without future observations or stored past observations.
Uses a single backward rendering pass to project each new cue map onto reference-map Gaussians and maintain an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian.
Derives a label-free decision threshold by sorting the self-supervised objective, with its margin supporting selective prediction.
On PASLCD, improves mean IoU from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 FPS.
Remains strictly causal while exceeding O-SCD’s reported offline result.

papers.abstract: Large, unlabeled datasets of prior experience have become increasingly available for agentic tasks in domains such as robotics and coding. A common recipe for these tasks is to train a policy using the prior data, and then further improve it with online rollouts. But while much work has studied how to use both the offline and online data for policy extraction, far less work has been done to understand how the prior data can be used to efficiently \textit{explore} during the online learning phase. Previous work has attempted to formalize this idea by defining the \textit{empowerment}, a measure of how many future states an agent can realize; states with higher empowerment require more exploration as there are more futures to explore. However, existing methods for estimating empowerment require online policy rollouts in the environment. We propose the first method for estimating empowerment from unlabeled prior data, without any environment interaction. By jointly learning an empowerment-maximizing policy together with its discounted state-occupancy measure, our estimator can be trained on unlabeled trajectories generated from any unknown policy. We demonstrate that our empowerment estimator qualitatively gives intuitive empowerment measures and show that the pretrained estimator can be used to improve exploration in the online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/ishirgarg/offline-empowerment}.
authors: Ishir Garg, Vivek Myers, Qiyang Li, Catherine Ji, Benjamin Eysenbach, Sergey Levine
bullets: Targets the underexplored use of prior offline data for exploration rather than only policy learning.
Introduces an estimator trained without environment interaction or knowledge of the data-generating policy.
Jointly learns an empowerment-maximizing policy and its discounted state-occupancy measure.
Shows qualitatively intuitive empowerment estimates and improved exploration in online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.
Scope: demonstrations are based on qualitative estimation and exploration improvements, without reported quantitative results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
authors: Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Zeyu Fang, Tian Lan
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of choosing research assignments while learning from the resulting experiences.
Uses a hierarchical framework: a Coordinator organizes search branches and directives, while Scientists generate hypotheses and execution plans.
Alternates GRPO-style updates for both hierarchy levels under a shared best-of-budget objective; execution uses a frozen shared Executor.
Provides theoretical results on objective alignment, coordination gains, private adaptation, and finite-budget regret.
On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD was best on 20 and achieved the highest aggregate normalized MLGym scores; comparisons involve mostly proprietary Scientist baselines.

papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting reliable lessons from flawed or mixed-quality attempts.
Uses selective hippocampal-style encoding and replay to diagnose shortcomings and compare attempts on the same task.
Merges overlapping memories and resolves conflicts with explicit applicability conditions instead of storing every lesson separately.
Improves performance on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web while retaining substantially fewer experiences than simple accumulation.
Benefits persist across base models with varying capabilities, including highly capable models.

papers.abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.
authors: unsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han, Seungryul Baek
bullets: Targets ambiguous references to adjacent body parts, garments, and visually similar motions.
Uses per-avatar semantic and motion memories to connect language with persistent Gaussian regions and joint trajectories.
An MLLM selects regions by appearance, relation, or function, while composable operators identify matching motion intervals.
Selections are traceable and extensible through category choices and operator programs.
On three human-annotated benchmarks, it outperforms baselines in part, 3D, and 4D referring segmentation, with minutes of per-avatar setup.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang, Yixuan Lin, Yuyang Hou, Bin Wu, Ruike Cao, Li Xiao, Yinsheng Li
bullets: Introduces UNICORNS, a benchmark with 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans and four evidence conditions.
Tests referential ambiguity, insufficient evidence, false presuppositions, and related challenges using eight categories plus answerable controls.
Six open-source 3D-LLMs show a large reliability gap: 61.22% on controls versus 40.94% on challenge categories for the strongest zero-shot model.
Proposes HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method using task, obligation, and supervised control-replay rewards.
HORN achieves 75.1 ± 1.0% on challenges and 77.2 ± 0.8% overall, without degrading control accuracy.

papers.abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
authors: Zhaiming Shen, Alexander Cloninger, Rongjie Lai, Wenjing Liao
bullets: Motivated by the gap between fixed-kernel interpretations of attention and the trainable query/key matrices used in practice.
Studies ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression tasks.
Shows through simulations that learned attention scores closely match oracle kernels for these function classes.
Develops a generalization-error framework linking transformer ICL to oracle kernel estimation.
Provides a constructive implementation using wide, shallow transformers, explaining prediction through query–context interactions.

papers.abstract: Simulation-to-real driving video diffusion models can translate photorealistic scenes, but they typically represent pedestrians and cyclists, vulnerable road users (VRUs), as generic object classes. This is insufficient for vulnerable road users whose safety-relevant appearance depends on articulated pose and identity. We present BodyBridge and Grounded Body Layers (GBL), a simulator-derived, pixel-aligned representation that combines scene geometry, canonical per-pixel body correspondence, and exact VRU masks. GBL provides explicit articulation to the video diffusion model, emphasizes VRU regions during control-branch post-training, and supports additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference. It also enables per-joint evaluation of generated VRUs and a failure taxonomy for identity errors. On CARLA-to-real translation, BodyBridge improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over the released depth-conditioned baseline. Replacing normal-map body control with canonical correspondence reduces body flips by 18%, while composition reduces near-range facing flips by 27%. These results show that explicit body grounding complements scene-level control and improves pose-faithful VRU generation. All code, data, and model checkpoints will be made publicly available to support reproducible, pedestrian-aware autonomous driving research.
authors: Mark Azer, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the limits of generic VRU representations, whose articulated pose and identity are safety-relevant.
Introduces Grounded Body Layers (GBL): simulator-derived, pixel-aligned body correspondence, scene geometry, and exact VRU masks.
Uses VRU-focused control-branch post-training and additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference.
On CARLA-to-real translation, improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over a released depth-conditioned baseline.
Canonical correspondence and composition reduce body flips by 18% and near-range facing flips by 27%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices, and source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches fail on real recordings, whose label-free prefix is 87.9--98.6% normal beats. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. The score offsets and decision rules were set on MIT-BIH only; the rate-invariant RR head (relA) was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once on Icentia11k chest-patch recordings under a pre-registered protocol. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT reached an arrhythmia macro-$F_1$ $J = \frac{1}{2}(\text{S-}F_1 + \text{V-}F_1) = 48.7\%$ [95% CI 42.1, 54.7] versus 34.5% without adaptation ($\Delta J = +14.1$ [+8.6, +19.3] pp; 59.8% versus 43.9% in non-AF) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In the 75-patient test subgroup of the historical split (73 analyzed), the gain was not significant (+6.1 [-8.5, +23.4] pp). Adaptation takes a median of 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
authors: JinKook Kim
bullets: Addresses patient/device domain shift when target recordings are heavily dominated by unlabeled normal beats.
Uses a closed-form symmetric positive-definite transport map estimated from normal beats in each recording’s first 5 minutes.
Adapts only normal and supraventricular prototypes while keeping ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed.
On 493 patients and 973 Icentia11k recordings, macro-F1 rose from 34.5% to 48.7%, outperforming five adjusted comparators.
The gain was not significant in a small 73-patient historical test subgroup; median adaptation time was 5.8 ms per record.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of NAGT (GA NS). (a) Dual-branch model and label-free adaptation pipeline. Each beat is encoded by a frozen convolutional encoder into an 8×8 SPD covariance descriptor C(x) and scored by its Log-Euclidean distance to the class prototypes; a parallel rate-invariant relative-RR branch (relA) adds RR logits and the fixed offsets δS = 1, δF = 0.5. From the label-free 5-min prefix, U1 normal anchors (non-premature beats with p(N) ≥ 0.5 under the four-dimensional RR head, 80% core of the patient’s own covariance cloud) define the AIRM mean M̂N and the closed-form congruence map Ap (Eq. Fig. 3. Error flows and the geometric abstention buffer. (a) Error flows removed or created by each design step, as a percentage of the true class, on MIT-BIH DS2 (Track B source), INCART (MIT-BIH-44 source) and Icentia11k; final RR configuration (relA, δS = 1, δF = 0.5) for every arm, 6-seed means (counts in Table 2; Section 2.3 additionally quotes the original four-dimensional RR-head counts of Table 2b,c). Outlined bars mark the step at which each flow appears: GN swallows S beats (S→N), GA All repels V (V→S), GA SV inflates N→V, and GA NS converts borderline N→V into N→F. Selected Icentia11k counts are given with leader lines. (b) DS1-CV grid of the F-logit offset δF (selected value circled): J versus N sensitivity for GA NS and GA SV. (c) N→V and N→F counts on DS1-CV as δF increases (dotted vertical segments: N→V gap between GA SV and GA NS); when F is effectively masked (large δF ), GA SV and GA NS coincide.

papers.title: Transport What Shares the Conduction Pathway: Normal-Anchored SPD Geometric Transport for Source-Free Patient Adaptation of Holter and Patch ECG

papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.
authors: Jessica Yang, Marcelo Beramendi Caballero, Ju-Chieh Chou, Karen Livescu
bullets: Self-supervised speech models use computationally expensive CNN local feature extractors that resemble simpler mel features.
The proposed universal extractor is learned by distillation from HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM teachers.
On SUPERB(-SG), it largely retains teacher performance and transfers to the unseen wav2vec 2.0 model.
It uses only 3% of the CNNs’ MACs and reduces overall inference runtime by more than 20%.
Scope: evaluation focuses on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks and the tested teacher/model families.

papers.title: Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
papers.tldr: A distilled two-layer speech feature extractor replaces costly CNN front ends while largely preserving downstream performance and reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Luoyi Zhang, Chan-Jan Hsu, Fernando Ruiloba Portilla, Jinchuan Tian, Shinji Watanabe, Carlos Busso
bullets: Targets perceptual errors and limited-diversity descriptions in existing audio post-training data.
Builds dense semantic, acoustic, and temporal descriptions, then creates challenging questions and incorrect reasoning traces.
Extends short traces into longer cognitive reasoning sequences through thought continuation.
Synthesizes 1.6M traces and trains Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization.
Reports accuracy gains on MMAU Test-mini, MMAR, and MMSU.

papers.abstract: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.

Improves conditional recovery and the share of predictions attributed to cross-modal interactions.
Conditional-recovery gains persist with Transformer-based fusion modules.

Figure 1: Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR): MSCR suppresses modality dominance and encourages the discovery of synergistic information. Raw data (X1, X2) are encoded into representations (Z1, Z2). These and their permuted variants (Z̃1, Z̃2) are fed into the fusion network to produce joint (pjoint) and shuffled (pshuf1, pshuf2) predictions, while the unimodal heads provide an additive reference (pref). The MSCR loss is built from three mechanisms: Ldom penalizes single-modality dominance by applying a smoothmax over modality sensitivities; Lsyn requires the joint prediction to outperform the unimodal reference by a margin m, with ∆ denoting the hinge argument; and a proficiency-aware gate (g) scales the regularizer according to the best unimodal loss (ℓbest).

papers.abstract: Human video demonstrations provide rich manipulation strategies for dexterous manipulation learning. We study a setting in which a fully specified simulated scene is used to generate videos that specify the demonstrated manipulation behavior. This setup provides access to scene information such as object geometry, articulation, and camera parameters, while allowing direct control over task and scene configuration. However, generated videos may contain geometric distortions, inaccurate contacts, and other physical inconsistencies, making the recovered motion difficult to execute directly on a robot. We present an end-to-end framework for converting such simulation-grounded videos into physically executable dexterous robot demonstrations. Our perception pipeline leverages the known scene through model-based object tracking with dense foundation-model features and depth-based hand-object alignment. The recovered human motion is then retargeted and physically grounded using residual reinforcement learning, where a backward curriculum and a cache of physically valid reset states enable the policy to correct imperfect video-derived references while preserving the demonstrated manipulation strategy. On clean ARCTIC demonstrations, our method achieves competitive performance with prior dexterous retargeting approaches and shows greater robustness when applied to references extracted from generated videos. We further demonstrate diverse rigid and articulated manipulation tasks in simulation and successful open-loop transfer of the optimized trajectories to a real dexterous robot.

papers.abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, Hengquan Huang, Shuang Qiu, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai
bullets: Targets query-dependent user preferences when only binary comparisons between candidate responses are available.

Evaluated on seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks with reference- and model-based preference simulators.

The agent generates the resulting response pair, obtains one binary preference, and updates both systems (4–5). After T rounds, the highest-scoring persona produces the personalized response, and the query-local BT increments are retained for later warm starts.

papers.abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long-term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query-relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE-Mem, Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query-guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix-length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length-normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE-Mem is a training-free, plug-in retrieval method for clip-based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE-Mem improves question-answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.
authors: Shidu Ren, Rong-cheng Tu, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
bullets: Addresses redundant memories and the mismatch between fixed retrieval depth and question-specific evidence needs.

Improves QA accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks.

papers.abstract: GUI world models are increasingly used to improve action selection by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, but it is unclear how much of the resulting gain comes from prediction itself rather than from the evaluator that interprets those predictions. We study this attribution problem through controlled interventions on GUI action selection. With candidates and predictions held fixed, lookahead gains can change with how the prediction is presented to the evaluator, so end-to-end gains cannot be attributed to prediction alone. We then introduce Direct Action Ranking (DAR), which learns from reference actions to score candidates without generating future screens, and compare it with a prediction-augmented variant under matched supervision. Predicted successors add no detectable ranking signal once evaluation is learned directly. Without retraining, DAR improves AndroidWorld task success by 5.8--16.4 points across three proposers, outperforms world-model lookahead, and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps, where every prediction-conditioned configuration falls below proposer confidence. These results suggest that GUI world models should be evaluated by their decision value, the incremental action-selection value of their predictions beyond a strong direct evaluator, rather than by prediction fidelity or end-to-end lookahead gain alone.
authors: Sizhe Tang, Hanhan Zhou, Jeffrey Svajlenko, Rashmi Gangadharaiah
bullets: Lookahead gains depend on how predicted screens are presented to the evaluator, so they cannot be attributed to prediction alone.
Direct Action Ranking (DAR) scores candidate actions from reference actions without generating future screens.

Without retraining, DAR improves AndroidWorld success by 5.8–16.4 points across three proposers and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps.
The study argues that world models should be assessed by incremental decision value, not prediction fidelity or lookahead gains alone.

papers.title: Beyond Next-Screen Prediction: The Decision Value of GUI World Models
papers.tldr: GUI world-model predictions may add little decision value beyond a strong evaluator that directly ranks candidate actions.

papers.abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. We introduce \textbf{WAQS} (\textbf{W}eight \textbf{A}bsorption for \textbf{Q}uadratic probing and affine \textbf{S}teering), a framework that obtains state-dependent steering, without additional inference-time computation. WAQS models a concept with a quadratic probe, whose gradient yields an affine, activation-dependent steering direction. We show that this affine intervention can be folded exactly into adjacent linear transformations through an offline weight update. Moreover, we prove that quadratic functions form the maximal class of smooth concept scores whose gradient-based interventions are affine and therefore exactly absorbable into linear layers. Under a Gaussian representation model, our formulation admits an interpretation as the difference of class-conditional Mahalanobis pulls and naturally generalizes linear discriminant and difference-in-means steering. To scale to high-dimensional representations, we introduce a low-rank parameterization of the quadratic term. Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy steering tasks, quadratic steering matches or improves upon constant linear steering while preserving model utility, with the absorbed implementation introducing no additional inference-time operations. Our results suggest that quadratic probes provide a practical middle ground between static linear steering and computationally expensive dynamic nonlinear interventions.
authors: Ding Zhu, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–expressiveness trade-off between fixed steering vectors and costly dynamic interventions.
Uses a quadratic concept probe whose gradient produces an activation-dependent affine steering direction.
Exactly folds this affine intervention into adjacent linear layers through an offline weight update.
Proves quadratic scores are the maximal smooth class yielding affine, exactly absorbable gradient interventions.
Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy tasks, it matches or improves linear steering while preserving utility; a low-rank form supports high-dimensional representations.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
authors: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee, Jonathan May, Shirley Ho
bullets: Speculative decoding uses a lightweight drafter to propose tokens that the target LLM verifies in parallel.
Existing block-diffusion drafters generate blocks quickly but predict tokens independently.
FlashMap conditions a continuous-flow language model on the target model’s hidden states to capture inter-token dependencies.
It generates the entire token block in one forward pass.
On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap outperforms matched DFlash across all benchmarks, with 7% higher average speedup.

papers.abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.
authors: Qishun Yang, Shu Yang, Difei Xu, Di Wang, Meng Ding
bullets: Evaluates privacy leakage when complete histories imply a sensitive relation but individual sessions do not.
Introduces 288 synthetic cases with hidden target annotations and compares six memory systems plus full-history and no-history controls.
Separately measures target-attribute visibility in stored/retrieved context and whether the final answer states the complete relation.
A paired test shows that removing shared identifiers or connecting clues can change relation disclosure even when target attributes remain visible.
Scope: synthetic cases focused on cross-session reconstruction during ordinary tasks.

papers.abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.
authors: Mankeerat Sidhu, Gangmuk Lim, Hetarth Chopra, Maximillian Eisenberg, Quan Hao Ng, Aryan Gosaliya, Shu Liu, Luka Govedi\v{c}, Jiaxin Shan, Hongkuan Zhou, Vikram Sharma Mailthody, P. Brighten Godfrey, Ion Stoica
bullets: Addresses the changing, interdependent choices involved in selecting accelerators, parallelism, engine settings, replicas, placement, and cost across multi-cloud fleets.
Uses a Recursive Language Model hierarchy to generate deployment hypotheses, while deterministic tools predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement.
Builds a fixed causal graph linking deployment decisions, runtime factors such as KV-cache pressure and communication overhead, and outcomes including latency and throughput.
Updates scoped causal relationships after deployments to create a reusable inference playbook and composes job-level configurations into cluster-wide plans.

Reports 1.18× higher goodput than the strongest baseline and 20% lower cost per token in a real heterogeneous cluster; ablations show the full planner outperforming tool-augmented and pure language-model variants.

papers.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
authors: Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
bullets: Targets real-time single-batch inference bottlenecks from kernel-launch overhead, data movement, and redundant recomputation across decisions.
Uses deep kernel fusion with launch overlap, an execution contract for cross-decision state reuse, and execution-state capsules for fast snapshot, restore, and fork operations.
Supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models through parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement.
Across evaluated policies and hardware, achieves 1.3–3.7× speedup at matched 16-bit precision and 3.38–12.66× over official eager implementations with reduced precision.
In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 reaches 94.04% success on Jetson AGX Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, near or above the reported FP16 reference.

papers.abstract: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.
authors: Sicheng Lyu, Xinyu Wang, Yu Gu, Lei Ding, Ziyang Song, Xiao-Wen Chang
bullets: A disagreement-based router selects when a low-precision agent should invoke its BF16 model, with evaluation based on end-to-end task success.
Paired branch interventions separate the effects of replacing one action, taking over later execution, or replacing both action and continuation.
In Qwen3 agents on tau2-bench, first-action BF16 replacement changed many outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled; the held-out telecom estimate was negative.
Replacing both action and continuation produced a positive net gain in only two of five exploratory lower-bit settings.
Same-precision references and even tool-argument ordering also changed outcomes, while an uncertainty trigger found more changes than random selection without clear net benefit.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the value of precision upgrades in closed-loop agents, directly addressing efficiency in AI systems.
papers.title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
papers.tldr: Precision fallbacks should be judged by their net task benefit under the exact intervention and continuation that will run, because they can rescue and spoil tasks in nearly equal measure.

papers.abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.
authors: Anjulie Agrusa, Andrei Panferov, Elizabeth Wei, Keith Wyss, Paul Gibbons, Erik Schultheis, Jinhang Choi, Frank Sun, Tijmen Blankevoort, Dan Alistarh
bullets: Evaluates NVFP4 training recipes on dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models for up to 1T tokens.
Proposes an optimized recipe combining established stable-training principles with unbiased gradient estimation that reduces quantization error.
Finds that every component of the optimized recipe improves the loss trajectory.
Shows selective high-precision layers are necessary for accuracy recovery at scale.
Finds de-biasing benefits vary across backward-pass tensors, motivating complementary error-reduction methods.

papers.selection_reason: Comparative study of low-precision FP4 pretraining recipes for LLMs; directly addresses training efficiency and energy reduction in AI systems.
papers.title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
papers.tldr: A systematic study identifies which techniques enable effective NVFP4 pretraining at medium scale, showing that selective high-precision layers and carefully targeted de-biasing are key to narrowing the loss gap to BF16.

papers.abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.
authors: Tara Dixit, Jessie Dong, Summer Li
bullets: NIST now labels mainly high-priority CVEs, creating a need to infer missing enrichment from text alone.
The study predicts all eight CVSS v3.1 base components, base score, severity tier, and CWE using CVEs from 2022–2023 and evaluates on 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs.
LoRA-tuned Phi-3.5-mini achieves 69.9% severity accuracy, 70.9% CWE accuracy, and exact vector matches for 48.8% of CVEs.
Deriving scores from predicted vectors improves TF-IDF logistic regression’s critical-severity recall from 50.7% to 73.3%.
The fine-tuned model outperforms TF-IDF by 2.8–4.7 accuracy points, while combining their predictions reaches 75.8% correct severity tiers across CVEs.

papers.tldr: Fine-tuning a small language model on CVE descriptions enables useful prediction of CVSS severity, vectors, and CWE labels for newly published vulnerabilities.

papers.abstract: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
authors: Haowen Tang, Wei Xia, Raoyuan Zhao, Hinrich Sch\"utze, Yihong Liu
bullets: They avoid fixed subword vocabularies by processing rendered text, benefiting typographical and multilingual settings.
Fine-tuning requires longer training and broader labelled-data coverage, with delayed learning and learning-rate-sensitive failures.
Pretrained pixel representations make task-relevant information less accessible during downstream adaptation.

After successful adaptation, they retain substantially more accuracy under typographical noise and outperform English-pretrained text models on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean-English performance.
The central trade-off is reduced input sensitivity at the cost of a more difficult adaptation bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.
authors: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song, Tingle Li, Haonan Chen, Edward H. Adelson
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting contact-rich robot data with force feedback and varied gripper geometry.
Trains a world model on 4.9 hours of bimanual human interaction using video, tactile images, sensor motion, and force.
Represents actions as tactile-sensor motion plus force change, creating a shared human–robot action space.
Jointly predicts scene, wrist, and tactile observations; scene prediction improves by 0.7–2.0 dB PSNR over scratch-trained baselines on held-out human data.
In robot rollouts, contact imprints transfer qualitatively, while visual and wrist-view predictions are inconsistent across tasks.

papers.abstract: BERT-based models require thousands of labeled samples to train. Larger models like GPT-X require only 1-5 examples per class. However, performance, cost and time tradeoffs of such models remain under-explored. In this work, we classify survey text data into 16 classes. We focus on experimental approaches and results on performance, cost, and time taken for this problem. We compare these parameters of a trained RoBERTa-based model, and an (off-the-shelf) GPT-3.5 model for text classification. Baseline experiments show that the time taken by GPT-3.5 for generating predictions on 10,000 records is 6 hours, whereas a RoBERTa-based model takes only 12 mins on a T4 GPU. To identify the best prompting approach for GPT-3.5, we explore batch prompting. We experiment with (1) batch-size, and (2) few-shot sampling. We find the best batch size is 20 with human few-shot curation. Experiments show the F1 score of a trained RoBERTa-based model (96%) is much higher than a GPT-3.5 model (83%). In case of GPT-3.5, batch prompting is beneficial in lowering inference costs by ~70%, without hindering task performance. We find the best approach is an ensemble of a RoBERTa-based and GPT-3.5 model (F1: 97.5%) incurring only 4.4% of inference cost compared to a standalone GPT-3.5.
authors: Shivam Mathur, Sri Harish Popuri, Priya Krishnan Sundararajan, Kevin Horecka, Michael Mugo
bullets: Compares a trained RoBERTa model with off-the-shelf GPT-3.5 for 16-class survey-text classification.
RoBERTa processes 10,000 records in 12 minutes on a T4 GPU, versus 6 hours for GPT-3.5.
RoBERTa achieves 96% F1, compared with 83% for GPT-3.5.
Batch prompting with batch size 20 and human-curated few-shot examples reduces GPT-3.5 inference cost by about 70% without hurting performance.
An RoBERTa–GPT-3.5 ensemble reaches 97.5% F1 at 4.4% of standalone GPT-3.5 inference cost.

papers.abstract: Safe, real-time motion planning is especially difficult when a dynamic obstacle actively pursues the ego agent, requiring rapid adaptation as the environment changes. We present TrajEdit, a hierarchical trajectory planner for pursuit-evasion that combines flow matching, trajectory editing, and safety filtering. Rather than regenerating trajectories from scratch at every step, TrajEdit follows the current plan under nominal conditions and adapts its remaining portion through FlowEdit as the pursuer approaches, and falls back to a control barrier function safety filter if the adversarial agent is within a safety threshold. Our use of FlowEdit for trajectory editing reduces computation time while maintaining a comparable success rate. We evaluate TrajEdit in 2D pursuit-evasion with static obstacles and an adversarial pursuer, demonstrating high success rates with low capture and collision rates, while achieving computational time savings over full replanning baselines.
authors: Wondmgezahu Teshome, Arya Honarpisheh, Octavia Camps, Mario Sznaier
bullets: Targets real-time motion planning against dynamic obstacles that actively pursue the ego agent.

Uses a hierarchical strategy: follow the current plan nominally, edit its remaining trajectory with FlowEdit as the pursuer approaches, and invoke a control barrier function filter near a safety threshold.
FlowEdit avoids regenerating trajectories from scratch, reducing computation time while maintaining a comparable success rate.
In 2D pursuit-evasion experiments with static obstacles, the method achieves high success with low capture and collision rates.
Scope is limited to the evaluated 2D pursuit-evasion setting; the abstract does not establish broader generalization.

papers.tldr: TrajEdit enables fast, safer trajectory adaptation in pursuit-evasion by editing existing plans with flow matching and applying a CBF safety filter when danger is imminent.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.

bullets: Addresses whether zero-shot LLM annotation quality can be predicted before labeling a new dataset.
Constructs two task families yielding 461 text-classification datasets.
Finds that LLM performance is predictable, but only to a certain degree.
Internal log-probabilities are more predictive than verbalized self-confidence.
Scope is limited to the constructed text-classification task families and datasets.

papers.title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
papers.tldr: LLM annotation performance on new datasets can be estimated to some extent, with internal log-probabilities providing the strongest predictive signal.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.
authors: Wen-Zhi Li, Sainyam Galhotra, Claire Cardie
bullets: RLVR can reduce reasoning diversity because limited on-policy rollouts under-sample distinct but equally rewarded solution modes.
Under-sampled reasoning behaviors are difficult for standard on-policy RLVR to recover.
TAR stores a compact bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them when suppression is detected.
Across six math benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 scales, TAR improves the balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation while reducing forgetting of correct base-model solutions.

papers.abstract: With advancements in learning-based policies, robots are increasingly being deployed in human-centric environments, such as manufacturing floors and homes, where safe and precise operation requires compensating for unknown loads while remaining compliant during human interactions. Reliably distinguishing between these interaction types is challenging with a single sensing modality, as force signals cannot separate payloads from human pushes, and vision is susceptible to occlusions. We propose a task-agnostic interaction estimation and adaptive control framework that addresses this challenge by fusing force history and 3D point cloud through a transformer-based classifier. Trained with modality dropout for occlusion resilience and fine-tuned from simulation to hardware, the classifier achieves 91.89% accuracy and maintains above 90% under complete occlusion of one modality. The classifier drives a system identification framework that selectively compensates for unknown payloads and a variable-impedance controller that switches between adaptive and reactive modes, while simultaneously estimating interaction forces for downstream tasks, such as human intent estimation. We validate the framework under external perturbations and unknown loads across single-arm manipulation, deployment with an imitation-learning-based policy, intent-driven target switching, and zero-shot bimanual deployment on two Franka arms lifting a box of unknown mass, demonstrating generalization to closed kinematic chains and unseen setups, enabling safe and precise deployment.
authors: Mateusz Jaszczuk, Paris Perdikaris, Nadia Figueroa
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity between unknown payloads and human pushes, which neither force sensing nor vision resolves reliably alone.
Fuses force history and 3D point clouds with a transformer classifier trained using modality dropout and adapted from simulation to hardware.
Achieves 91.89% classification accuracy and remains above 90% when either sensing modality is completely occluded.
Uses the estimate to selectively compensate payloads, switch between adaptive and reactive impedance control, and estimate interaction forces.
Validated across single-arm manipulation, imitation-learning deployment, intent-driven switching, and zero-shot bimanual box lifting, including unseen setups.

papers.tldr: A transformer that fuses force histories and 3D vision distinguishes payloads from human interactions to enable safer, adaptive impedance control under occlusion and unknown loads.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for training reasoning models, but its computational cost makes efficient data selection increasingly important. Since training examples contribute unequally to learning, selecting a small, informative subset can offer a more efficient alternative to using the entire data pool. The training-free selection method estimates prompt value with hidden states from complete greedy rollouts. However, in our datasets, $26$--$32\%$ of these rollouts fail to terminate within the generation budget. We introduce LIFT, a training-free data selector that identifies impactful prompts using only partial reasoning rollouts. At its core, LIFT uses Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL), a score inspired by pointwise $\mathcal{V}$-information that accumulates token-level log-likelihood ratios between a question-conditioned context and a null context with the question removed. This enables prompt scoring from a short rollout prefix rather than a complete trajectory. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, prefixes retaining at least 90\% and 95\% of the full-rollout PRCL score, respectively, require only 26\% and 4.7\% of the tokens generated by full rollouts. Compared with SHIFT, LIFT reduces selection cost by 3.7--9.1$\times$ while achieving competitive downstream RLVR performance, with the highest six-benchmark average in three of six settings.
authors: Lei Jiang, Honghui Bao, Yue Zhou, Zhengyao Gu, Langzhou He, Natalie Parde
bullets: Complete greedy rollouts used for prompt scoring can fail to terminate within the generation budget 26–32% of the time.
LIFT scores prompts with Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL), based on token-level log-likelihood ratios between question-conditioned and null contexts.
Short prefixes can retain at least 90–95% of full-rollout PRCL scores while using only 26% or 4.7% of full-rollout tokens across the evaluated models.
Compared with SHIFT, LIFT reduces selection cost by 3.7–9.1× and achieves competitive RLVR results, attaining the highest six-benchmark average in three of six settings.
