papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model's output probability distribution. We study hidden trajectories: the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. We introduce Drift-TTA, which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. We develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models. On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively. Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation.
authors: Amirhossein Sabour, Amir Khasahmadi, Mengliu Zhao
bullets: Existing TTA methods mainly use final-layer weights or output probabilities, while this work exploits ordered intermediate representations.
Drift-TTA adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and learns to reduce hidden-trajectory drift.
It supports source-dependent alignment with clean targets and source-free learning from inputs at varying corruption severities.
An online variant updates only a scalar gate to control adaptation strength, keeping the backbone and adapters frozen.
On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, source-free online Drift-TTA improves accuracy by 13.3 points for ViT-B/16 and 11.6 points for CLIP ViT-B/16, while also reducing calibration error.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of Drift-TTA. A frozen pretrained backbone is augmented with zeroinitialized low-rank adapters attached to selected linear maps. The mean-pooled representations h1, . . . ,hL produced across the backbone form the hidden trajectory. The learned adapters move corrupted trajectories toward their clean counterparts while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. After training, the adapters can be used directly with fixed weights. For online adaptation, DriftTTA-online keeps the backbone and adapter weights frozen and updates only the strength of each learned correction.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces online test-time adaptation via hidden trajectory alignment, directly fitting test-time learning under distribution shift.
papers.title: Hidden Trajectories Don't Lie: Correcting Corruption Drift for Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Drift-TTA improves test-time adaptation by aligning corrupted models’ hidden representation trajectories with cleaner ones, enabling effective source-free online correction.

papers.abstract: Policy gradients for autoregressive sequence models differentiate each token's log-probability while holding the conditioning history fixed. This discards information about how earlier decisions shape later conditional distributions, creating a credit-assignment bottleneck when rewards are sparse. We introduce History-Reparameterized (HR) policy gradients, which replace the frozen prefix in the score function with a differentiable reparameterized or relaxed history, allowing gradients of downstream log-probabilities to propagate backward through the generated trajectory. The resulting history-pathwise term is generally biased when added directly, so we derive Optimal HR (OHR), a centered control-variate estimator with a closed-form coefficient that minimizes the trace of the gradient variance at the population level. The variance reduction is governed by temporal structure in the policy dynamics: random or weakly structured policies provide little benefit, while policies with learned sequential dependencies yield informative history-pathwise corrections. For discrete tokens, the choice of relaxation is crucial: embedding-level relaxation yields substantial variance reduction that grows with horizon, whereas straight-through Gumbel-Softmax yields essentially none in our diagnostics. We validate the method on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze with a recurrent policy, and an autoregressive Transformer model for small Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances.
authors: Mohammad Hossein Amani, Leonardo Bocchieri, Maxime Peyrard, Cl\'ement Hongler, Robert West
bullets: Standard autoregressive policy gradients freeze prior histories, limiting how downstream decisions inform earlier actions.
HR gradients use differentiable or relaxed histories to add a history-pathwise gradient term, while OHR centers it and chooses a closed-form variance-minimizing coefficient.
Benefits depend on policy dynamics: weakly structured or random policies gain little, whereas learned sequential dependencies provide useful corrections.
Embedding-level relaxations reduce variance increasingly with sequence horizon; straight-through Gumbel-Softmax shows essentially no reduction in the reported diagnostics.
The approach is evaluated on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze, and small autoregressive Transformer TSP instances.

papers.selection_reason: Policy-gradient credit assignment and variance reduction for sequential policies is technically transferable to reinforcement learning for embodied agents.
papers.title: On Reparameterizing the Score Function
papers.tldr: History-Reparameterized policy gradients improve sparse-reward credit assignment by backpropagating through generated histories, with an optimal control-variate estimator that can reduce variance when policies have meaningful sequential structure.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.
authors: Man-Ling Sung, William Hartmann, Jiangying Zhou
bullets: Addresses information loss and growing memory requirements in long, complex reasoning tasks.
Uses external memory to retain intermediate information without adding it to the model’s active context.
Reduces computation time for problems requiring repeated intermediate computations.
Improves performance on complex mathematics problems in experiments with small models and GPT-2.
Evaluation is limited to a few mathematics problems and the reported model sizes.

papers.abstract: Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video-to-action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.
authors: Hyunwoo Ryu, Eric Ming Chen, Max Wilcoxson, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Addresses the scalability bottleneck of training inverse-dynamics models on large human-collected video-action datasets.
Learns action mappings by attempting to execute visual plans, collecting resulting video-action pairs, and iteratively retraining.
Outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control with learned video plans.
Achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans and strong results on Minecraft BASALT and survival tasks.
Also performs competitively offline using expert action labels without environment interaction.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Minecraft Diamond Challenge. Success rates across twelve acquisition milestones. Offline methods learn from VPT human data without environment interaction. Online methods learn by interacting with the environment for about 10M steps (∼140 in-game hours) without expert action labels. In the offline setting, Mirror (supervised) sets a new state of the art. In the online setting, Mirror (self-improving) is the only method to reach the iron pickaxe without action labels or rewards. Mirror is evaluated on 128 episodes of 60 minutes with respawning, following VPT and Dreamer V4. Offline baselines are from Dreamer V4 (Hafner et al., 2025b). Online baselines at 10M environment steps are from Dreamer V3 (Hafner et al., 2025a).

Figure 8: Imitation learning performance across three benchmark suites. Left: learning curves on 13 DeepMind Control (DMC) tasks, four OGBench tasks, and seven Atari games. Colors identify methods; dashed method curves use an oracle VP and solid method curves use a generative VP. The horizontal dashed line marks expert performance. Curves average tasks equally, with shaded regions showing ±1 standard error across three seeds per task. The Atari VIPER curve is digitized from Escontrela et al. (2023) over its first 1M decisions and rescaled to % of expert. Right: final performance at 1M environment transitions (mean ± SE, equal task weights), separated by planner type.

Figure 7: Text-conditioned video planning. We evaluate text-conditioned control on 10 tasks across two unseen environments (see Appendix C.1.4). Each task is specified only through a text prompt, with no task-specific fine-tuning. VIPER (Escontrela et al., 2023) is included as a rewardfree video-based baseline. Combined with our self-improving V2A approach, the agent achieves high success rates although it has never seen expert demonstrations on these tasks. Left: Success rates of each method. Right: Text guidance leads the agent to complete different tasks.

Figure 3: The causal video planner. (a) Tokenized frames and text are fed into the 14B-parameter Cosmos3-Nano (NVIDIA, 2026) model, forming a causal stream of contexts whose keys and values are cached and reused. The denoiser generates K future frames while cross-attending to the context KV cache, so each observation and instruction is encoded only once. (b) Attention mask. Video history is encoded block-causally. The future plan attends to this history and bidirectionally to itself. Sliding-window attention lets the planner generalize beyond the window while keeping the KV cache within a constant budget.

Figure 1: Enabling long-horizon exploration with a video planner. Left: Random exploration struggles to reach later stages of long-horizon tasks that require specific sequences of actions. Right: The video planner guides exploration. As the V2A model learns from achieved transitions, the agent follows the plan more accurately and reaches progressively later stages of the task. These new transitions further improve the model, eventually enabling the agent to execute the full plan.

(1) Once per plan, the planner reads the agent’s inventory, health, and whether a GUI is open, and sends a subgoal caption and a guidance scale w to the video planner; the V2A model never sees them. (2) Guidance-scale rules; the dashed one is used only during training. (3) Subgoals in the order the planner picks them from an empty inventory. Each 3×3 craft happens at a crafting table placed for it and picked up afterwards.

(a) The VP inherits long-horizon planning capabilities learned from video pre-training, while the V2A model learns to ground the video plans to action via online interaction. (b) The constructed waterfalls are diverse and similar to human creations. (c) Mirror achieves near-human performance on FindCave.
Figure 2: Re-planning holds the agent at the milestone until noise supplies the critical action.

Figure 10: Rolling cache at inference. (1) Each new observation is encoded once by the context encoder, which attends to the 12 s cache. (2) The resulting keys and values are appended and the oldest context is evicted, keeping the cache size fixed. (3) The denoiser generates the next 1.6 s of video while attending to the last 8 s of cached context and, optionally, to a control-level caption. Cache cells schematically group frames.

Figure 17: Per-game performance on Atari. Scores on seven games, expressed as a percentage of each game’s expert score. Curves show the mean ± one standard error over three seeds.

Figure 14: Text-conditioned planning on Camp. We demonstrate text-conditioned planning on the camp environment. While our self-improving approach is able to solve many tasks, it struggles on tasks with fine-grained environment interactions such as placing torches in the cave. Meanwhile, VIPER, our action-free baseline, struggles to learn the action space of Minecraft. BC solves some tasks, but remains limited in its generalization ability.

Figure 13: The Wan2.2 VAE loses the VPT cursor. The same frame with (a) VPT’s cursor and (b) the high-visibility cursor, before and after a round trip through the Wan2.2 VAE. VPT’s small cursor nearly vanishes in the reconstruction, which is why we draw a larger, outlined cursor for GUI-heavy tasks.

Figure 6: Emergent in-context learning from failure. (a) We challenge our agent to escape a lava lake without fine-tuning. (b) Retaining context between deaths causes a directional bias in the agent’s trajectories, indicating in-context adaptation. (c) Shared history allows the agent to learn from its past failures in-context, leading to higher escape rates. Retaining recurrent state does not provide a comparable benefit for VPT BC.

Figure 18: MakeWaterfall comparisons. Mirror is capable of the long horizon planning necessary for MakeWaterfall. The agent must make a waterfall, remember its location, and move to another location to take a picture of it. Even though BC, UniTeam and KAIROS are trained with action labels, they achieve 0% success on this long-horizon task. They often go out of distribution. GoUp, which relies on scripted actions, cannot adapt to unseen scenarios such as when underwater. While it is able to place the water bucket with a pre-programmed instruction, it does not know what to do when underwater. The VLA approaches, STEVE-1, GROOT, JARVIS-VLA, and OpenHA, struggle at following the task instructions. VIPER, our action-free baseline, struggles to learn the Minecraft action space.
Figure 16: Per-task performance on OGBench. Success rate on four single-task environments. Curves show the mean ± one standard error over three seeds.

Figure 9: Variable prediction length training. Prediction windows of variable length over the same 32 s clip. The clean history is encoded once by the context encoder and shared by all prediction windows. With sliding-window attention, the clean history tokens and the noisy plan windows attend to the preceding 12 s and 8 s clean frames, respectively.

Figure 12: Video post-processing for the diamond task. (a) The original VPT video recordings do not include the cursor inside GUI menus. (b) As in VPT’s data loader (Baker et al., 2022), we draw the cursor from the mouse position log. However, VPT’s original 16×16 cursor is too small for the Wan2.2 VAE, which blurs or drops it (Figure 13). Thus, for the diamond task we draw a highvisibility cursor: VPT’s cursor enlarged 2×, tinted coral, and outlined in black and white. (c) The VAE also blurs the small item counts or turns them into other digits, so we crop the 184×24-pixel hotbar from the video, enlarge it 3× with nearest-neighbor upsampling, and paste it back at the bottom center, moving the health and food bars up. (d) Finally, we resize the 640 × 360 frames to 320 × 192 with bilinear interpolation and antialiasing. Of the filters we tried, it is the blurriest but keeps all task-relevant detail and causes the fewest VAE artifacts (reconstruction PSNR 32.7 dB, versus 24.5–30.4 dB for bilinear without antialiasing, bicubic, area, and Lanczos).

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.
authors: Guangya Hao, Yiting Duan, Longyan Tan, Yunbo Long, Hao Wu, Ge Zheng, Alexandra Brintrup, Zhuokai Zhao
bullets: Addresses policy drift, collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting when external supervision is unavailable.
Perturbs an anchor policy to create nearby policies, samples one trajectory per policy, and aggregates their answers into group-relative learning signals.
Keeps the anchor fixed within each block and refreshes it from the student between blocks to balance stability and adaptation.
Across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% over the base model and 16.6% over the strongest test-time adaptation baseline.
Reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ESRL. ESRL first constructs a population of perturbed policies around a shared anchor and generates one rollout from each policy. Majority voting provides label-free rewards, which are converted into group-relative advantages. The student is then updated with an advantage-weighted log-likelihood objective. The anchor remains fixed within each block of B prompts and is refreshed from the latest student at the next block boundary.

papers.abstract: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
authors: Shuyang Xiang
bullets: Prompt-dependent hidden-state differences decay approximately as a power law, t^-α.
Trained models forget faster (α≈0.55–0.7) than untrained models (α≈0.2–0.5).
A finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformer has a prompt-dependent offset bounded by O(P(log t)^{L−1}/t), under bounded logits and nonzero pre-norm activations.
An exactly solvable relay model matches the bound and reproduces the increasing local exponent observed in untrained networks.
Logit-bias experiments indicate that attention dilution is necessary—and, in the studied settings, sufficient—for the observed forgetting.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of prompt retention and forgetting in autoregressive transformers, relevant to LLM architecture and context behavior.
papers.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
papers.tldr: Transformers gradually forget prompt-specific information as generation continues, with direct dilution dominating and relay effects adding only logarithmic corrections.

papers.abstract: Reducing actuator count simplifies robot hardware but also removes independent inputs for maneuvering. The original Rollbot steered by modulating a quasi-stable helical orbit, but moved slowly and relied on external motion capture. Rollbot 2 preserves the single-actuator design while its redesigned mass distribution enables near-straight rolling and more direct travel toward commanded paths and beacon targets. Onboard inertial and ultra-wideband sensing support learned steering, beacon seeking, and waypoint following through one motor-velocity command. Rollbot 2 autonomously approaches UWB beacons without motion capture and completes a 468~m manually commanded indoor route at 0.87~m/s. On the shared 4.8~m ``N'' waypoint benchmark, all 16 trials complete the path with a mean traversal time of 10.8~s and mean time-averaged deviation of 7~cm. Its fastest traversal takes 8.0~s, over 70 times faster than the original Rollbot's 564~s run despite minor protocol differences. These results show how mechanical redesign, onboard sensing, and learning-based control improve the agility and autonomy of a single-actuator spherical robot.

papers.abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.
authors: Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Ziyi Wang, Zirui Zhou
bullets: Establishes existence of a prefix for an input–output pair when the target is in the pretrained Transformer’s output range.
Computes the prefix explicitly by solving multiple linear systems.
Shows the range assumption is necessary: desired outputs may be unreachable otherwise.
Theoretical results apply under fairly general architectural assumptions.
Experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B show strong control over generated outputs.

papers.abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine-grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation-decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock-wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss-free SLP framework that generates variable-duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi-scale motion-derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference-time body-conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state-of-the-art performance in sign language production.
authors: Youngmin Kim, Seoyeong Hwang, Sujung Hong, Seong Jae Hwang

A Latent Articulatory Clock predicts block durations and when generation should terminate.
Body-conditioned hand refinement improves coordination; experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily report state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. JOINT trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. DECOUPLED trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. AGENT gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144 dataset-budget combinations: DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from AGENT to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, JOINT leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 5-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward DECOUPLED across eight classification datasets (Spearman $\rho=-0.67$). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select AGENT or fusion, then JOINT or DECOUPLED. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4% of cells versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.028 versus 0.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 5-NN accuracy. Target-task diagnostics thus support selecting among the three paradigms before candidate fitting.

papers.abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Zhenyu Bi, Sirui Ding, Xuan Wang
bullets: Diagnoses context internalization through fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation.
Aggregates query-relevant evidence from a frozen document cache, then encodes only the query and memory-token suffix into LoRA updates.
Uses multi-style supervision to preserve evidence and better follow answer-format instructions.
Across 17 tasks, reaches 0.663 macro F1 versus 0.671 for full-context in-context learning, with 5.9× higher decoding throughput in the reported setting.
Generated LoRA is more robust than learned-KV under long intervening text and combines effectively with retained document KV.

papers.abstract: Does persistent memory accumulated from previous attempts help an LLM agent solve new problems, and does memory design affect that benefit? We study programmatic Chinese-character drawing across five agent conditions attempting the same 668 items. Accumulated memory produces modest aggregate gains despite substantial growth in the memory stores: free-form notes improve first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points, while a design combining free-form memory with reusable code improves it by 2.8 points. The two designs do not differ significantly overall, but the code bank shows a suggestive advantage on later, harder items. A separate post-hoc comparison finds a much larger improvement when the code-bank agent receives privileged, target-specific structural supervision. The agent can therefore exploit highly informative structural guidance, although the privileged per-item information does not establish what could have been learned from experience alone. These results suggest that memory design may affect where accumulated experience becomes useful, even when its average benefit is modest.
authors: Peilin Wu, Yi-Zhuang You
bullets: The study tests five agent conditions on 668 programmatic Chinese-character drawing items.
Free-form notes raise first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points; combining notes with reusable code raises it by 2.8 points.
The two memory designs show no significant overall difference, but the code bank may help more on later, harder items.
Privileged target-specific structural guidance yields a much larger improvement, but does not show what experience alone could teach.
Overall, memory provides modest average gains while influencing where accumulated experience is useful.

papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
authors: Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama
bullets: Reframes T2I evaluation as constraint satisfaction over objects, attributes, and relations.
Tests nine constraint classes, including logical operators such as ∀, ∃, counting, and implication, across four T2I models.
Performance drops from 98% on single-object attributes to 53% on complex conditional multi-object relations.
Compositional generalization declines from 84% for single constraints to 20% for multiple constraints; unsatisfiable prompts are recognized correctly only 23% of the time by the best model.
On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.88–0.98 against human judgments.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.
authors: Sahar Refaei Ghalibafan, Samira Nazari, Christian Herglotz, Maksim Jenihhin, Mahdi Taheri
bullets: Addresses differing client data difficulty and compute budgets in federated early-exit ViT inference.
Uses client-specific thresholds based on label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, with input-level adjustments from entropy, confidence, class margin, and exit depth.
Aggregates updates only from clients that modified a parameter.
Reports 32.0% CIFAR-10 depth savings at 88.70% accuracy and 30% ImageNet-1K savings at 73.7% top-1 accuracy.
On matched non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy reaches 72.28%, while robustness-aware routing achieves 70.01% accuracy with 32.55% savings.

papers.abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.

Shows generalization across object classes, lighting, clutter levels, and from simulation to reality.

papers.abstract: Developing autonomous electric wheelchairs capable of long-horizon sidewalk navigation is critical for accessible personal mobility, yet existing approaches either focus on indoor map-based navigation or rely on expensive, complex sensor stacks to achieve full autonomy. In this work, we propose to tackle outdoor sidewalk navigation by leveraging visual navigation foundation models and large-scale navigation datasets, which offer strong generalization using lightweight hardware. To this end, we present ChairNav, a novel framework that adapts a general visual navigation model into a personalized electric wheelchair navigation system using a three-stage data pyramid. To address the scarcity of in-domain data, ChairNav first pre-trains on large-scale cross-embodiment datasets transformed into the wheelchair domain, followed by mid-training on a small number of wheelchair demonstrations to eliminate remaining domain gaps. Finally, a post-training stage refines the deployed model from user interventions to personalize its behavior. We deploy ChairNav on a commercial electric wheelchair equipped with an RGB-D camera and an onboard NVIDIA Jetson compute module. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of each stage in our data pyramid: pre-training reduces lateral ADE by 18%, and post-training increases the mean distance between user interventions from 29.2 m to 57.4 m. Further evaluation on kilometer-scale urban sidewalk routes shows that our system operates autonomously for 93.4% of total driving time, demonstrating its potential for everyday accessible mobility. Demo video and more details are at https://vail.cs.ucla.edu/ChairNav/.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.

papers.abstract: When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments. Project website: https://www.proroklab.org/compositional-motion-styles/
authors: Heedo Woo, Antonio Marino, Eduardo Sebasti\'an, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving distinct motion styles while executing separate task commands on robots with redundant degrees of freedom.

Retargets recordings to the target robot, uses weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering to discover styles without preselecting their number, and trains a reinforcement-learning composition policy.
Evaluated on a Unitree Go2 in two simulators and on physical hardware.
Improves kinematic coherence over baselines and tracks velocity commands beyond the recorded-data support while retaining distinguishable styles.
Demonstrated across cross-simulator and real-world deployments.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
authors: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
bullets: Native MLLMs tokenize image patches directly, creating substantial visual-token redundancy that existing ViT-oriented compression methods do not address.
Analysis finds redundancy is heterogeneous and independently distributed across height and width, while early-layer tokens are broadly indiscriminable.
PACE estimates direction-aware spatial importance by decoupling Multimodal-RoPE attention along height and width with negligible overhead.
It allocates token budgets through Pareto optimization across performance, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage.
Experiments report near-lossless performance at 25–50% visual-token retention, with improvements on several benchmarks and over 2× FLOPs reduction.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration
authors: Patrick Wienholt, Frederik Hauke, Christiane Kuhl, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
bullets: Medical MLLMs’ default yes/no threshold can be poorly calibrated for binary clinical tasks.
The method renormalizes yes and no token probabilities from one forward pass to produce a continuous decision score.
Validation-selected thresholds can substantially improve task-specific operating points; for normal chest radiographs, sensitivity was 0.945 and specificity 0.696.
Normalization achieved the best AUROC on 4 of 6 medical imaging datasets, including 0.819 on CheXpert.
Inference took 53–79 ms per decision on one GPU; evaluation covered MedGemma and Gemma-3 models.

Each dataset was split into a validation set, used exclusively to select the decision threshold, and a test set, used only for the final performance evaluation. We compared four models, namely Gemma-3 and MedGemma each in a 4B and a 27B variant, using three scoring methods: the normalized yes/no token probability, the raw yes token probability, and a text-elicited probability generated directly as output. papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires distinguishing subtle differences in local attributes and spatial relations, yet remains challenging for existing vision-language models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) offer a new opportunity through generation pathways that preserve rich visual information complementary to understanding. However, existing generation-assisted understanding methods mainly rely on generative supervision or explicit generation and have not systematically explored direct use of native generation-side representations. To address this gap, we systematically analyze what generation-side representations offer for fine-grained understanding, finding that they are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, capture task-relevant changes missed by understanding-side representations, and depend on correct spatial organization for this advantage. Guided by these findings, we design GAFU, a post-training framework that unlocks native generation-side information for fine-grained understanding. It compresses generation-side visual representations into compact \(G\) tokens that preserve fine-grained visual details, enabling task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway. Experiments show that GAFU consistently outperforms SFT baselines trained on the same data across diverse visual understanding tasks and UMM architectures, with maximum relative improvements of 20.00\%, 17.94\%, and 8.62\% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information from the generation pathway into gains in fine-grained visual understanding, providing an effective path toward synergy between generation and understanding in UMMs.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Zhiheng Liu, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Kaixuan Wang, Bohao Li, Xihui Liu
bullets: Fine-grained understanding of subtle attributes and spatial relations remains difficult for vision-language models.
Generation-side representations are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, but their benefit depends on correct spatial organization.
GAFU compresses these representations into compact G tokens that preserve visual detail and support task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway.
Across multiple tasks and UMM architectures, GAFU outperforms same-data SFT baselines, with reported maximum relative gains of 20.00%, 17.94%, and 8.62%.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.

papers.abstract: A key design choice in visual world models is what information the latent state is encouraged to preserve. Models that learn a latent space with only a latent-prediction objective adapt to environment dynamics, but the predictive objective alone admits collapsed solutions and provides no explicit constraint on the visual information retained by the latent. Models built directly on pretrained visual features inherit a strong visual prior, but tie prediction and planning to a frozen state space. We propose Anchor-WM, which instead uses pretrained visual features as a teacher for learning a compact latent state rather than as the world-model state itself. Anchor-WM learns this compact latent with action-conditioned dynamics, while distilling the dense DINO representations through a training-only distillation head. This encourages the compact latent to retain visual information captured by the pretrained representation while discouraging representational collapse. At inference, the DINO encoder and distillation head are discarded, allowing prediction and planning to operate entirely in the learned latent space. Anchor-WM achieves the best average success rate across the four evaluated environments while enabling substantially faster planning than world models operating directly on DINO patch features. These results show that pretrained visual features can effectively guide world-model learning without defining the state space used for prediction and planning.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Nan Lin, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses latent-state collapse and the loss of visual information in prediction-only world models.
Learns an action-conditioned compact latent while distilling dense DINO representations through a temporary training head.
Discards the DINO encoder and distillation head at inference, enabling planning entirely in the learned latent space.
Achieves the best average success rate across four evaluated environments and substantially faster planning than models using DINO patch features.
Shows that pretrained visual features can guide, rather than define, the state space for visual world models.

At inference, the DINO encoder and distillation head are discarded, and planning is performed entirely in the learned latent space by optimizing an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent approaches the encoded goal latent.

papers.abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Junjie Liao, Zhining Zhang, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Across four agent environments, multi-turn RL gains are evaluated through environment-specific grounded visual question answering.
Vision-encoder probe accuracy stays relatively stable, while probe accuracy in LLM layers improves after RL.
Attention analysis shows that LLM layers attend more to visual tokens during RL training.
A fixed attention-bias intervention partially recovers VQA gains without parameter updates or gradients.
The findings suggest RL teaches VLMs where to attend, but not how to perceive visual content.

papers.abstract: Video world models learn how visual environments evolve by predicting missing or future content. However, physical-state information can provide useful context for predicting how environments evolve. Prior work incorporates this information through different mechanisms: domain-specific physical laws can complicate multi-domain training, while supervision on individual frames or frame pairs gives limited attention to how physical state evolves over time. We introduce Time-JEPA, which fine-tunes a video world model using low-dimensional, temporally aligned physical time series as auxiliary supervision. Physical time series connect video representations with physical state at corresponding temporal positions, encouraging the model to preserve how physical state evolves. In multiple domains including autonomous driving, robot manipulation, and human motion, Time-JEPA improves current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction over matched video-fine-tuned controls across both condition and state-variable distribution shifts. Multi-domain training provides aggregate gains over matched single-domain training in all three tasks. External evaluations further suggest that time-series supervision improves sensitivity to physical anomalies and the representation of physical interactions, including in unseen scenarios. Aggregate gains on a second video backbone indicate that the method can be applied to more backbones. These results suggest that physical time series help video world models better understand the physical world.
authors: Shenyi Li, Ziyang Zhang, Wen Wu, Ming Liu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Uses low-dimensional, temporally aligned physical time series as auxiliary supervision during video-world-model fine-tuning.
Encourages representations to preserve how physical states evolve, rather than supervising only individual frames or frame pairs.
Improves current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, and kinematic reconstruction in driving, manipulation, and human-motion domains.
Multi-domain training yields aggregate gains over matched single-domain training, including under condition and state-variable distribution shifts.
External evaluations indicate greater sensitivity to physical anomalies and interactions, with gains also observed on a second video backbone.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Time-JEPA training and evaluation. Training combines masked latent prediction with regression of aligned, pooled, and normalized physical state values from full-clip video features. The EMA target encoder supplies latent supervision. Video-only evaluation covers current-state decoding, multi-horizon future-state prediction, kinematic reconstruction, and external physical evaluations. and spatial patch locations. At each temporal position, Time-JEPA then applies mean pooling across spatial patch locations to produce one pooled temporal feature. An auxiliary physical-state regression head applies a two-layer pointwise nonlinear projection independently to each pooled temporal feature and regresses normalized state values for the corresponding tubelet. This minimal pointwise design concentrates temporal representation learning in the online encoder. We compute the time-series regression loss Ltime as a validity-masked Smooth-L1 error between the auxiliary-head outputs and their aligned state values.

papers.abstract: Modeling human-object interaction (HOI) in real environments requires jointly representing whole-body motion, manipulated objects, and scene geometry, yet existing datasets trade off scalable capture against structured, scene-aligned supervision. We introduce SituHOI, a large-scale RGB-D dataset containing 18,429 annotated clips across 16 indoor rooms and approximately 86 hours of quality-screened activity. It pairs recordings from a single moving RGB-D camera with static scene scans, object geometry, language descriptions, and estimated human and object trajectories. Using the scans as persistent references, our pipeline combines camera localization and depth-based metric alignment with human mesh recovery, object tracking, and temporal refinement to register all geometric annotations in a shared floor-aligned frame. These data support FlexHOI-Bench, a goal-conditioned joint motion prediction benchmark with variable observation and prediction durations. Given observed histories, scene and object geometry, and a terminal object pose, models predict future human and object motion. We provide SharedHOI as a reference predictor and evaluate world-space accuracy and human-object coordination. On a MoCap subset, our pipeline reduces human G-MPJPE from 195.4 to 68.3 mm and object translation error from 43.0 to 28.7 mm. SharedHOI leads four adapted baselines on all three aggregate FlexHOI-Bench metrics. Data will be released upon acceptance. An anonymized code repository is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/iclr2027-anonymous-code-1DFB.

The pipeline improves MoCap-subset errors from 195.4 to 68.3 mm for human G-MPJPE and 43.0 to 28.7 mm for object translation; SharedHOI leads four adapted baselines on all aggregate metrics.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.
authors: Janghoon Cho, Shubhankar Borse, Reza Pourreza, Juntae Lee, Jihwan Bang, Munawar Hayat, Fatih Porikli
bullets: Frames pruning as selecting one shared, fixed-budget visual-token subset per image for diverse downstream questions.
Uses auxiliary QA generated by a frontier VLM and a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen.
Introduces QA mini-batch greedy, which builds nested subsets by estimating token gains from sampled QA components.
On Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma 4 E4B across 900 images from nine benchmarks, searched subsets outperform evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation.
Scope: optimization requires substantial offline computation—one frontier-VLM call and about 0.5 H100 GPU-hours per image—and covers keep ratios up to 0.3.

papers.abstract: Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible. Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize. These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model. We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training. Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains. Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.
authors: Daniel Swoboda, Hector Geffner
bullets: Addresses the gap between tractable symbolic abstractions and real geometric constraints in robotic rearrangement.
Uses a relational graph neural network over a simple symbolic model, supervised by a motion planner that reveals hidden action preconditions.
Combines the learned heuristic with greedy best-first search and generalizes across object counts, plan lengths, arrangements, and multiple domains.
Solves more problems than classical and learning-based baselines while using roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods.
Ranks a geometrically feasible action first in 94% of sampled states, compared with 22% for random choice.

figures.caption: Figure 1: REAP learns which symbolically applicable actions are geometrically feasible, without modeling the geometric constraints. (1) Grasping the target o1 is symbolically applicable, but not geometrically feasible since other objects block the target. (2) A relational GNN, whose input state includes the goal, predicts a cost Q(s, a) for each applicable action and applies to any number of objects. Feasible picks of blocking objects get low costs, infeasible picks high costs. (3) At test time, a plan is found by greedy execution or greedy best-first search on Q, with the motion planner checking each expanded action. Q is learned by an RL algorithm that uses ε-greedy WA⋆ to guide the exploration and penalizes infeasible actions.

Figure 2: REAP instantiates the same relational-GNN architecture trained with motion-planner feedback over hidden geometric preconditions across five evaluation environments, each with a different hidden geometric precondition. Gripper clearance on the open table, lateral grasp clearance in the confined shelf, blocking in a multi-level shelf, front-facing retrieval past blockers (Access-19), and finger/arm interference in 3D stacking. At the same time, REAP also learns the cost-to-go of the underlying planning problems, to guide search towards efficient solutions.

papers.abstract: Sparse-frame video-language models can change their answers when only the sampling timestamps shift. Raw agreement exposes this problem, but it need not rank errors better than token confidence or identify which additional observation will repair an answer. We argue that answer risk and action value must be estimated separately. PhaseGuard+ probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets, predicts the reliability of the phase-vote answer, and predicts the example-wise correctness gain of a specific rescue action. The second score routes only examples expected to benefit from denser frames or a stronger VLM. Both predictors use lightweight models trained on public data; the VLMs remain frozen. We use 256 Perception Test videos for method development and evaluate on a disjoint 256-video test set comprising 554 Physics questions. For Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC rises from 68.0% with token softmax to 74.8% (+6.8 pp, 95% CI [2.6, 10.7] pp). Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B reaches 67.87% accuracy, compared with 63.66% for budget-matched random routing (+4.21 percentage points, CI [1.89, 6.40]). All four tested rescue pairs significantly outperform random routing. Temporal sensitivity becomes actionable when the system learns both whether an answer is unreliable and whether an available action is likely to fix it.
authors: Shujia Liu
bullets: Sparse-frame video-language models can change answers when sampling timestamps shift.
The method probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets and forms a phase-vote answer.
Separate lightweight predictors estimate answer reliability and the correctness gain from denser frames or a stronger VLM.
On Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC improves from 68.0% to 74.8% over token softmax.
Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B achieves 67.87% accuracy versus 63.66% for random routing; all four rescue pairs outperform random routing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Phase-aware selective re-observation. (a) For a held-out Perception Test collision question, four controlled two-frame phases from the same frozen Qwen3-VL-8B yield [B,A,A,B] (A: beige–black pen, B: mouse, C: notebook; gold B). The 2:2 tie is resolved by the earliestphase rule, giving ȳq = B with phase consensus sq = 50%. (b) The observable perturbation trace xq supports two separately supervised estimates: current-answer reliability fθ(xq) and the signed correctness gain bϕ,a(xq) of a specified action a. (c) For a pool of Q questions, the policy ranks predicted action benefits and re-observes only the top K = max(1, round(ρQ)) questions with Qwen3-VL-32B/8F; all remaining questions retain their phase-vote answers. The displayed example follows the blue no-re-observation branch, while the orange branch visualizes the candidate action and its counterfactual output.

Figure 3: Why answer uncertainty is not action value. Two held-out test examples are shown under the same 30% re-observation budget. Each curve ranks all test questions by the corresponding routing score; the yellow marker locates the displayed question and the vertical dashed line denotes the routing cutoff. Left: token-softmax and predicted answer risk keep an incorrect phase-vote answer, whereas PHASEGUARD+ predicts positive benefit, invokes Qwen3-VL-32B/8F, and corrects the answer. Right: token-softmax and answer risk route an initially correct answer, but the rescue action changes it to an incorrect one; PHASEGUARD+ predicts low benefit and retains the correct phase-vote answer. The examples illustrate that the probability of current error and the signed gain of a particular rescue action are different quantities.

Figure 4: Budgeted recovery across all four locked action pairs. Each panel reuses one predictor frozen on the development set and varies only the fraction routed on the 554-question test set. The blue marker denotes the development-selected rate; its annotation is the accuracy gain over expected matched-random routing at the same budget. Action-value routing is most useful in the constrainedbudget regime; the curves may cross at larger budgets because a rescue action can also overturn a correct answer.

At the locked 30% budget, action-value routing reaches 67.87%, versus 63.66% for matched random.

papers.abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero. The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7-14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5-16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8-3.2x). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.
authors: Tingan Jin
bullets: Addresses the limitation that a single visual observation does not reveal an object’s physical response.
Uses a Bayesian contact memory of three calibration pushes, predicted pose, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space.
On 512 held-out objects, contact memory reduces 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6–12.8% across all 8 seeds; gains also hold for 128 out-of-range-physics objects.
The full extension improves over a plain predictor by 15.5–16.6%; gains emerge after contact rather than at contact onset.
Raw push measurements perform similarly, while the Bayesian summary compresses trials into eight interpretable values.
