(2) The Bayesian contact memory: posterior mean normal, tangential and angular response at two lever arms and two uncertainties, shown for the rough (𝜇 = 0.35) and the frictionless version of the same object. The tangential responses 𝑣𝑡 reveal friction. (3) A motion head turns the memory and the query context into predicted poses (outlines). (4) The pose enters the V-JEPA 2 predictor as tokens and through a Fourier pose head that corrects the predicted features. The query context also feeds the predictor. Blue marks our additions; the no-memory arm has the same architecture with 𝑚 = 0.

Fig. 4. Predicted 1-s poses on the first four confirmation objects (seed order, no selection; one model per arm, seed 1101, final checkpoint). Gray: the true pose of the frictionless (light) and rough (dark) version of the same object after the same push; faint: start. Orange dashed: the no-memory predictor, which must predict one pose for both versions because its inputs are identical. Blue: IMPULSE, solid for the frictionless and dotted for the rough version. Red disk and arrow: pusher and push direction. Below each panel: 1-s position errors in pixels (frictionless / rough).

Fig. 3. Confirmation, seed by seed. Blue dots are the 8 training seeds (each averaged over all fresh objects); black bars show the mean with its 95% interval over seeds and objects. Every seed lies below zero (lower error with memory) in every cell.

Fig. 6. The memory’s gain emerges after contact. Relative change of the calibrated feature error with IMPULSE versus no memory (𝜇 = 0.35, selected checkpoint; 95% intervals over seeds and objects). The gray band marks where 90% of pushes first touch the object.

Fig. 1. Same look, same push, different futures. Three T-blocks that look identical receive the same push (red disk: the pusher) but differ in hidden inertia ratio 𝜌, restitution 𝑒 and friction 𝜇. Faint copies show the block every 0.25 s; the solid block is its pose after 1 s. A single frame cannot tell the three apart, but a few test pushes can. (Illustrative rollouts of the task simulator.)

Fig. 5. Measured information ladder on the 512 fresh objects (post hoc; selected checkpoint; mean over 8 seeds). P1: pose tokens; P2: pose tokens plus the Fourier pose head. Each row feeds no memory, the memory, the true parameters (oracle) or the true future pose through the same pathway. The Fourier pose head lengthens the whole ladder, and the memory’s gain grows with it: the memory collects 39% of the oracle’s gain on P1 and 51% on P2.

papers.abstract: Reliable fetal brain biometry on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosing congenital brain anomalies, but artificial intelligence models often lose accuracy under domain shifts. We developed BioTTA, a backbone-agnostic, source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation framework that adapts pretrained models online to individual unlabeled target volumes. This retrospective multicohort study included 394 reconstructed 3D fetal brain MRI volumes at 20-39 gestational weeks, with 11 biometric measurements annotated by radiologists. BioTTA was developed on single-center turbo spin-echo MRI and evaluated on three datasets representing cross-sequence, cross-center, and cross-nation shifts. Biometry accuracy was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and the percentage of correct measurements within 4 mm. A web-based reporting platform mapped measurements onto normative growth trajectories and was evaluated against radiologists in four multicenter disease cohorts covering germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage, ventriculomegaly, and cerebellar abnormality. Across all three target datasets, BioTTA outperformed auto-SVRTK, source-only models, and FetalSynthGen, while matching models finetuned with target labels. MAEs ranged from 1.10 to 1.46 mm with a convolutional backbone and from 1.46 to 2.25 mm with a transformer backbone. Diagnostic accuracy ranged from 82.1% to 95.0%, comparable to a senior radiologist. BioTTA supports accurate, generalizable fetal brain biometry and standardized prenatal brain growth assessment across heterogeneous MRI sources.

papers.abstract: Code generation has become a core capability of large language models (LLMs), and code data is central to the pre-training process that develops it. As obtaining public code of sufficient quality becomes more difficult, further progress cannot rely on corpus expansion alone. Tiered data management instead applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller data pools, producing data states suited to different training objectives. Following this perspective, we present UltraData-Code as four connected data states spanning repository archival at L0, standardized natural code at L1, algorithmic selection at L2, and task-oriented synthesis at L3. L0 preserves repository data and provenance for reprocessing, while L1 applies scalable filtering, normalization, and near-deduplication for broad pre-training. L2 selects high-quality algorithmically relevant files using language-adaptive relevance signals and quality constraints, yielding approximately 400B tokens of UltraData-Code-L2 across 11 programming languages for focused continual pre-training. L3 converts selected implementations into structured programming exercises, yielding approximately 150B tokens of UltraData-Code-L3 across the same 11 languages for task-oriented mid-training or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Under controlled 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 percentage points (pp) on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E. Replacing half of the L2 training tokens with L3 yields a further gain of 8.42pp and 8.07pp on the two benchmarks, respectively. Both gains increase when the training budget scales to 100B tokens. We have released our datasets and classifiers to support further research on LLMs.

Produces approximately 400B tokens of L2 and 150B tokens of L3 across 11 programming languages.
In 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80pp on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E.
Replacing half of L2 with L3 adds 8.42pp and 8.07pp, with larger gains at a 100B-token training budget.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the capacity to represent and reason about physical space, underlies embodied perception and real-world visual understanding. Existing benchmarks probe it through spatial relations, perspective-taking, and mental modeling. What remains underexamined is whether a model can maintain a coherent scene representation across views, since pairwise comparison alone cannot reveal which view departs from the truth. We thus introduce Same Space or Not (SSoN), a benchmark of cross-view contradiction resolution comprising 1,000 questions from seven indoor scene sources and six categories of controlled 3D edits. Each question presents three views of an unchanged scene and one view of an edited variant. Models must identify the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without a designated trusted reference or a marked target. Our pipeline iteratively translates human review into generation constraints. Automated checks and exhaustive human validation screen out both trivial visual shortcuts and questions lacking sufficient evidence for a unique answer. Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, compared with 39.7% for the strongest vision-language models (VLMs), falling to 34.9% when a valid visual explanation is also required. We investigate prompting, camera information, and 3D reconstruction as interventions. On a 100-question intervention set with a 24% baseline, prompting and 3D reconstruction remain below 50% answer accuracy, except when ground-truth camera information is supplied, which reaches 61% answer accuracy but only 48% True solve accuracy. On a held-out 201-question test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 21.89% accuracy, 33.33% after answer-only fine-tuning, and 41.79% after fine-tuning on both rationales and answers. These results identify cross-view contradiction resolution as a substantial weakness of current VLMs that can be partly addressed by targeted supervision.
authors: Huizi Cao, Guanyu Xu, Zhixuan Liang, Ming Yin, Jiuxiang Gu, Manling Li, Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu

Prompting and 3D reconstruction generally remain below 50% accuracy; ground-truth camera information improves answer accuracy to 61% but true solving to 48%.
On a held-out test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 21.89% to 41.79% with fine-tuning on both answers and rationales.

papers.abstract: AI-based 3D generation models such as Hunyuan 3D and Meshy can produce visually appealing 3D shapes from an image or text prompt.However, they typically focus on an object's external appearance, often producing incomplete or implausible interior geometry. Consequently, the generated shapes are not guaranteed to be functionally valid, limiting their direct use in downstream applications such as simulation and fabrication. In this paper, we present a computational approach to functionalize AI-generated 3D shapes through interior geometry construction. Our key observations are that a part's functional role defines its interior geometry, and such geometry is often smooth, relatively simple, and closely related to the part's external shape. Inspired by these observations, we introduce an interior-aware part graph to encode information necessary for constructing interior geometry within an AI-generated 3D shape, and build the graph via VLM-based shape segmentation and graph attribute inference. Guided by the graph, we model the interior geometry of each part as a generalized cylinder and infer its parameters from the part's external geometry through an optimization. The resulting 3D shapes are functionally valid while preserving their AI-generated external appearance. We demonstrate our approach on a variety of AI-generated 3D shapes, including vessels, containers, and storage furniture, and fabricate selected examples for functional validation.

papers.abstract: Line-parallel language models advance multiple lines concurrently for substantial speedups. However, frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM) enforce a fixed commitment schedule across lines. Because dependencies vary within text, a fixed schedule cannot hold back a line whose prerequisites remain uncomputed, forcing premature commitments and cascading reasoning errors. To address this limitation, we introduce the Lattice Language Model (LatLM), making commitment schedules an adaptive decoding-time choice. Text occupies a 2D lattice where eligible frontier tokens are scored each round; a policy commits confident candidates while deferring unready ones for extended context. One forward pass supervises entire sampled trajectories via 2D causal masking, while an append-only cache retains exact states. At 482M parameters, we establish two findings. (1) LatLM matches a data- and capacity-matched autoregressive model on held-out text when decoded sequentially, while its adaptive parallel decoder achieves near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks using 25--41% as many decoding rounds. (2) When cross-line dependencies cause LCLM's fixed schedule to fail, deferred commitment substantially improves accuracy while retaining parallelism where dependencies permit. On mixed dependency chains, LatLM achieves 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM's 78.5%, using fewer than half the decoding rounds of the autoregressive baseline.
authors: Shaorong Zhang, Shiyuan Li, Longxuan Yu, Greg Ver Steeg

papers.abstract: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.
authors: Chuansai Zhou, Yanlin Liu, Bingning Huang, Shidi Xi, Chao Huang, Boxing Chen, Mingming Zhu, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Zongzuo Wang
bullets: Addresses context-window overflow from multi-turn kernel refinement and sparse terminal rewards in GRPO.
Uses a compaction-aware, segment-level objective to improve step-level credit assignment.
Provides cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback through a lightweight agent harness.
Injects Ascend-specific knowledge during agentic RL training and evaluation.
On Ascend hardware, outperforms reported baselines, including GRPO, in correctness and speedup on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench.

papers.abstract: Collaborative inference serves as a critical methodology in edge intelligence. Existing collaborative inference methods operate by splitting the deep neural network (DNN) model between edge devices and cloud servers. However, these methods need to load different models for multiple split points when the communication or device changes, thus resulting in long switching times and substantial storage overhead on the edge side. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Split Network (DS-Net), which not only enables efficient split point switching but also enhances the collaborative speed and accuracy across various scenarios. Specifically, we design a dynamic switching framework that enables flexible selection among multiple split points within a single model, thereby reducing storage, memory, and switching overhead. To mitigate the feature distribution shifts and task-relevant information loss caused by dynamic splitting and high-ratio compression, we further propose a hierarchical compensation mechanism. Local alignment calibrates the decoded feature distribution at each split point, while task-specific global compensation restores task-relevant information at the global level. In addition, we incorporate sample-adaptive global compensation selection into split-point selection based on sample complexity and runtime resource conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-Net reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and achieves millisecond-level switching latency. Moreover, under a 10 Mbps bandwidth constraint on the Nano platform, DS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative methods by achieving 1.2% higher accuracy on the COCO dataset, reducing latency by 42.5%, and improving throughput by a factor of 1.8$\times$.
authors: Xinyun Zhang, Li Wang, Lei Jin, Lianming Xu, Zhu Han
bullets: Addresses storage and switching delays caused by maintaining separate models for different split points and changing communication or device conditions.
Uses a single dynamic model with flexible split-point selection, reducing edge memory overhead and enabling millisecond-level switching.
Applies local feature-distribution alignment and task-specific global compensation to recover information lost through dynamic splitting and compression.
Selects global compensation adaptively based on sample complexity and runtime resources.
On Nano under 10 Mbps bandwidth, reports 74.6% lower memory overhead, 42.5% lower latency, 1.8× higher throughput, and 1.2% higher COCO accuracy than prior collaborative methods.

papers.abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.
authors: Bowei He, Yankai Chen, Xiaokun Zhang, Changjiang Han, Ye Yuan, Chong Li, Xue Liu
bullets: The study models agentic data using task, environment, and trajectory cardinalities, plus reward density, under a synthesis budget.
Across tested LLMs, domains, and PPO/GRPO, scaling exponents rank environment > task > trajectory; world diversity chiefly drives the environment advantage.
Fitted scaling laws price synthesis strategies through per-axis discounts and identify axis-specific synthetic-to-real collapse thresholds.
A constrained, Chinchilla-style budget allocation recipe is derived and validated at held-out scale.
Following the recipe achieves up to 1.7× compute efficiency compared with primarily scaling trajectories.

papers.abstract: Motion planning in unstructured environments is a bottleneck for robot deployment. Current visuomotor policies predominantly rely on external cameras, introducing perceptual blind spots and fragility due to occlusions, clutter, and calibration constraints. To overcome these limitations, we propose ESCAPE, an online egocentric sensing framework for collision-free trajectory generation. ESCAPE aggregates sparse measurements from distributed depth sensors, converting them into a structured, obstacle-aware point cloud representation. Our policy leverages a flow matching-based generative framework, and trains on a high-quality dataset comprising over 100K safety-critical trajectories. With joint optimization of goal-reaching and collision objectives, it produces safe trajectories directly from these egocentric inputs. Crucially, ESCAPE is trained entirely in simulation and transfers zero-shot to physical hardware without any real-world fine-tuning. Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ESCAPE achieves stable motion planning using only egocentric perception, outperforming external-view and voxelized-planning baselines across both simulation and real-world evaluations.
authors: Weiqing Shen, Wenhao Huang, Baokang Zhang, Shuo Shang, Yanmiao Hu, Haojun Li, Yifan Han, Wenzhao Lian

papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
authors: Kangcong Li, Hangfan Zhang, Shuyue Hu, Shengji Tang, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of extracting reliable, actionable lessons from context-dependent interaction feedback.
Maintains explicit, revisable experience-based memory and uses it for test-time training within each episode.
Updates an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen; the adapted model performs both actions and reflection.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite across two model families, outperforming trajectory-based test-time training in all six settings.
Task success improves by up to 12.14 percentage points; adapting the reflection policy contributes an additional 7.14-point benefit versus frozen reflection.

papers.abstract: Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of $2.0$--$2.6$ over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64--512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89~FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.
authors: Jianneng Huang, Wenjia Rao
bullets: Targets the sequential, expensive leaf-sphere construction bottleneck in inner sphere trees for non-convex collision detection.
Predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry in a single shot.
Uses differentiable coverage feedback to fill residual gaps across scales, followed by geometric projection for validity.
Reduces mean leaf-generation time by 2.0–2.6× versus single-core CPU construction across 64–512 target spheres.
Integrated into Jolt Physics and Bullet, achieving 55.89 FPS in the reported alpha-puzzle benchmark among compared representations.

A differentiable renderer generates five coverage-feedback maps, which are concatenated with the original input and processed by a second encoder. A correction head refines the base spheres, while medium- and detail-sphere heads predict additional candidates. The three groups are concatenated and geometrically projected to obtain IST leaves. Layer annotations give the output shape of each Conv3D stage as (channels, depth, height, width); for example, (24,96,96,96) denotes 24 channels at 96× 96× 96 resolution, and B is the batch size.

Training used four RTX 4090 GPUs, and a separate ML-IST model was trained from GT-IST labels for each K.
Figure 2: ML-IST inner-sphere sets for complex nonconvex models. Each pair shows the input surface mesh and the corresponding ML-IST prediction.

Figure 7: Runtime frame rate of four collision representations in the alpha-puzzle benchmark. ML-IST reaches 55.89 FPS, compared with 31.33 FPS for GT-IST, 26.79 FPS for GImpact, and 2.57 FPS for convex hulls with convex decomposition.

papers.title: Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning
papers.tldr: ML-IST uses machine learning to rapidly generate valid inner-sphere-tree leaves, accelerating collision-representation construction while preserving coverage of complex geometry.

papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
authors: Minyoung Go, Yongjun Park
bullets: KV-cache memory grows with context length, while existing non-uniform head compression methods can be unstable across workloads.
The method finds that active-head composition shifts between prefill and decode but remains stable across later content tokens after filtering format tokens.
PeekKV performs a one-token peek to jointly score head groups and token importance, then allocates cache budgets and retains the highest-scoring tokens.
It applies directly to unseen workloads and models because it requires neither offline profiling nor additional training.
Across four benchmarks, it is closest to full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench; reported retention reaches 95.7% and 95.9% of full-cache accuracy at low memory budgets on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to make accurate predictions from demonstrations, but prediction success alone does not reveal the extent to which the underlying concept has been recovered. Existing evaluations typically assess recovery at the level of the whole concept, making it difficult to identify which components are recovered and to separate model limitations from ambiguity in the demonstrations. We introduce a component-level framework for concept recovery that decomposes concepts into their defining components and uses controlled structural interventions to evaluate both component-level and whole-concept recovery under identifiable demonstrations. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and three composition forms, we find that models often achieve high prediction accuracy despite poor whole-concept recovery, with systematic over-specification of relevant attributes and level constraints. Individual structural components are generally insufficient for whole-concept recovery, whereas jointly specifying complementary components, particularly relevant attributes and their level constraints, substantially improves recovery. However, this improvement is fragile: a single plausible but unnecessary level constraint can substantially disrupt recovery. Finally, joint supervision of recovery and implicit prediction substantially improves recovery while preserving prediction performance, with the learned capability transferring across composition forms. Overall, our component-level analysis provides a more diagnostic view of what models recover from demonstrations than the existing holistic view.
authors: Xufeng Liu, Fang Wan, Yi Liu
bullets: Whole-concept prediction accuracy can mask failures in recovering the underlying concept.
Controlled structural interventions separate component-level recovery from ambiguity in demonstrations.
Models tend to over-specify relevant attributes and level constraints.
Complementary components improve recovery, but one plausible unnecessary constraint can disrupt it.
Jointly training recovery with implicit prediction improves recovery without reducing prediction and transfers across composition forms.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our component-level framework for concept recovery. The top panel illustrates the three composition forms, while the lower panels show the evaluation, localization, and recovery stages. We first decompose recovered concepts into defining components and evaluate at the component level. We then use controlled interventions on structural information to localize their effects on recovery. Finally, we use supervised learning to finetune the model to recover the structured concept while preserving its implicit-prediction capability.

Figure 1: Holistic versus component-level evaluation of concept recovery. Given a target concept, we generate demonstrations from the concept and provide them to an LLM for concept recovery. Holistic evaluation assesses whether the recovered concept is correct as a whole, without revealing which concept-defining components are recovered correctly or incorrectly. We instead adopt a component-level view, using demonstrations sufficient to uniquely identify the target concept and evaluating recovery at the level of individual concept-defining components.

papers.selection_reason: Component-level analysis of concept recovery in in-context learning informs understanding of LLM reasoning and context, within language foundation models.
papers.title: Beyond Prediction: A Component-Level Study of Concept Recovery in In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: A component-level framework reveals that LLMs can predict correctly while recovering concepts poorly, and that recovery improves with complementary structural cues but remains fragile to unnecessary constraints.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
authors: Jiakun Fan, Min Xiao, Qiang Wang, Neiwen Ling, Zhichao Liu, Zhihao Jia, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Zijun Wei
bullets: Diffusion drafters can achieve higher mean accepted tokens without improving throughput because early prefix rejections invalidate later predictions and larger proposals may increase latency.
Training factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction components to combine mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss.
Inference factorizes throughput into mean accepted tokens divided by per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and block-size selection.
Across six benchmarks, DScout reaches mean speedups of 3.84× on Qwen3-4B and 4.14× on Qwen3-8B over autoregressive decoding.
Its workload-specific configuration policy adds up to 9.75% mean speedup over DScout’s fixed configuration.

papers.abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.
authors: Harikrishnan P M, Goutham Vignesh, Siva Prasad, Zishan Ahmad, Mahesh Basveshwar Deshmukhe, Varun V, Rohit Agrawal, Vishal Vaddina
bullets: A small VLM localizes evidence for each extracted field and calibrates confidence in both the value and its supporting evidence.
Fine-tuning the VLM improves evidence quality and expands selective-prediction coverage at strict confidence thresholds.
Open-weight VLM internal states substantially outperform output log-probabilities for in-distribution confidence estimation.
This advantage weakens under distribution shift, but target-domain labeling of roughly 120 fields restores evidence-confidence quality.
The framework is evaluated across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, with scope limited by reduced cross-distribution calibration transfer.

papers.title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence

papers.abstract: Vector quantization is widely used for large-scale data compression and approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). Multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) is a practical paradigm that represents database vectors with compact codes and supports efficient retrieval through asymmetric distance computation (ADC). However, existing shallow MCQs encode vectors independently within each inverted file (IVF) cluster, without exploiting local references. Therefore, we propose Spatio-Topological Linkage Quantization (STLQ), a topological shallow MCQ method that organizes each IVF cluster as a directed-forest with compact codes and scaling coefficients. Its basic encoding phase first quantizes vectors independently, while the linked encoding phase re-encodes relative residuals with respect to selected reconstructed parents, reusing local reconstruction information to obtain finer representations. The corresponding linked-ADC preserves linear scanning complexity. STLQ further compresses the scaling coefficients and directed-forest structure to control the additional topology overhead. Extensive experiments show that STLQ achieves higher recall than the evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, although at a higher offline construction cost. Meanwhile, it has a competitive recall-QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs. The code is available at https://github.com/ighxiy/STLQ.
authors: Kuizhi Liu, Junying Zhang, Xindi Ma, Xiangyu Wang, Qi Jiang, Sheng Gao, Chen Gong, Jianfeng Ma
bullets: Targets shallow multi-codebook quantization methods that encode vectors independently and miss local references.
Organizes each IVF cluster as a directed forest using compact codes and scaling coefficients.
Re-encodes residuals relative to reconstructed parent vectors, reusing local information for finer representations.
Compresses the forest structure and scaling coefficients to limit topology overhead; linked-ADC retains linear scanning complexity.
Reports higher recall than evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, with higher offline construction cost, and a competitive recall–QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. STLQ technical overview. Basic encoding generates independent codes and coefficients, while linked encoding accepts parent-dependent representations only when they reduce reconstruction MSE. Compact and dispersed clusters use outward-expanding and virtual-relay topologies, respectively. Training alternates between the two encoding phases. After base set encoding, coefficients and forest topology are compressed for storage. Spiral and elliptical galaxies hint the cluster structure entropy and topologies. Credit: NASA, ESA, S. Beckwith (STScI) and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA). [Public domain], via NASA (https://www.nasa.gov/).
Fig. 7. Error distribution of (a) SIFT1M-8B and (b) SIFT1M-16B in Eq. 4 on top-100 ground truth. Figures with “Summation” on x-axis show the per vector sum of inner-product and norm terms

papers.abstract: Recognizing micro-expressions in real-world conversations is challenging, as these facial movements are brief and faint, and their interpretations are strongly dependent on the contextual circumstances of their occurrence. Most existing methods are de-contextualized, as they analyze isolated video clips while disregarding the semantic and acoustic cues in the surrounding dialogue that help explain the emergence of an expression. Decades of psychological studies have shown that social context exerts influences on facial behavior over two key dimensions: how an expression is interpreted and how strongly it is generated to begin with. However, existing micro-expression research rarely incorporates such contextual factors into its models. As an example, provocative utterances from an interlocutor may elicit suppressed negative affective reactions, which isolated silent clips are unable to account for. We propose TriCoME, a trimodal dataset consisting of visual, audio and text data sourced from real-world conversations. In this dataset, each micro-expression is paired with its concurrent utterance and preceding context. We further annotate the context based on conversational role to denote two categories: external stimuli from an interlocutor's utterance and internal background from the subject's own utterance. On this basis, we propose the Hierarchical Focusing Fusion Network (HFFNet), which aligns acoustic and semantic streams at fine granularity, compresses long dialogue sequences, modulates attention toward conversational roles via a context-type embedding, and routes each sample between visual-only and multimodal decisions based on visual confidence to prevent noisy context from degrading recognition performance.
authors: Junbo Wang, Yan Zhao, Shigang Wang, Jian Wei, Qiming Zhang, Yu Wu
bullets: Micro-expressions are brief, subtle, and difficult to interpret without surrounding conversational context.
TriCoME pairs each expression with concurrent utterances and preceding context across visual, audio, and text modalities.
Context is annotated by conversational role, distinguishing interlocutor-generated stimuli from the subject’s own internal background.
HFFNet hierarchically fuses aligned acoustic and semantic cues, models long dialogue context, and focuses on conversational roles.
A confidence-based routing mechanism falls back to visual-only recognition when contextual signals may introduce noise.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of the proposed Hierarchical Focusing Fusion Network (HFFNet) for context-aware micro-expression recognition. The pipeline comprises three stages. (1) Multi-modal Feature Extraction: MMNet extracts visual features Fvisual from video frames; Wav2Vec 2.0 with a sliding-window strategy extracts acoustic features Saudio from raw waveforms; BERT extracts semantic features Stext from transcribed text. (2) Context-Aware Sentence Encoding: A Cross-Modal Transformer (CmT) fuses Saudio and Stext through fine-grained interaction, followed by a Sequence Compressor that condenses the fused sequence into a compact representation; a Contextual Transformer (CoT) then injects context type embeddings tc ∈ {0, 1} to distinguish interlocutor utterances (external triggers) from self-statements (internal background), yielding the sentence feature Fsentence. (3) Intelligent Gating & Adaptive Routing: Fvisual and Fsentence interact via a cross-modal fusion block and an enhanced gating network with element-wise gate vector g; an adaptive router dynamically selects between the visual-only prediction Lvis and the multimodal prediction Lmm based on visual confidence, producing the final emotion classification.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR-free, multi-vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper-bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine-grained document semantics and improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off over state-of-the-art base-lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced-Optimal-Transport-for-EVDR.
authors: Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem caused by excessive tokens in OCR-free, multi-vector VLM-based visual document retrieval.
Formulates token compression as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem balancing token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage.
Uses alternating optimization to jointly optimize these compression objectives.
Provides a theoretical guarantee that lower transport cost bounds MaxSim retrieval error, supporting ranking stability.
Experiments on ViDoRe V1 and V3 show a better efficiency–effectiveness trade-off than existing baselines while retaining fine-grained semantics.

FLOPs are estimated via a late-interaction proxy proportional to corpus size, expected query-document token interactions, and embedding dimension. Our method establishes a superior Pareto frontier compared to recent stateof-the-art baselines [15,27].

Fig. 2: Overview: Visual Token Compression. Offline, N visual tokens X are compressed into K anchors Y (K ≪ N). Our Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) formulation jointly optimizes semantic redundancy (cost C), token importance (source µ), and anchor capacity (target ν) to enable efficient online MaxSim retrieval.

papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
authors: Zhen Li, Mingfa Feng, Yiming Zhang, Yang Yu, Changhai Zhou, Pengxiang Li, Dongkuan Wu, Congkai Xie, Hongxia Yang
bullets: Matching weights and numerical formats alone does not guarantee consistent policy evaluation across engines.
The framework combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and native W4A4 GEMM kernels without changing the RL objective.
Long-horizon experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B achieve stable training and benchmark quality close to BF16, outperforming naive TE NVFP4 in evaluation quality.
On a single NVIDIA B300 node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s—1.39× BF16 and 1.47× TE NVFP4 throughput for complete learner updates.
The framework, kernels, diagnostics, and configurations are released; results focus on the reported model and hardware setup.

papers.abstract: In certain real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled data is excessively expensive, motivating increasing interest in adapting models without annotations. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide pseudo-labels for unlabeled images through image-text similarity, enabling adaptation without manual labeling. The previous unsupervised vision-language model adaption methods assume access to an adaptation vocabulary containing all class names. However, a complete vocabulary is difficult to construct in real-world scenarios, as unlabeled data may contain classes that are overlooked or fall outside the current task scope. Thus, we propose Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (VI-UVA), where only a subset of class names are available during adaptation. The vocabulary incompleteness induces an adaptation bias toward provided classes, which degrades omitted-class recognition. To address this issue, we propose Label Space Reconstruction (LSR), which reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning, thereby extending adaptation beyond the incomplete vocabulary and mitigating the adaptation bias. Furthermore, we derive an omitted-class semantic discrepancy bound for LSR and identify the key factors affecting the bound. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Si Qin, Jiawei Tang, Yaxin Hou, Yan Chen, Yutong Xie, Chen Li, Yuheng Jia
bullets: Existing unsupervised VLM adaptation assumes all relevant class names are available, which can bias adaptation toward known classes.
The proposed VI-UVA setting uses only a subset of class names during adaptation.
Label Space Reconstruction (LSR) infers a latent label space from unlabeled images and integrates it into prompt tuning.
The method derives a bound on omitted-class semantic discrepancy and analyzes factors influencing it.
Experiments on eight benchmarks show LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Comparison between unsupervised VLM adaptation (UVA) and vocabulary-incomplete unsupervised VLM adaptation (VI-UVA). During adaptation, all class names are available for UVA, while only a subset of class names is available for VI-UVA. During evaluation, UVA and VI-UVA are both tested on the complete vocabulary including provided-class names and omitted-class names. (b) Omitted-group recall measures the proportion of omitted-class samples assigned to any omitted class, which indicates how well the model avoids vocabulary overfitting. On the DTD dataset, our method outperforms the best adaptation method by 5.0 and 10.0 percentage points in omitted-group recall and omitted-class accuracy, respectively.
Figure 2: Average results of omitted-group recall (%) and omitted-class accuracy (%) across eight datasets at different omission ratios γ.

Second, we apply the CMSP to all unlabeled images to generate textual embeddings, cluster them into semantic anchors, and filter out unreliable anchors. Third, for each retained anchor, we retrieve the corresponding pseudo-token sequence and textual representation to construct a pseudovocabulary and a pseudo-labeled dataset, respectively. Then, we perform prompt tuning with the pseudo-vocabulary and pseudo-labeled dataset to preserve omitted-class recognition.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models answer questions about images and also generate images with one shared set of weights. This creates a post-training risk that single-purpose models do not have: fine-tuning one capability can damage another that works in a different modality. We measure this cross-modal forgetting for LoRA post-training of Janus-Pro-7B. Every target is chosen by how poorly the base model already handles it, from a poetic register to a language it barely speaks, so that retention is tested against a real intervention; we then evaluate the capabilities we never trained, first after a single run and then after chaining three. A single run looks entirely safe: nothing we did not train degrades on four public benchmarks or in free-form English, even when the adapter cuts held-out Welsh perplexity by 76% with a relative weight change under 2%. That safety belongs to the run, not to the recipe. Chaining three runs destroys the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude above the never-adapted model, on the very measures that stayed flat before. The cause is in the objective, which constrains only the modality being trained and leaves the other head unconstrained: cutting the learning rate to one fifth does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage to the capabilities we never trained, at no cost to what is learned. What is learned also stays inside its own modality, with Welsh acquired from text closing only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.
authors: Francesco Colasurdo, Ivan Slobozhan, Joaquin Vanschoren, Anna Vettoruzzo
bullets: The study measures whether adapting one modality harms capabilities in another for Janus-Pro-7B.
A single LoRA run caused no observed degradation on four benchmarks or free-form English, despite substantially improving held-out Welsh perplexity.
Chaining three runs erased a capability learned earlier and increased general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude.
Reducing the learning rate did not prevent collapse; anchoring the other modality’s head did, without sacrificing the trained capability.
Knowledge transfer across modalities was weak: text-based Welsh learning closed only 3% of the English–Welsh gap in image generation.

papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-modal forgetting in unified multimodal post-training and proposes anchoring to prevent collapse, relevant to multimodal foundation models and continual learning.
papers.title: Cross-Modal Forgetting and Transfer in Unified Multimodal Post-Training
papers.tldr: LoRA post-training of unified multimodal models appears safe after one run but can cause severe cross-modal forgetting when three runs are chained, which is prevented by anchoring the untrained head.

papers.abstract: Characters, locations, and actions recur throughout a movie, so many of its moments differ only in fine-grained details. Grounding such a moment in a full-length movie requires resolving that detail rather than matching the attributes it shares with other moments, yet existing temporal movie grounding benchmarks rarely test this. We introduce CoM$^2$-Bench, a benchmark of confusable query pairs, where the two queries in each pair share most attributes but differ in a single distinguishing detail within a full movie, posing a challenge for recent temporal grounding approaches. To locate where grounding breaks down, we analyze a retrieve-then-localize pipeline, in which a retriever first selects a short candidate chunk and a localizer then performs temporal grounding within it. Separating the two stages lets us attribute each failure to either retrieval or localization. We find that retrieval is the major bottleneck: state-of-the-art retrievers often select a moment's confusable counterpart, because their choices follow the content the two moments share rather than the detail that tells them apart. To address these failures, we propose a simple, training-free remedy, Agentic Window Search (AWS): an MLLM agent $\textit{Decomposes}$ the query into attribute-level sub-queries, then $\textit{Inspects}$ each candidate window against them and $\textit{Expands}$ the window when evidence is cut off at its edge. AWS works with existing retrievers and localizers without additional training, raising mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8.
authors: Dong-Hee Kim, Seonwoo Choi, Changbeen Kim, Juyeon Ko, Youngju Choi, Il Hyeon Mun, Hyunwoo J. Kim, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Introduces paired queries that share most attributes but differ in one distinguishing detail.
Evaluates retrieve-then-localize pipelines on full-length movies and separates retrieval from localization failures.
Finds retrieval is the main bottleneck: systems often select a confusable counterpart based on shared content.
Proposes training-free Agentic Window Search, which decomposes queries, inspects candidate windows, and expands truncated windows.
Improves mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8 when used with existing retrievers and localizers.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose multimodal assistants, making multimodal safety alignment an important challenge. Safety depends on the interplay between textual and visual content, with visual context often playing a critical role. However, VLMs may fail to use visual information appropriately, either overlooking safety-relevant visual content or over-interpreting sensitive visual content, leading to unsafe responses or over-refusal. Existing multimodal safety alignment datasets largely follow the response-preference paradigm, which teaches models how to respond but provides limited supervision on how visual context should inform the safety judgment, making it difficult to balance safety and over-refusal. To address this limitation, we introduce ContraSafe-VL, a Contrastive Safety preference dataset for Vision-Language Models. For each fixed textual query, ContraSafe-VL constructs paired visual contexts that result in multimodal queries with different safety labels, providing direct supervision for how visual context should inform multimodal safety judgments. It further provides response preference pairs based on harmlessness and helpfulness to encourage models to generate responses that are both safe and helpful. Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks demonstrate that training with ContraSafe-VL improves cross-modal safety recognition and achieves a better safety--over-refusal trade-off while preserving general multimodal capabilities. The dataset will be publicly released.

bullets: Addresses VLM failures to notice safety-relevant visual content or overreact to benign sensitive content.

Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show improved cross-modal safety recognition and a better safety–over-refusal trade-off.
The dataset is intended for public release and aims to preserve general multimodal capabilities.

papers.abstract: AI-generated video (AIGV) detection is increasingly important for mitigating misinformation, impersonation, and other malicious uses of synthetic media, yet existing detectors often generalize poorly to unseen generators in open-world settings. To better understand this challenge, we analyze the failure modes of AIGV detectors under cross-generator out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts and observe that detector representations strongly encode generator-specific cues, which are associated with substantial ID-OOD performance drops. Further analysis shows that naively perturbing generator-sensitive tokens can even reduce OOD performance, indicating that generator-related cues and detection-relevant evidence are only partially separable. Motivated by these findings, we propose Forensic Obfuscation of geneRator-specific cues via Gradient-guided Embedding perturbation (FORGE), a token-aware adversarial training framework for open-world AIGV detection. FORGE identifies tokens that are strongly associated with generator-specific shortcuts yet less critical to real/fake discrimination, and selectively perturbs them during training to suppress generator-dependent patterns while preserving useful forensic evidence. Through synchronized adversarial training between an attacker and a detector, FORGE encourages the detector to learn more transferable generator-invariant forensic representations. Experiments on 29 held-out benchmark entries show that FORGE achieves an average F1 of 92.62, outperforming eight strong baselines by 5.31 points, while also remaining robust under four common post-processing attacks. We will release our code and datasets upon acceptance.
authors: Qi Zhou, Yuanfan Li, Huiqi Deng, Hongbin Pei, Yazhe Tang
bullets: Existing detectors often overfit to generator-specific cues, causing substantial performance drops on unseen generators.
Naively perturbing these cues can hurt detection because generator signals and real/fake evidence are only partly separable.
FORGE uses token-aware, gradient-guided adversarial embedding perturbations to reduce reliance on generator-dependent patterns.
Synchronized attacker–detector training encourages generator-invariant forensic representations.
On 29 held-out benchmark entries, FORGE reaches 92.62 average F1, surpasses eight baselines by 5.31 points, and remains robust to four post-processing attacks.

papers.abstract: Long-video agents must map hours or days of multimodal evidence into a bounded context while respecting token and latency budgets, making memory design a context-management challenge. Existing memory systems largely rely on hand-designed policies, leaving open how to jointly optimize memory design for performance and efficiency. We propose Long Video Meta-memory Harness (LVMH), an automated multi-agent framework that formulates memory-policy development as multi-objective code search around a fixed answer model. To guard against self-certification and development-set overfitting, LVMH separates implementation from independent review and enforces protected observation boundaries. Persistent meta-memory records past proposals, traces, costs, and failures to guide subsequent policy revisions. Through this harness, we discover Self-Evolving Evidence Memory (SEEM), a "text-first, vision-second" policy that answers from compact structured event memory and evidence specialists, consulting localized frames through a selective visual gate. The policy evolved on EgoLifeQA generalizes to unseen benchmarks, outperforming Meta-Harness on both Ego-R1 Bench and Video-MME (L) with GPT-5 mini. Across the three benchmarks, SEEM with GPT-5 achieves 65.7% average accuracy, surpassing the previous state of the art by 7.7 percentage points with approximately 32x lower average evaluation token use and 91x shorter average response time.
authors: Liwei Che, Benlin Liu, Dai Li, Xiangyan Li, Zijian Wu, Changjiang Li, Minghao Guo, Chengzhi Mao, Vladimir Pavlovic, Ranjay Krishna

papers.abstract: Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on. The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame. Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing. We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm. After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended. It performs calibration, plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm's own poses. We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions.

Provides real and synthetic datasets with robot/camera parameters and fitted 3DGS reconstructions.

papers.abstract: We present RhinoNet, a simplicial complex-based point cloud neural network, that creates a geometry-preserving embedding of high-dimensional point clouds. RhinoNet takes collections of datasets, also called {\em data cohorts}, and processes each dataset (point cloud) within the cohort as a simplicial complex. These simplicial complexes have datapoints as vertices and edges learned by Vietoris-Rips filtration. Using simplicial wavelets and MLP layers, RhinoNet computes a vector representation of each dataset in a latent space produced by an autoencoder. The latent space is optimized such that an optimal transport distance between pairs of point clouds is preserved between the latent representations. We apply RhinoNet to single-cell datasets collected on patients---a common source of such high-dimensional data. RhinoNet creates a patient level representation, known in biological contexts as a phenoscape. We establish that RhinoNet generates organized phenoscapes, whereas other methods such as static maps do not. Next we show that we can generate entire point clouds by sampling and decoding this phenoscape. We show two modes of generation via 1) latent flow matching and 2) geodesic interpolation in latent space, followed by a decoding back into the point cloud space. RhinoNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-cell and spatial data cohorts relative to tested baselines. Overall, RhinoNet lifts the concepts of representation learning and generative modeling to the point cloud or population level and defines a neural model for phenoscaping.
authors: Siddharth Viswanath, Hiren Madhu, Eddie Cavallin, Benjamin Jones, Alistair Wilkinson, Christopher Tape, Michael Perlmutter, Rex Ying, Ian Adelstein, Smita Krishnaswamy

papers.abstract: Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
authors: Yanjun Li, Jiarui Ye, Weiyu Guo, Zixiao He, Kangjie Ye, Dihan Wang, Yishuo Cheng, Zishang Xiang, Mingju Gao, Hao Tang

Adds no inference-time overhead because language components are used only during training.
Achieves 79.17% average success on HumanoidArena and improves real-world task success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: A robotic agent operating in an unknown environment must gather sufficient task-relevant information before acting. However, determining when the available information is sufficient remains a challenge. We propose a conceptual hybrid neuro-symbolic framework for task-sufficient active perception in unknown environments. After interpreting a requested task, the agent generates an initial plan and iteratively reevaluates it as new information becomes available. At each iteration, it can acquire a more informative viewpoint, inspect or manipulate candidate objects, ask the user for clarification, or perform the task. Neural perception modules update an object-centric belief state, while a symbolic decision layer determines whether the remaining uncertainty justifies further information gathering. The framework will be implemented on a mobile manipulator comprising a humanoid torso and a mobile base, with complementary evaluation in simulation. The proposed approach aims to enable robots to determine not only how to gather additional information, but also when further perception is no longer necessary.

papers.abstract: Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data-efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi-object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single-step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual-strategy that performs single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 61.24% success on unseen objects, and achieves high success rates in separated layouts. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real deployment through a vision-based policy trained solely on simulation data. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Aurora-Xiong/MoDex.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich insertion requires precise geometric alignment despite uncertainty in perception, geometry, and con- trol. When this uncertainty causes unintended contact, the re- sulting contact provides local information that can guide correc- tive motion. Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) is well suited to this setting because it optimizes through forward simulation without requiring gradients through contact dynamics. However, standard SMPC methods typically use generic proposal distributions that do not exploit observed contact to determine where to search next. We introduce ContactKernels, a contact-adaptive proposal kernel that uses geometry-conditioned wrench measurements to estimate contact location and local contact geometry. The estimated contact state directly adapts the proposal distribution: contact location biases the search toward corrective motions, while the contact normal shapes the sampling covariance. We evaluate ContactKernels with Predictive Sampling (PS) and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control across multiple insertion geometries in simulation and on a real robot. In simulation, ContactKernels improves mean insertion success by over 50 % points across both controllers. On the real robot, it increases insertion success from 53.3 % to 90.0 % and reduces mean time to insertion by 33 %. These results show that contact information can improve sampling-based control not only as feedback, but also by directly determining where the controller searches

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.
authors: Junjie Yang, Qiming Zhang, Yuyan Li, Shuqi Shen, Yusong Huang, Yanggang Sheng, Wenpeng Xu, Ziyi Shi, Tianshun Li, Yijie Chen, Yujia Wang, Jun Ma, Xinhu Zheng, Hongliang Lu, Hai Yang

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet existing planners organize trajectory generation along the Gaussian-noise axis, treating driving utility only as an auxiliary guidance or selection signal. We instead formulate diffusion along a driving-quality axis. We propose QualiDrive, which constructs scene-specific quality ladders by ranking observed trajectories according to measured driving utility and learns to reverse this ordered degradation through ordered low-to-high-quality refinement. Each reverse step is conditioned on the scene, ego state, current trajectory, and target quality level, progressively refining trajectories toward higher driving quality. On NAVSIM, QualiDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on v1 and a state-of-the-art 92.74 EPDMS on v2. QualiDrive improves Oracle EPDMS only modestly over endpoint-only quality supervision (98.52 to 98.57), but substantially increases the fractions of candidates above 0.95 and 0.98 EPDMS from 12.94%/9.71% to 21.53%/15.93%, raising selected EPDMS from 92.63 to 92.74. These results suggest that diffusion is not merely a process of denoising, but one of progressive quality-ordered refinement.

papers.abstract: Long-range throwing on unstructured terrain is a key capability for mobile robots in delivery and retrieval tasks, but it requires high release velocity, coordinated whole-body motion, and robustness to terrain-induced disturbances. We present a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for a wheeled-quadruped manipulator that combines kinetic-chain arm modeling with SQP-based trajectory optimization and a reference-guided reinforcement learning policy for coordinated base motion. The manipulator is first reduced to a kinetic-chain model and optimized under kinematic and dynamic constraints to produce a high-speed throwing reference. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a throwing distance of 16.68 m. When whole-body coordination is enabled, the system further increases the release speed to 16.64 m/s and the throwing distance to 28.25 m. We then integrate the mobility of the wheeled-quadruped platform and validate the complete policy through hardware experiments on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads. The results show that kinetic-chain optimization and whole-body coordination together enable robust long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.

The resulting policy enables terrain-robust long-range throwing and is evaluated across multiple real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin, Yikeng Chen, Qiwei Liang, Zinan Xie, Zhengtu Liang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Targets the joint problem of selecting layers to remove and choosing recovery procedures after pruning.
